News.title: Afghan national who pinned down and raped two girls, 14, in flat after plying them with alcohol is jailed
News.content:
BEAST CAGED Afghan national who pinned down and raped two girls, 14, in flat after plying them with alcohol is jailed







Next

A SICK Afghan national has been jailed for raping two 14-year-old girls after luring them to his flat and plying them with alcohol.

Sultani Bakatash held the girls down and dragged them across a carpet when they tried to flee his home in Bolton.



The 29-year-old then raped both teens as they “drifted in and out of consciousness”.

Bakatash has been in the UK for two years and has been granted indefinite leave to remain, with his mother, two brothers and two sisters also living in Britain.



He was today jailed for 14 years after he was found guilty of two counts of rape, one of sexual assault and one of assault by penetration following a four-week trial.

Bolton Crown Court heard Bakatash met up with the girls after befriending one of them on Snapchat.

Prosecutor Rebecca Rimmer said: “Once at his flat, the Crown say, he plied those two girls with alcohol to the point they were so drunk they were drifting in and out of consciousness before seizing the opportunity to rape and abuse them.

“Persisting, despite their efforts to push him away and hide in the toilet from him.

“A man, the Crown say, intent on sexual gratification regardless of what [the girls] wanted.”

The court was told the girls had travelled to Bolton after one of them befriended Bakatash online when she met him in an Asda when she was 13.



He told the girl she was “too young” but still kept in contact with her and agreed to meet up with her.

Jurors heard both girls told Bakatash they were 14 when they met up but that “didn’t dissuade” him from carrying out the sexual acts that followed.

All three went in a Uber to his flat and as they approached the home, Bakatash told them “to be quiet and put their hoods up”.

Once inside, the girls drank vodka and coke while he had one sip and he “encouraged” them to drink more to the point they became “drunk and were falling over”.

Bakatash then “dragged” both girls on to the floor, kissed them and groped them.



The first girl stuck her hand in his face, but Bakatash wouldn’t move away and sexually assaulted her.

She later told how she remembered going to the toilet before finding herself on Bakatash’s bed, where he allegedly raped her.

He then sexually assaulted and raped the second girl in the bedroom after she “kicked her legs and tried to push him off”.

Both girls eventually managed to flee the flat and spoke to a neighbour who raised the alarm.

When officers arrived they found the “extremely distressed” teens, who were both “intoxicated” and drifting in and out of consciousness.



The girls were examined and the first had “carpet burns to her knees” and numerous bruises while the second girl had abrasions and bruises to her body.

Bakatash was arrested at this brother’s address the next day and answered no comment in interview.

He later claimed in a statement that he believed the girls were aged 18 and 19 and they had “instigated” consensual sexual activity.

But he changed his position ahead of the trial and denied any sexual activity took place – cruelly suggesting the girls were “telling a pack of lies”.

Chief Superintendent Helen Critchley, District Commander for Bolton for GMP, said: “I would like to thank both survivors for their immense bravery during these proceedings.



“Their unwavering strength and courage has been instrumental in securing this conviction.

“Bakatash denied all counts against him. He denied manipulating, grooming and assaulting both girls. He denied the pain and hurt he subjected them to. He showed a blatant disregard for his actions and the long-term impact this would have on the victims. But today a jury rightfully found him guilty on all counts.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“This trial will have been no doubt a difficult time for the girls and their families, and it is only with their support that we have managed to keep Bakatash behind bars.

“I urge anyone who may have experienced similar abuse to please come forward and report. You will always be listened to, respected, and supported.”

News.title: New headteacher suspends 25 pupils for ‘zipping bags loudly & looking out window’ as parents blast ‘military base’ rules
News.content:
BAD EDUCATION New headteacher suspends 25 pupils for ‘zipping bags loudly & looking out window’ as parents blast ‘military base’ rules







Next

A NEW headteacher has suspended 25 pupils for minor offences such as zipping up a bag “too loudly” and “staring out of a classroom window”.

Dan Jeffries, interim principal at Frome Community College in Somerset, dished out the suspensions just days into term, saying in a statement his priority is “ensuring every pupil receives a disruption-free education”.



But furious parents have slammed the crackdown, branding the school “like a military base”.

Disgruntled mothers and fathers are claiming kids have been hauled up for the most minor of misdemeanours.



One mum, Natalie Morris, claimed that her daughter was suspended in her first week for “nervously laughing”, reports the Daily Mail.

She told the outlet that her girl has special educational needs and additional sensory needs, and was simply overwhelmed by “strange faces” in a new environment.



Other pupils were said to have been suspended for offences including being a minute late to class.

One parent said the environment had taken a toll on pupils’ mental health, with one child reportedly hiding in the toilets to avoid trouble.

Ann-Marie Ramsey claims parents were being ignored, alleging kids were even being pulled up over hair and nail colour.



However, not all parents are against the new regime.

Mum Liz Halliwell welcomed the shake-up, saying she was glad to see rules being enforced “fair and consistent for everybody”.

While other comments on social media commend Mr Jeffries’ discipline, questioning why more schools don’t follow suit.

Ex-rugby union player Jeffries insisted the suspensions were not for uniform or lateness, but for repeated “defiance”.

He asserted that pupils needing to disrupt lessons four times under school policy before facing suspension.



In a statement, he said: “My first weeks have been fantastic, and the vast majority of our pupils, families, and staff have offered overwhelming support for this shared vision.

“While online rumors can create unnecessary worry, our door is always open.

“We strongly encourage any parent with questions, concerns, or feedback to contact the school directly so we can work together constructively.”

He also said the school holds “high expectations for behaviour, with these standards made to prepare young people for successful futures”, and pointed out it has received no formal complaints from parents.

Jeffries is the latest head to face backlash over zero-tolerance discipline, following in the footsteps of Serge Cefai.



Cefai was dubbed Britain’s “strictest” headteacher, for his no-nonsense approach against kids who used “mental health” as an excuse for laziness, at St Thomas the Apostle school in Peckham.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Headteacher Jon Richardson was also branded the ‘UK’s strictest’ after kicking a student out of Strood Academy in Kent for his haircut.

Both have been accused of running old-fashioned regimes, while supporters credit them for their high standards.

News.title: Nurse, 35, marries BUS and proudly shows off tattoo dedicated to ‘love of her life’ after bizarre wedding ceremony
News.content:
Next

A NURSE who married a public bus boasts a new tattoo dedicated to the “love of her life” after a bizarre wedding ceremony.

Yeline Lizbeth Patiño, 35, has experienced an attraction to vehicles for most of her life and although she has past dated men in the past, something always felt missing.



In 2022, Yeline moved to Bogota, Colombia, and fell madly in love with a fleet of red articulated busses on Route 60.

Now, with a tattoo of the bus on her side, a shiny ring and a marriage “certificate”, Yeline and Bogota’s A60–F60 convoy are Colombia’s most unconventional nuptials.



The pair were married in secret in October 2024 at an intimate service, complete with a white dress, a wedding cake and a pearl ring.

Recalling their love affair, she said: “Its structure, colour, and material captivate me – they are, I dare say, my reason for living.”



“I decided to start a relationship with it and marry it in a ceremony – one held in secret, as I did not want to reveal it to the world at the time.”

Yeline commemorated her one-year anniversary with a large tattoo on her torso showing the front of her articulated bus and the city’s cathedral.



The nurse recently decided to go public with her marriage as she fears their future is in trouble.

She said: “I made this public for one reason only: I am terrified – truly terrified – that TransMilenio will cancel that route.”

With the introduction of the capital city’s new metro, Yeline is afraid the route could disappear within the next two years.



Yeline said she is willing to risk her reputation, her career and life to raise awareness of the route, in the hope of drumming up enough support so that the company will “find it impossible to cancel the service”.

She continued: “I feel such a sense of helplessness and pain because TransMilenio knows what this means to me.

“I am asking for just one thing: that there be a TransMilenio articulated bus bearing the number ‘60’ on its route – it doesn’t matter where it goes.”

She has called on human rights organisation and fellow mechanophiles and objectophiles to help her cause.

She said: “It is the most immense and beautiful love imaginable.



“I would like international support.

“To preserve the route’s identity within the system, I want everyone to stand in solidarity with my cause so we can gather signatures or submit joint requests – perhaps form a fan club for the route, or do something to prevent its removal – if there is no other way.”

Yeline is a nurse and professional singer from Pasto who moved to Bogota to pursue her artistic dreams and it was there that she fell for Route 60.

She said: “It felt like a real encounter, even though I didn’t realise at the time that my love for it was genuine.”

She later took a job as a night cleaner at the bus depot so she can wash the fleet and stay beside it.



She said she was just happy to be near them.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Yeline first experienced mechanophilia when she was just 10-years-old when seh fell “head over heels” for a rans Sandoná bus that ran from the municipality of San Pablo to Pasto.

She explained: “Through my mechanophilia, I perceive that a bus takes on a distinct identity – one that completely possesses it – whenever it runs a specific route.”

News.title: Desperate search for missing schoolgirl, 13, last seen boarding bus outside city shopping centre five days ago
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FRANTIC HUNT Desperate search for missing schoolgirl, 13, last seen boarding bus outside city shopping centre five days ago







Next

THE frantic search for a 13-year-old girl who was last seen boarding a bus outside a shopping centre continues, almost a week on since she went missing.

Lilia was last spotted at around 1.50pm on Saturday afternoon boarding the 247 at the Trafford Centre, Manchester.



Police were alerted to her disappearance on Friday.

She is described as a slim, white girl around 5ft 5 tall, with light brown hair and glasses.



She was last seen wearing a black zip-up hooded top, light blue baggy jeans and a black Nike backpack.

It is not clear how long she stayed on the bus, or which stop she got off at.

The sighting forms an essential part of the search mission.

Cops are appealing to anyone with relevant CCTV or Ring doorbell footage to come forward.

Issuing a personal appeal not long after she vanished, her mum Jessica said: “Lilia, you’re not in any trouble, I’m really, really worried.

“It’s been four nights now and you need to be safe.



“Please come home, we all love you very much.”

In their statement, Greater Manchester Police said: “Lilia you are not in any trouble.

“They simply want you to come home.”

Cops have set up a Major Incident Portal where the public can submit information via the police website.

News.title: Enemies ‘drilled’ & daylight killings – how top holiday coast became a mob boss hotspot… & why it’s getting MORE violent
News.content:
Next

SUN, sea and shootings: Brits have flocked to this charming coastline for decades to get their tan on – but a spate of broad daylight killings in one region has shattered its picture-postcard image.

Panic has long gripped the sunny holiday hotspot, terrorised by gangs carrying out brutal score-settling murders and kidnappings – but experts warn the latest shootings mark a new wave of bloody slaughter.





Three brutal shootings have rocked the Spanish coast in recent weeks.

The most recent struck on Monday afternoon, when a man was shot dead in the quiet hamlet of Zalea, on the outskirts of Malaga.

Further along the Costa del Sol, in Marbella, two shootings rocked the holiday town in just two weeks.

A man was blasted in the leg near a ritzy hotel in broad daylight, sparking a dramatic police chase along the resort’s famous Golden Mile.

Just two weeks earlier, a man was shot dead in the street before his killers sped off from the scene.

Recent outbreaks of gangland violence in the Costa del Sol expose how a huge network of international organised crime groups operate out of the area’s picturesque towns.





In August alone Málaga recorded as many as five shootings – but the incidents are far from the region’s first taste of gory gang-linked violence.

In 2019, a man was found alive but in excruciating pain after a rival had drilled holes through his toes.

Hitmen have been shipped in from abroad to carry out targeted assassinations, bombs have been planted in Benahavís and kidnappings carried out as conflicting clans battle it out.

Gangsters have been attracted to the Costa del Sol since the 70s after the death of the Fascist dictator General Franco.

As cheaper commercial air travel saw Spain welcome increasing numbers of British tourists with the popularity of package holidays, the UK also exported many of its criminals.

An extradition treaty with the UK expired in 1978, meaning British criminals could hole up in the holiday hotspot without fear of being shipped back home to face justice.

By the time the legal loophole had been fixed, the crime bosses had already flooded in, capitalising on the coast’s burgeoning tourism industry.

The idyllic coastline soon gained notoriety as a gangster’s paradise, where criminal kingpins could hide out unbothered by the pesky arms of the law.



So many wanted crime bosses line its shores that the area gained a chilling new nickname: the Costa del Crime.

At first, authorities turned a blind eye to the criminal class filling up the country’s southern resort towns – so long as they didn’t commit crimes there – for one key reason. They brought cash to splash, and a lot of it.

With plenty of money flowing in from ordinary holidaymakers as well as retired gangsters, the country’s tourist industry boomed and luxury resorts developed.

It was a great opportunity to hide in plain sight and for criminals to launder their cash.

Professor Michele Riccardi is the Deputy Director of Transcrime, Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore and an expert in how organised crime groups launder their ill-gotten gains.

He told The Sun: “Spain, and especially the Costa del Sol has been a place where a good number of the most wanted criminals went for both operational reasons, mostly related to cocaine trafficking coming from Latin America, but also for money laundering.

“There was on the one side, a good opportunity to invest like in real estate, in tourism. So they could exploit that demand for tourism, but also hide in the midst of normal tourists.”

The operational appeal of the coastline was simple.

Spain had become the gateway to Europe for the international drug trade, with cocaine shipped from South America and hashish from the North of Africa.

Critically, Morocco is just 10 miles across the sea from the Costa del Sol.



And so the Costa del Sol, stretching 55 miles from Málaga to Estepona, was propelled into infamy.

One town in particular became the hottest destination for the global criminal elite: Marbella.

Chris Dalby, an organised crime researcher and Head of Intelligence at Dyami, a security firm, told The Sun: “Marbella has almost everything an international criminal could want.

“You have extraordinary wealth, a huge transient international population and luxury developments where somebody spending enormous amounts of money doesn’t necessarily stand out.

“At the same time, you are sitting beside some of Europe’s most important drug-trafficking routes: Morocco is across the Strait, Algeciras is a major container port and Gibraltar is nearby.

“The proliferation of criminals became a self-fulfilling prophecy. The more there were, the more expertise could be found, the more deals could be made.”

“Spanish authorities have identified more than 100 organised-crime groups across dozens of nationalities on the Costa del Sol.

“It became a place where a British trafficker could meet a Dutch-Moroccan broker, an Albanian cocaine supplier and a Spanish logistics crew.”



Professor Riccardi said: “Marbella is quite a strategic place, it’s quite close to Gibraltar, is quite close to Algeciras, which is an important port for drug trafficking in Europe.”

Its luxury meant that the flash cars of mobsters didn’t look out of place and crime bosses felt safe – until they weren’t.

As Spanish authorities began to catch wind of the criminals filling up its sunbeds, running operations from Marbella and Málaga became riskier.

Criminals started searching for boltholes in countries outside the EU, but also countries whose governments were less cooperative in targeting international crime, Professor Riccardi said.

They were looking for destinations “where it was more difficult to have good international cooperation on both criminal things like extradition, but also money laundering cooperation”.

He explained: “Among these places, the UAE started to emerge. In the 2010s they began to settle in Dubai, but also in the Emirates in general, because at that stage, their governments were not so great in terms of extradition and international cooperation.”

“Dubai has become a strategic place for driving and coordinating drug trafficking businesses and other criminal businesses, but also for money laundering, for example, in luxury, in real estate.”

But not all criminals moved – some people still need to be by the sea to traffic drugs and other goods to Europe.



Analysts suspect that the top tier of criminals may have scarpered to the UAE but left their lower ranking lackeys to keep doing their dirty work on the Costa del Sol.

It means the Spanish holiday coast may see an increase in lower-level turf war killings and violence.

Professor Riccardi said: “What was observed, although this is a kind of plausible speculation, is that Spain and in particular Marbella area remain more on very operational, with lower-rank players, lower-rank criminals while the Emirates became for higher-rank criminals.

“And therefore – and this is a hypothesis – Marbella began hosting not just higher-rank criminals.



“It may see what happens when lower-rank multiple criminal groups are involved, like market fights, violence, killings, kidnapping, and so on.”

It’s not just British gangs with gangsters charging about the Costa del Sol. Italian mafia, Dutch criminal networks and feared “soldiers” from Marseille clans in France.

The violence that explodes onto the streets can mean these groups are contesting territory, or failing to find a balance between their crime empires, Professor Riccardi said.

He added: “We have multiple criminal groups, criminal actors involved, which have not found an agreement and therefore fight for the same market.

“And the second reason may be that this place has become the place for lower rank members of criminal organisation, while the bosses, the coordinators are elsewhere.

“The Emirates may be an option, but also other countries, which are increasingly important, such as Turkey.

“Shootings, and killings especially, are just a last resort measure.



“When you have visible killings and violence, this can be the signal of the fact that an agreement and equilibrium has not been found, first of all, or that other type of criminal actors maybe more violent ones, have entered the market.”

Analyst Dalby said: “Marbella acquired something much harder to replicate: the people you need to commit crimes at scale.

“If you needed a money launderer, a trafficker, somebody who could move drugs through a port, somebody who could sell them elsewhere in Europe, or somebody who could provide violence, those connections were increasingly available on the Costa del Sol.

“Over time, that produced this extraordinary concentration of criminal groups from across Europe and beyond.

“They formed a constantly shifting patchwork of alliances, business relationships and betrayals. Groups might cooperate on one shipment and then fall out over missing drugs, unpaid debts or stolen money.

“That accumulation of relationships is part of what has ultimately taken Marbella down the increasingly violent path we see today.”

Marbella is reckoning with the crime gangsters have brought to its shores, with huge crackdowns and specialised police operations.

Police arrested three suspected gang members after the September 8 shooting outside a hotel.

Former Marbella mayor Pepe Bernal said that a plan to combat gang crime in the city launched in 2024 was “a recognition by law enforcement that there is a problem here”.

He said the mob bosses used to be known, but tolerated: “Before, these people came to just to spend their money or to enjoy it.



“Now they are not in the limelight, they are not known, but they are here with their organisations. And that’s dangerous.”

Dalby said that criminals are “rational about risk”, but that because of the huge networks built up over the years in Marbella, the city is difficult to replicate.

He said: “The Costa Blanca around Alicante, and the wider Spanish Mediterranean coast through Murcia, Valencia and Ibiza, are probably the most obvious candidates for some displacement.”

“We are already seeing substantial criminal infrastructure there. A major operation this summer found a network with operational bases in Alicante, Murcia, Cartagena, Almería and Ibiza, providing boats, storage, transport, safe houses, communications and financial services to other criminal groups.

“Outside Spain, the French Riviera has some of the same luxury and financial characteristics.

“There is recent evidence of senior international traffickers and money-laundering networks establishing themselves there: Europol dismantled one such network this year and seized more than €5 million in high-end property on the Riviera.”

News.title: Met refers itself to police watchdog over ‘contact’ with Putney Pusher suspect after he was found dead at home
News.content:
Next

THE Met Police has referred itself to the police watchdog over “contact” with the Putney Pusher suspect – after he was found dead at his home.

Nicholas Brandram’s heartbroken family blamed the force after his body was discovered at his property in Chiswick, West London.



The 44-year-old’s family claimed that he “took his own life after months of immense pressure”.

Brandram was investigated over the Putney Bridge incident, which saw a woman pushed into the path of an on-coming bus in May 2017.



The force described the wealthy banker’s death on Tuesday evening as ‘’unexpected’’ but not suspicious.

But it has since referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) over the case.

An IOPC spokesman said: “We have received a mandatory referral from the Met Police relating to prior contact officers had with Nicholas Brandram, who was sadly found unresponsive and declared deceased on 15 September.

“We are currently assessing the referral before deciding whether further action is required from us.”



Brandram’s furious family today protested his innocence and slammed the force for failing to “clear his name” before his death.

Ambulance and police crews discovered the body of Mr Brandram, a descendant of Queen Victoria, at his home on Tuesday evening.

The ex-Army officer’s relatives claimed there was no forensic evidence linking him to the crime or placing him on the bridge at the time.

They also told how he had carried the weight of the allegations for months.

Issuing a statement, they said: “The Met Police knew he was not [the Putney Pusher].



“And yet, when Nick died, they had still failed formally to clear his name. That is a source of profound grief and anger for our family.

“There was no forensic evidence linking Nick to it, no evidence placing him on Putney Bridge at that time, and no credible evidence that he was the man shown in the footage.

“In fact, the evidence proved the opposite. Despite that, the police chose to arrest Nick rather than invite him to attend for interview.

“He lived with the shame, anxiety, humiliation and extraordinary pressure created by a wholly unnecessary investigation.”

Shocking images showed the 12-ton bus narrowly missing the woman on the bridge spanning the River Thames in South West London.



Detectives interviewed 50 men and arrested three suspects, including an American investment banker who wasn’t in the country at the time.

But no one was ever charged in connection with the incident.

The investigation was wound down in 2018 over a lack of viable leads.

Brandram’s arrest followed his separation from his second wife, with whom he had a young son.

It is understood police were contacted by someone close to his estranged wife with information about the Putney Pusher.



The banker was held on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm (GBH).

While in custody he was further arrested on suspicion of possessing Class A and B drugs, believed to be cocaine and cannabis.

He was bailed later that day.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

His bail – which extends for a maximum of three months – was cancelled last week.

Detectives informed him he was being kept under investigation though without any conditions or length of time.

News.title: Belarus deploys tanks & drone units to Nato’s ‘weakest link’ in war games to simulating destruction of enemy targets
News.content:
Next

BELARUS is simulating war games with tanks and drone units near Nato’s “weakest link” next to Poland’s border.

Russia‘s closest ally has scrambled military training deployments to the defence pact’s doorstep – in Vladimir Putin‘s latest threat to the West.



The menacing four-day drills are taking place in Brest and Grodno regions, bordering Poland and Lithuania.

Grodno sits adjacent to the Suwalki Gap, a strategic 40-mile-wide strip that connects the Baltic states to the rest of Nato.



Wedged between the heavily militarised Russian exclave Kaliningrad and Belarus, it has been described as Nato’s “weakest link”.

Were the gap to be blockaded, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia could be completely cut off from allied land reinforcements.



The fresh Belarussian military exercises are taking place within striking distance of the Suwalki Gap.

Terrifying footage on Belarus state TV showed columns of armoured vehicles moving into position as troops marched on.



Tank battalions were ordered to conduct searches and eliminate supposed enemy reconnaissance and sabotage groups during the practice runs.

Commanders also tested artillery, concealed firing positions, drones and mobile teams designed to counter hostile unmanned aircraft.

General Pavel Muraveiko, chief of the Belarusian General Staff, claimed emphasis was being put on faster battlefield decision-making.



He said: “We are deliberately placing emphasis on training headquarters staff, because today a great deal depends on decision-making [and] on how quickly officials work.”

The manoeuvres are “purely defensive,” according to the Minsk regime.

Belarus, headed by Putin bootlicker Alexander Lukashenko, allowed Russia to launch its full-scale invasion of Ukraine from its territory in 2022.

In recent days, Lithuania has simultaneously been holding exercises of its own across 12 municipalities.

Meanwhile, a separate multinational drill near the Belarusian border involves about 2,500 troops from eight countries.



Poland is also constructing fortified positions, surveillance systems and anti-drone defences along its eastern frontier.

Nato has faced the threat of increased Russian drone carnage in recent days.

The alliance has been forced to scramble jets several times in the last week – including when Boris Johnson was allegedly targeted in an attack on a train.

Poland was today forced to shut down major airports and suspend dozens of flights amid a “military operation” in response to Russian strikes on Ukraine.

Explosions were reported close to the Polish-Ukrainian border while thousands of attack threat alerts were sounded in the region.



Two airports in Lublin and Rzeszow were suspended due to “operations of military aviation”, authorities said.

The Polish Armed Forces said the operations were “in connection with strikes carried out by the Russian Federation using jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles on the western territory of Ukraine“.

They added: “Ground-based air defense systems and radar reconnaissance systems have reached a state of readiness.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The actions were aimed at “securing airspace and its protection especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions”, the military said.

Both airports have since resumed operations following the temporary closure.

News.title: Human remains ‘unearthed by wildfires’ at UK beauty spot revealed as mum who vanished six years ago – as man arrested
News.content:
'MURDER' RIDDLE Human remains ‘unearthed by wildfires’ at UK beauty spot revealed as mum who vanished six years ago – as man arrested







Next

BONES discovered at a beauty spot have been identified as a mum-of-three who vanished six years ago, with cops launching a murder probe.

Joanne Sheen, 44, was travelling from Fareham to her home city of Southampton, Hampshire, when she vanished on December 2019.



The last known sighting was on December 5, when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton by train with a friend.

She was reported missing by her family in February 2020.



Police have now arrested a 56-year-old man from Southampton on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder.

It comes after a wildfire exposed a woman’s bones in West London on August 12, with cops racing to identify them.

Hampshire Police today confirmed the bones belong to Jo.

Five people were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to murder her in 2020, but were released with no further action.



In 2023, cops searched a house in Southampton, and deployed a boat to search the Solent.

They raided more homes in the port city last year.

Cops launched a fresh probe after Jo’s bones were found on Padstow Walk, an area nicknamed The Pits, in London.

The area is close to Bedfont Lakes Country Park, with cops confirming recent fires in the area had unearthed the remains.

Police said more than 10 addresses have been searched and several water searches since Jo disappeared.



Anyone with information about her movements in either city in 2019 have been urged to contact cops, with CrimeStoppers offering a £20,000 reward.

Jo’s daughters Hayley and Layla previously described their mum as a “lovely, loving person”.

Hayley said in 2020: “You can’t imagine what it is like with a loved one, when you don’t know where they are, you don’t know if they’re okay.

“Your mind is always turning on every single possibility that could’ve happened. It’s like turmoil but every day is the same. It just starts over every day.”

A Hampshire Police spokesperson said: “As part of our investigation, we have today arrested a 56-year-old man from Southampton on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder. He remains in custody at this time as our enquiries continue.



“As our investigation enters this next stage, we are working closely with our colleagues in the Metropolitan Police to establish exactly what happened to Joanne.

“Her death is being treated as murder, and we remain committed to identifying and bringing those responsible to justice.”

Detective Chief Inspector Toby Elcock added: “This is a significant development in what has been a long and complex investigation and provides us with several new lines of enquiry, which we are exploring with our dedicated team.



“While this tragic discovery is not the outcome Joanne’s family, or any of us, had hoped for, we hope the identification of her remains can at least begin to provide some answers after many years of uncertainty.

“Throughout this investigation, Joanne’s family have shown tremendous strength and dignity in the face of unimaginable circumstances, and our thoughts remain with them at this incredibly difficult time.

“As our investigation progresses, we remain committed to establishing exactly what happened to Joanne and ensuring that those responsible are held accountable.

“There may still be people who have information about Joanne’s disappearance, her movements before she went missing, or how she came to be in Feltham.

“The passage of time does not lessen the importance of that information.



“No matter how small or insignificant it may seem, we would urge anyone who may know something to come forward.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We understand that coming forward may feel difficult, particularly if you are worried about the consequences, but we are asking you to think about the family who are left without their loved one and who are waiting for answers. Please do the right thing. If you know something, now is the time to come forward.

“We are also pleased that Crimestoppers has agreed to reinstate its £20,000 reward offer in support of our investigation. If anyone has information but does not feel comfortable speaking directly to police, I would encourage them to contact Crimestoppers anonymously.”

News.title: Remains found after wildfire identified as mother-of-three missing since 2019
News.content:
Human remains discovered in woodland in south-west London following a wildfire have been identified as a woman who has been missing since 2019.

Mother-of-three Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019.

Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham on 12 August after bones were discovered in an area of shrubland damaged by a fire the previous week.

A 56-year-old man from Southampton has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and he remains in police custody.

Detectives in London have now handed the investigation over to Hampshire Police after the remains were identified as those of Sheen.

Sheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force described as "long and complex".

News.title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
News.content:
King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society.

Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.

It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.

He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.

The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.

News.title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high
News.content:
The Bank of England has held interest rates for the sixth time in a row but said they are likely to rise if high energy prices caused by the conflict in the Middle East continue.

The main Bank rate has been kept at 3.75% despite an uptick in the rate of inflation.

The US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted global energy supplies which has led to a sharp increase in petrol and diesel prices.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said the longer the volatility in energy prices persists, "the bigger the impact it will have on inflation and the more likely it is we will need to raise [the] Bank rate to ensure that inflation falls back to our 2% target".

The Bank now forecasts that inflation will rise more than it previously thought and warned that the price cap on household gas and electricity bills for January is "now expected to rise substantially further".

Speaking after the Bank's decision, Bailey said the direct impact of higher energy prices was clear, but officials were still assessing how far those costs would feed through into wider inflation across the economy.

The Bank's main interest rate is a crucial benchmark for banks and other lenders in setting interest rates for individuals and businesses who want to borrow or save money.

The Bank of England uses interest rates to help control inflation, the pace at which prices are rising.

The UK's central bank aims to keep inflation at a target of 2%, but it has been above that rate for nearly two years.

On Wednesday, official figures showed inflation had risen to 3.1% in August from 2.9% in July.

News.title: Father's tribute to 'sweetest little boy' Noah Woods
News.content:
People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire turned up to help with the search for Noah, who was from nearby East Bergholt.

Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the River Stour on the Suffolk-Essex border.

Reflecting on the community response, Woods wrote in his Facebook post: "It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation.

"You have all taken Noah into your own hearts, with all the overwhelming help, we were all just trying to bring him home to us safe and sound."

He thanked everyone who came together to search for "our boy" - listing emergency services, businesses and venues in the village - and "all of the people who gave up their time in their busy schedules to help us when we most needed it".

"The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives."

He finished the post by addressing his son.

"It has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short three years you were with us."

Suffolk Police said his death was not being treated as suspicious, but that officers still had inquiries to complete before submitting a file for the coroner.

Supt Tom Pearse thanked the family for their "patience and understanding throughout the searches".

"It was clear from the media coverage we saw that they not only had all of Suffolk behind them, but an outpouring of goodwill from across the entire country and beyond.

"I know how grateful Noah's family are for all the support and kind messages they have received, but would reiterate our plea to now allow them the time, space and privacy they need at this deeply distressing time."

News.title: Verified video shows wreckage of Saudi fighter jet shot down over Yemen
News.content:
Footage verified by the BBC shows the wreckage of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet which the Iran-backed Houthi group says it shot down over Yemen.

The US-made aircraft was "downed using a locally manufactured surface-to-air missile" as it "conducted hostile operations" over the Marib region, according to a Houthi statement on Wednesday.

Experts have told BBC Verify the incident is a "propaganda coup" that shows the Houthis' military capability has advanced and they are prepared to further escalate its conflict with Saudi Arabia.

Using satellite imagery to match features in the landscape seen in the footage, BBC Verify was able to pinpoint the crash site to an isolated location in the hills west of the Yemeni city of Marib.

The long-running conflict between a Saudi-led military coalition and the Houthis has escalated in the last week after the armed group launched an offensive against pro-government forces.

This led to the Houthis seizing key territory near the south-west coast, close to vital international shipping channels in the Bab al-Mandab strait.

News.title: UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes
News.content:
"Civilians in Iran are caught between gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government and the nation's deadly conflict with the United States and Israel," the fact-finding mission warned in a statement on Thursday.

For their latest report to the UN Human Rights Council, the mission's three independent experts investigated two of the deadliest attacks on civilians during the conflict.

On 28 February, when the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, Tomahawk missiles struck Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the southern town of Minab, killing at least 156 people, including 120 children, according to local authorities.

The fact-finding mission's experts said the school was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) naval complex also attacked that day, but that the school was clearly identifiable and that no information indicated that it was used for military purposes.

The experts said that, based on the evidence gathered - including media reports indicating that a preliminary US military inquiry found US forces responsible, and the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses Tomahawk missiles - they had reasonable grounds to believe that the strike on the school was carried out by the US.

They also concluded that the school was "the intended point of impact and that the damage did not result from an errant strike or collateral damage" from the attack on the IRGC complex, citing survivors as saying the school was struck twice.

The US military has yet to release the findings of its investigation into the Minab strike, but Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said it would "never target civilian targets".

Also on 28 February, Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM) dispersed clouds of tungsten pellets over a sports complex and residential area in the town of Lamerd, killing at least 21 civilians, including seven children, according to local authorities.

Again, the fact-finding mission's experts said the sports complex was clearly identifiable and that no information indicated it was used for military purposes.

They concluded by saying there were reasonable grounds to believe that the strike was carried out by the US, citing evidence including the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses PrSM missiles.

The US military has said it carried no strikes on Lamerd that day and disputed reports identifying the weapon used as a PrSM.

In both incidents, the fact-finding mission's experts said there were "reasonable grounds to believe that the US committed the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack resulting in loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects".

News.title: Canada welcomes EU proposal to become 'associate member'
News.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the European Union's ambition for Canada to become its first "associate member", calling for closer cooperation on defence, critical minerals and energy security.

Carney told the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".

His comments came a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to Canada's associate membership, a status that does not currently exist.

US President Donald Trump earlier called the idea "laughable" and threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".

Canada and the US are locked in an escalating trade dispute, with each side imposing tit-for-tat tariffs after bilateral talks collapsed last month.

"Today our societies are being battered by new storms," Carney said during his address, naming them as climate change, "the erosion of democratic norms" and the "weaponisation of trade".

"Economic integration is now being weaponised, tariffs being used to exert pressure," he said.

"Financial mechanisms have been used for coercion. Supply chains constitute weak points to be exploited."

He said a Canada-EU alliance would create a "beacon for other democracies", while stressing the two sides were not seeking to form a new power bloc.

"I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival - only with better manners," he told MEPs.

"This is about sovereignty, our ability to live as we wish. We do not seek power to dominate others."

Asked about the proposal on Wednesday, Trump told reporters: "If I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, on many things.

"If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility."

Responding to Trump's comments at a press conference following his address, Carney said: "This alliance is a positive process, that's my response to the American president."

"Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak, no-one is going to dictate our culture, or with whom we can strike agreements internationally," he added.

Carney said Canada was "not in a position, nor seeking, to become a full member of the European Union", describing the proposal as a "different framework".

News.title: Family of 'Putney pusher' suspect say he was innocent and blame police for his death
News.content:
The family said that police "chose to arrest Nick rather than invite him to attend for interview".

"They searched his home, and the Met Police press team then released information which inevitably led to speculation and Nick being identified in subsequent reporting," they said.

"For Nick, the consequences did not disappear. He was left for months carrying the stigma of an appalling allegation which the police themselves clearly recognised was unsupported by the evidence.

"He lived with the shame, anxiety, humiliation, and extraordinary pressure created by a wholly unnecessary investigation."

They said the police were repeatedly asked to end their investigation and warned about the impact the investigation was having on Brandram's mental health, saying: "Even then, the investigation was not brought to an end. As a result, Nick is dead."

While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, Brandram was also arrested on suspicion of possession of class A and class B drugs.

On Thursday, an IOPC spokesperson said: "We have received a mandatory referral from the Met Police relating to prior contact officers had with Nicholas Brandram, who was sadly found unresponsive and declared deceased on 15 September.

"We are currently assessing the referral before deciding whether further action is required from us."

Shortly after the Putney Bridge incident on 5 May 2017, investigating officer Sgt Mat Knowles said: "It was only due to the superb quick reactions of the bus driver that she was not hit by the vehicle."

Bus driver Oliver Salbris told the Sunday Times following the incident: "If I hadn't swerved, I would have smashed her head.

"It was reflex. The consequences would have been terrible for her â and for me."

The Met said at the time that about 15 minutes after the push, the jogger came back the other way across the bridge and ignored the victim when she tried to speak to him.

Detectives identified more than 50 people of interest following the incident.

The Met had initially closed its investigation in 2018 after three men had been arrested and released without charge.

News.title: RNLI station out-of-service after anti-migrant protests
News.content:
Portsmouth's lifeboat station remains temporarily out of service following anti-migrant protests.

Protesters blocked roads in the city on 6 September after about 120 people arrived at the Eastney Landing ferry port area following a Channel small boat crossing. The RNLI helped bring them ashore.

The RNLI also said it helped to ensure the safety of anti-migrant demonstrators who went into the sea.

Following the protest, the charity's chief executive said staff had faced "unacceptable" online and physical abuse. The lifeboat station was taken out of service on 10 September, meanwhile, abuse aimed at volunteers also forced the lifeboat museum in Poole to shut for several days.

The RNLI said: "Search and rescue cover continues to be provided through established contingency arrangements, including flank RNLI stations and other declared assets.

"We hope to have the lifeboat station back on service as soon as possible."

After abuse was directed at its crews tasked to assist the incident, its chief executive issued a statement.

Peter Sparkes said: "Recent events have generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding about the RNLI â our purpose, our tasking, and particularly our lifesaving work in the Channel.

"Sadly, as a result, some of our volunteers and staff have been the subject of online and, in the worst cases, physical abuse.

"The RNLI's people represent the very best in our society, they selflessly give up their time to keep others safe."

He added: "Stand by them, not against them and their families. I am extremely proud of and grateful for their vital lifesaving work."

The protest in Portsmouth followed a separate demonstration the previous day, in which hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters brought the Port of Dover to a standstill.

The protests led the RNLI to also review its security procedures. As part of this, volunteers were told to consider not wearing RNLI-branded clothing in some circumstances while representing the charity.

News.title: Tower block arsonist jailed for setting woman alight
News.content:
A man who set a woman on fire inside a flat, after dousing her in petrol and vodka, has been jailed for 11 years and nine months.

Reece Brivitt, 33, set the victim alight inside a tower block flat on Milton Grove, Stafford, on 22 October.

The victim suffered serious burns to her chest and legs, leaving her with life-changing injuries, the court heard.

Brivitt admitted charges of arson with intent to endanger life as well as wounding with intent and was sentenced at Stafford Crown Court on Wednesday.

Brivitt was also served with an indefinite restraining order against the victim.

Det Con Jessica Scott, of Staffordshire Police, said the arsonist had "subjected his victim to a cruel attack, which has left her with life-changing injuries".

"The incident not only threatened the life of the victim, but of all those who were in the flats at the time," she added.

The swift actions of firefighters meant the fire was extinguished quickly, preventing further injuries, she explained.

Delivery group manager Mark Walchester, from Staffordshire Fire and Rescue Service, said: "Crews worked quickly to minimise the risk posed to those in the flat block during this incident and to ensure the fire was extinguished as quickly as possible.

"Fires in flat blocks and houses of multiple occupancy have the potential to devastate lives."

News.title: Tributes paid to 'deeply caring' dad killed in Swiss Alps plane crash
News.content:
Authorities said the plane took off from Sion airport in the RhÃ´ne Valley and, for unknown reasons, crashed into a mountain slope about 10 minutes later.

Emergency teams from the Valais Rescue Organisation, police and firefighters were sent to the scene along with three helicopters.

Amcanu announced his death with "profound sadness", describing Davies as "strong-willed, spirited, determined and deeply caring".

The statement also said family was "at the centre of Owain's life".

"He was devoted to his wife Michelle, immensely proud of his children Aron and Ffion, and adored being a grandfather to Oakley and Albie, " it said.

His son Aron described him as "a real character", and said he was "immensely proud of everything he achieved".

"He was my mentor throughout my life, personally and in business, and I know many people at Amcanu will feel that they have lost a mentor too," he said.

The firm was founded by his father, Spencer Davies OBE, in Burry Port in 1975, and he took over the leadership of the business in 2000.

Amcanu noted Davies was "a proud Welshman and Welsh speaker" and had been a trustee of Wales Air Ambulance Charity since 2017.

The charity's chair of trustees Dr Kyle Jacques said Davies had made a "significant contribution to the Wales Air Ambulance and the vital service we provide".

"Owain was a valued colleague and friend, whose loyalty and generosity of spirit meant so much to us. He will be greatly missed," he added.

Earlier in his life, Davies served for nearly 25 years as a helmsman with Burry Port Lifeboat, the firm said.

News.title: Crocodile attack suspect has bail extended
News.content:
A man who was arrested after a three-year-old boy was seriously injured in a crocodile enclosure is still on bail.

The boy was visiting Johnsons of Old Hurst near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, with his family on 18 June, when he ended up in the enclosure and was attacked by at least one of the reptiles.

A 30-year-old man from Norfolk was arrested at the time on suspicion of attempted murder and was bailed until 18 September after being assessed as not "fit for interview".

A police spokesperson confirmed the individual, who was not known to the child, had been rebailed until 17 December.

The BBC understands the arrested man has learning disabilities and was on a trip with carers.

The parents of the boy said their child received injuries to his arms, neck, head, face and suffered broken bones and underwent seven surgeries.

In the latest update on a fundraising page set up by the family, his parents said he had returned home and faced lengthy rehabilitation.

The Care Quality Commission launched an investigation in July into the care that the man - later arrested - had been receiving.

Norfolk County Council â which did not provide any care for the man â has also launched an inquiry under the Care Act 2014.

News.title: Conservatives urge Burnham to rule out tax rises at Budget
News.content:
Griffith - who was appointed as shadow chancellor last month - told an audience at a further education college that taxes in the UK had reached "nosebleed territory" and that Healey "must end uncertainty today and rule out any new taxes".

"He must rule out increasing taxes on small businesses and the self-employed."

Griffith described business owners and the self-employed as "economic heroes", adding: "Any government worth its salt would do everything it could to help them because whilst not every acorn grows into a mighty oak we need green shoots that are nurtured not trampled upon."

He said the IR35 regime had "crushed the dreams of self-employed people" and promised that a Conservative government would "replace it with a new system that respects the right of the self-employed to choose their status and only prevents actual abuse".

The IR35 rules are designed to prevent people avoiding tax by posing as self-employed contractors rather than employees but some freelancers argue the system has led to unfair treatment.

Griffith also urged the chancellor to pause the rollout of Making Tax Digital, the new system for the self-employed to register their income with HMRC.

"For the self-employed, many of whom will have started out in colleges such as this, there is this special torture of Making Tax Digital."

He acknowledged that the previous Conservative government had been responsible for setting up the system and said that "despite well-intentioned, the execution has left a lot to be desired".

Griffith told the audience that he had commissioned Lord Mackinlay of Richborough, the former South Thanet MP, and Robert Colvile, the outgoing director of the Centre for Policy Studies think tank, to produce a report on reducing regulations for small businesses.

Over the weekend, the Mail on Sunday reported, external that the Conservatives could promise to abolish inheritance tax if they win the next election, with the policy potentially being announced at the party's annual conference in October.

Speaking to the BBC ahead of his speech, Griffith said he would "love" to cut the tax but it would have to be "subject to an ability to set out properly how we would fund that".

"I'm going to be responsible and only want to make promises I can keep," he said.

He added that he had recently been on a fact-finding trip to Sweden, which scrapped inheritance taxes in 2005.

Reform UK has previously said it wanted to cut inheritance tax, but speaking at the party's conference, the party's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said it would not be a priority.

"It's a bold chancellor that would say I'd rather privilege 36,000 families than 40 million [income] taxpayers," he told a Reform conference fringe event.

Asked if getting rid of inheritance tax would amount to a tax cut for the wealthy, Griffith argued that it would boost growth and that the wealthiest people were often able to "arrange their affairs" to avoid the tax.

News.title: Barclays workers ask for more money to return to the office
News.content:
Thousands of Barclays staff are demanding concessions from the bank after it said it wants employees to work from the office more often.

Staff who have been expected to work in the office for two days per week should be in the office for at least three days a week from next month, according to the company.

Unite, which represents about 36,000 Barclays staff, is calling for the bank to reverse its decision. The union is also pressing for exemptions and a payment to offset increased travel and childcare costs.

Barclays said many employees already work in the office for three or more days and that being on-site fostered collaboration and helped people learn from eachother.

It added that it recognised "the benefits of balancing flexibility for colleagues with the importance of working together in our physical locations".

The bank sent a memo to staff in July outlining its expectations, which include that senior leaders work at least four days per week in the office.

But the bank is facing a growing backlash against the proposed rules change, first reported in the Financial Times, external,

Unite national officer Rick Coyle said thousands of employees have signed an open letter calling for Barclays to reverse the decision, and the number of signatories "continues to rise".

He added that Barclays is "trying to fix a problem that doesn't exist" in making its working-from-home rules less flexible.

The open letter, external says workers are delivering "strong financial results and improved customer services" with its current working from home policy.

It adds that thousands of workers have made suggestions, which the union has condensed into a series of demands.

These include:

an exemption for people whose commutes are longer than 40 minutes or 35 miles

exemptions during Christmas, summer, and school holidays

a maximum one day in the office for carers

flexibility for wrap-around childcare, and childcare vouchers and onsite creches to be explored

a one-off payment to offset costs

"Our minimum time in office requirements vary by business area, reflecting the nature of the work and the needs of the business," a spokesperson for the bank said.

Barclays declined to say how many staff would be affected by the rule change. However, the BBC understands that there are different requirements depending on teams, with, for example, investment bankers in the office for five days per week.

The coronavirus pandemic forced many businesses to allow working from home, depending on the nature of the business.

Since then, many organisations have been increasingly recalling workers to the office.

There is evidence that hybrid working may be the best fit for many workers and businesses.

But a lot of large organisations including Amazon, Boots and JP Morgan took the decision to bring in policies requiring head office staff to be in every day after the pandemic.

This week, Ewan Venters, the executive chair of fashion brand Paul Smith, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast that working from home "just doesn't work" for young people and urged the government to stay out of decisions over where employees work.

In June, digital bank Revolut said it was shifting away from its "remote-first" policy for new recruits in 2027, but for other employees that policy wouldn't change.

News.title: Eleanor Donaldson to appeal trial of the facts verdict
News.content:
Eleanor Donaldson has applied to appeal the verdict from her trial of the facts, which found she had done the acts in relation to all five charges she faced.

Four of those charges were of aiding and abetting the offending committed by her husband Jeffrey Donaldson.

The former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader was convicted of 18 counts of sex abuse, including one count of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.

The Northern Ireland Courts Service confirmed on Thursday that an application for leave to appeal had been lodged to the Court of Appeal by Eleanor Donaldson's legal team.

She faced a trial of the facts after being found unfit for a conventional trial on mental health grounds.

It ran alongside her husband's trial at Newry Crown Court in May and June.

She cannot be given a prison sentence but could be given a treatment order or an absolute discharge.

The judge from her trial is due to decide on this in October.

Jeffrey Donaldson's solicitor has said he is also to appeal against his convictions.

News.title: Virtual queue for disabled at Alton Towers praised
News.content:
A new virtual queuing system for visitors with accessibility needs to be introduced first at Alton Towers has been praised by charities.

The upgraded ride access pass (Rap), to be in use later at other Merlin-run parks like Thorpe Park and Legoland Windsor Resort, enables queuing for rides via an app rather than in physical lines.

The news follows a backlash in February when proposed changes led to visitors with conditions such as ADHD and autism being told they would not be able to use a physical Rap.

There will be no change to the eligibility criteria for the pass, available to those who have problems queuing for long periods because of a physical, emotional or learning need, Merlin says.

Staffordshire-based Alton Towers will start accepting the revamped pass at the end of the year, with Merlin's other theme parks taking it on next year.

During the row earlier in the year, families of children with additional needs told the BBC the restrictions would mean their children could not visit because of waiting in long queues, or sensory overload felt in crowded environments.

Under the plan, visitors to places like Alton Towers, Chessington World of Adventures and Legoland Windsor over half-term who had "difficulty with crowds" would no longer have qualified.

Merlin backtracked on the proposal days later following an online petition against it signed by more than 25,000, saying they had listened to the feedback and would pause the changes while considering other options.

News.title: Kennedy Center claims it’s only closing for seven days after Trump says it could be ‘ripped down’
News.content:

The Department of Justice insists that the Kennedy Center is only “temporarily” closing for seven days to address “advanced deterioration” after the institution’s Donald Trump-dominated board voted to shutter the building for repairs, fueling speculation that the president could try to demolish it altogether.

The board’s executive director and chief operating officer decided to temporarily close the Kennedy Center due to “acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration” of the building, according to government lawyers.

That decision from Matt Floca was “separate from any Board decision related to closure for ongoing renovations,” lawyers with the Justice Department wrote in court filings Thursday.

The venue’s closure may be “extended” after workers “assess existing safety risks in those portions of the main building exhibiting severe structural deterioration,” according to the Justice Department.

Thursday’s filing follows an extraordinary 24 hours for the living memorial to the assassinated former president, as workers installed fencing and orange barricades around the property while Trump publicly mulled whether to demolish the building entirely after courts blocked his attempts to rename it after himself.

open image in gallery Donald Trump appeared to review a placard about the Kennedy Center while onboard Air Force One one day after the venue’s board voted to close it down without his name on it ( AFP/Getty )

Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, a Kennedy Center board member who is leading the legal battle against Trump’s efforts, has requested an emergency court hearing on the building’s closure, which her legal team says violates an injunction that was issued earlier this year.

She alerted Washington, D.C. Judge Christopher R. Cooper to Trump’s remarks on Wednesday night, telling reporters that the building “will end up being ripped down” unless the president is given “recognition” for his takeover of the memorial.

He later appeared to be reviewing a placard reading “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED” while sitting on Air Force One — images that Beatty’s legal team have now included in court filings.

“Given the emergency nature of this matter and Defendants’ 10 a.m. filing deadline for their response to Plaintiff’s motion, Plaintiff wanted to make sure the Court and Defendants are aware of this new information,” lawyers wrote.

Bill Pulte, Trump’s director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency and former Acting Director of National Intelligence, was aboard Air Force One when AFP photojournalist Brendan Smialowski captured images of the president reviewing the placard.

Pulte did not respond to a text message from The Independent asking for more information about the poster.

open image in gallery Workers installed fencing and barricades around the Kennedy Center on September 16 after the board voted to shutter the institution ( Reuters )

Judge Cooper is mulling whether to hold an emergency hearing on the institution’s closure, which will likely raise more questions about the president’s alleged plans to “demolish” the campus to make way for his own memorial.

Floca said in a sworn declaration to Judge Cooper that he independently decided to close the building over “acute risks to public safety” and claimed that a message over the Kennedy Center’s speakers telling people to leave stemmed from an improperly triggered alarm.

“I did not authorize that alarm, nor am I aware of a legitimate reason why that alarm may have been triggered,” he wrote in court filings.

Beatty’s legal team said Floca’s explanation for the closure “cannot be squared with the record.”

The Kennedy Center is only temporarily closing the building as “a plain pretext to justify shutting down the Center permanently,” her lawyers wrote in response to the Justice Department’s latest filings.

“It is a recipe for Defendants extending their shutdown forever and closing the Kennedy Center for the next two years — the very thing this Court said they could not do without its permission,” they wrote.

“It goes without saying that demolishing the Kennedy Center’s main building would violate the Court’s preliminary injunction,” they added.

Beatty is now asking for a judge’s “crystal clear” order to prevent Trump’s demolition.

In May, the judge blocked the president from renaming the venue after himself, writing that Congress made it “crystal clear” that the building is only to be named after former President John F. Kennedy, “and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial” based on a “unilateral say-so” from a Trump-appointed board.

Last week, Cooper blocked the board from trying to rename the venue after Trump, again, after board members proposed adding “renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump” to the facade.

“Closing the Kennedy Center without Judge Cooper’s approval appears to directly violate his order. This is an assault on the rule of law,” Beatty’s counsel Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group said in a statement Wednesday.

“The board cannot simply ignore Judge Cooper’s rulings whenever it suits them. In this country, no one — including the president — is above the law,” they said.

Last month, after government lawyers repeatedly argued that the performing arts venue is falling into “financial ruin” and rapidly deteriorating in a state of “terminal decline” without Trump at the helm, the Justice Department suggested that it could fall into such extreme disrepair that will require it “to be taken down.

Trump, with his “unrivaled expertise and experience in real estate and construction” and “prominence” as president to raise money for the venue, must be memorialized on the building’s marble facade — or the Kennedy Center will “deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down,” according to the Justice Department.

The Independent has requested further comment from Beatty’s legal team.

Andrew Feinberg contributed reporting from Washington, D.C.

The Pentagon has reportedly sent out an email seeking troops to appear alongside Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at a major speech later this month – but only if they meet strict fitness and grooming standards.

The Wall Street Journal reports that the message was fired out to Army commanders Tuesday asking them to nominate troops who meet the approved “physical standards” with a view to their appearing alongside the secretary at his “State of the Force” address on September 30.

The email states that the soldiers – who will be invited to participate in a workout with Hegseth – would be expected to pass the Army’s preferred waist-to-height ratio and fitness tests and have “impeccable grooming and uniform standards (no exception),” according to the Journal.

They will ultimately be chosen based on “demonstrated leadership quality and professional character,” the email reportedly explained.

It added that preferred candidates will be “consistently rated as top performers within their formations,” have a “clear record of integrity, discipline and selfless service,” “demonstrate strong presence, clear communication and sound judgment under pressure” and “serve as role models for their peers and subordinates.”

open image in gallery Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is seeking only the only fittest and most ‘impeccably’ groomed troops to appear alongside him at an upcoming speech ( Getty )

A Pentagon official declined to comment but chief spokesman Sean Parnell previously told The Independent: “Secretary Hegseth maintains the highest expectations for our service members to uphold the professional standards of appearance, fitness, and discipline that define our warfighting force, and he continues to emphasize consistent enforcement of hair, weight, and grooming standards across all ranks.”

Discussing the email on The Daily Show, host Josh Johnson joked: “I have never heard anyone say the phrase ‘waste-to-height ratio’ before. This man cannot count the number of missiles you need to fight a war with Iran but when it comes to male physique he’s in A Beautiful Mind?”

Hegseth’s fixation with personal appearance standards has become a feature of his tenure leading the Department of Defense.

He raised the issue in a March 2025 memo to senior military leaders in which he called for a review of all fitness, body composition, and grooming standards, “which includes but is not limited to beards.”

The secretary went further in another memo the following August in which he called for a “clean-shaven military” before giving full vent to his feelings when he summoned the top U.S. generals and admirals to Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia a year ago to lecture them on his vision of the “warrior ethos” and denounce “woke” politics in the military.

open image in gallery The secretary has placed an emphasis on personal appearance standards and made a point of taking part in workouts with servicemembers to set an example ( Department of Defense )

“Today, at my direction, the era of unprofessional appearance is over,” he told his highly-decorated audience. “No more beardos. The age of rampant and ridiculous shaving profiles is done.

“We don’t have a military full of Nordic pagans. No more beards, long hair, superficial individual expression. We’re going to cut our hair, shave our beards, and adhere to standards. If you want a beard, you can join special forces. If not, then shave.”

He subsequently declined to meet with U.S. soldiers stationed at Camp Humphreys in South Korea when he visited last October if they had been granted “shaver waivers,” handing them a medical exemption from shaving.

That same month, he had overweight members of the Texas National Guard sent home from Operation Midway Blitz in Chicago after they appeared in a viral photo.

More recently, he reportedly lashed out at the Navy after encountering sailors with beards during a shipboard inspection in June and was accused of “body shaming” a Canadian cadet instructor by posting her picture on X with a derisory comment as trade tensions between the U.S. and Canada came to a head.

Earlier this week, outgoing Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie filed a resolution to impeach Hegseth, forcing the House of Representatives to hold a vote on the matter within two days.

Massie accused the secretary of violating his oath of office, abusing his powers and high crimes and misdemeanors, citing military operations in Iran, Caribbean boat strikes and disputes over free speech.

Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt has written to Fifa president Gianni Infantino requesting an independent investigation into plans for private investment in the World Cup and how the disciplinary case of Folarin Balogun was handled, the Press Association understands.

The move increases the pressure on Infantino following opposition from three continental confederations to his proposal. The plan aimed to establish a commercial entity to manage Fifa tournaments, including the men’s and women’s World Cups, and offload a 20 per cent stake to private investors.

Hewitt’s letter demanding answers was first revealed by The Times on Thursday. Alongside her FA role, she serves as a Fifa vice-president and holds a seat on the Fifa Council.

It is understood by the Press Association that the correspondence requests an external review regarding the private investor scheme, as well as explanation over Fifa’s disciplinary committee opting to suspend a one-game ban handed to United States forward Balogun during the tournament.

Debbie Hewitt wants answers from Infantino (James Manning/PA) ( PA Wire )

The decision to pause Balogun’s suspension came before US president Donald Trump admitted he personally contacted Infantino to request that the red card given to the forward against Bosnia and Herzegovina be re-examined.

Although Infantino issued an apology on 5 August regarding the procedures surrounding the private investment strategy, and Fifa’s management board pledged an evaluation would occur, the governing body has never confirmed who is carrying out the review.

European football body Uefa has stated it has "lost confidence" in Infantino, launching legal proceedings within the US court system to compel the disclosure of files relating to the private investment scheme.

Uefa has additionally committed to backing a viable opponent to challenge Infantino at the Fifa Congress next March, ahead of the official nomination deadline on 18 November.

Infantino has already announced his intention to stand for re-election, retaining robust backing across South America, Africa and several nations in the Middle East, including Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

Meanwhile, the Belgian football association (RBFA) continues to examine its legal avenues regarding the Balogun situation, as the suspended sanction permitted the American attacker to feature in their World Cup last-16 encounter against Belgium.
