The government’s former cost-of-living tsar had warned Andy Burnham must stop acting like “Father Christmas”, telling the prime minister that British businesses aren't a “piggy bank” to be raided.

Iceland boss Richard Walker served as Sir Keir Starmer’s expert ‘cost-of-living champion’ during his tenure, but left his post days before Mr Burrnham took office.

He told Mr Burnham that he needed to start making “unpopular decisions” ahead of next month’s Budget, warning the prime minister “real crunch time is coming up now”.

Lord Walker told LBC: “Andy Burnham has been Father Christmas so far, and it would be great if he’d start to get a bit more unpopular.

“For the last 50 years, chancellors on the left or the right haven’t been too dramatic on raising taxes or reducing spending because they’ve been able to borrow a little bit more.

open image in gallery The government’s former cost-of-living tsar had warned Andy Burnham must stop acting like “Father Christmas” ( AP )

“Borrowing, increasing borrowing, is now off the table as an option. The bond markets are teaching us that lesson. Therefore, tough choices are now needed.

“We cannot, for the sake of all of us, keep taxing business and view it as some piggy bank that can constantly be raided, because as I said, it's only business that, that creates growth.

“Therefore, we have to now start reducing spending, or at least cutting the rate of increase of spending.”

He added: “The real crunch time is coming up now. You know, the nights are drawing in, it's getting colder, and it's time to make some hard choices.”

Mr Burnham has made a slew of promises since entering No 10 over the summer, including moves to introduce a £2 cap on bus fares, cut VAT on household electricity bills, and end rough sleeping. But questions have been raised on how he will fund his pledges.

open image in gallery Iceland boss Lord Richard Walker served as Sir Keir Starmer’s expert ‘cost-of-living champion’ during his tenure ( LBC )

On Wednesday, he admitted next month’s Budget will be “challenging” for his government after official figures revealed inflation has soared to a five-month high.

Chancellor John Healey is set to deliver the first Budget since Mr Burnham entered No 10 next month, amid concerns over the impact of Donald Trump’s war on Iran and funding for UK defence.

The major political headache comes against a backdrop of rising inflation rates, with the most recent official figures showing another jump on Wednesday.

The Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey warned interest rates could rise in the coming months if the Iran war continued.

Mr Burnham told broadcasters that the current climate would mean next month’s Budget will be “challenging”, but insisted his government “will not take risks with people’s living standards”.

“It is going to be challenging, because the picture around the world is challenging, particularly the situation in the Middle East, and we will look carefully at all those things,” he said.

Appealing to the fact that more of us are taking a closer look at the ingredients in our hair and skincare, the formula is also made without a list of certain synthetic ingredients that many of us try to avoid. Whether you want to impart vibrancy and a healthy-looking shine onto your roots and strands while covering greys with ease, you can choose from seven shades. Far-left streamer Hasan Piker said the United States is “pound for pound” worse than al-Qaeda, the Islamist terrorist network that carried out the 9/11 attacks.

Piker, a self-described socialist whose Twitch streams draw millions of views, made the comments in an interview with Axios that the outlet previewed Thursday. Piker later accused Axios of turning his “nuanced answer” into clickbait.

Ahead of the November midterms Republicans have sought to portray Piker as emblematic of the Democratic Party’s “radical left.” GOP lawmakers have pointed to Piker’s previous controversial statements, including his assertion that “America deserved 9/11” and that Hamas is “a thousand times better” than Israel.

The 35-year-old, from New Jersey, has also caused division within the Democratic Party. Some Democrats have appeared alongside Piker on the campaign trail, including Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, while others have denounced him.

In the Axios interview preview, reporter Alex Thompson asked Piker: “You once said that America is the top dog in terrorism… Do you think America then is worse than al-Qaeda?”

open image in gallery Hasan Piker, a popular left-wing streamer, said that the US is 'pound-for-pound' worse than al-Qaeda, in an interview clip released by Axios ( Axios, X )

“Pound for pound as far as the number of deaths, yes,” Piker replied. “We have caused tremendous terror all around the world.”

Elsewhere in the clip, Piker highlighted the February air strike on a school in Minab, Iran, which killed more than 150 people, including about 120 children.

U.S. military investigators reportedly reached the preliminary conclusion in March that American forces were likely responsible, while a recent U.N. fact-finding mission said it had “reasonable grounds” to believe the U.S. was to blame. The Pentagon has not publicly released its findings, and President Donald Trump told reporters in June: “I don’t think it was us.”

“One clear example of this is what we did in Minab, right?” Piker said. “There’s no distinction between blowing up a school, triple tapping it with Tomahawk missiles, if you’re killing 140 school girls; that is an act of terror.”

“This doesn’t mean that all Americans are terrorists,” he continued. “But the reality of the matter is we have to create an environment of accountability to ensure things like that never happen again.”

In recent weeks, Republicans have repeatedly invoked Piker as they seek to cast the Democratic Party’s left flank as too extreme. They’ve also criticized Democratic candidates and officeholders for their ties to him.

“You have [Democrats] associating themselves with someone like Hasan Piker, who said that we deserved 9/11…They’re sympathetic to Islamic jihadists,” Arizona Senator Katie Britt said earlier this month.

An image of Piker, shown shirtless, also briefly appeared on a jumbotron at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, earlier this month, according to Newsweek.

Democrats have taken varying approaches to Piker.

Last month, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries called the streamer’s comments about Jews “malicious” and said they “should not be tolerated by anyone in the public square.”

His remarks followed Piker’s statement on his stream: “If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews.”

open image in gallery Republicans have criticized Democratic candidates and officeholders, including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, for their ties to Piker ( AP )

El-Sayed, who is running for the U.S. Senate in Michigan, has also criticized some of Piker’s past remarks, calling his statement that America deserved 9/11 “dumb.”

But El-Sayed has resisted calls to fully denounce Piker, and defended him in an interview last month.

“They’re trying to equate him and David Duke and him and Nick Fuentes,” El-Sayed said. “There are a lot of things he says that I deeply agree with. People deserve healthcare. We shouldn’t be fighting dumb wars. The war in Iran is ridiculous. Donald Trump is a fascist. All true.”

Other Democrats have castigated their colleagues for dwelling too much on Piker, arguing that Republicans are using the controversy as a political trap.

“I guarantee you that 80%+ of Dems have no idea who Hasan Piker is. This is a dumb distraction and Dems should stop taking the bait,” Democratic strategist Tom Bonier wrote on social media last month.

Piker has denied allegations of antisemitism, apologized to viewers offended by his comments about the September 11 attacks and said some of his remarks have been taken out of context.

News.title: Interest rate increase ‘likely’, warns Bank of England
News.content:
Andrew Bailey has said that interest rates are likely to rise if the Middle East war rages on, warning inflation is now on course to hit 4pc.

The Bank of England opted to hold borrowing costs at 3.75pc on Thursday, the sixth time in a row it has left them unchanged.

However, the Governor said a “material” increase in energy prices since July would push up inflation to twice the Bank’s 2pc target.

He warned the outlook for inflation “continues to be on the upside” and criticised the “seeming loss of urgency to find solutions” to the war in Iran.

Oil prices are back above $100 a barrel and analysts expect average gas and electricity bills to rise above £2,000 this winter as the conflict continues.

Mr Bailey said: “So far, higher global energy costs have had a limited effect on price and wage setting in the UK.

“But the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise Bank Rate to ensure that inflation falls back to our 2pc target.”

Investors expect the Bank to raise interest rates as soon as November, which has pushed average mortgage rates to their highest level in three years.

The average five-year fixed mortgage deal has risen to 5.87pc, according to Moneyfacts, which is the highest level since November 2023 and up from 4.95pc before the Iran war.

Thursday’s rate hold leaves the Bank out of step with central banks around the world after the US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank voted to raise borrowing costs this month.

However, economists said there had been a change in tone from policymakers over the threat posed by energy prices and whether this would feed into the wider economy.

The Bank of England predicted that inflation would hit 4pc early next year, just as most workers are negotiating pay rises.

Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said: “It seems as though a majority of the MPC is on the cusp of wanting to tighten policy.”

In a warning on the impending pain facing households, Mr Bailey told the Chancellor that energy bills would rise by 24pc early next year under the Ofgem price cap.

This will push up annual average bills by £413 to £2,136, which the Governor blamed on the war in the Middle East.

The Governor is required to write a formal letter to the Chancellor every time inflation is more than a percentage point above its 2pc target.

Official data showed inflation rose to 3.1pc in August.

Mr Bailey said: “The energy price shock has been the most important factor driving recent short-term movements in inflation.”

Despite expectations of higher rates, the FTSE 100 rose on Thursday at its steepest pace since July, climbing more than 1pc, as the Bank of England eased the pressure on the UK bond market.

Policymakers also confirmed a Telegraph report that the Bank will stop selling the long-dated bonds it amassed during the financial crisis and lockdown.

The Bank will continue actively selling £20bn of government bonds per year until the rest of the stockpile is wound down to zero in 2034.

The announcement triggered a sharp fall in the cost of borrowing for the Treasury, with the yield on 30-year UK gilts falling at the fastest pace since May.

News.title: Next-generation antivenom fights India’s deadliest snakes
News.content:
The process to make antivenom has barely changed in a century: snakes are milked, their venom is injected into horses, and their antibodies are harvested to form the basis of the product. The resulting treatments are difficult to administer, can trigger severe side effects, and the quality varies from batch to batch.

“The big four snakes contribute to 70 per cent of poisonous bites [in India]… so 30 per cent of poisonous snakes are not covered, even to begin with,” said Dr Yogesh Jain, a public health physician in Chhattisgarh state and a member of The Global Snakebite Taskforce.

“But there are huge quality and efficacy issues even against these 70 per cent of bites. We’re relying on a 100-year-old technique of getting antivenoms, and at least 50,000 people are dying every year,” he told The Telegraph.

“There’s a real need for new technology. We don’t have a safe and appropriate antivenom for the largest majority of people in rural India.”

Now, scientists are hopeful that they have developed a potential alternative.

In the latest study, published last week, researchers showed that an experimental antivenom cocktail with five components protected mice against lethal doses of antivenom in Indian cobras, even when delayed by up to 20 minutes – a scenario that mimics the real-world lag between a bite and treatment.

“If you go 10 years back, people didn’t think you could make sufficiently simple products with new, modern biotechnology that could cover all these different snake venoms,” said Prof Andreas Laustsen-Kiel, head of the Section of Biologics Engineering at the Technical University of Denmark and co-author of the paper.

“People simply believed it was too complex, too expensive to manufacture, and so on… But the data we are gathering is convincing enough to say this is something that could make a huge dent in the lost lives and limbs snakebite causes every year.”

The antivenom itself was based on lab-made nanobodies – antibodies derived from a group of animals including camels, llamas and some species of shark. Scientists believe their structure means they could be a more potent, more precise, more temperature-stable alternative to man-made monoclonal antibodies – and cheaper to manufacture.

“The latest study builds on an earlier discovery of nanobodies that can protect across a broad spectrum of African snakes,” said Prof Nicholas Casewell, director of the Centre for Snakebite Research and Interventions at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, who has previously collaborated with Prof Laustsen-Kiel.

“In this paper they have iterated and demonstrated that a narrow number of nanobodies can protect against Indian cobras and king cobras. This demonstration brings the nanobody technology closer to market,” he added.

But that is likely still years away, depending on how much funding the researchers can attract. The next steps – a larger animal study, scaling up manufacture, and launching human trials – are expensive.

“If money was no issue, we could probably be testing in humans in 1.5 to three years from now,” said Prof Laustsen-Kiel. “But since money is a big issue, it is more likely that human trials won’t be able to start until 2.5 to four years from now.

“But I really think that this [study shows] there’s no doubt that biotech can deliver better antivenoms. The question is whether people are willing to fund it,” he said.

News.title: Manchester United hounded off pitch by own fans
News.content:
The joke goes that Michael Carrick has already bettered Ruben Amorim’s efforts by reaching the third round of the League Cup, but Manchester United will need to find a way past free-flowing Brighton if they are to go any further.

United were eliminated in the second round by League Two Grimsby Town last season, but start the competition a stage later because they are one of nine Premier League clubs playing in European competition.

Brighton knocked United out of the FA Cup in the third round, with Danny Welbeck scoring at Old Trafford, meaning the club played just 40 matches in 2025-26.

Carrick will want to make a better fist of the cup competitions, but he could really use a win of any kind after taking just four points from United’s first four league games of the new season.

The no-show at Hull and derby defeat by City’s 10 men were especially dispiriting, and the relationship between the club and supporters is becoming increasingly strained.

There were no flags on the Stretford End for the game against City, as fans voiced their opposition to what they view as a heavy-handed ticketing policy. The club says the measures are to stop ticket-touting but critics believe many innocent season-ticket holders are being caught in the crossfire and having their tickets revoked.

Discontent is never too far away given the continued presence of the Glazer family, and confidence is fragile regarding the club’s sporting direction under Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos.

The news that 15-year-old JJ Gabriel, possibly the country’s outstanding academy player in his year group, wants out (broken by Matt Law in a Telegraph Sport exclusive) nagged at some of those fears.



Gabriel could have been in contention for a place on the bench this evening, but that is now surely out of the question even if United say they have not given up hope of persuading him to stay.

News.content:
“But that is why we cannot say it does not work for anyone. There are players who play every three days with no issues. They are very robust, their performances do not change too much. There are other players where the risk is bigger and the performances are different. I have to learn who is ready to play games every three days and who needs a rest so their performance level is not affected. I thought I had it quite clear in my mind with some, but with others, it is new, even for them, because they have not played as many games. We are learning.”

Liverpool were knocked out in the fourth round of this competition last season, losing 3-0 at home against Crystal Palace. Joe Gomez returns to the squad for the hosts tonight after an injury early in pre-season but Giovanni Leoni, Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Federico Chiesa remain out.

Tottenham are still without a league win or goal this season. Their 0-0 draw at home against Everton Saturday means they sit just above the relegation zone. Tottenham overcame Charlton in the second round, convincingly winning 5-1 at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium last month.

“I think we are working well,” Tottenham boss Roberto De Zerbi said. “We played 30 minutes, 25 minutes very well [against Everton]. In that moment we could score two goals. News.title: England cruise to victory led by ‘absolute freak’ Brook
News.content:
Whatever his returns, there has been an extra focus to Brook’s approach this summer, possibly because he has learnt from a grievous indiscretion in Wellington last winter. While others chase the Indian Premier League, he is totally committed to England, taking his break while that tournament is on and playing every match in all formats for his country.

Brook had come to the crease at the fall of the first wicket and, while it is early days, England appear to have added another arrow to their quiver. They handed a debut to opener Aneurin Donald, with his cap presented in the pre-match huddle by Pietersen, the new “specialist mentor”.

Donald has been selected as an “intent merchant”, charged with going extremely hard from the first over, aping Phil Salt, who is missing with a quad injury. He did what he was asked to do, smearing his first ball for two, then pulling six to leg and hammering four through the offside before the first over was out. Another big shot, off Wellalage, in the second saw him well caught in the deep, but 12 off five had kickstarted the innings.

News.title: Max Dowman-mania could make League Cup hottest ticket in town
News.content:
At this rate, Arsenal supporters will be looking forward to Carabao Cup matches as eagerly as any Premier League or Champions League game, simply because it will be a chance to watch Dowman again. The forward’s age and inexperience means he is still used sparingly in those high-priority competitions. The League Cup, by contrast, may prove to be his domain over the coming months.

Dowman’s double at Portman Road made him just the second 16-year-old to score two goals in a game for a Premier League side. The first was Wayne Rooney, for Everton against Wrexham in 2002.

The two goals underlined why there is so much excitement around Dowman. The first was a demonstration of his prodigious dribbling ability, as he weaved through Ipswich’s defence and buried his shot with the weaker right foot. The second showed his composure: a slotted finish, rolled in with ease.

News.title: UK borrowing costs hit 19-year high as global bond rout intensifies
News.content:
The cost of UK government borrowing hit its highest level since 2007 in a fresh global debt sell-off.

The yield on 10-year gilts, a benchmark for what the Treasury pays to borrow money, rose from 5.37pc to a fresh 19-year high of 5.41pc on Tuesday as rising oil prices risk reigniting inflation.

Mortgage experts have warned that residential and buy-to-let mortgage rates are set to climb towards 5pc, as market turmoil threatens to filter through to household finances.

Short-term debt costs have also jumped, with the yield on two-year UK bonds surpassing 4.9pc for the first time in three years.

The bond chaos came as Andy Haldane, a former Bank of England chief economist, warned that Labour risked becoming “just a traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok videos”.

He told LBC that John Healey’s original plan for a “low drama budget” had been “torpedoed” by higher borrowing costs and “events over the last couple of weeks”.

He said: “I think that [the bond market turmoil] will mean some hard choices next month at the Budget.”

“Few hard choices so far, but one is looming on the horizon, how any hole to the budget headroom is made good on. Is that a question of tax rises, or is it a question of taking the knife to public spending.”

Mr Haldane has been advising Labour since Andy Burnham took power.

It comes as the US Federal Reserve and the Bank of England face pressure to raise interest rates this week to combat rising prices.

Anthony Brinkman, a portfolio manager at Principal Asset Management, said: “The recent gilt market movements seem to be intent on showing central banks they are out of time – the market is expecting action.”

Borrowing costs around the world are rising after a 20pc surge in oil prices so far this month.

Brent crude tipped above $109 a barrel this week after Houthi rebels in Yemen, considered a proxy for Iran’s forces, seized control of a key port in the Red Sea, threatening shipping.

The US Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates on Wednesday in the face of the inflation threat.

As a result, the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds has surged above 5pc for the first time since 2007.

News.title: AI could transform global inequalities or ‘widen the gap’, warns Bill Gates
News.content:
“AI could be a great equaliser, or [it could] widen the gap”, says Mr Gates. “This is not a long-range prediction. It’s a present-tense choice”.

“We can harness AI for good. But it won’t happen by accident. After all, the market is an extraordinary engine of innovation, but a terrible guarantor of equal opportunity.

“With AI, the gap could grow even faster … That is what makes this moment so urgent. Things are changing rapidly, and the window to shape who benefits from AI, and how soon, is short”.

The key issue holding back the deployment of AI in the developing world revolves around the availability of local data and, in turn, the ability for the technology to scale in environments very different from where it is currently being created.

An app that is trained on billions of hours of American English, will struggle at first with British English (see your spell check) but is next to useless if your local language is Swahili or Chichewa.

More profoundly, an AI tool that allows a farmer in Hampshire to control his combine harvester remotely, will offer little to a smallholder in South Sudan who works the land by hand and faces a completely different array of pests, weather conditions and costs.

The same is true for health. “A community health worker in Rwanda examining a baby with a fever faces different questions than a clinician in a well-resourced hospital - and the AI supporting her needs to reflect that”, says Mr Gates.

He adds: “Most of the world is invisible to today’s AI models. These AI systems were trained primarily on what exists on the internet – and the internet reflects a deeply unequal world. More than 90 percent of the data used to train early, large language models came from English-language sources. The communities that stand the most to gain from AI are largely absent from the knowledge base these tools are built on. They are not just underserved. They are not in the picture at all”.

The new investment aims to help correct that. Mark Suzman, CEO of the Gates Foundation, says investments are already being made with companies including Microsoft and Google to build databases of a much wider range of languages, for instance.

Africa alone has more than 2,000 languages, and for AI’s to be effective there they have to understand what and how people actually speak - “their dialects, accents, and slang, too”.

The investments, he says, are being made on the condition that the intelligence and knowledge they accumulate are made freely available for others to use.

Languages for AI “are true public goods, almost definitional public goods. They need to be freely available to everybody. Once they’re created, they are public goods that can be uploaded onto any AI,” said Mr Suzman.

Sports.title: West Ham stars told how to use volatile Millwall atmosphere to their advantage ahead of first derby in 14 years
Sports.content:
Next

MATT JARVIS has urged West Ham players to embrace the fierce atmosphere at The Den on Saturday when they face rivals Millwall.

The pair have not met in 14 years, with their last clash coming in 2012 during the Hammers’ last spell in the Championship.



But they will finally reunite in South East London this weekend for what will be the 100th competitive clash in their 127-year-long feud.

Former Hammers star Jarvis did not take to the field against the Lions while wearing Claret and Blue, but he is no stranger to The Den and the intimidating atmosphere it can produce.



And he reckons that the gravity of the clash will not be lost on the Hammers’ current crop of stars, as they search for a first away win against Millwall since 1988.

Jarvis told SunSport, on behalf of ElevenLabs: “You’re going to be looking away at Saturday, and every player will come out in the press and say, ‘It’s just another game. We’re just going to continue as we have done.’



“But you will be told by the fans that this game is so important. It doesn’t matter about the one on Tuesday and about the one the following week. This game is massively important.

“Recent results suggest that West Ham are in great form and it’s just going to be another game, they’re going to go out and play their thing.

“But once you go and play Millwall at The Den, that atmosphere – you’ll feel it from the crowd. You’ll feel it from the team talk before the game about how much this game means to everyone.”

The momentous occasion certainly won’t be lost on the home crowd in New Cross, who will be making sure the feisty fixture lives up to its reputation.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Jarvis has featured in front of the same crowd himself while with Gillingham, and suggested that West Ham’s stars should embrace the hostilities and try to channel them into their own performance.

He said of the home crowd aggro: “Sometimes, depending on the situation in the game, you can use it to your advantage.

“I was a winger, so you hear absolutely everything because you’re literally next to the fans for the majority of the game. I took the corners, so they’re literally on you. They can touch you, you can hear everything.

“You try and use everything as a positive. If I’m getting hammered by the away fans, then I know that I’m doing something well.



“So you actually rile them up a little bit, but you know that you’re obviously performing.”

The trick, according to former Wolves and England star, is striking the balance between allowing the energy to fuel you while not getting caught up in the spectacle.

He continued: “You are trying to zone in on what your roles and responsibilities are in that game. If you switch off for one moment and they score, you know that you’re going to be in serious trouble from either your team-mates or the manager or the fans.

“So it is really great to soak up all of the atmosphere, everything before the game. You have a good look around when you walk out. You feed off it.



“Then once that game starts, you’ve got to be able to zone into: ‘Right, what do I have to do here? Who am I picking up from a corner? He will not score from that corner.’

“That’s the hardest and the best part about the game.”

The fixture has seen its fair share of bone-headed decisions over the years, with the last Dockers Derby seeing Jarvis’ former team-mate Kevin Nolan sent off within the opening ten minutes.

The Hammers went on to win that one thanks to a thumping strike from Winston Reid, but Jarvis – who spent seven years on Millwall’s books as a youngster before being released at 16 – is hoping it won’t come to that this time around.



He explained: “You’re hoping that this squad that’s just started to find a bit of form will have that mentality to not go into stupid challenges to start with. They’re not going to get a petulant yellow card or a sending off that’s just going to have a big impact on the game.

“So you’re hoping that they can be in a position where they can go and play their game the way that they have been, but knowing the surroundings, the supporters, the atmosphere, everything that goes into this game.

“It hasn’t happened for such a long time as well, so there’s going to be bragging rights for all of the fanbases. The players will fully, fully know this, and they’ll be playing it down, but it will have been drilled into them, the importance of this result.”

If all of that falls into place, Jarvis sees West Ham walking out as the victors – though he would not be surprised to see the match end up a bit more scrappy than your average Championship showdown.

The former winger tipped the favourites to live up to their billing, especially with Millwall’s injuries and the fact that, per Transfermarkt, the Hammers’ squad is worth more than triple that of their rivals.

Jarvis added: “I would say, looking at Millwall this season, they’re still going to be up in and around it like they have been the last few years. They’ve just had a couple of difficult results.

“So I would say it is going to be a frantic, frantic game. I can see both teams scoring, and I will go for a 3-1 away win.

“The new (West Ham) players that have come in have settled really well. They’ve either scored, they’ve got man of the match, they’ve got an assist, so their confidence is high. The team’s confidence is high.

“They’ve gone down to Bolton, they’ve gone goals behind, they’ve come back and won. This breeds so much confidence within the team.

“I feel like that’s where West Ham are building at the moment. That ability to not panic, to go, ‘We have got a great squad, we’ve got great players. Whatever happens in this game, whoever’s playing, we’ve got a real chance of coming back or winning the game.’

“So I would be optimistic that, at the moment, from what we’ve seen, they are in that mindset.”

MANCHESTER UNITED hit another low point on Wednesday, squandering a two-goal lead to lose at home against Brighton.

The Red Devils went 2-0 up within 10 minutes at Old Trafford thanks to goals from Shea Lacey and Mason Mount.



Charalampos Kostoulas got one back for the visitors on the brink of half-time before United threw it all away after the break, with Pascal Gross equalising and Maxim De Cuyper netting a 70th-minute winner.

Another disappointing display laid bare United’s main issues on the pitch, especially in attack.



Benjamin Sesko failed to threaten the Brighton defence and goalkeeper, not even managing one shot.

It is not the first time a United striker has struggled to impress in recent years.



The Red Devils have faced a huge challenge to find and keep a No9 who can hit the target consistently.

SunSport has looked at some of the strikers to have walked through the doors at Old Trafford over the last decade and how they have performed.

Anthony Martial (2015-2024)

Anthony Martial made 317 appearances for United after joining from Monaco in a £36m transfer as a 19-year-old.

Sports.title: Chelsea owners to decide on Stamford Bridge future as prospect of new stadium looms with Blues facing EIGHT-year rebuild
Sports.content:
Next

CHELSEA’S new majority owners face a huge decision over the future of Stamford Bridge with the Blues potentially facing an EIGHT-YEAR stadium rebuild.

According to a report in the Daily Mail, Clearlake Capital have made deciding what to do with the club’s famous home one of their key priorities following their takeover as majority shareholders.



And insiders have claimed the options have now been narrowed down to two – complete demolition and rebuild of Stamford Bridge, or a sensational move to a new site.

A stand-by-stand redevelopment of the existing ground is reportedly viewed by Clearlake as not worthwhile, despite previous attempts to modernise the historic stadium.



Stamford Bridge, built in 1877, currently holds 40,044 supporters, leaving Chelsea with a significantly smaller capacity and means to generate matchday revenue than many of their Premier League rivals.

The Sun previously reported that the club could be looking at a capacity of at least 60,000 for a completely new ground.

One possible destination is Earl’s Court, just a mile from the current stadium.

While the area’s development masterplan does not include a football stadium, the Mail reports that people inside Chelsea believe there may still be enough land available to find a solution.

But any move would come with a major hurdle, the Chelsea Pitch Owners.

The supporters’ organisation owns the freehold of Stamford Bridge, as well as the pitch, turnstiles and Chelsea Football Club naming rights.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

A permanent move would require the necessary approval from the CPO, while a rebuild on the existing site would also require its agreement.

Staying at Stamford Bridge would be an extremely complex solution that would cost huge money and lots of time.

With upgrading the current stadium not seen as an option razing and rebuilding Stamford Bridge could leave Chelsea needing to play their home matches elsewhere for up to eight years of the complexity of the project.

Wembley Stadium could therefore become a potential temporary home, just as it did for Tottenham during their own stadium rebuild – although that took less than two full seasons.

The Sun has previously identified Wembley and Twickenham as possible temporary venues if Chelsea were forced out of Stamford Bridge.



There is, however, no final decision yet, while the report claims plans have been worked on privately for both a Stamford Bridge rebuild and a potential new stadium.

The scale of what Chelsea could ultimately build is enormous. Previous concepts have included a futuristic, brick-built 60,000-capacity Stamford Bridge, while a completely new site would give the club a blank canvas for a modern stadium with corporate facilities, fan zones, cutting-edge technology and potentially a retractable roof.

The financial stakes are huge, too. The Sun previously estimated a move could cost around £1.5billion, while a complete overhaul of Stamford Bridge could approach £1.6billion.

Sports.title: Kevin Miller dead at 57: Former Premier League goalkeeper dies suddenly as current club Wigan lead tributes
Sports.content:
Next

FORMER Watford and Crystal Palace star Kevin Miller has suddenly passed away at the age of 57.

The ex-goalkeeper had moved into coaching following the end of his playing career, and joined Wigan as a goalkeeping coach in the summer.



But the club have tragically had to announce his passing just months later, after Miller died overnight on Tuesday.

A club statement read: “Everyone at Wigan Athletic is deeply saddened and devastated to learn about the sudden passing of goalkeeping coach Kevin Miller.



“Although Kevin’s time with Latics was far too short, he quickly became a much loved and respected member of our first-team staff.

“His experience, professionalism and passion for goalkeeping were clear for all to see, while his uplifting personality made a lasting impression on everyone who had the privilege of working alongside him.

“Kevin’s contribution to football was significant, but for those who worked alongside him, it was the person he was that will be remembered most.

“Kevin was a husband, father, hugely respected colleague, dedicated coach and someone who made a genuine impact on those around him, both on and off the pitch.

“His sudden passing has left everyone at the club deeply saddened and devastated.”

Miller joined the Latics in the summer as he followed his former Exeter colleague Gary Caldwell to Wigan.



He played more than 200 times for the Devon outfit across two stints, and returned as a goalkeeping coach in 2022 – before stepping down from his role in June.

Exeter also released a statement honouring the star, writing: “As a player, Kevin had a commanding presence and a fierce competitive spirit.

“For those who watched Kevin play, he will be remembered not only for the saves and clean sheets, but for the personality he brought to the team. Kevin was never afraid to make his voice heard, organise those in front of him and put his body on the line for the team.

“His time in Devon left a lasting impression on those around the club, and his contribution remains a big part of Exeter City’s story.”

Miller began his career playing non-League football in Cornwall with Falmouth Town and Newquay, before landing at Exeter in 1989.



He would go on to star for Watford and then Crystal Palace between 1994 and 1999, making 128 and 66 league appearances for the sides respectively.

He also spent time with Barnsley, Bristol Rovers, Southampton and Torquay, before ending his career with non-League Bodmin Town.

Sports.title: Arsenal complete incredible transfer for Liverpool wonderkid Vincent Joseph, 16, as teen striker joins academy
Sports.content:
Next

ARSENAL have announced the capture of rising star Vincent Joseph from Liverpool.

Joseph, 16, has become the latest in a long list of academy prospects to join the Gunners this summer in an aggressive recruitment drive.

The teenager joins Arsenal as part of their first year scholarship intake given his young age and could potentially pen a pro deal once he turns 17 in January.



Joseph shone for Liverpool’s Under-18s last season, scoring three goals in his first two games at U18 level.



He has also impressed for England Under-16s too, scoring eight times and providing one assist in his nine caps for the Young Lions.

Joseph announced his exit from Liverpool on Tuesday night, writing on Instagram: “After nine unforgettable years, the time has come to say goodbye.

“Thank you for the memories, and for making my time here truly special. YNWA.”

Joseph becomes the third top-rated youngster to join the Gunners in the space of two weeks, following Georgian wonderkid Andria Bartishvili and 40-goal prospect Mylo Bernard through the door.

Meanwhile Arsenal also lured Manchester United duo James Scanlon and Habeeb Ogunneye away from Old Trafford earlier this month.

That followed the signing of Elijah Upson – son of former West Ham and Arsenal ace Matthew – from North London rivals Tottenham earlier in the window.

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Igor Tyjon has joined from Backburn Rovers, Axel Donczew has arrived from Cardiff City and Phoenix Blayney has signed from Northern Irish club Larne.



There will be other new faces arriving in the coming months, too.

Pre-contract agreements were made last season for highly-rated Ecuadorian twins Edwin and Holger Quintero to join when they turn 18 next August.

And Irish starlet Victor Ozhianvuna will join from Shamrock Rovers on his 18th birthday in January.

Sports.title: Man Utd wonderkid Gabriel attracting interest from top European clubs
Sports.content:
Real Madrid, Barcelona, Paris Saint-Germain and Bayern Munich, along with several Premier League clubs, are interested in Manchester United forward JJ Gabriel.

The 15-year-old has made it clear he wants to leave Man Utd and has asked to be deregistered immediately to become a free agent.

Gabriel and his team feel United had ample opportunities to involve him more in pre-season and in first-team squads since the season started, including in the Champions League.

United's hierarchy will keep trying to convince Gabriel to stay while he is still registered with them.

However, it is understood Gabriel has made up his mind and, as far as he's concerned, has played his last game for the club.

Gabriel turns 16 on October 6 and cannot sign a scholarship agreement until then, or a professional contract until he turns 17.

What will happen next?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Dan Khan updates Sky Sports on 15-year-old prodigy JJ Gabriel's decision to leave Manchester United

Premier League rules state that a youth registration can only be cancelled if the club, player and parent or carer agree. If they cannot reach an agreement, the Premier League can make a binding decision.

Conversations now with Gabriel's team and his family will be key, and it will be up to Man Utd chief executive Omar Berrada, director of football Jason Wilcox and academy director Stephen Torpey to attempt to de-escalate the situation.

But the biggest clubs around the Premier League and the rest of Europe will all be monitoring the situation with Gabriel as it evolves.

He was not included in the A-list for Champions League participation and featured for eight minutes for the first team in pre-season, and there is a feeling he has not been afforded as many opportunities as other young players around the squad.

However, those inside Carrington believe not much more could have been done to show a pathway through to the senior team for the young star.

In the last 12 months, Gabriel met former United head coach Ruben Amorim in his office as a first step towards the first team, followed by a meeting not too soon after with Sir Alex Ferguson.

Gabriel then trained with the first team last season and was part of Carrick's pre-season squad at times this summer as well, making his debut against Atletico Madrid in Stockholm last month.

However, Gabriel has started this season incredibly well. He scored a hat-trick against Sabah last week in the UEFA Youth League and has two goals and two assists in Premier League 2 so far this season.

Gabriel became the youngest winner of United's Jimmy Murphy Young Player of the Year award last season after scoring more than 20 goals for the U18s.

Carrick: We have to be careful with Gabriel situation

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Michael Carrick has urged care in the handling of Manchester United teenager JJ Gabriel, after the 15-year-old requested to leave the club earlier this week

Man Utd head coach Michael Carrick has asked for Gabriel's welfare to be protected amid the doubts over the teenager's future at the club.

Carrick told Sky Sports on Wednesday: "We have to be a little bit careful on that one. He's a 15-year-old boy.

"It's more about the welfare, the care and the attention of JJ as a child, really.

"The situation is what it is, but we have to be careful about the exposure and how much we jump on that."

Merson: Massive blow if Gabriel leaves

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Paul Merson says the likes of teenage sensations Max Dowman at Arsenal and JJ Gabriel, who's asked to leave Manchester United, need to be patient as they look to build their careers

Sky Sports' Paul Merson:

"First of all, he's an unbelievable talent. The problem now is with the lad and probably his agents and his family - I don't know him so I'm only thinking from the outside.

"When you're watching Max Dowman at Arsenal and Rio Ngumoha getting given a chance at Liverpool and doing very well, he's probably thinking, 'I should be playing at Man Utd now as well'.

"This is the problem you're going to have with the kids of this day and age. They're so talented that they want to play straight away. When I was playing, it was unheard of at 16.

"It'll be a massive blow for Man Utd. Believe me, this kid is an unbelievable talent. They'll have every club in the world wanting him."

Sports.title: Breach, Matthews return for Red Roses vs Canada as Mitchell rings changes
Sports.content:
Jess Breach and Alex Matthews return to start for England's Red Roses against Canada in the first of three WXV Tests between the sides on Saturday, as head coach John Mitchell makes nine changes.

Breach and Matthews, both of whom played major roles in 2025's Women's Rugby World Cup glory - as England beat Canada in the final - come into the side on the right wing and at No 8 respectively.

Mitchell's side face Canada in Tests on Saturday in Exeter, Friday October 16 in Toronto, and Friday October 23 in Ottawa. They also face New Zealand on Saturday September 26 at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

Hooker Bryony Field scored on her international debut last weekend in the dominant win over Australia and earns a maiden start in an all-changed front row featuring Hannah Botterman and Maud Muir. Morwenna Talling is also back among the starting contingent from the second row.

Image: Meg Jones (left) captains England again as Alex Matthews (centre), Jess Breach (right) return to the side vs Canada

Lucy Packer - another try scorer against the Wallaroos - is named at scrum-half with fly-half Zoe Harrison outside her. Helena Rowland is reinstated to the midfield alongside captain Meg Jones.

Three Exeter Chiefs players - Claudia Moloney-MacDonald, Maddie Feaunati and Flo Robinson - are in the squad as the Red Roses prepare to play at their club stadium, Sandy Park, for the first time since September 2023.

"This is the first Test of an exciting three-Test series between the No 1 and No 3 teams in the world," head coach Mitchell said.

Image: No 8 Alex Matthews scored two tries in the 2025 Women's Rugby World Cup final success vs Canada

"You need rivalries in our sport and our rivalry with Canada is one that has evolved to a great level. They are a well-coached team who will bring a different challenge to the one Australia presented. We will be expected to raise our standards."

England's squad contains 974 Test caps, while 14 players in the matchday 23 were involved in the World Cup final triumph over Canada at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

Sports.title: Alonso: Chelsea didn't need a reset - they just needed an update
Sports.content:
Xabi Alonso says Chelsea were in need of "an update" rather than a full reset when he was appointed manager this summer.

The 44-year-old signed a four-year contract in May and took over a Blues side that finished 10th in the Premier League, after parting ways with both Enzo Maresca and Liam Rosenior during a tumultuous campaign at Stamford Bridge.

That meant missing out on European football for the third time in four seasons.

"Not a reset - it was an update, I would say. To change or to take decisions in another direction," he said in an exclusive interview with Sky Sports.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from the Premier League clash between Chelsea and Hull.

"My main concern is the squad, the team, the players that we have, in which stage of their career they are, in which moments we want to bring them, what we have, what we can improve.

"Those were, for me, the important decisions, the important things to analyse before coming here. Once we agreed we wanted to take one direction, it was about taking decisions.

"Some of them we took, others will have to be taken, but we are convinced with all of them.

"Now it's competition time. It's not about improving, now it's with the team that we have to work hard, improve, knowing that we have to learn from mistakes, from the good things as well, and we are in that moment."

Alonso has taken charge of six games in all competitions so far; two wins, one draw and a defeat in the league and two wins from two in the Carabao Cup.

Brentford

Chelsea Friday 18th September 7:00pm Kick off 8:00pm

Next up, his Chelsea side make the short trip to the Gtech Community Stadium to take on Brentford in a west London derby on Friday night, which is live on Sky Sports.

"If I look for perfection, I will be frustrated always," he said.

"What I'm looking for is to reach a good level, good continuity, good solidity; to be a team that knows what they're going to do and have this confidence and this conviction whenever you are facing any opposition.

"We are in the process. We will get there when some processes are quicker or longer, but we are working to have that feeling and when you see that we are going on the pitch we have that belief that we know what we are going to do.

"The early days are just for games and I'm not that focused about the other teams. I'm very focused about my own team and all my players and the development that we will do, the process and the improvement that we have to make.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Chelsea head coach Xabi Alonso discusses the ownership changes at the club after Todd Boehly sold his minority stakes to Clearlake Capital and stepped down as chairman.

"We need to learn quick because the competition is furious in the Premier League and I'm sure that the Chelsea of the first day and the Chelsea of the last day in the Premier League will be different and I'm sure that it will be better. It will be getting better and better with weeks and with games."

Asked when people should just his team, he added: "It's not for me to answer.

"I prefer not to ask things from people. I prefer to do things.

"And knowing that, I am aware everything takes time in football, but time will tell."

Alonso: Joao Pedro could feature for Chelsea vs Brentford

Alonso has said Joao Pedro could feature against Brentford on Friday Night Football - despite pulling out of the Brazil squad with injury.

it was announced on Wednesday night that Pedro has withdrawn from the Brazil squad - raising concerns about his fitness levels as Chelsea look to get back to winning ways.

"In terms of injuries and in terms of the squad, we are having the last training session [on Friday]," Alonso said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Thierry Henry analyses Joao Pedro role in the Chelsea team this season and explains how he is vital to their system and success.

"No one is ruled out. I remain cautious and we wait. We will see [on Friday] if he's ready to play. We will take a decision."

Asked what he can say about Pedro's injury issues, Alonso simply replied: "No."

Asked if he could play against Brentford on Friday, but then not play for Brazil, Alonso said: "It is a possibility."

Then asked if Pedro is disappointed to be missing out of Brazil, especially given he was not selected for the World Cup, Alonso replied: "He has moved on from the summer, he has moved on from the World Cup.

"He has shown this desire, determination to have a great season so far. The summer is far away now.

"He will be [in the Brazil squad] in the future. I'm pretty sure he is going to be."

Sports.title: McManamon to fight Yu on undercard of heavyweight world title fight
Sports.content:
Britain’s Marie McManamon will meet Hong Kong Muay Thai star Yu Yau Pui in an atomweight clash on ONE Fight Night 48, live on Sky Sports on October 3.

McManamon is one of the UK's premier female Muay Thai athletes. A force in the ring, she has used her relentless cardio and whipping kicks to earn both Victory League and Roar Fighting Championship Titles.

Coming off a loss to Selina Flores, McManamon, a former ONE world title challenger, is going straight back into another top-level contest.

A dangerous striker who can end a contest at any given moment, Yu Yau Pui began competing in the weekly ONE Friday Fights series in 2023 and after four knockout wins in five fights, the Chinese striker won a lucrative $100,000 contract to ONE Championship.

Image: Marie McManamon challenges Allycia Hellen Rodrigues for the world Muay Thai championship

ONE Fight Night 48, live on Sky Sports in the early hours of Saturday October 3, will be headlined by Middlesbrough's Paul Elliott in a ONE Championship heavyweight world title bout against Shamil Erdogan.

The card also features America's Luke Lessei versus England's Charlie Guest in an important Muay Thai match which will see the winner push for a crack at Nico Carrillo's featherweight title.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel’s shot at redemption begins with England’s tricky Nations League tests
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel has been back around the Premier League grounds this season and it is worth dwelling on one particular interaction he had with a colleague inside a VIP enclosure, which has doubtless been repeated elsewhere. “People are killing me,” the England manager said. At which point he might have added: Still.

It is two months since England’s 2-1 World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in the United States and the emotion tied up in it continues to swirl. Heartbreak, pain, frustration; everything in this kind of area has touched everybody with an investment in the team. It was a result to leave scars that may never heal.

Then things begin to diverge because on one hand there is an anger among a section of the fanbase – those who have struggled to make their peace with a glorious opportunity spurned. They lay the blame for the surrender of a 1-0 lead with five minutes to go at Tuchel’s door.

On the other, there is an appreciation of how Tuchel’s team fought to reach the semi-finals for only the fourth time in England’s history; the personality they showed; the stirring moments along the way, chiefly the last-16 win over Mexico at the Azteca Stadium.

It was not nothing to dig deep and find a way past Norway in the quarter-finals after extra-time. The victory over Croatia in the opening group game was a thriller. When England beat France in the third-place playoff, it added up to a best World Cup finish since 1966.

It is difficult to quantify the number of haters. Just as it is those who have retained a sense of perspective. Both groups co-exist and Tuchel has been affected rather more by the former. He remains bruised by the fallout from the World Cup; bemused, too, because it is not as if England reach the semi-finals as a matter of course.

It is the tension that tracks Tuchel as he prepares for his next cycle in charge, running up to the Euro 2028 finals when England will be co-hosts. On Friday, he names his squad for the opening four Nations League ties, against Spain (home), Czechia (home and away) and Croatia (away).

Tuchel wants to look forward. As does the Football Association. He would do well to move on from the criticism of the Argentina defeat, however over-the-top he thought it was, however much it coloured the view of what he achieved at the tournament.

There is a reason why the England job has been described as impossible. It is because of the overbearing levels of expectation, how hard it is to dodge the recriminations after defeat, how the reactions make it more difficult for the team moving forward. It is a vicious circle that will be broken one way. Better not to overanalyse it. Just to accept it.

View image in fullscreen It may not have been the result fans or the manager wanted but Thomas Tuchel delivered the best World Cup showing since 1966 for England with a win in the third-place playoff. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

Tuchel can draw strength from the FA’s faith in him. Perhaps the best way to illustrate it is that it would not have wanted to get rid of him had England lost to the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the last 32. That went down as one of the most stressful England games in memory, the team 1-0 down with 15 minutes to go, even Tuchel wondering whether it was the end of his tournament before Harry Kane’s two goals drove the comeback. The captain deserves the Ballon d’Or purely for staving off an Iceland 2016-style disaster.

The FA loved how Tuchel’s in-game changes made the difference, as they did at other stages of the World Cup. It loved the team spirit he oversaw. Tuchel has spoken a good deal about the brotherhood among his players. It was real, not something for the cameras. The FA has set great store by this. Quite simply, it stands full square behind Tuchel. It considers the notion that he ought to have resigned or been sacked after a semi-final finish as absurd.

Tuchel’s stated mission at the World Cup was to put a second star on the shirt and he fell short. Did his death-or-glory rhetoric, which he did row back on slightly during the tournament, make the end worse? Then again, it was surely preferable to aim for glory. How would people have felt if he said the quarters or semis would have been fine?

England were the fourth seeds and, privately, the FA worried that punching above their ranking and winning the tournament would be beyond them, especially after the draw. It gave England the latest possible start and a long gap between their first and second group matches, followed by a more condensed schedule.

It was always going to be brutally challenging with the travel and heat. There is genuine optimism about the Euros, particularly as it is in effect a home tournament. The FA pushed hard to be a host alongside Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland for a reason.

Can England as a nation move on from the Argentina defeat? Can Tuchel’s explanations for his moves during it be accepted? It feels like an important starting point for the campaign ahead.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Tuchel could not get anything out of his players in the second half as Argentina dialled up all-out fury mode, and that is on him. England, though, were physically spent, a consequence of playing at altitude against Mexico with 10 men and for 120 minutes against Norway in Miami in 40C heat.

View image in fullscreen England face Spain next Saturday for the first time since defeat in the Euro 2024 final. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

England started to sink back long before the second-half hydration break when Tuchel introduced the defender Ezri Konsa for the winger Anthony Gordon and went to a five-man defence. They were well into grim survival football. Tuchel could do nothing to change the flow, to get his players on the ball. Again that is on him.

The decision to reinforce the defence, to double down, was a clinical one, taken after considering the available evidence. To Tuchel, it felt like the percentage call, maybe the least bad option. It failed. And when it failed, the optics were horrible. Would more positive changes have led to a better outcome? It is hard to say. The bottom line was that England were well beaten.

It is time to look forward and it is a good thing that England are back in Nations League Group A with testing fixtures, none more so than the opener against Spain at Wembley next Saturday.

It was damaging – more so than the FA realised – to be in Group B last time and have more straightforward matches against Ireland, Finland and Greece (even if Greece at Wembley was not straightforward, England losing 2-1). Neither was the World Cup qualification group too taxing. The hope is the Nations League will better prepare England for the Euros.

Tuchel has numerous selection teasers for his squad as he contends with the probable absence of four of his World Cup players through injury: John Stones, Dan Burn, Djed Spence and Jordan Henderson. Tino Livramento, Levi Colwill, Jarrad Branthwaite and Lewis Hall are pushing for recalls in defence.

Does Kobbie Mainoo keep his place in midfield after his washout of a World Cup? He has been good for Manchester United despite their poor start. Alex Scott and Myles Lewis-Skelly are hoping for recalls. As are Cole Palmer and Phil Foden in the No 10 positions. Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke have not restarted well at Arsenal. There is a lot of energy around Josh King and Ryo Ngumoha. Ditto Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Liam Delap.

All eyes will be on Tuchel at the announcement and his tone, as much as anything, will be instructive. Being overly defensive did not work out the last time.

Sports.title: Alessandro Costacurta: ‘San Siro is an icon – it’s incredibly beautiful but it’s not functional’
Sports.content:
Alessandro Costacurta lasted 15 minutes of his first game at San Siro. He was, admittedly, not playing, but tagging along to watch his older brother’s favourite team.

“I grew up in the province of Varese, north of Milan,” he says. “So as a kid I was a Varese fan. It was my brother who supported Milan. The first time I went to San Siro, I was 12, my brother was 14. I think it was Milan-Bologna. But San Siro wasn’t covered back then, and suddenly this downpour started, so much rain. We were with our dad and after a quarter of an hour he just said: ‘No, that’s it, we’ve got to go.’ So that was the first time I saw San Siro.”

But happily, far from the last. Costacurta was recruited into Milan’s academy a year later and played 663 times for their first team – helping them win Serie A seven times and the European Cup five, either side of its Champions League rebrand. Only his fellow defenders Paolo Maldini (902) and Franco Baresi (719) have made more appearances for the Rossoneri. Many of those were alongside him.

At one point, Costacurta refers to that Milan team as the “best in the world for 25 years”. He quickly corrects himself to “one of the best”. If he wanted to avoid boastfulness then let me say it for him: the back four he formed with Maldini, Baresi and Mauro Tassotti might be – for quality and longevity – the greatest ever.

View image in fullscreen Alessandro Costacurta (front row, second right) celebrates with his Milan teammates after they won the 1989 European Cup final. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

And they played in one of the planet’s most famous arenas. We are speaking in the days leading up to San Siro’s 100th birthday, an occasion that feels more profound for the knowledge it will not host football games much longer. Milan and Inter completed a joint-purchase of the stadium, and a surrounding parcel of land, from the city council at the end of 2025. They plan to begin construction of a new ground early next year.

A necessary step, for Costacurta. “San Siro is not a modern stadium,” he says. “It’s an icon, it’s incredibly beautiful, but it’s not functional.” He reels off a list of shortcomings, from a shortage of elevators to dated lounges. A mention of the stadium’s infamously grim toilets draws a sheepish grin. “That’s the first thing I wanted to say!”

It will be replaced by a multifunction venue designed by the architect firms Foster + Partners and Manica, with the area around the stadium being regenerated with new retail and hospitality facilities. The realisation of a new stadium has been a central pillar of the vision set out by Milan’s owners, RedBird, since its takeover in 2022.

The project is shared with their co-tenants at San Siro, Inter. There is something in that collaboration that reflects the nature of the rivalry – less bitter than we see between neighbours elsewhere.

“Milan is a particular thing,” says Costacurta. “It’s rare to breathe such friendly air when you go to different derbies around the world. There are chants of course, but also a lot of mixing between fans. And when I was playing, between players too.”

View image in fullscreen The camaraderie between the Milan teams was demonstrated in 2005 as Inter’s Marco Materazzi and Milan’s Rui Costa waited together for flares on the pitch to be cleared during their Champions League quarter-final second leg. Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/Reuters

Still, the games against Inter were the best ones to win – especially when your team was officially the “away” one. “When you’re playing in any great team, the biggest satisfaction of all is ‘conquering’ another great team’s home stadium. I remember a 6-0 when we were ‘away’ to Inter [in May 2001]. At 4-0 we could see their fans walking out.”

Construction is intended to be completed in 2031, ready to host games as well at Euro 2032. It will be a boon to Milan and Inter, providing revenue streams that can make them more competitive on a continental stage, at a time when Serie A – like every other league – has struggled to keep up with the Premier League’s earning power.

Even accepting all this, we can acknowledge the sadness of saying farewell to San Siro. Costacurta has visited Europe’s most famous grounds as a player and spectator. What makes San Siro unique, he says, is the steepness of the stands.

“Lots of stadiums are made this way,” he says, holding his hands at a shallow angle. “San Siro is like this.” Now he is pointing his fingers straight downward. “The first time I was out beside the pitch as a ballboy – which everyone does when you get to the youth team – it made me almost afraid. It felt like all those people were going to fall on top of me.”

View image in fullscreen Fans enjoy the atmosphere in the stadium during the Serie A match between Milan and Brescia at the San Siro in May 2004. Photograph: New Press/Getty Images

“Maybe [Real Madrid’s Santiago] Bernabéu is a bit like that. But still, like San Siro? I don’t think so. In Rome, they have a different way of making you feel close – that anthem they sing before kick-off at Roma is beautiful. But it’s different. At San Siro, when you’re up there at the top, it’s like you’re in a tower above the pitch, leaning out of the window.”

San Siro was opened on 19 September 1926, the realisation of the then Milan president Piero Pirelli’s vision for a football-specific stadium unlike anything in Italy at the time. There was no running track, only four stands with capacity for 35,000 spectators.

Pirelli was said to have taken inspiration from stadiums in England, but San Siro was also a product of its setting. Stables, hay barns and storage space were incorporated below the stands to serve the horse racing track next door.

View image in fullscreen The San Siro Stadium seen from the adjacent Hippodrome soon after it was built in 1926. Photograph: Touring Club Italiano/Universal Images Group/Getty Images

The stadium was bought by Milan’s city council in 1935 and expanded with connecting sections between stands. Inter joined Milan as co-tenants in 1947 before a second tier was added, opening in 1955. In 1980 the stadium was renamed for Giuseppe Meazza, the two-time World Cup-winning midfielder for Italy who played 14 seasons with Inter and two with Milan, though it has remained San Siro to most fans.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen A second tier was added to the stadium, opening in 1955. Photograph: Keystone/Getty Images

View image in fullscreen A view of the stadium exterior in the 1950s. Photograph: FC Internazionale Archive/FC Internazionale/Getty Images

Construction of the final third tier, with a roof at last to shield supporters from the rain, was completed before the 1990 World Cup. Costacurta played the first match after its opening, a 1-0 defeat in the return leg of Milan’s Coppa Italia final against Juventus.

“I remember there was more noise, but the main thing I remember is the pitch,” says Costacurta. “They hadn’t understood how to manage the airflow with the extra tier, and the pitch was really ugly. For a year and a half, our pitch was the worst in Europe.”

Clearly, they adapted. Milan went on a record-breaking 58-game unbeaten run in Serie A from May 1991 through to March 1993. Maybe that ugly pitch even became an asset?

“I think it was a disadvantage for visiting teams that came to San Siro,” says Costacurta. “And San Siro is a stadium that puts a lot of pressure on, there’s this incredible noise.”

He switches to the English word, “Roar!”, for emphasis. He’s not wrong. San Siro on a big occasion is astonishingly loud, to the point that you can find it hard to hear people speaking right next to you.

View image in fullscreen The construction of the final third tier was completed ahead of the Italia 90 World Cup. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

View image in fullscreen Dancers on the pitch during the 1990 World Cup opening ceremony. Photograph: Michael Kunkel/Bongarts/Getty Images

“Nobody’s really talking on the pitch though,” says Costacurta, who insists the real conversations take place on the training ground. Managers bawling from the touchline are engaged in a futile act. “They hope they can pass a message down the line but, trust me, the message almost never gets there.”

But fans have their ways of getting a message across. San Siro still had standing sections when Costacurta made his first-team debut in 1987. “People would be holding onto the railing beside the pitch, sticking their heads out, shouting, shouting, shouting.

“I was lucky because I came through the youth team, so I didn’t take the hardest insults. They said things to me in a Milanese dialect. Insults, but amusing ones. They called me “pè de ghisa”, which means iron foot, because I didn’t have an acceptable level of technical ability for a team like that yet. But my teammates who weren’t from the youth team got proper insults.”

He won them round in the end. Costacurta laughs at the memory of the “rubbish” chant fans made for him. “It was just ‘Billy! [his nickname] Billy! Vai! Vai! Vai!” [Billy! Billy! Go! Go! Go!] The worst chant of any player at Milan.” But on the day of his final game at San Siro, thousands waited outside the stadium to thank him.

View image in fullscreen Milan supporters display a banner paying tribute to Costacurta during his final match for the club in May 2007. Photograph: Luca Bruno/AP

View image in fullscreen Costacurta acknowledges the fans after his last match for the club. Photograph: Alessandro Garofalo/Reuters

Memories like that will always remain, even when San Siro joins him in retirement. Milan and Inter have said that some part of the old stadium will be preserved in the new development. Costacurta, who became a fan of Arsenal over the years too, admiring Arsène Wenger’s teams from affair, finds encouragement in their move away from Highbury, now converted into apartments.

“I played there in the European Super Cup,” he says. “Nil-nil. [Milan won 2-0 in the return leg at San Siro.] Great. Beautiful. Iconic. I think everyone suffered the change at first, but the Emirates is great now. So why not?”

Sports.title: Football Daily | Michael Carrick risks untimely spell in the ‘crisis’ box seat with Manchester United
Sports.content:
RINSE AND REPEAT?

Following the conclusion of this weekend’s round of Premier League fixtures, football fans have what promises to be an exceptionally long, uninspiring and largely inconsequential international break to endure. In most parts of the world, various nations have nothing more exciting than friendlies scheduled. In Europe, it’s the return of the Nations League. A competition apparently conceived for no other reason than to allow Cristiano Ronaldo to spuriously claim he has won two major international trophies, this Uefa wheeze is about to kick off for the fifth time. Almost unique among tournaments that have enjoyed such longevity, its format remains fairly baffling to many of those who will actually be playing in it and all but the keenest students of the game. In truth, hardly anyone cares about the Nations League and quite literally nobody gives two hoots about its opening games.

As is customary in the absence of anything more interesting to report on, hacks will be keeping their ears cupped towards the continent in the hope that some loose-lipped South American Premier League star cuts a promo about a perceived dissatisfaction with their lot. Otherwise, the first top-flight head coach whose club is deemed to be “in crisis” will be lined up in the collective media crosshairs and, as things stand, it is Michael Carrick who is in the box seat.

“Under pressure?” he replied to assorted reporters in the wake of Manchester United’s dismal capitulation after going 2-0 up against Brighton in the Milk Cup. “That doesn’t bother me one bit.” As words of defiance go, they may have sounded more convincing if they hadn’t been uttered by a man who appears to have aged 20 years across his first six games in proper charge, only two of which have been won. “I understand what goes on and how the world works,” he added with a sigh.

In recent years there has been a recurring rinse-and-repeat cycle as far as what goes on and how the world works at United. Specifically one involving the dismissal of head coaches following widespread media speculation regarding their abilities to paper over the giant chasms caused by boardroom penny-pinching, dismal player recruitment and ongoing fan dissatisfaction, for which somebody – anybody but the owners and their besuited yes-men – must carry the can. Whether it’s Ole, Erik, Ruben, or the new incumbent, the story only ever seems to end one way, and just six games into the new season, it already seems the die has been cast for the cycle to begin again. Outwitted by Fabian Hürzeler, while his players were torn apart out on the field, Carrick can’t be absolved of all blame for United’s many shortcomings on and off the field. Anything but a win in Sunday’s crisis klaxon derby at Fulham and his future, or lack of one at Old Trafford, will be a tedious but unavoidable talking point for what promise to be 16 already very long days.

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

Join Michael Butler from 7.30pm for hot Milk Cup minute-by-minute updates from Manchester City 3-1 Norwich, while Scott Murray will be your guide at 8pm for the night’s Bigger Vase action in his clockwatch, featuring Real Sociedad 1-1 Bournemouth, plus Crystal Palace 1-0 Lech Poznan.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“You can try to kill me here. But it’s my scar, it’s not your scar. No one is more hurt than me, no one wanted it more. They can endlessly torture you and think: ‘If I had done different substitutions, then we would have won the match.’ You just don’t know it” – Thomas Tuchel stands by his heavily criticised defensive regression during the Geopolitics World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina, adding that the opposition tactics forced his hand: “Sorry for the language, [they played eff]-it football: ‘We have nothing to lose. Let’s [eff] it.’”

View image in fullscreen Thomas Tuchel on the celebrity beat earlier this week. Photograph: Alberto Pezzali/AP

double quotation mark I met Ludek Miklosko once. In fact, shaking my hand was one of the first things he had to endure after signing for West Ham in the summer of 1990. (The history books say he signed earlier, but he wasn’t officially unveiled until the summer.) I was working in the club shop at Upton Park (a cabin by the gates). He seemed baffled that now he was finally here and had escaped the communist regime, he was being introduced to a child as ‘our new goalkeeper’. He was very nice about it, though; I showed him the new kit, and he went on to meet the groundsman and have a look at the pitch. My lasting memory was of his truly massive hands. Lovely fella” – Jimmy O’Brien.

double quotation mark I was struck by the phrase that Madrid’s Carlos Espí ‘dug his side out of a hole’ (yesterday’s Football Daily). Surely, one cannot dig oneself out of a hole? Digging, by definition, takes you further into the ground. Unless the goal was to arrive in China, climbing out of a hole would be more appropriate” – Christopher D’Cruz.

double quotation mark Amalgamating the themes of yesterday’s three letters, Spurs fans can at least be hopeful about one thing. Since a player who spends much of the time rolling around knacked near the corner flag can’t be interfering with play, then at least none of their forward line will be caught offside much this year” – Jon Millard.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Jimmy O’Brien. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: Real Madrid leading race to sign JJ Gabriel from Manchester United
Sports.content:
Real Madrid are leading the race to sign the Manchester United teenager JJ Gabriel after he told the Premier League club he wants to cancel his registration.

The 15-year-old has attracted interest from across Europe as his reputation has grown with academy performances. Barcelona have been keen to acquire him and Bayern Munich are known to admire the winger. It is understood Gabriel prefers a move to Europe and having an Irish passport would enable that.

Although surprised by Gabriel’s decision, some at United felt he might not sign a professional contract as other clubs circled. United, however, still feel they may be able to rectify the matter having developed him since he joined at 11. He would be eligible to sign as a scholar when he turns 16 next month and as a professional a year later.

A move to Real Madrid comes with the prospect of accelerated progression to senior football with their B team, Castilla, who play in the regionalised Spanish third tier.

Had Gabriel not informed United of his desire to leave, he would have been called up by Michael Carrick for the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton on Wednesday. If he had played he would have become the youngest player in the club’s history.

“I just think we’ve got to be really careful of the whole situation,” Carrick said of Gabriel after the defeat by Brighton. “He’s a young boy. He’s 15, and for me, definitely, and from a club point of view, looking after our younger players – their welfare, their wellbeing, their exposure – we’ve got to be really conscious of that in this situation.”

Gabriel featured in a pre-season friendly against Atlético Madrid in Stockholm and has regularly trained with the first-team recently.

Sports.title: Carlos Espí gives Real Madrid hope in the face of Barcelona’s La Liga storm | Sid Lowe
Sports.content:
José Mourinho called and Carlos Espí came to his side. It was late, it was noisy and it was almost over – the match and maybe even something more – when Real Madrid’s coach took the forward who is also his flatmate to one side on Tuesday night. Standing close, Mourinho had a message to deliver; he also had a piece of paper. Small, folded, half-hidden in his hand, it was not big enough for much more than a single word, shown almost surreptitiously, the request written on it, like what he had whispered in Espí’s ear, left to your imagination. Put ball in goal, perhaps. Or: Help. So he did.

Madrid needed him to, which they should not have. Two goals up inside half an hour at Elche on Tuesday night, they could have added a third or a fourth, maybe even a fifth, before half-time.
