But, thinking it was as done as it really should have been, their minds perhaps on Sunday’s derby at Atlético too, they had stopped again, drifting. Vinícius Júnior had gone, Arda Guler had gone, Aurélien Tchouaméni might as well have done, barely able to move any more, and now, somehow, the game was going. Goals from Abiel Osorio in the 71st minute and Fer Niño in the 83rd had made it 2-2.

View image in fullscreen Fer Niño scored the equaliser for Elche to make it 2-2 against Real Madrid in the 83rd minute. Photograph: Kai Forsterling/EPA

Antonio Rüdiger was parading the touchline, hands on his head, wearing a look that said: wait, what?! And, control long since lost, the ball not theirs, it could still get worse: somewhere in the notebook, amid all the arrows and the scrawls no one can make sense of, the last, barely decipherable scribble said: “88. Elche are going for the winner too!” All around the Martinez Valero a chant went round: Yes, we can! They had more possession and as many shots on target, had deserved to draw level and maybe even to lead after a second half they had dominated, and genuinely thought they could too. Which was of course their first mistake, the hope what killed them.

With crushing inevitability, the next note says something about Espí and just wide, the one after says 4’ and the one after that just ESPÍ. A step forward, the whole Elche line following to their inevitable demise, and there was the space. On as a substitute, rested to begin with, Jude Bellingham’s superb run and pass released Kylian Mbappé who laid off for Espí to score, staff and subs, dressed in pink, racing down the touchline. He had only gone and done it again. It had been 11.16pm, the 88th minute, when Mourinho slipped him that note; it was 11.21pm when he stood in the corner, pumping his fists. On the pitch four minutes, the 21-year-old who scored an injury-time winner on the opening weekend, had saved them.

Born in Tavernes, a little way up the east coast from Elche, his family waiting for him at the side of the pitch after the match on Tuesday night, no one had heard of Espí this time last year. By then the end of the year, there was a case to say that he was the single most important player in Spain last season but even then, even when Madrid paid his buyout clause, he wasn’t exactly famous. The day he scored against Espanyol in the first week of the season, his Wikipedia page was the most read in the whole country. One detail not on there is that he is a trained oboe player.

That night at Cornella he saved Madrid, like he had saved Levante. No one had an impact on a team like he had on them, scoring 11 goals in 25 games to rescue them for relegation. Maybe saving teams is just what he does. Big strong, a traditional No 9, who does not mind mixing it with centre-backs – Thibaut Courtois called him a “beast” for going into battle with Rüdiger in training. At Madrid, teammates have taken to calling him Joselu Junior. He has scored twice in 42 minutes, delivering four points already. No one at the club has a better ratio.

View image in fullscreen Kylian Mbappé assisted Carlos Espí’s winning goal. Photograph: Kai Forsterling/EPA

This was huge, not just about Tuesday night. Matchday six, a full round of midweek matches, has not finished yet. La Liga did the worst first – Real Sociedad and Celta played out a 0-0 draw two weeks ago – and left the best for last. Betis and Villarreal, the two teams Lamine Yamal says he likes watching the most – if only because he is usually too busy to be in front of the telly when Barcelona play – are both in action on Thursday. But plenty has already happened and something amazing did not: Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang did not score, for the first time. As for Levante and Athletic, they did not even play, although they did turn up and, amid the biblical storm and safety alerts, the league did not actually announce it was off until five minutes after it was due to start and long after the referee had taken one look at the knee-high lake at the end of the tunnel and declared it “reckless” to even get to the pitch, let alone play.

This was the week in which Rayo finally played the last of their unexpectedly successful but ultimately empty games in exile at Léganes, leaving the balance at Butarque: three matches, two wins, one draw, thousands of unoccupied seats and something (else) broken for ever. In which Atlético put four past Osasuna. In which Valencia, under new caretaker management, won for the first time and scored for just the second. And in which Sevilla – Sevilla! – went fourth, a third of the points needed for survival already secure and never to be taken from them. It was also the week in which Atlético scored four, and Barcelona scored seven.

Quick Guide La Liga matchday six results Show Real Sociedad 0-0 Celta (played on 3 September), Rayo 2-1 Espanyol, Alaves 0-1 Valencia, Elche 2-3 Real Madrid, Atlético 4-0 Osasuna, Deportivo 0-1 Sevilla, Barcelona 7-2 Racing. Thursday: Betis v Getafe, Malaga v Villarreal. Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

At the end of the match at the Camp Nou the thunder and lightning also came rolling in, if not quite as violently as at Levante, and delivered every headline writer’s dream – Barcelona are the storm, said AS, while El Mundo Deportivo went for “torrential football” – tragically, no one went for liquid football. The Racing Santander midfielder Sergio Canales described his opponents as “madness”. You do not even have to know about football to see it, he said, which is handy: “Barcelona have it all.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

On a night when they had João Cancelo scoring two belters, Karim Adeyemi channeling Pelé and Gabriel Jesus curling in a gorgeous first goal for the club. Barcelona gave Racing a chance, sending on Wojciech Szczesny, and still did not give them a chance. They scored seven and could have scored 17. Lamine Yamal only scored one; he also had one disallowed, hit the post, and missed a penalty.

They also have Raphinha. And while everyone goes on about Lamine Yamal and Mbappé and the Ballon d’Or and Hansi Flick goes on about how he will be happy when the bloody thing is over, Raphinha, who was not even nominated, quietly goes about showing that right now he is better than both of them – and anyone else in fact. The man who is just filling in at No 9 has 11 goals already this season, a start so good only two men have ever done it before: Lionel Messi and Brazil forward Ronaldo. With seven wins from seven competitive games, this is Barcelona’s best-ever start. They scored two against the man who in the summer conceded just one in eight World Cup games. In their other six matches they have scored: five, five, five, five, four and seven. They have won every league match.

View image in fullscreen Raphinha poses like Spider-Man to celebrate his hat-trick against Racing. Photograph: Joan Monfort/AP

Which is why Madrid needed Espí so badly on Tuesday night. Already defeated at Betis – where Espí came on and scored an outrageous volley that would have been the winner, only for it to be ruled out – Madrid faced the prospect of dropping points again. Still not entirely convincing, they had let another team back into the game – last weekend, Rayo too should have finished off but were suddenly alive. Madrid have “lost” three of the last four second halves – and, with two minutes left, faced the prospect of slipping five points behind Barcelona … with the derby to come this weekend. Of course, it would not have been over: there are still 32 weeks left and Billie Joe Armstrong’s mum hasn’t even sneaked into his room yet. But this is not a Barcelona team that looks likely to allow many second chances and five points would have been a significant gap even at this stage. But then Espí did it again.

After that win at Espanyol on the opening day, the first time their new striker saved them, Mourinho said that he and Espí lived together at the club’s Valdebebas training ground: the two of them, the coaching staff and Marc Cucurella, like the characters in some heartwarming sitcom, a bunch of flatmates thrown together and making it work somehow. “Espí’s a funny kid,” Mourinho said; he’s also one he can call on when you need him.

Sports.title: Raheem Sterling’s bleak tale a reminder of absurd path young footballers face | Jonathan Liew
Sports.content:
“What’s your name?”

“Raheem.”

“What’s your surname?”

“Sterling.”

This is how a story ends. At 9.13 on a glorious May morning, by the side of the A327, sitting in the passenger seat of a wrecked Lamborghini, feverishly stashing canisters of nitrous oxide into the back, having to recite one’s name from scratch. A police officer asks him who was driving the car at the time it smashed into a metal pole on a country road in Hampshire. Sterling says nothing. There’s nobody sitting in the driver’s seat.

As it transpired in court in Basingstoke this week, Sterling had been up driving all night by the time police started getting calls from members of the public concerned that someone was bobbing and weaving up the M3 in an unpredictable, uncontrollable manner. And of course there is an acrid and tasteless irony in the fact that this was exactly what Sterling was known for on the pitch: weaving in and out of traffic, no order or reason to it, following a logic that existed only in his own head.

We can, and we should, and the district judge did, take an extremely dim view of the serious and life-threatening crime to which Sterling has admitted. We can also acknowledge that football is the one and only reason any of this remotely registered on our radar. You are not angry at the other dangerous drivers, whose names you do not know and will never look up. You are angry at this one in particular, a £50m footballer four years ago, now facing the possibility of prison and a sporting career that may just have come to a hard stop at the age of 31.

View image in fullscreen ‘The end of Sterling as a going concern really happened much earlier, about the time his Arsenal loan deal ended.’ Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

Yep: younger than Kepa Arrizabalaga, younger than Solly March, younger than Ariana Grande. And let’s be real, the end of Sterling as a going concern really happened much earlier, about the time his Arsenal loan deal ended and Enzo Maresca made clear he had no further use for him at Chelsea and he was made to train on his own after 8pm despite having young children, and Maresca said this was no big deal, because people in the fishing industry also work hard hours.

In a way, Sterling became a victim of the cycle he helped to catalyse. At the age of 15, he became one of the first big-money academy transfers when he moved from Queens Park Rangers to Liverpool for a fee of up to £2m. More than a decade on, the increasing emphasis on one‑on‑one duels, on straight-line speed and dynamic dribbling, on unpredictable and unmapped movement, has generated a kind of fetish for unscarred teenage footballers, a self-perpetuating market in child labour that nobody has ever really begun to question, much less challenge.

The Premier League’s centre of gravity has been shifting younger for years, to the point where last season half its players were 25 or younger. The three youngest Premier League debuts (Jeremy Monga, Max Dowman, Ethan Nwaneri) have taken place since 2022. Farther afield players such as Lamine Yamal (La Liga debut at 15) and Cavan Sullivan (Major League Soccer debut at 14) have begun to normalise the trope of the child footballer, the athlete propelled to global superstardom before they can legally buy a vape.

This week it has been widely reported that JJ Gabriel, a talented and highly coveted 15-year-old attacking midfielder, has demanded to leave the Manchester United academy. Let’s assume for the sake of argument that Gabriel didn’t walk into the offices of the Daily Telegraph and plant this story himself. So what we really have here, in essence, is an entire locus of gossip – briefings, counter-briefings, whispers, internet spume, back-page splashes – centred on a child.

View image in fullscreen It has been widely reported that JJ Gabriel has demanded to leave Manchester United. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

And before we even get into the myriad safeguarding issues, it’s worth reflecting on the financial incentives involved here. As scouting networks broaden and deepen, as clubs increasingly remodel themselves as trading vehicles, the premium on exclusive young talent has become unignorable. Should Gabriel leave United he will undoubtedly have his pick of Europe’s top clubs.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Players and their representatives have also begun to recognise their rarefied value in this market. In a previous era Michael Carrick might have had the luxury of integrating Gabriel gradually into the United first team, taking a long-term view of his development, much as Mikel Arteta has done with Dowman at Arsenal. But of course if Lamine Yamal is playing first-team football at 15, then why not JJ Gabriel? If every big club in Europe is looking for the next big star, then who ultimately holds the power in this relationship: the kid or one of the biggest football clubs in the world?

And this is absurd, and it is intentionally absurd, and it is no defence of Sterling’s subsequent actions to point out that this is basically a ridiculous path upon which to dispatch a human being: festooned with unimaginable riches as a teenager, placed at the very centre of things, cast on to the scrap heap by 29. This is an unbelievably weird life, one that starts so wildly and violently beyond the boundaries of normative society that it’s a wonder anyone manages to stay remotely sane within it.

The life-changing money, the scrutiny, the lack of privacy, the intermediaries and handlers, the winnowing of trust, the noise beyond the windows, the strangers demanding a piece of you, at a time when – remember – you are still a child and this entire lifestyle has been sold to you as the ultimate aspiration. Remember, you’re supporting the whole family now. Gabriel’s original surname, taken from his father and agent, was reportedly changed from O’Cearuill to Gabriel because it was easier to pronounce and therefore more marketable.

I guess the point here is that nobody has as much agency over their career as they might like. The young modern footballer exists at the mercy of forces barely within their control. Their job is contingent on so many others: the coaches who train their skills, the medical staff who manage their workload, the teammates who pass to them, the support network that might just dissuade them from getting into a car with a load of nitrous oxide balloons in the early hours of the morning.

And by any measure, Sterling is one of the lucky ones. The teenager who made it, who scaled the peaks, won 82 international caps, four league titles, worked under one of the greatest managers of all time, who tasted the manna even if it eventually choked him. How many other thousands of lives you will never see have been fruitlessly and callously bent and twisted towards this world: skills you will never witness, names you will never hear? How much humanity are we prepared to fling into this machine in order for it to provide us with entertainment?

Perhaps in the post-Ronaldo/Messi era we are beginning to shake the idea that great individual players can bend the arc of history to their will, a fallacy we may as well call the Ballon d’Or Industrial Complex. Injuries, circumstance, tactical trends, physical shifts, the inevitability of time and tide: these are the handmaidens of talent, its trade winds, its lucky charms. Gaze at any footballing prodigy from afar and you’ll see a seductive blur of gift and privilege. But look closely enough and you’ll notice that the driver’s seat is empty.

Sports.title: Rancour, road trips and revival: tale of battle for Brighton’s future hits the stage
Sports.content:
It was the tip-off that changed Ian Hart’s life for ever. The funeral director from Worthing was co-editor of the Brighton fanzine Gull’s Eye when he received a phone call from Gordon Lucking, a Crystal Palace director, in July 1995.

“Gordon always wanted to join the Brighton board, but they didn’t want him there,” Hart says. “Ron Noades [the Palace chair] welcomed him with open arms. One of his [Lucking’s] employees had been on this golf day and someone got pissed in the evening and said: ‘You’ll never guess what’s happened – Brighton have sold the Goldstone Ground and are moving to Portsmouth.’ Gordon loved it, because it was another nail in Brighton’s coffin.”

Hart initially struggled to believe that Brighton’s home since 1902 could be in danger, but decided to confront the chief executive, David Bellotti, at his office. “I parked the hearse outside, went in and asked him straight whether they had sold the ground and were moving to Portsmouth,” Hart writes in his book, Brighton & Hove Albion: From Every Angle, which was released last year. “All the colour drained from his face.”

View image in fullscreen Ian Hart is the producer of Stand or Fall, which will be performed at Brighton’s Theatre Royal from 23-26 September. Photograph: James Boardman

The subsequent battle between the supporters and owners was the start of a nomadic period in Brighton’s history that will be revisited this month in a new play to coincide with the club’s 125th anniversary. Stand or Fall, written by the Brighton fan Mark Brailsford, follows a group of fans from the last days at the Goldstone in 1997, their exile 70 miles away in Gillingham and then at the Withdean Stadium in Brighton before the club find a new home at the Amex Stadium.

Hart is a producer for the play that will run for four nights from 23 September at the city’s Theatre Royal. An exhibition, also entitled Stand or Fall, detailing what he describes as the club’s civil war, opened at the Brighton Museum in August and continues until the end of the year.

View image in fullscreen In February 1997, thousands of supporters from clubs across the UK and Europe converged on Brighton’s Goldstone Ground for Fans United day to show their solidarity. Photograph: Andrew Hasson/Alamy

“We were all thrown together, all different demographics: a funeral director, a punk performance poet, a chartered accountant, plasterers and labourers,” Hart says of the action group that included the punk poet John Baine, better known as Attila the Stockbroker.

“A few days after everyone found out the Goldstone Ground was being sold, we had a fans’ meeting at [the pub] Chapman’s, which is now the Railway, in Worthing. There were probably 40 or 50 people from all walks of life and it grew from there.

“A year later, there were 500 people who couldn’t get inside listening on loudspeakers outside the Concorde [nightclub] when things were getting really serious.”

View image in fullscreen Brighton fans dig up the turf to take as a souvenir after Brighton’s last game at the Goldstone Ground. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

In April 1996, 600 spectators ran on to the Goldstone Ground pitch after a win against Carlisle, calling for Bellotti’s resignation. Some fans tore up seats in the directors’ box as attempts were made to storm the boardroom. Then came the meeting with York that has gone down in Brighton folklore, as fans waited until the 16th minute to invade the pitch, causing the game to be abandoned.

“It was not a riot, it was a legitimate protest,” Hart says. “The FA and the Football League were a bit like Neville Chamberlain at Munich, waving a piece of paper saying everything was going to be fine. They thought they could give us a load of bullshit and we would just take it.”

View image in fullscreen Fans leave the Goldstone Ground for the last time. Photograph: Paul Popper/Popperfoto/Getty Images

The Goldstone Ground was demolished a year later after Brighton came within 27 minutes of relegation from the Football League, only to be saved by Robbie Reinelt’s equaliser against Hereford. At one stage they had been 13 points adrift at the bottom of Division Three (now League Two). Brighton finished 91st in the Football League again the following year, playing home games in Gillingham after Portsmouth reneged on their offer to groundshare.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“We lost a generation of fans, which we’ve got back now, but for years you used to be driving past parks in Worthing seeing football teams training on a Saturday morning with kits and no Brighton shirts. It was horrible,” Hart says. “I was a coach at Worthing United from under-six to under-16 and I banned anybody not wearing a Brighton or Worthing shirt.”

View image in fullscreen From 1999 to 2011 Brighton played at Withdean Stadium, which had a capacity of 8,850. Photograph: Andrew Cowie/Shutterstock

Dick Knight became chair of Brighton in 1997 via a supporter‑led consortium and steadied the ship as they moved back to the city, albeit at the Withdean, primarily an athletics stadium. It was when Tony Bloom took over as chair in 2009 that Brighton really began to take flight, moving into the Amex Stadium two years later before being promoted to the Premier League in 2017.

The club reached the last 16 of the Europa League in their first European campaign in 2024 and will compete in the Conference League this season. Hart is hoping they could complete the quest for a major trophy.

View image in fullscreen In 2011, the Seagulls moved to the 22,500-capacity Amex Stadium, which opened with a friendly against Tottenham. Photograph: Simon Dack/Alamy

“It would be brilliant and Tony did promise us a trophy at the 1983 [FA Cup final] reunion dinner a few years ago,” he says. “We were having a drink with him in Tromsø [before the Conference League playoff in Norway last month] and as much as he promised us a trophy I don’t want to get weighed down by expectation.

“The great thing about the play is that there are highs and lows, but you can’t really celebrate the highs unless you have the lows. It makes the whole story even more incredible.”

Sports.title: ‘It is for every fan who has ever followed us’: Bournemouth’s European debut caps journey from the brink
Sports.content:
It is 13 years since Bournemouth, a couple of months after finishing runners-up to Doncaster in the third tier, hosted Real Madrid. It was a balmy summer’s day, officially Carlo Ancelotti’s first match in charge, and, a few hours after checking into the Haven hotel on the Sandbanks peninsula, a wave of galácticos took to the pitch: Cristiano Ronaldo, Luka Modric, Kaká, Karim Benzema, the list goes on.

An early, wayward Ronaldo free-kick broke the wrist of an 11-year‑old boy before Madrid ran out 6-0 winners in a bucket-list friendly.

“I retired a month earlier, and I thought: ‘Yeah, that’s typical, isn’t it?’” says Steve Fletcher, a bona fide Bournemouth legend and now club ambassador who scored 121 goals across 728 appearances, a smile unravelling on his face. “You play for a club for 20 years, and then you go and get the biggest team in the world to come down. I wanted to say to Eddie Howe: ‘Can I have five minutes on the pitch?’ For them to play here was utterly ridiculous.”

It was one of the stranger days in Bournemouth’s recent history and on Thursday they will take another step when they face Real Sociedad in their first competitive game against European opposition. On the final day of last season, Bournemouth’s staff and players celebrated qualifying for the Europa League by gathering around a “Rayanair” flag depicting their Brazil forward piloting a plane, giddy supporters providing the perfect backdrop for the pictures, and those fans have since booked trips to Prague, Oslo and Vigo.

Perhaps it was fate that Andoni Iraola, who grew up in the Basque Country, would guide Bournemouth to San Sebastián. “It is going to be a momentous occasion, an I-was-there moment,” Fletcher says. He has exchanged messages this week with Iraola, who sent best wishes, including for a win.

The scale of the achievement is not lost on Fletcher. Iraola, who will return to Bournemouth with Liverpool on Sunday – with his assistants Tommy Elphick and Shaun Cooper, both of whom also played for the club in the third tier – was the mastermind. “I always say to people around Bournemouth: ‘Don’t ever take this for granted,’” Fletcher says.

“It is for every supporter who has ever followed Bournemouth: past, present, for the people who passed away, grandparents, great‑grandparents. I think everyone will feel very emotional on Thursday.”

View image in fullscreen Bournemouth reveal their ‘Rayanair’ banner after qualifying for the Europa League. Photograph: Robin Jones/AFC Bournemouth/Getty Images

La Real are playing in Europe for the sixth time in seven seasons but for Bournemouth, coached by Marco Rose, this is new ground. It was not unplanned, though. At the end of 2023, when Bournemouth were 14th in the Premier League, their bullish American billionaire owner, Bill Foley, predicted they would play in Europe within five years. Foley’s motto “Always Advance, Never Retreat” adorns a wall in the boardroom.

“He created the Golden Knights, the ice hockey team in Las Vegas, and they won the Stanley Cup within six seasons,” Fletcher says. “He has obviously got a crystal ball, he can see things and believes in people … I always think there should be a movie made about this time at AFC Bournemouth.”

View image in fullscreen Young fans waiting to catch a glimpse of the star-studded Real Madrid team in 2013. Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The Guardian

Fletcher was influential in Bournemouth making it this far. His winning goal at home against Grimsby on the penultimate day of the 2008-09 season ensured Bournemouth would not fall into non-league, the club having begun the season on -17 points after failing to exit administration. He subsequently worked in the recruitment department, as first‑team coach to Howe, Gary O’Neil and Scott Parker and then as a player liaison officer. “I’ve still got kit man and groundsman to go,” he says, laughing.

Adam Smith, the 35-year-old Bournemouth captain into his 15th season at the club, including a loan in League One in 2010-11, remembers the days of training at Canford school, round the corner from the state-of-the-art facility they moved into 18 months ago. Did Europe feel plausible when he signed from Tottenham as a teenager? “I would never have believed you; I’d just think it’s bonkers,” Smith says.

Quick Guide Benfica dispatch Amorim's Milan Show Ruben Amorim’s Milan were beaten 2-0 by Marco Silva’s Benfica in the Europa League. Dodi Lukebakio put the Portuguese side ahead at San Siro in the 16th minute and Jakub Kaminski added a second early in the second half. Bayer Leverkusen, finalists in 2024, began their Europa League campaign with a 2-0 win against the Slovenian champions Celje while Lyon were 2-1 winners at Anderlecht. The Cypriot champions Omonia Nicosia stunned the La Liga side Celta Vigo 1-0 while Rangers’ conquerors Jagiellonia Bialystok were denied a point at the Greek giants Olympiacos by Roman Yaremchuk’s late winner. Sparta Prague thrashed Ararat-Armenia 4-1 while Sturm Graz against Rennes and Hapoel Be’er Sheva versus Dinamo Zagreb both ended goalless. Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Fletcher references Neil Vacher, the former club secretary and current club historian who grew up as a supporter in the 1960s. “Would he have dreamed that we could even be in the top flight, never mind playing in Europe?”

Bournemouth have been in the top flight for all but two seasons since their promotion in 2015, but Europe hits differently. Most of the squad watched the August draw in the canteen and until this season David Brooks was used to midweek European matches meaning a night on the sofa.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

He watched his Wales teammate Brennan Johnson lift the Europa League and Conference League in successive seasons with Tottenham and Crystal Palace respectively, and another, Neco Williams, excel in the Europa League for Nottingham Forest.

View image in fullscreen Bournemouth’s Steve Fletcher (left) and Burton’s Shaun Kelly battle for the ball in a League Two match in 2010. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

“I was delighted for them, but for selfish reasons you want to be involved in teams like that, competing in Europe,” he says. “Everyone’s raring to go and wanting to showcase their talents, and hopefully we can go far. We always cause the big teams in the Premier League problems and I don’t think it should be any different in Europe. The club’s journey has been well documented and to finish it off with a European trophy would be really nice.”

The Madrid game coincided with Bournemouth opening a stand named after Ted MacDougall, another much-loved striker. At the time the pressure was on to ensure the stadium was ready for the landmark fixture, and if that sounds familiar then that is because this summer Bournemouth had to upgrade their ground to meet Uefa regulations. Their first home game is against Sturm Graz next month; the week after, Milan – whose red-and-black stripes inspired Bournemouth’s kit at the start of the 70s – come to town. “Just to mutter the words Milan, AC Milan, in the same sentence as AFC Bournemouth, in a competitive fixture, is crazy,” Fletcher says. “I think of Maldini, Baresi, Van Basten, Gullit.”

The stand at the other end of the ground has been named after Fletcher since 2010. Viktoria Plzen and Hapoel Be’er Sheva will visit in December and January. “A lot of people might come to Bournemouth and go: ‘Who is Steve Fletcher?’ Because I’m not one of the great footballers, but I’m very proud of the career I had,” the 54-year-old says.

View image in fullscreen More than 11,000 crammed into Dean Court in 2013 to watch Cristiano Ronaldo and co at Bournemouth. Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen Bournemouth hosted Madrid on a balmy afternoon in 2013. Thirteen years later they are embarking on their first European campaign. Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The Guardian

“I’ve had Premier League managers before games, an hour and a half before kick-off, look over and say: ‘That’s your stand, very well done.’ People like José Mourinho and Pep Guardiola said that and when I walked away I got straight on the phone to my parents and said: ‘You won’t believe what’s just happened.’”

There will probably be a pervading sense of disbelief among the Bournemouth supporters in San Sebastián and those tuning in from home on Thursday. “There will probably be people coming to our European games in their 80s and 90s who will have watched the club from year dot,” Fletcher says. “For us to be mixing it with some of the giants of European football is magical.

“It’s beyond anybody’s wildest dreams, and we still have to pinch ourselves. But at the same time, we have to enjoy it, embrace it. I hope there’s many more happy times to come. To think we’re playing someone like Milan in a competitive game is incredible. Wouldn’t it be amazing if in the next few years we could play Real Madrid?”

Sports.title: Wigan announce sudden death of goalkeeping coach Kevin Miller as tributes paid
Sports.content:
Wigan Athletic have been rocked by the sudden and unexpected passing of goalkeeper coach Kevin Miller.

Miller only linked up with the Latics over the summer to reunite with former Exeter City boss Gary Caldwell having stepped down as goalkeeper coach for the Grecians in June.

"Everyone at Wigan Athletic is deeply saddened and devastated to learn about the sudden passing of Goalkeeping Coach Kevin Miller," a statement read on Wigan's official website.

"Kevin joined the Club earlier this summer, linking up with Gary Caldwell, a close friend and colleague, and the wider First-Team staff after more than three years as Goalkeeping Coach at Exeter City and an impressive playing career that spanned over 18 years.

"Although Kevin’s time with Latics was far too short, he quickly became a much-loved and respected member of our First-Team staff. His experience, professionalism and passion for goalkeeping were clear for all to see, while his uplifting personality made a lasting impression on everyone who had the privilege of working alongside him.

"In a playing career of almost two decades, Kevin made more than 700 career appearances, including in the Premier League. He began his professional career with Exeter City, helping the Club to the Fourth Division title, before going on to represent Birmingham City, Watford, Crystal Palace, Barnsley, Bristol Rovers, Derby, Southampton and Torquay.

"Following an impressive career, Kevin moved into coaching and management, eventually returning to St James Park as Goalkeeping Coach in 2022, where he was able to pass on the considerable knowledge and experience he had gained throughout his career to the next generation of goalkeepers.

"Kevin’s contribution to football was significant, but for those who worked alongside him, it was the person he was that will be remembered most. Kevin was a husband, father, hugely respected colleague, dedicated coach and someone who made a genuine impact on those around him, both on and off the pitch.

"His sudden passing has left everyone at the Club deeply saddened and devastated.

"Our thoughts and prayers are with Kevin’s wife, Fiona, daughter, Esme, close family, friends, colleagues and all who knew and loved him.

"The Club asks for total privacy for Kevin’s family and friends at this difficult time.

"Everyone at Wigan Athletic sends its deepest condolences to Kevin’s loved ones."

1 Miller only joined Wigan as a goalkeeper coach in the summer Credit: Getty

Exeter City's statement

Exeter also paid tribute to the 57-year-old, stating: "Kevin was an incredibly popular figure during his time at St James Park, earning a place in the hearts of supporters with his performances between the posts and his wholehearted commitment to the club.

"At just 57, his passing is a huge loss to his family, friends and everyone who knew him. Exeter City Football Club sends its deepest condolences to Kevin's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time. Our thoughts are also with Gary Caldwell and our former staff at Wigan Athletic.

"The club will be supporting those who were close to Kevin and will be commemorating Kevin’s time with us and his memory in an appropriate way.

"Once a Grecian, always a Grecian."

Teams and individuals pay respects

A number of teams and individuals took to social media to pay their respects to the former Exeter shotstopper.

"Wigan Warriors would like to share our condolences following the sad news of the passing of goalkeeper Coach Kevin Miller," the official Wigan Warriors account posted.

"Our thoughts are with those at Wigan Athletic, Kevin's family, friends and colleagues at this sad time."

Former side Barnsley FC, meanwhile, wrote: "Our thoughts are with everyone at Wigan Athletic and Kevin's family. Tragic news. Once a Red, Always a Red."

Former Alan Tonge, who played for Exeter before retiring at 24, posted: "RIP Big Kev. Devastated."

Sports.title: Brentford vs Chelsea LIVE commentary: Joao Pedro and two Blues stars in doubt for Friday night clash
Sports.content:
Brentford vs Chelsea LIVE commentary: Joao Pedro and two Blues stars in doubt for Friday night clash

Premier League Gameweek 5 kicks off with a West London derby as Chelsea face Brentford on Friday night.

The Blues are looking to bounce back against the Bees following two disappointing results against Hull and Arsenal.



3 Joao Pedro has been crucial for Chelsea so far, and saved them a point last time out against Hull Credit: Getty

Meanwhile, Brentford are unbeaten across six matches in all competitions this season - winning three and drawing three.

Keith Andrews' side are seventh in the Premier League table on six points, and they will now be looking for their second league win of the campaign in their final fixture ahead of the international break.

Additionally, Xabi Alonso faces a significant injury criss after three key first-team players were absent from training, including starman Joao Pedro.



The Brazilian forward missed a majority of Tuesday's training at Cobham.

The 24-year-old has been a standout Chelsea player during this season, registering three goals and three assists in only five appearances.



Additionally, Alonso faces an even bigger injury crisis as captain Reece James and midfielder Moises Caicedo were also missing from the main group.

However, Tuesday's training session did see summer recruits Marco Palestra and Jordan Henderson participate after waiting to make their long-awaited debuts.



How to follow Brentford v Chelsea

The fixture will be played on Friday, September 18.

It is scheduled to kick off at the Gtech Stadium at 8pm.

talkSPORT will have live commentary of the match to open up the weekend of Premier League action.

3 Andrews has enjoyed a fantastic start to the season, including a 3-0 win against Spurs Credit: Getty

Coverage will start at 7pm with Hugh Woozencroft before commentary will be from Joe Shennan and former Arsenal defender Martin Keown.

Listen talkSPORT through the website or find us on DAB digital radio through your smart speaker and on 1089 or 1053 AM.



Download and listen to all our live commentaries via the talkSPORT app, whilst talkSPORT is also available to watch on Samsung TV Plus.

Subscribe to the talkSPORT YouTube channel for news, views and analysis plus our regular goals show and for more, 

For the latest odds and bet boosts for every big event, visit talkSPORT BET.

talkSPORT.com will also have all the action in our dedicated Premier League blog.



The match will be broadcast live on Sky Sports Main Event and Sky Sports Premier League from 7pm.

3 James' injuries have also raised concerns whether he has a future at right-back for Chelsea Credit: Getty

Brentford v Chelsea: Recent head-to-head record Chelsea 2-0 Brentford - January 2026 - Premier League Brentford 2-2 Chelsea - September 2025 - Premier League Brentford 0-0 Chelsea - April 2025 - Premier League Chelsea 2-1 Brentford - December 2025 - Premier League Brentford 2-2 Chelsea - March 2024 - Premier League

Brentford v Chelsea: Team news

Brentford will be without the services of Joshua Dasilva, Antoni Milambo, Nathan Collins, Sepp van den Berg, and Kafe Furo for the derby.

Additionally, Mathias Jensen is a doubt for the Premier League clash and Igor Thiago will be aiming to score his first goal of the campaign.



As for Chelsea, Pedro, Caicedo, and James both missed training on Tuesday, yet there's been no suggestion of an injury.

On the other hand, Palmer and Rogers have been in excellent form this season and will be certain starters for the fixture.

Brentford v Chelsea: What's been said?

Following Pedro pulling out of the Brazil squad, Alonso said on Thursday: "In terms of injuries and the squad, we are having the last training session tomorrow so no one is ruled out for us for Friday.

"I prefer to be cautious. We will take the final decision on every player.



He added: "He's [Moises] getting closer and tomorrow we will make the final decision.

"Moi is one of the top midfielders in the world. Any team with Moi in the middle is a better team - and we are aware of that.

"We will see tomorrow, he has not been able to play and we've had to cope with that situation."

On James, he said: "No, it was just a decision for Tuesday. Tomorrow, we will decide."

Sports.title: Gary Neville points finger at JJ Gabriel’s representatives for ‘nuclear option’ at Man United
Sports.content:
Gary Neville has criticised JJ Gabriel's representatives for the way they have handled the teenager's demands to leave Manchester United.

talkSPORT understands that the talented teenager has asked to leave the Manchester giants, with La Liga powerhouse Real Madrid reportedly interested in the 15-year-old.

3 Man United were stunned by Gabriel's demands to leave the club Credit: Getty

The news came as a shock to United, who were looking to hand Gabriel his senior debut in Wednesday's 3-2 EFL Cup defeat to Brighton & Hove Albion, just five days after scoring a hat-trick on his UEFA Youth League debut.

Gabriel has reportedly sent in formal notice to cancel his registration at the club in order to become a free agent.

United are desperate to retain the services of a player who club legend Ryan Giggs recently dubbed a 'generational talent'.

Giggs came through the United ranks and cemented his place as a club icon, but only after they poached the Welshman from rivals Manchester City.

The Premier League side are wary about letting Gabriel depart for pastures new and seeing him develop into a world class star elsewhere, just as Giggs did.

What did Neville say?

Neville has since lambasted Gabriel's representatives for the way they have acted as the teen pushes to leave United.

"There was this big announcement from a prominent journalist that's obviously been leaked," Neville began on the latest episode of Stick to Football.

"If the club's not going to leak that, it's not in the club's interest to leak this, not on the back of the weekend.

"So, the players representatives have definitely leaked this.

3 Neville has criticised Gabriel's representatives for taking the 'nuclear option' Credit: Getty

"They've decided they want to go the nuclear option and go: 'Bang, we're JJ Gabriel to leave Man United'.

"That to me is my concern is that who's representing him thinks that's good for the kid."

Keane echoed Neville's sentiments, adding: "Are you telling me he can’t wait? If you are 15 years of age and you’re talking about playing for Man United’s first team, just wait. Can you wait another six weeks if United get through the cup?

"Carrick’s under pressure. Obviously, [Sir Alex] Ferguson would throw young lads into the first team. But United, they need wins [right now].

"I don’t think United are in a position where they go: ‘We can write off a cup game tonight and play a couple of young lads'.

"'We need to get momentum into the season. If some 15-year-old is spitting his dummy out, we’ll deal with that.’"

Neville uses Dowman example

Neville went on to outline how Arsenal's protection of Max Dowman should be used as an example on how to handle the Gabriel situation.

"I just don’t see the logic from any representatives of a 15-year-old boy who think it’s a good idea to put his name in lights right now," he continued.

3 16-year-old Dowman has already made a handful of first-team appearances for Arsenal Credit: Getty

"You want to try and sort of douse the flames, don’t you? You don’t want to add fuel to a fire.

"Max Dowman, if you remember last year when he came on, you know, Sky probably asked for an interview at the end of the game.

"Arsenal said no. They got him straight back into the changing room. He’s back at school on the Monday morning."

Sports.title: Premier League club given green light to increase stadium capacity by 22,000 seats in £550m project
Sports.content:
Premier League club given green light to increase stadium capacity by 22,000 seats in £550m project

Nottingham Forest have been granted planning permission to increase the capacity of the City Ground to 52,500.

The club are set to redevelop three of their four stands in a project which is expected to cost £550million.

3 Forest have had plans approved to expand the City Ground to 52,500 seats Credit: KSS/Nottingham Forest

It will see the stadium become the sixth-largest in the Premier League.

Forest first unveiled their plans back in 2019, which would have initially seen the capacity raised to 38,000.

Under those proposals, the club were set to demolish and rebuild the Peter Taylor Stand.

Despite receiving the green light for those plans, Forest expanded their proposal in January.

Both the Trent End and Brian Clough Stand will also now be redeveloped in a two-stage project.

Forest granted planning permission

It comes after planning permission was approved by Rushcliffe Borough Council.

Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis is understood to be keen for the City Ground to comply with Champions League standards once the expansion is completed.

Meanwhile, both the Peter Taylor Stand and Trent End are hoped to remain operational in some capacity throughout the work.

Following the approval of the plans, council leader Cllr Neil Clarke said: "Given the significance of these latest applications I am very pleased the Planning Committee, through its independent process, saw it fit to grant permission to assist the club with its plans.

"I am very pleased that the applications have now been passed and we look forward to working with the club further as they progress."

3 A £550million redevelopment project can now get underway at the City Ground Credit: Getty

Forest have played home matches at the City Ground since it opened in 1898.

However, the stadium has not been expanded since 1996, when the Trent End was expanded ahead of that summer's Euros.

What are Forest's stadium plans?

The club now plan to raise the capacity of the City Ground from 31,212 to 52,500 once the work is completed.

Their project is set to be split across two phases of redevelopment.

As part of the first stage, the capacity will initially be raised to 45,000 seats.

This will see the Peter Taylor Stand tripled in size from a 5,000 capacity to 15,000.

3 The City Ground currently holds 31,212 fans and was last expanded in 1996 Credit: Getty

An additional 5,000 seats will also be added by filling in the corners on each side of the Trent End.

The second phase will then see the Brian Clough Stand expanded by 7,500 seats to take the total capacity to 52,500.

It comes as Forest compete in their fifth successive Premier League season.

The club's current spell in the top-flight is their longest sustained stay for 33 years.

An expanded City Ground was included on a list of 22 proposed venues to host the 2035 Women's World Cup in November.

England will co-host the tournament alongside Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

Sports.title: Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso gives cryptic update on Joao Pedro injury
Sports.content:
Xabi Alonso was tight-lipped on whether Joao Pedro will be involved Chelsea's upcoming Premier League meeting with Brentford.

The Brazilian played the full 90 minutes of the Blues' recent 2-2 draw with Hull City, scoring one and assisting another to maintain his superb start to the season.

2 Pedro has made a flying start to the 2026/27 Premier League season

Pedro has now been directly involved in six goals in the opening four league games of the season, scoring three times.

And his good form at club level didn't go unnoticed after he was named in the Brazil squad for the upcoming friendly double-header with Australia and next month's game against India.

Pedro withdrawn from Brazil squad

However, the Brazilian FA recently announced that Pedro will miss the international meetings with the Socceroos and the Blue Tigers due to injury, with Fluminense midfielder Matheus Martinelli called up as his replacement.

"Fluminense athlete Martinelli was called up on Wednesday, September 16, by coach Carlo Ancelotti for the Brazil National Team's friendlies against Australia and India in the upcoming FIFA international window," a statement read

"The player will replace Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who is injured."

But Alonso refused to definitively rule Pedro out of Friday's West London Derby at the Gtech Community Stadium.

What did Alonso say on Pedro?

Speaking to the press on Thursday afternoon, the Chelsea boss was asked about Pedro, to which he replied: "In terms of injuries and the squad, we are having the last training session tomorrow so no one is ruled out for us for Friday.

"I prefer to be cautious. We will take the final decision on every player."

Chelsea team news

Moises Caicedo has been a big miss for Chelsea having been absent from their last three squads.

Alonso revealed he could be involved for the clash against Brentford.

2 Alonso spoke to the media on Thursday Credit: Getty

The Blues boss said: "He's getting closer and tomorrow we will make the final decision."

He later added: "Moi is one of the top midfielders in the world. Any team with Moi in the middle is a better team - and we are aware of that.

"We will see tomorrow, he has not been able to play and we've had to cope with that situation."

Reece James also missed training earlier this week amid further injury fears for the Chelsea captain.

Alonso was also coy on what the current status of the defender is.

He added: "No, it was just a decision for Tuesday. Tomorrow, we will decide."

Sports.title: England World Cup star ruled out of Nations League games as club confirm injury blow
Sports.content:
England World Cup star ruled out of Nations League games as club confirm injury blow

John Stones has been ruled out of England's upcoming Nations League matches.

The Inter Milan defender has suffered a thigh injury, his club have confirmed.

3 Stones has been ruled out of England's upcoming Nations League matches through injury Credit: Getty

Stones is set to be sidelined for a minimum of three-and-a-half weeks after straining a muscle in his left thigh.

However, Inter fear he could be out for up to a month, missing their next four matches in all competitions.

Stones ruled out

At best, the 32-year-old will not return to action until after the upcoming international break.

It follows tests on the issue, which Stones picked up in Monday's 5-3 win over Udinese.

The 32-year-old joined Inter on a two-year deal in July following his Manchester City exit.

Stones has since made four appearances for the Serie A giants, with the clash with Udinese representing his first start.

He was forced off in the 62nd minute, though, after picking up the injury.

Thomas Tuchel is set to name his first England squad since the World Cup on Friday.

The Three Lions return to action against Spain at Wembley Stadium on September 26.

They then travel to take on the Czech Republic and Croatia as part of their Nations League campaign.

3 Stones is set to be sidelined for up to a month following tests, Inter have confirmed Credit: Getty

England conclude the international break on October 6 at home to the Czech Republic.

Those matches will be followed by a visit from Croatia and a trip to Spain in November.

The World Cup semi-finalists will then begin their qualification campaign for Euro 2028 next year.

England selection headache

Tuchel now faces a potential defensive headache in the absence of Stones.

The former City man featured five times at the World Cup as England finished third in North America.

As well as starting their opener against Croatia, Stones played every minute of both the quarter-final and semi-final matches.

3 Tuchel faces a defensive headache ahead of naming his England squad on Friday Credit: Getty

Of the players in Tuchel's World Cup squad, only Harry Kane had more caps than Stones' 94.

The centre-back has been a member of the Three Lions' selections for the last six major tournaments.

Sports.title: Unai Emery makes worrying Alejandro Garnacho admission after failing to play in third straight Aston Villa game
Sports.content:
Unai Emery makes worrying Alejandro Garnacho admission after failing to play in third straight Aston Villa game

Unai Emery admitted Alejandro Garnacho is behind his teammates in the Aston Villa pecking order.

The Argentina international was left as an unused substitute during Villa's 3-1 victory over Coventry City in the Carabao Cup.

3 Emery is the most recent manager to try and bring out the full potential of Garnacho Credit: Getty

Despite Emery making seven changes to the Villans' starting XI following their defeat to Nottingham Forest last weekend, Garnacho remained on the bench for the entire 90 minutes.

Johan Manzambi, Alysson, Nicolas Jackson and Emi Buendia were all brought on in the second half, but still no Garnacho.

Villa secured a comfortable win over their Premier League rivals after goals came from former Chelsea stars Tammy Abraham and Ross Barkley.

The 22-year-old winger has now failed to make an appearance for three consecutive matches, and has only played 31 minutes of competitive action this season.

Following the match, the Villa boss openly admitted the former Manchester United star needs to work harder to be more involved.

He said: "[He has to] continue working. Work, work, train, work. When he can have minutes to play, try and play well.

"George [Hemmings] is playing fantastic, Alysson is also understanding things well and is giving us things I want.

"Alysson is also understanding things well and is giving us things I want. [Ibrahim] Mbaye also responded well. We want a competitive team and players to compete in the style we have.

"Garnacho is a little bit behind because of some circumstances we had in pre-season. It is time to be patient for the time he needs."

Mbaye made his full debut for the club, while Hemmings made his sixth successive start of the campaign.

3 Mbaye assisted Barkley for the third Villa goal on his debut Credit: Getty

Additionally, fellow summer recruits Taylor Harwood-Bellis and Matteo Ruggeri were all handed their first starts for Villa.

Pre-season disruption

Garnacho's start to life in Birmingham was severely disrupted by a facial injury during pre-season which forced him to miss the Super Cup final against Paris Saint-Germain.

Prior to the defeat against Forest, Emery highlighted the Chelsea loanee's dedication.

He said: "His attitude is very important, he is getting the commitment we need to achieve it.

"Now he needs time. Time, hard work every day, and he is showing it with his attitude."

"Progressively, I am seeing him better. The most important thing is being consistent and demanding through the attitude he has.

3 Alejandro Garnacho is yet to start a game for Villa Credit: Getty

"Then, I believe and I trust that he will achieve his best performance."

Villa have an agreement to sign Garnacho for an alleged £42.5m if he reaches a set number of appearances.

Although the condition for an obligation to buy requires a limited number of appearances, Villa showed with Harvey Elliott they are prepared to limit player opportunities with loanees who arrive on this formula.

Last season, it was clear Emery didn't want to sign Liverpool's Elliott for £35million which led to him not making the set amount of appearances.

Sports.title: Jurgen Klopp hits out at leaks after naming 44 players in first Germany squad
Sports.content:
Jurgen Klopp hits out at leaks after naming 44 players in first Germany squad

Jurgen Klopp has taken aim at members of the press who leaked the Germany squad ahead of Thursday's announcement.

Klopp, who succeeded Julian Nagelsmann for Die Mannschaft, named two separate squads, totalling 44 players, for the upcoming international break as the UEFA Nations League gets underway.



3 Klopp named two separate squads for the start of the UEFA Nations League Credit: Getty

The first will take on Netherlands and Greece later this month, while the second face Serbia and Greece, again, next month after FIFA merged the September and October international break.

Elversberg's Felix Keidel was among the surprise inclusions in Klopp's squad, the 23-year-old in line to make his international bow next month.

Keidel caught the eye during Elversberg's recent 2-1 defeat to defending Bundesliga champions Bayern Munich.



And the former Liverpool boss referenced Keidel when speaking with the press to explain his decision.

Klopp, though, criticised those who leaked his picks before the official announcement on Thursday.



What did Klopp say?

"I spoke to Felix Keidel again last night and asked him what the last 16 or 17 hours had been like after someone leaked that he will be in the squad," Klopp revealed.

The 59-year-old then went on the offensive to criticise those who had leaked his selections, continuing: "And by the way, I can say that I don’t give a damn that it came out early.



"I have absolutely no problem with that.

"I just think it’s a bit pathetic to make a living by putting things out there earlier than people actually need to know them. But whatever."

3 Keidel was a surprise inclusion in the Germany squad

It's not the first time Klopp has criticised the press, threatening to quit his role as Germany boss just minutes after his appointment if the media didn't leave his family alone.

Who else made the Germany squad?

A number of familiar faces have made the Germany squad for the upcoming international break.



Bayern Munich pair Joshua Kimmich and Jamal Musiala have both made the cut, so, too, has Arsenal forward Kai Havertz.

Goalkeeper Marc-Andre ter Stegen has also returned to the international stage.

Klopp has since confirmed that the Ajax man will succeed the recently-retired Manuel Neuer as first-choice between the sticks.

"Yes, for the moment, there is one, Marc-Andre ter Stegen," Klopp said when asked who'd be his number one goalkeeper.



3 Ter Stegen has big gloves to fill for the Germany national team

"A team needs stability and a spine, and then you can add a lot of youth around that. I’ve known him for ages. Manuel Neuer was the best goalkeeper in the world for a long time.

"Nevertheless, everyone knew that Ter Stegen was world-class too. He then suffered an injury at an unfortunate time. At the moment, he is fit and the same goalkeeper he was before.

"He brings experience with him. He is making a very good impression. Everything depends on performance."



Elsewhere, Brighton's Pascal Gross, along with Deniz Undav and Leroy Sane, were overlooked by Klopp.

Sports.title: Aussie HYROX athlete apologises after soiling herself during competition that sparked uproar around the world - as she reveals she's forfeited her win
Sports.content:
Australian HYROX athlete Joanna Wietrzyk has issued a public apology following her win in an endurance event in Beijing – after she soiled herself during the race.

The 24-year-old, from Melbourne, refused to drop out of the event despite streams of faeces running down her legs as she powered to victory during the gruelling competition last Saturday.

Wietrzyk's decision to push on sparked ferocious criticism of the organisers for allowing the her to continue competing.

The Australian athlete issued a statement today apologising to other competitors and revealing she had forfeited her win at the event.

She wrote on Instagram: 'I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing.

'I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness.

'Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice.

'I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused.'

Australian HYROX athlete Joanna Wietrzyk (above) issued an apology on Thursday after refusing to quit a competition despite soiling herself on Saturday

Wietrzyk (above) forfeited her win at the event and apologised to other competitors

Wietrzyk said she'd reflected on the incident and was 'genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected'.

'I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away,' she wrote.

'On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned.'

The Melbourne athlete then thanked those who supported her during the days of backlash following the event.

'Thank you to those standing by me, both as an athlete and as a person, during this time, and to everyone who has reached out with kindness and support,' Wietrzyk wrote.

'It means more to me than I can properly express right now. I will be taking some time to recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise.'

Daily Mail previously revealed major sponsor Puma had distanced itself from the athlete by scrubbing references to her from its various country websites.

The incident on Saturday also prompted HYROX co-founder Moritz Fürste to issue a personal statement pledging to implement immediate rule changes.

Massive backlash from the incident (above) prompted HYROX co-founder Moritz Fürste to issue a personal statement pledging to implement immediate rule changes

Prior to the weekend's incident, official event rules punished athletes for minor infringements such as littering on the course or clearing their nose on the floor, but here were no rules relating to faecal matter.

Wietrzyk's statement drew hundreds of comments within minutes of being uploaded.

Commenters were deeply divided on whether the apology was sincere or the result of public pressure.

'This apology is just not good enough, not least because it has come far too late ... Truly terrible sportsmanship putting your fellow athletes health at serious risk, never mind the spectators and volunteers,' one wrote.

'Hindsight is a wonderful thing but during that moment and time nobody knows exactly how they would have reacted,' another said.

'A real person would've apologised the same day. Not after almost a week later,' another wrote.

'True actions of a fighter, not many people understand the mindset of the best in the world,' another said.

Wietrzyk turned off comments under the statement, and her other posts, within an hour of sharing it.

Wietrzyk initially made a post saying 'a win is a win' after the HYROX event

Commenters under the apology from Wietrzyk (above) were divided over whether it was delivered too late

The Melbourne athlete had initially shared a post following her accident declaring 'a win is a win' but later removed it and refused to publicly comment on the situation.

Her coach, Chris Bayens, shared a statement on Monday calling out 'hatred and personal attacks' on Wietrzyk.

'The mental health of athletes is shaped far more by the community around them, and right now that community should take a hard look at itself,' Bayens wrote.

'No one is perfect, not in sport, not on social media, not in real life. What happened was extraordinary. The hatred that has followed is ugly.'

Bayens vowed to continue supporting her and stressed that no one was prepared for what happened and that the decision to continue was made on the fly.

'Decisions were made under competition conditions by an athlete, judges and officials, all responding to a situation none of them could reasonably have prepared for,' he said.

'It is very easy to construct the perfect response once the moment has passed. Hindsight gives people time, information and distance that simply did not exist for those actually living it.

'Those decisions can be reviewed and lessons can be taken from them. But judging someone's intent, character or morality through the clarity of hindsight is neither fair nor honest.'

Her coach Chris Bayens has leapt to her defence, accusing critics of spreading negativity

Prior to Wietrzyk's accident, HYROX had no rules relating to faecal matter

Bayens followed the statement with a more comical take on the situation on Wednesday, writing: 'I had a few things on my Bingo card for the 26-27 HYROX season.

This was absolutely not one of them. I was hoping for a slightly smoother start.'

-

Sports.title: Lewis Hamilton forced to deny claims he asked for Ferrari staff member 'to be replaced' as behind-the-scenes tensions mount following spat with engineer and clash with Charles Leclerc
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton forced to deny claims he asked for Ferrari staff member 'to be replaced' as behind-the-scenes tensions mount following spat with engineer and clash with Charles Leclerc

Lewis Hamilton has denied a report that he demanded the sacking of a Ferrari staff member.

Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera reported on Tuesday that Hamilton, 41, wanted a trackside employee replaced.

The publication also claimed that Hamilton's relationship with team principal Fred Vasseur was strained.

But the Brit, who sits third in the Formula One Drivers' Championship, has denied these claims in a statement on Instagram.

He wrote: 'I’ve seen some of the stories that have gone out and I want to clear it up here. I’ve never asked for anyone on my team to be replaced.

'Everyone I work with works hard every day, and their dedication is what moves us forward.

Lewis Hamilton has denied calling for a member of Ferrari's trackside team to be replaced

'I always try to empower and lift people to be the best versions of themselves or at least see the best in themselves.

'I may not always achieve that but it’s my intention and what I’m here to do. We all work together and that will continue.'

Hamilton also shared a picture of himself alongside Ferrari staff members.

The report in Italy came after a tense Spanish Grand Prix weekend, which saw Hamilton entangled in a frosty exchange with his engineer after he crashed in practice.

The 'car-killing' Madring claimed another victim when Hamilton – who was on course to set the fastest time of the session – veered off track and into the barriers ahead of qualifying.

The collision caused major damage to the front wing of the car, with seven-time world champion Hamilton told to leave the car and allow for a recovery vehicle to return it to the garage.

However, the 41-year-old defied orders from his engineer and reversed out of the barriers before making his way onto the track, seemingly eager to return the car himself.

He was repeatedly told to 'stop the car' but ploughed on with a tyre puncture, before eventually limping to a halt.

The Brit held clear-the-air talks with Charles Leclerc (right) following their clash at Monza

Meanwhile, at the preceding Italian GP, he was embroiled in an explosive clash with team-mate Charles Leclerc.

Hamilton was squeezed off the track by Leclerc, clearly the Monegasque's error, in the second half of the first chicane in early exchanges of positions last Sunday. 'Charles pushed me off,' the seven-time world champion complained at the time.

Leclerc crashed out moments later at the Parabolica in an unrelated event, again his mistake, and it was a big bang. Hamilton went on to finish sixth – a combination of failure that amounted to a poor result for Ferrari on home turf.

In a message to team principal Fred Vasseur, the seven-time world champion said: ‘Here there are no rules. And that’s something that needs to change. When I was at Mercedes we had written rules of engagement. And we never had it too bad.

‘There was a moment with me and Nico a couple of times. But more often than not, it was good. Here there are no rules.'

But speaking ahead of the new home of the Spanish Grand Prix, Hamilton revealed he had held crunch talks with his team-mate: 'What is great is that there was no shying away from having a discussion. We sat face to face, just him (Charles) and me, and talked about it and we were both honest and open and then we quashed it and moved on.

'That shows maturity from him and it is healthy. It is a relationship we have built over time.

'Of course, there are going to be frustrations along the way. And there will be more times where we are close because we are approximate in pace and we both want to win as much as each other and do well for the team, but, yes, it is really positive.

'It has been really positive. I spoke to Fred (Vasseur, Ferrari's team principal) on Monday and we had clearing out discussions.

'Naturally we are going to have different opinions, but we come together to find a way forward and that is the positive of where we have got to over the past 15 months, when we can have really great communication internally and same with me and Charles.

'If you look at the history of the sport, this happened before, so it is no biggie.'

Sports.title: Ruben Amorim is ALREADY making excuses at AC Milan: Former Man United boss says his players are not 'perfect' for his system - and aims thinly-veiled dig at Old Trafford stars - before warning he will 'fail BIG'
Sports.content:
Ruben Amorim is ALREADY making excuses at AC Milan: Former Man United boss says his players are not 'perfect' for his system - and aims thinly-veiled dig at Old Trafford stars - before warning he will 'fail BIG'

Ruben Amorim has thrown shade at his AC Milan squad for not fitting his system, as he compared the Italian side's defeat to Benfica to his struggles at Manchester United.

Amorim suffered his first defeat at the Milan helm on Wednesday night as his side were beaten 2-0 by the Portuguese outfit at the San Siro in the Europa League.

One of the issues Amorim persistently complained about during his nightmare tenure at Old Trafford was that his players did not suit his style of play, which consists of a back three.

And just five games into his new role at AC Milan, the Portuguese coach struck an all-too familiar tone when asked about his squad.

'I think you are a little bit right,' Amorim told Sky Italia. 'I know at Manchester United and Milan, two big clubs with the pressure to win, people expect everything in just a few months, and I feel the same pressure here.

'I think this team is a little bit different, they are more accustomed to working with three defenders, they are a little bit faster, a little bit stronger.

Ruben Amorim compared his struggles at AC Milan to those he had at Man United

Milan were beaten 2-0 by Benfica at the San Siro in the Europa League on Wednesday night

'Of course, I don't have the clear characteristics that are perfect at this moment, but it is impossible when you take on a new team to have those perfect characteristics right away.'

Amorim requested patience and admitted that failure is once again possible, no matter the size of the club.

He added: 'I know it will take time, but I also know that there is big pressure at this club, yet I prefer this kind of job because if I need to fail one day, I want to fail big.

'I have a lot of passion for this club, I want to help this club to be better, I don't know if I will have the time, but I look at my players and I think they are listening to everything that I say in training, and that gives me hope we can solve these problems.'

The comments came under much criticism on social media, from supporters and journalists alike.

TNT Sports commentator Adam Summerton, who is known for being British broadcaster's voice of the Serie A, particularly took issue with Amorim's complaints.

Taking to social media, Summerton said: 'One of the best things Ruben Amorim could do right now is stop talking. He says way too much.'

Sports.title: River home to 500 CROCODILES to host Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoeing at 2032 Brisbane Games
Sports.content:
Athletes at the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games risk being torn apart by hungry crocodiles in front of a global audience.

They fear the threat of saltwater crocs after a river in Australia containing more than 500 of them was given the green light for the 2032 Olympic Games.

The Fitzroy River in Rockhampton, Queensland, has been given the go-ahead by organisers for the Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoeing events after passing its test with 'flying colours'.

In 2023, local authorities captured a monster 4.5-metre long Saltie after its presence had led to the cancellation of a local regatta. Last year, a four-metre behemoth snatched and killed a 16-month-old Rottweiler named Nigel.

'I'm sure I'd row faster!' three-time Olympic rowing gold medallist Drew Ginn told BBC Sport.

'I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on.

'Things like relocating crocodiles out of the river, you sort of go, "does international rowing want to have the athletes in jeopardy of that sort of stuff?"'

A river hosting more than 500 crocodiles has been given the green light for the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games

The Fitzroy River by Rockhampton (pictured) saw a dog killed by a crocodile last year

Five-hundred-and-foorty-two rowers signed a letter to the state government asking for a specific facility to be built in south-east Queensland due to concerns over the site, which also has a strong current. The Fitzroy River is six or seven hours away from Brisbane, where the main Games are taking place.

The river is roughly 300 miles long, meaning it hosts an average of 1.67 crocodiles per mile. Near Rockhampton, the waters are around 50 to 100 metres wide.

Rockhampton mayor Tony Williams has warned athletes to be 'croc-wise'.

'We're not shying away from it, there are crocodiles in the system,' he told AAP.

'There's crocodile management that can be put in place.

'I've swum in the river... being aware that they inhabit the rivers, you've just got to be croc-wise.'

The problem was raised at a recent International Olympic Committee meeting.

But organisers have not mentioned rehoming the snappy crocs and are instead adopting a positive attitude.

A total of 542 athletes signed a letter to the state government requesting a change of venue

Brisbane 2032 President Andrew Liveris said last year: 'There are sharks in the ocean and we're still surfing. It's a can do, not a can't do - please change the mindset here.'

Meanwhile, Queensland's premier, David Crisafulli, said: 'The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours. It’s official, signed, sealed and delivered.'

A report into the river, ordered by the Games Independent Infrastructure and Co-ordination Authority, did not consider the crocodiles but merely how the river would perform under various weather conditions.

The report did stress that 'contingency plans are in place at events for when crocodiles are spotted and Olympic officials have previously been assured of rower safety'.

Local crocodile farmer John Lever told AAP that the crocs were not a major worry.

'There's very few crocodiles in the freshwater, downstream side of the river (near the course) - I think we've had four removed in 40 years,' he said.

'They're not of concern. The schools are out there every day with their rowing teams.'

'Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games, consistent with the requirements of Olympic and Paralympic Rowing,' World Rowing President Jean-Christophe Rolland said.

Thomas Konietzko, president of Paddle Worldwide, which deals with canoeing, said: 'The quality and depth of the technical work undertaken has significantly improved our understanding of the field of play and provides confidence to us and our athletes that the course can deliver fair competition for Canoe Sprint athletes.'

Sports.title: The truth behind Max Verstappen's 100-influencer racing challenge: Daily Mail Sport's HENRY WILLIAMS reveals the one rule everybody HAD to follow, the pre-race warning Red Bull star sent him and how he fared in Silverstone bonanza
Sports.content:
The truth behind Max Verstappen's 100-influencer racing challenge: Daily Mail Sport's HENRY WILLIAMS reveals the one rule everybody HAD to follow, the pre-race warning Red Bull star sent him and how he fared in Silverstone bonanza

For those of us that love sport, there are few opportunities to live the life of the athletes we admire.

These rare chances may be limited to: running a marathon, scoring the winner in Sunday league, beating your mates on the 18th in front of a packed-out clubhouse.

On Wednesday evening I was one of the luckiest 100 people in the world, as I was asked to take on Max Verstappen in 'Max vs 100' - Red Bull's latest ingenious way of capturing a market that goes way beyond energy drink consumers.

This was the closest I'll ever get to being a professional sportsperson, and it's a thrill I'll never forget.

Taking on the four-time world champion was a daunting prospect, softened somewhat by the fact that all 101 of us were out of place: One hundred of us were out of place imitating professionals. Max Verstappen was out of place being at the back of any grid - not that he was for long.

A few hours before the race, Max, wearing casual Red Bull attire, briskly walked through the paddock to his pit. I caught up with him and asked:

Henry Williams lasted just two corners in his attempt to beat Formula One's Max Verstapppen

'Are you going to beat me, Max?'

'I'm going to try my best!' he replied.

A cheeky question answered with immense respect. A response that I would put to him after the race.

Once the buzz of our first interaction had worn off, the nerves set in for qualifying. One flying lap, one attempt to get myself far enough away from Max that he had to at least get up to speed before overtaking me.

'Don't spin out, don't spin out, don't spin out' I uttered to myself time after time. I wanted to give myself the best opportunity possible. Knowing that if I avoided messing up, I could be a few rows ahead of him, at least.

The track was part-karting, part-Silverstone race circuit. Our first taste of it was on a smaller version on Tuesday, where we had a full practice schedule put on for us. This consisted of a: practice session, qualifying and a sprint race.

All before we took on VCARB driver, Arvid Lindblad, in a 50-kart simulation of the following day's showdown with Max.

Are you starting to see what I mean when I liken this to the experience of a professional driver?

Whereas on Tuesday there was comfort in the fact that we had ample opportunity to bounce back from errors on the track, Wednesday was an entirely different ballgame.

My group 'Team Priory' was the final to be released for qualifying. Having seen many come and go before us, the nerves had longer to fester.

Daily Mail Sport's Henry was invited to compete against the Red Bull driver and 99 other influencers at Silverstone

Henry qualified in 73rd for the 30-lap race, with his qualifying attempt impeded by traffic

It was a bit of a mess for myself, truth be told. On the out lap, I had planned to give myself as much distance to the car ahead as possible. Adrenaline quickly aborted that plan for me, and I found myself bunched up with two others.

Which leads me on to the Motley Crew of competitors Max had to contend with. It was largely a mix of creators and influencers. From Love Island winners, to F1 fanatics, it was an eclectic mix of enthusiastic hopefuls. In front of me for qualifying was Quecee, a Dutch streamer and Molly Carlson, a cliff-diving Red Bull athlete.
