Two of the abducted teachers were subsequently killed by the terrorists, while the other surviving victims were rescued on 10 July.

On 29 July, the Nigerian government arraigned the five men, who were previously convicted for terrorism earlier this year, in connection with the kidnap.

The five received life sentences for terrorism in two judgements handed down by the Federal High Court in Abuja.

They include Mahmud Usman Muhammad (also known as Abu Bara’a and Abbas Mukhtar),and Abubakar Abbas (also known as Isah Adam, Mahmud al-Nigeri and Malam Mamuda). The State Security Service (SSS) said Mr Muhammad was a self-proclaimed Emir of Ansaru, while Mr Abbas described himself as the group’s deputy and chief of staff.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The remaining defendants are Abdulrazak Umar (also known as Abu Khalifa and Abu Khalid), Yunusa Musa (also known as Yunusa bin Musa), and Shamsu Adamu Sani (also known as Abu Itisar).

They were alleged to be members of the Jama’atu Ansarul Muslimina fi-Biladis Sudan (Ansarul) terrorist group.

They pleaded not guilty to the charges before trial judge Salim Ibrahim.

Led in evidence by the prosecution lawyer, Rotimi Oyedepo, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), witness AAA told the court on Thursday that she was in court in respect of the kidnapping in Oriire LGA of Oyo State.

“I am a class teacher in one of the schools.

“On May 15, armed men invaded our schools, carted away students and teachers and took us into the forest and we were there for 56 days,” she said.

When she was asked how it all started, the witness said: “school activities had just started when we heard gunshots.”

She said seven teachers and 39 students were kidnapped.

When the lawyer asked him if the terrorists were friendly during the period of captivity, the witness responded: “Friendly? In what sense sir?”

The witness, who told the court that their abductors mainly spoke in Hausa, said few of them could speak Yoruba.

“Some of them are Kogi boys,” she said.

Re-arraignment

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the men were re-arraigned on Thursday on seven charges before trial judge, Mr Ibrahim.

The prosecution lawyer, Mr Oyedepo, said he would open the case against the defendants in line with Section 273 of the Criminal Justice Act following the defendants’ not-guilty pleas.

Mr Oyedepo, the Director of Public Prosecutions of the Federation, said that due to the sensitive nature of the matter, the prosecution would apply for witness protection.

“I urge my lord to invoke the provision of Section 232 of ACJA for witness protection; either to be screened or masked and for names that are in acronyms to be ascribed to them,” he said.

The defendants’ counsel, Bala Dakum, did not object to the prosecution.

The lawyer, however, applied for the permission of court to enable him to view the witness during cross-examination.

The judge, Mr Ibrahim, granted the applications from both the prosecution and the defence lawyers.

Background

The Nigerian government arraigned the five men in July, two of whom were convicted Ansarul commanders. The three other defendants were also convicted and jailed for their connection with terrorism.

The five men were arraigned before Judge Ibrahim on 29 July on pre-existing charges and four fresh ones covering the impact of the defendants’ alleged terror activities nationwide.

This came after the SSS expressed dissatisfaction with the life sentence earlier imposed on each of the five defendants in two separate terrorism cases.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that Judge Emeka Nwite sentenced Messrs Muhammad and Abbas to life imprisonment on 20 July, after they pleaded guilty to 32 charges brought by the SSS.

Three days later, Judge Ibrahim sentenced the three other newly charged defendants – Messrs Umar, Musa and Sani – to life imprisonment after they pleaded guilty to six of out 10 terrorism charges, including allegations of their complicity in the abduction of pupils and teachers in Oriire Local Government Area of Oyo State in May this year.

The three men were to proceed to full trial on the four remaining charges before the prosecution re-filed an amended version of the indictment, adding six counts and bringing in the two jailed Ansarul leaders as co-defendants.

The prosecution opened trial of all five defendants on Thursday regarding amended seven charges.

In the wake of the court’s verdict, the SSS rejected the life imprisonment imposed on the convicts, saying the penalty was not commensurate with the gravity of their offences. It vowed to appeal against the judgement and push for the death penalty.

World.title: Kogi renovates three PHCs in each LGA – Official
World.content:
The Chief Medical Director, Kogi Hospitals Management Board, Ayo Olayemi, says renovation of Primary Healthcare Centres (PHCs) across the state is improving healthcare delivery and patient safety.

Mr Olayemi said this in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) on Thursday in Lokoja, to commemorate World Patient Safety Day, marked annually on 17 September.

He said Governor Ahmed Ododo had renovated three PHCs in each of the state’s 21 Local Government Areas, bringing the total number of renovated facilities to 63.

Mr Olayemi said the government had also constructed seven additional PHCs in locations with large populations that previously relied on a single facility for primary healthcare services.

He said the interventions were aimed at improving access to quality healthcare and creating safer environments for patients seeking medical attention across the state.

“The primary healthcare system in the state is being strengthened,” he said, adding that functional facilities could improve timely diagnosis, treatment and follow-up care for patients.

Mr Olayemi, however, identified human resources as a major challenge in the health sector, but expressed optimism that the situation would improve with continued government intervention.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Human resources is a challenge,” he said, expressing confidence that the situation would change soon as measures were being implemented to address the shortage.

The chief medical director emphasised the importance of patients understanding their rights and speaking up whenever they were uncertain about treatment or suspected an error during healthcare delivery.

“As a patient, you have a right,” he said, urging patients to ask questions about their diagnosis, prescribed medicines, possible side effects and available treatment options.

He said medical errors could occur at different stages of healthcare delivery, including diagnosis, laboratory investigations, prescribing, dispensing and treatment, requiring vigilance from healthcare providers and patients.

Mr Olayemi cited medication errors as an example, noting that patients should seek clarification whenever the medicines or dosages supplied differed from what doctors had prescribed.

He said healthcare facilities in the state had functional complaint systems through which patients could report suspected errors, concerns and other issues encountered while receiving healthcare services.

He encouraged patients to lodge complaints through the Servicom system or approach the chief medical director of facilities where they were receiving care for necessary intervention.

According to him, complaints should not merely be received but reviewed and used to identify weaknesses, address gaps and improve healthcare services across facilities.

The World Patient Safety Day, established by the World Health Assembly in 2019, is observed annually to raise awareness and promote action on patient safety globally.

The 2026 theme is “Safe care for non-communicable diseases,” with the slogan “Safe care for life!”, focusing attention on safer treatment for people living with chronic conditions.

The World Health Organisation says the 2026 campaign focuses on preventing avoidable harm among people living with non-communicable diseases through safer and more responsive healthcare practices.

Mr Olayemi said that strengthening primary healthcare, improving infrastructure, and addressing human resource gaps were important steps towards ensuring safer healthcare services for patients across Kogi.

He expressed optimism that continued government commitment and the dedication of healthcare workers would improve healthcare delivery and change the current narrative across the state.

World.title: NDA Admission: Group cautions against making recruitment religious contest
World.content:
A group, Gospel Reggae Team Initiative (GRTI), has expressed concern over a statement attributed to the Abuja Chapter of the Muslim Rights Concern (MURIC) alleging religious imbalance in the recently released admission list for the 78 Regular Course of the Nigerian Defence Academy (NDA), Kaduna.

MURIC recently frowned at what it described as a clear religious imbalance in the 2026 NDA 78 Regular Course admission list released recently.

The Islamic organisation, in a statement by its Chairman, Ustaz Salahudeen, said the composition of the admission committee and the ratio of Muslims and Christians admitted in each state raised serious concerns.

According to Mr Salahudeen, all key officers superintending the admission process are of the same faith, naming the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), the Chairman of the NDA Selection Board, the Commandant of NDA, the NDA Registrar and the NDA Provost as all being Christian.

He said this lopsided hierarchy raises legitimate concerns about balance, fairness, objectivity and adherence to the Federal Character principle enshrined in Section 14(3) of the 1999 Constitution.

However, the GRTI, in a statement on Tuesday by its Founder/Coordinator, Lucy Awe, and shared with PREMIUM TIMES, said as a Christian body, which believes in the unity of Nigeria, viewing issues of admission into the NDA through the lens of religion is deeply troubling.

“As Christians who believe deeply in the unity, peace and sovereignty of Nigeria, we find the attempt to assess admission into Nigeria’s premier military training institution primarily through the lens of Christianity and Islam deeply troubling,” the statement said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It, therefore, appealed to the State Security Service (also known as Department of State Services) and other relevant security and public institutions to remain vigilant and, where appropriate, encourage restraint in public commentary that could unnecessarily introduce religious tension into sensitive national processes.

It explained that its position is not meant to prevent anyone from raising legitimate concerns about the institution’s admission process, but that such concerns should be presented and assessed on the basis of objective criteria, evidence and established laws and regulations, rather than religious assumptions.

The group also quoted one of its trustees, Odoh Okenyodo, as saying that, “The Nigerian Defence Academy is not a Christian institution. It is not a Muslim institution. It belongs to Nigeria. Its responsibility is to train Nigerians who will serve the Nigerian state, irrespective of their religion, ethnicity, region or social background.

“The fundamental questions in military recruitment should therefore be whether candidates meet the established requirements and demonstrate the competence, character, discipline and commitment necessary to serve Nigeria.”

GRTI said it is particularly concerned about attempts to establish religious ratios among candidates admitted from various states and to draw conclusions about fairness primarily from whether candidates are identified as Christians or Muslims.

“This raises an important question: What legitimate recruitment criterion requires the NDA admission process to be reduced to a Christian-Muslim arithmetic?

“Federal character and equitable representation are important constitutional principles. However, these principles should not be interpreted as requiring every government institution to reproduce a particular religious ratio.

“There is a fundamental difference between ensuring equitable representation across Nigeria’s diverse communities and allocating opportunities according to religious identity.

“The latter could create an unhealthy precedent in which competence and qualification gradually become secondary to religious considerations.” It stated.

The group noted that the repeated introduction of religious considerations into government appointments, recruitment, admissions and other public processes deserves careful reflection.

It argued that if allowed to become a recurring feature of public discourse, such practices could place pressure on government institutions to consider religious identity where competence, integrity and national loyalty ought to remain paramount.

According to GRTI, this is particularly sensitive when dealing with the military and other security institutions.

“Nigeria needs security personnel whose primary allegiance is to the Federal Republic of Nigeria and its Constitution, rather than to religious, ethnic or sectional interests.

“We therefore encourage all stakeholders to approach matters concerning security-sector recruitment with a strong sense of responsibility and patriotism,” it added.

The group said if there are genuine concerns about the NDA admission process, the appropriate questions are clear: What were the published admission criteria; What were the applicable cut-off marks; Were the criteria applied consistently; Were candidates treated fairly and equally; and was there any violation of applicable law or recruitment policy?

GRTI said that, as a Christian organisation, it is appealing for restraints “because we believe Christianity does not require Christians to demand religious quotas in every Nigerian institution. We equally reject any expectation that Muslims should receive preferential treatment simply because they are Muslims.”

World.title: Dangote Refinery IPO could add $60bn to NGX market capitalisation – Minister
World.content:
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Jumoke Oduwole, has said the proposed Initial Public Offering (IPO) of Dangote Petroleum Refinery & Petrochemicals FZE could boost Nigeria’s investment and capital market sectors.

Mrs Oduwole said if fully subscribed, the offering and subsequent listing could add approximately $60 billion to the total equity market capitalisation of the Nigerian Exchange (NGX).

The minister stated this in a statement on Wednesday in support of the refinery’s IPO.

“If fully subscribed, the offering and subsequent listing could add approximately $60 billion to the total equity market capitalisation of the Nigerian Exchange (NGX), significantly expanding the size of Nigeria’s listed equity market,” she said.

The minister noted the transaction could attract new investors, broaden the range of companies listed on the exchange and demonstrate the capacity of Nigeria’s capital market to support enterprises operating at scale.

“Less than three years ago, access by Free Zone Entities to Nigeria’s capital market was a live regulatory constraint being raised directly by investors. Today, a Free Zone Entity operating from Nigeria has launched Africa’s largest-ever IPO.

“This is translating into investment, and it is precisely the kind of reform-to-investment conversion we want to institutionalize,” Mrs Oduwole said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

She recalled that the issue of access to the capital market by Free Zone Entities had been raised during engagements with private-sector operators, including Dangote Refinery and other Free Zone operators.

Mrs Oduwole urged investors to contribute to Nigeria’s economic development, saying the country’s business environment was becoming more conducive to investment.

“Our ambition is not merely to attract capital, but to shape an environment in which capital can land, grow and create lasting value. Our message to domestic and global investors is clear: Nigeria is a market where you can build at scale, mobilise capital at scale and compete globally.

“We will continue to deepen the reforms necessary to unlock productive investment and connect Nigerian enterprise and production more competitively to African and global markets,” she said.

Dangote Refinery IPO

The Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals FZE plan to raise capital from the public through an Initial Public Offering (IPO) after its Chairman, Aliko Dangote, announced plans to list the refinery and widened its ownership.

The company signed the IPO documents on 7 September and formally opened the public offer on 14 September. The offer comprises 4.1 billion ordinary shares at N525 per share, with the company seeking to raise about N2.15 trillion if fully subscribed. The offer is scheduled to close on 13 October.

The IPO is being presented by Mr Dangote as a way of broadening ownership of the refinery beyond its existing investors. At the launch, he said the exercise was intended to make wealth creation available to ordinary people rather than being primarily a fundraising exercise.

How the IPO works

An IPO is the process through which a privately held company offers shares to members of the public for the first time. Investors who are allotted shares become shareholders in the company and may receive dividends if the company declares them. The value of their shares can also rise or fall depending on the market and the company’s performance.

In the Dangote Refinery offer, investors can apply for a minimum of 10 shares at N525 each, meaning the minimum subscription is N5,250. Applications are to be made through Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)-approved receiving agents and electronic application channels. After the offer closes, the applications will be processed and shares allotted in accordance with the terms of the offer.

The company is seeking to raise about N2.15 trillion through the offer. The funds are expected to support the refinery’s expansion plans, including its proposed increase in refining capacity. Reuters reported that the company plans to more than double capacity to about 1.4 million barrels per day by 2029, with the expansion estimated at $14.3 billion.

Nigerians’ reactions

The IPO has generated substantial interest among Nigerian retail investors, with several investment platforms reporting unusually heavy traffic when the offer opened.

There are reports of surge in demand overwhelming parts of Nigeria’s fintech investment infrastructure, with platforms including Bamboo, Cowrywise and InvestNaija experiencing difficulties as investors rushed to participate. Bamboo said its traffic increased sharply shortly after the offer opened.

Some Nigerians have expressed excitement about the opportunity to own shares in a major Nigerian industrial company, with social media users joking about becoming “business partners” with Mr Dangote after subscribing to the offer.

However, the enthusiasm has also been accompanied by caution. The Securities and Exchange Commission has warned prospective investors to use only approved subscription channels and to verify platforms and receiving agents, amid concerns about fraudulent websites, social-media accounts and unsolicited messages targeting people interested in the IPO.

World.title: Cross River, Okomu National Parks added to CITES elephant monitoring network
World.content:
Cross River National Park and Okomu National Park in Nigeria have been added to the Monitoring the Illegal Killing of Elephants (MIKE) Programme of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES).

In a statement published on its website , CITES said the designation brings the number of MIKE sites across Africa to 74.

The organisation said the network has expanded significantly from its original 39 sites in 2001, describing the latest additions as a major step towards strengthening Africa’s capacity for systematic elephant monitoring.

With financial support from the European Union, CITES said the expansion reflects the commitment of elephant range states to evidence-based conservation.

The five newly designated sites are Digya National Park and Bia National Park in Ghana; Cross River National Park and Okomu National Park in Nigeria; and Gambella National Park in Ethiopia.

CITES described Digya National Park, located along the shores of Lake Volta in Ghana’s forest-savanna transition zone, as one of the country’s largest protected areas.

Bia National Park, which forms part of the Bia Biosphere Reserve recognised under UNESCO’s Man and the Biosphere Programme, borders Côte d’Ivoire and plays an important role in cross-border conservation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“In Nigeria, Cross River National Park has joined the network, a major protected area in the southeast dominated by moist tropical rainforest and bordering Cameroon, placing it within a wider transboundary conservation landscape. Also added is Okomu National Park, in southwestern Nigeria, which protects the last remaining fragment of lowland rainforest within the wider Okomu Forest Reserve,” CITES said.

The organisation said the addition of the sites would strengthen the MIKE Programme’s ability to track poaching trends and guide conservation action in areas where it is most urgently needed.

Declining elephant populations in Nigeria

The designation of the two Nigerian parks comes amid persistent threats to the country’s declining elephant population.

An extensive PREMIUM TIMES investigation published last year revealed how human-elephant conflict is threatening Nigeria’s remaining wild elephants.

Nigeria is among the few African countries with both forest and savanna elephant populations, scientifically known as Loxodonta cyclotis and Loxodonta africana, respectively.

It is estimated that about 90 per cent of Nigeria’s elephants are found in or near protected areas, including national parks and game reserves, while about 10 per cent live outside protected areas.

Human-elephant conflict has emerged as a major threat to the declining elephant population across Nigeria’s ecological zones.

The problem is compounded by illegal logging, agricultural expansion and extreme weather events, among other factors.

According to the Natural Resources Conservation Council (NARESCON), major threats to Nigeria’s elephants include poaching and the illegal ivory trade, habitat loss and fragmentation, livestock grazing, human-elephant conflict, and legal and institutional challenges.

Data from the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) show that Nigeria’s elephant population has declined over the past three decades from an estimated 1,200–1,500 to about 300–400.

Of the remaining population, about 200–300 are estimated to be forest elephants, while roughly 100 are savanna elephants.

The IUCN classifies the African forest elephant as critically endangered and the African savanna elephant as endangered.

In August 2024, the Federal Government, with support from the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) and the Elephant Protection Initiative, adopted a 10-year plan for protecting Nigeria’s remaining elephants.

The plan, seen by PREMIUM TIMES, outlines the status of the country’s elephant population and provides a framework for the long-term conservation of the species across Nigeria.

Cross River National Park is one of the largest remaining forest blocks in the Guinean Forest biodiversity hotspot.

The park comprises the Oban and Okwangwo divisions, both of which harbour threatened and vulnerable wildlife species, including chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), Cross River gorillas (Gorilla gorilla diehli), white-bellied pangolins (Phataginus tricuspis) and forest elephants.

The park’s location along Nigeria’s border with Cameroon also gives it importance within a wider transboundary conservation landscape. Okomu National Park is a 200-square-kilometer protected lowland rainforest located in the Ovia South-West Local Government Area of Edo State, Nigeria.

Strengthening conservation efforts

CITES said the MIKE Programme has, for more than two decades, provided governments with tools to understand changes in elephant populations and develop targeted conservation responses.

It said the expansion of the network represents both the programme’s growth and the continued collaboration among participating countries.

CITES Secretary-General, Ivonne Higuero, said the expanded network would strengthen efforts to monitor and respond to elephant killings.

“CITES Parties have remained committed to evidence-based elephant conservation, and this expansion of the CITES MIKE network strengthens our collective ability to not only respond to illegal killing through reliable, continent-wide monitoring, but also advance our goals for people and wildlife within the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and the CITES Strategic Vision 2021-2030,” she said.

CITES said one of the significant aspects of the expansion is its focus on West Africa.

According to the IUCN African Elephant Database, West Africa holds less than three per cent of Africa’s total elephant population and accounts for less than five per cent of the continent’s elephant range.

The organisation said the region’s remaining elephant populations survive in highly fragmented groups, making systematic monitoring particularly important.

The expansion also includes Gambella National Park in Ethiopia, which CITES said hosts the country’s largest elephant population and forms part of a major transboundary wildlife landscape extending into South Sudan.

According to CITES, the new sites will improve the geographic coverage and completeness of data on the threats facing elephant populations across Africa.

It said the expansion also contributes to the implementation of CITES Resolution Conf. 10.10 (Rev. CoP20), which calls for the selection of monitoring sites and, where appropriate, expansion of the MIKE network to the maximum extent possible.

What happens next?

CITES said the next phase would involve onboarding the newly designated sites into the MIKE system.

Working with MIKE National Focal Points, the CITES MIKE team will conduct induction sessions and practical training for rangers and site focal points.

The training will ensure that elephant mortality is recorded and reported consistently under MIKE protocols, including deaths from all causes and not only illegal killing.

CITES said the addition of each site strengthens a continent-wide system of data collection, collaboration and conservation action.

“The MIKE Programme welcomes the commitment of Ethiopia, Ghana and Nigeria to regular data submission and continued collaboration under CITES,” the organisation said.

It added that other countries had expressed interest in nominating sites and that the MIKE Programme was engaging with them to support further expansion of the network.

About CITES

The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) was signed on 3 March 1973 and entered into force on 1 July 1975.

With 185 Parties—184 countries and the European Union—CITES regulates international trade in more than 41,000 species of wild animals and plants.

The convention seeks to ensure that international wildlife trade is legal, sustainable and traceable through scientific assessment, legal compliance and enforcement.

CITES said its work supports the CITES Strategic Vision 2021–2030, the goals and targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.

Nigeria signed CITES in 1974 and ratified the convention in 1975.

As a Party to the convention, Nigeria is required to implement relevant provisions of CITES, including measures to protect endangered species and combat the illegal trafficking of protected animals and their body parts.

World.title: King’s College: Glory, decay and battle over the future
World.content:
For generations of Nigerians, King’s College, Lagos, has been more than a secondary school; it has been a symbol of academic excellence and a training ground for future leaders.

Founded during the colonial era, this institution shaped generations of Nigerians who later attained prominent positions across government, business, academia, and various professional sectors.

Its name became associated with discipline, academic excellence and the idea of bringing young Nigerians from different parts of the country together to learn and grow.

But decades of inadequate investment and deteriorating infrastructure have raised questions about whether the institution still reflects the reputation for which it became renowned.

Against this backdrop, the Federal Government and the King’s College Old Boys Association (KCOBA) agreed on a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) concession for the institution.

The proposal has generated controversy, with education unions opposing the move.

While the government insists the arrangement is not a sale or privatisation, the dispute has triggered heated debates over how best to preserve the school’s legacy while addressing its deteriorating infrastructure and standards.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The workers’ unions have raised concerns about the proposed arrangement, particularly its implications for staff, the future of the school, and the possibility that it could set a precedent for other unity colleges.

At the centre of the disagreement is a fundamental question: how can government restore the quality and infrastructure of institutions that once represented the pinnacle of public education?

The Minister of Education, Tunji Alausa, said the federal government had no plan to sell any of the country’s Federal Unity Colleges.

He described reports to the contrary as misinformation, stressing that the government retained responsibility and ownership of the institutions.

“Federal Government of Nigeria, through the Federal Ministry of Education, is not going to sell any of our Federal Unity Colleges; that is the government position, and go and write it down and hold on to that.

“So, if the unions start telling you that, ‘Oh, they are protesting because they want to sell unity colleges,’ that is absolutely false.

“We are not selling any of our Federal Unity Colleges. Government still has its responsibility.”

He said the arrangement involving King’s College was intended to address the school’s infrastructure and management challenges while restoring its historic status.

He said that King’s College was established to provide an environment capable of producing leaders, much like some renowned institutions globally that have historically served as pipelines for national leadership.

He cited Eton College in the UK and Ivy League universities in the US as examples of institutions that have played important roles in developing generations of leaders.

Mr Alausa argued that Nigeria once had similar institutions, pointing to King’s College, Lagos, and Barewa College, Zaria, as examples of schools that produced prominent Nigerians across generations.

However, he said the condition of some Unity Colleges had deteriorated significantly after decades of accumulated infrastructure deficits.

Mr Alausa recalled that after assuming office, he and the Minister of State for Education, Suwaiba Ahmad, split the country’s regions to inspect the condition of Unity Colleges.

He said his visit to King’s College was conducted unannounced and began at about 7:30 a.m.

Mr Alausa reported encountering a school struggling with serious infrastructure and environmental challenges during the inspection.

He described the toilets and bathrooms as being in poor condition and the students’ dormitories as severely dilapidated.

The minister also expressed concern about the condition of the dining facilities, classrooms and laboratories, saying some areas were poorly lit and had accumulated refuse.

He said the school had also experienced prolonged electricity challenges, recalling how he contacted the management of the electricity distribution company serving the area and insisted that power be restored to the school.

“I will not leave this school today if you do not come and connect this school back to electricity,” he recalled telling the company’s chairman.

He said electricity was subsequently restored to the Senior Secondary School, explaining that the condition he encountered was not limited to one section of King’s College, adding that the Junior Secondary School also required substantial rehabilitation.

Mr Alausa also revealed that another issue that caught his attention during the inspection was the use of parts of the school premises as a car park.

The minister said he observed about 200 vehicles parked in one part of the compound, with additional vehicles near the gate.

He questioned the safety implications of operating a public car park within the premises of a school largely occupied by children.

The minister said he directed the cancellation of the arrangement, expressing concern that unrestricted access to the school could expose students to security risks.

This incident, according to him, highlights the larger management difficulties faced by several Unity Colleges.

For the federal government, the King’s College controversy is therefore not simply about the management of one school but part of a larger debate about the sustainability of public education and the future of the country’s Unity Colleges.

Mr Alausa said government funding alone might not be sufficient to close decades of infrastructure gaps across the schools.

He estimated that the cost of rehabilitating unity colleges would run into hundreds of billions of naira, noting that the government had other competing priorities, including healthcare, security and broader infrastructure.

He said even a hypothetical allocation of N2 trillion would not be sufficient to completely address the infrastructure needs of the 115 Unity Colleges.

The minister said the government was consequently exploring alternative funding and management models while insisting that ownership of the schools would remain with the federal government.

He cited an ongoing effort to repurpose about $20 million from a World Bank-supported programme for the comprehensive rehabilitation of selected Unity Colleges.

He said the federal government was also exploring public-private partnership models for some schools.

Mr Alausa said KCOBA approached the government with a proposal to take responsibility for rehabilitating and managing King’s College through a non-profit arrangement.

He said the association had previously invested substantially in the school but believed more needed to be done to restore its former standard.

“They want their past back,” he said, referring to the Old Boys’ desire to restore the institution that shaped their lives.

Mr Alausa said members of the association included accomplished professionals and business leaders who were willing to commit resources to the school without seeking financial profit.

He said the proposed arrangement would be guided by stringent key performance indicators, with the Ministry of Education monitoring implementation through an oversight team.

The minister also maintained that the arrangement would not result in an increase in school fees.

Beyond infrastructure, however, the government has raised concerns about whether some unity colleges are still fulfilling the original objective for which they were established.

Mr Alausa said King’s College, which was intended to bring together students from different parts of the country, had experienced a shift in its admission pattern.

He alleged that more than 60 per cent of its students currently came from one geopolitical zone.

For him, this undermines the original philosophy of unity colleges as institutions where young Nigerians from different backgrounds could live and learn together.

Sharing similar sentiments, Ms Ahmad stressed that the government’s priority was to improve the learning environment and ensure that students received quality education.

She said no teacher would lose their job as a result of the arrangement and that redeployment would be carried out in line with the Public Service Rules.

She added that teachers would have the opportunity to indicate where they wished to be redeployed.

The minister of state also emphasised the importance of dialogue, noting that the government had already begun engaging with unions and had established committees to review concerns regarding the Memorandum of Understanding and to monitor its implementation.

According to her, the agreement is not cast in stone, and legitimate concerns that could improve its implementation would be considered.

For the Joint Workers Union of the Federal Ministry of Education, however, the issue goes beyond whether the government calls the arrangement a concession, a management agreement, or a partnership.

The Chairman of the Joint Workers Union, Abraham Onuche, said their opposition was not simply about the condition of King’s College but also about the process through which the proposed arrangement was reached.

He contended that proper consultation with the unions and other stakeholders should precede any major decision affecting Federal Unity Colleges.

Mr Onuche argued that allowing KCOBA to manage King’s College could establish a precedent for old students’ associations of other Unity Colleges to seek similar arrangements.

“If that King’s College goes, as we follow in law, that’s what they call precedent.

“That means old boys have set precedent, and tomorrow, another old boys association can say they also want to take over the management of their own school.

“Our demand now is one, that the minister should revoke that decision concerning King’s College and other schools,” he said.

Analysts say the concern is particularly significant because many Unity Colleges have active alumni associations with strong emotional and financial connections to their former schools.

The unions fear that a precedent could gradually change the character of the Federal Unity Colleges, even if the government currently says there is no plan to replicate the King’s College model.

Chigozie Ngadi, chairperson of the Association of Senior Civil Servants of Nigeria (ASCSN), Federal Ministry of Education chapter, said the union’s primary concern was ensuring that children from less privileged families continued to have access to quality education.

Mr Ngadi said the Old Boys Association should contribute to the school without taking it away from the public.

“We are speaking for Nigerians. We are speaking for downtrodden Nigerians to have access to good education.

“We are only demanding that poor children should have access to King’s College and quality education.

“The old boys association should give back to that society that made them what they are and not take from it,” he said.

Mr Ngadi said the unions were not opposed to partnerships that could improve infrastructure in schools.

He said their preference, however, was for arrangements that would preserve public ownership and ensure that the schools remain accessible to children irrespective of their economic background.

Observers say the dispute has expanded into a broader debate regarding the future of public education in Nigeria.

The government’s primary focus is on rapidly securing resources to stop further institutional decay, arguing that decades of neglect and failing infrastructure demand immediate action.

Conversely, unions urge caution, questioning whether public institutions should be handed over to alumni associations—even non-profit ones.

They underscore the need to protect public ownership, maintain student access, and avoid setting a risky precedent without proper consultation.

While both sides agree that the current situation is unsustainable, students remain caught in the middle of the conflict.

(NAN)

World.title: When rain becomes a governance test, By AbdulAzeez Aliyu Elayo
World.content:
A flooded Abuja street or road

At last Friday’s sermon in my neighbourhood mosque, the Anas Ibn Malik Islamic Centre Masjid at AMSSCO Platinum City Estate, Galadimawa, Abuja, the Imam, Bashir Bello Shagari, spoke on the theme, “Rain: A Blessing, Mercy, Trial and Lesson.”

It was a timely sermon. Across Abuja, rainfall, once received mainly with gratitude and relief, increasingly evokes mixed feelings. Rain nourishes crops, replenishes water sources, cools the atmosphere and sustains human and animal life. Yet, for many residents, it has also become associated with flooded homes, submerged roads, damaged property, disrupted livelihoods and avoidable deaths.

The sermon invited worshippers to look beyond rain as an ordinary meteorological event. It presented rain as a blessing for which humanity must be grateful, a mercy that sustains creation, a possible trial when it causes harm, and a lesson about responsibility and accountability.

That message should not end within the walls of the mosque. It speaks directly to Nigeria’s environmental and climate challenges and, more importantly, to the quality of our public policies and governance in addressing them.

Rain as mercy and a public good

The Qur’an describes rain as an expression of divine mercy: “And He is the One who sends down the rain after they have despaired, and He spreads His mercy” (Qur’an 42:28). It also asks humanity to reflect: “Have you considered the water that you drink? Is it you who bring it down from the clouds, or are We the One who sends it down?” (Qur’an 56:68–69).

These verses establish water as more than a commodity. It is a common resource upon which life depends. The obligation to receive it with gratitude must, therefore, include responsibility for using it appropriately, preparing for the risks associated with it and protecting the environment through which it flows.

Gratitude cannot be reduced to words while drains are filled with refuse, green areas are converted into housing estates, trees are removed without replacement, and buildings are approved on natural waterways. It must be expressed through responsible conduct, environmental stewardship and policies that preserve this gift for present and future generations. That is the essence of sustainability.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Islamic concept of khilafah, humanity’s trusteeship over the earth, provides a compelling foundation for sustainability. Human beings may use the earth’s resources within nature’s capacity to regenerate and absorb the effects of human activity, but we do not possess an unlimited moral licence to degrade them. Development that destroys the ecological systems on which society depends is neither responsible nor sustainable. Environmental degradation usually brings both immediate warnings and long-term consequences.

Abuja’s recurring warning

This message has acquired particular urgency in the Federal Capital Territory. Flooding in August 2026 affected several parts of Abuja, including Wuse II, Gudu, Gaduwa, Durumi, Maitama, Katampe, Mabushi, Lugbe and Gwarinpa. The FCT Administration subsequently announced the removal of structures obstructing waterways and, in September, began a citywide drainage-clearing exercise during the peak of the rainy season.

These actions are necessary, but they raise difficult governance questions. What weaknesses in planning approval and enforcement allowed such developments to occur? Were environmental impact assessments undertaken? Why do drainage systems remain blocked until flooding becomes an emergency? Why must residents repeatedly lose homes and businesses before preventive action begins?

Flooding is often described as a natural disaster, but rainfall alone does not explain its human consequences. Heavy rain becomes catastrophic when it meets poor drainage, uncontrolled development, indiscriminate waste disposal, inadequate infrastructure and weak enforcement of planning regulations.

Abuja’s experience illustrates the difference between weather and disaster. The government cannot prevent rain, but public decisions help determine whether rainwater passes through functioning drainage channels or through people’s homes.

Citizens also carry responsibilities. Individual behaviour is a central part of environmental stewardship and climate action. Throwing plastic bottles, food containers and household waste into drains may appear to be a private act, but its consequences are collective. When thousands of such actions converge, drainage channels become refuse dumps and entire communities are placed at risk.

The sermon reminded worshippers: “Do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction” (Qur’an 2:195). That instruction applies to a motorist attempting to cross raging floodwater. It also speaks to every private action and official failure that creates the conditions for preventable harm.

Lessons from Jos and Keana

The sermon also brought back memories of my childhood in Jos and Keana. At the time, the last Saturday of every month was reserved for compulsory environmental sanitation. I remember that virtually every household kept basic implements such as cutlasses, hoes, rakes and brooms. Families used them to clear overgrown surroundings, remove refuse and open drainage channels.

The practice did more than keep our communities clean. It instilled discipline and gave citizens a sense of responsibility and ownership in protecting their environment. Children grew up understanding that environmental sanitation was not the responsibility of the government alone. Every household had a role to play.

That lesson became even more relevant after flooding in Keana, Nasarawa State, in 2025. Reports indicated that the flood destroyed houses and farmlands and disrupted livelihoods. Although no lives were reported lost, the damage showed how quickly rainfall can change from blessing to trial when communities and institutions are inadequately prepared.

The communal ethic I witnessed growing up appears to be weakening. Urbanisation, changing lifestyles and growing dependence on government have gradually displaced a culture of shared environmental responsibility. Today’s climate realities require us to restore that spirit in a more organised and sustainable form.

Government must provide effective waste-management services, drainage infrastructure, planning enforcement and early-warning systems. Citizens must complement these measures by keeping their surroundings clean, protecting drainage channels, planting trees and refusing to turn waterways into refuse dumps. Sustainable environmental governance succeeds when sound public policy is matched by responsible citizenship.

A national pattern of preventable tragedy

The danger extends far beyond the FCT and Keana. Federal flood projections for 2026 identified thousands of communities across 33 states as exposed to varying levels of risk. Yet Nigeria’s flood season continues to follow a painfully familiar cycle. Forecasts are issued, warnings are publicised, rains intensify, communities are displaced, emergency relief is distributed, and public attention fades until the next disaster.

The catastrophe in Mokwa, Niger State, in May 2025, remains one of the clearest warnings. Hundreds of lives were reportedly lost, homes were destroyed, and thousands of residents were displaced. Farmland and infrastructure were also devastated. The tragedy affected food production, household incomes, public health and local economic activity.

The devastating Maiduguri flood of 2024 similarly showed what happens when extreme rainfall intersects with vulnerable infrastructure and inadequate disaster preparedness. Homes, public facilities, and livelihoods disappeared underwater, leaving hundreds of thousands of people displaced.

These disasters show why Nigeria must continue strengthening prevention and preparedness alongside emergency response.

Relief materials are essential after a disaster, but their distribution should not be mistaken for a complete disaster-management policy. Good governance is measured not only by how officials respond after a tragedy, but also by what institutions did before it occurred.

From seasonal reaction to climate governance

Climate change is increasing the intensity and unpredictability of extreme weather. Yet climate change must not become an excuse for administrative failure. It may intensify rainfall, but it does not dump refuse into drains, approve construction on floodplains, neglect critical infrastructure or prevent governments from enforcing building regulations.

Nigeria must move from seasonal flood response to year-round climate governance.

First, flood-risk information produced by the Nigerian Meteorological Agency and the Nigeria Hydrological Services Agency should be integrated into state and local development decisions. Forecasts should determine where construction is permitted, which communities require early evacuation plans and where infrastructure investment must be prioritised.

Second, planning approvals must become more transparent. Residents should be able to determine whether developments around them comply with approved land-use plans and environmental standards. Officials and developers responsible for illegal construction on waterways must be held accountable. Enforcement should be consistent, lawful, transparent and humane.

Third, drainage maintenance should be treated as routine public infrastructure management, not an emergency activity undertaken after flooding begins. Budgets for drainage construction and maintenance should be publicly disclosed, while completed projects should be independently monitored.

Fourth, governments must invest in nature-based solutions. Wetlands, green corridors, urban trees and permeable surfaces absorb and slow rainwater. Paving every available space and removing vegetation may create the appearance of rapid development, but it increases runoff and transfers the cost to vulnerable communities.

Fifth, governments must improve waste management by providing reliable collection services and enforcing sanitation regulations. Households, markets and businesses must also stop treating drainage channels and waterways as dumping grounds.

Finally, disaster preparedness must reach the community level. Flood warnings should be communicated in clear local languages through mosques, churches, traditional institutions, schools, community associations and digital platforms. Communities need evacuation routes, emergency contacts and practical guidance on avoiding flooded roads and assisting affected people without creating further casualties.

Faith must produce responsibility

One of the most striking aspects of Mr Shagari’s sermon was its emphasis on “beneficial rain.” The Prophet Muhammad (SAW) prayed for rain during a drought. When rainfall became excessive, he prayed that its harm be diverted. This reflects a balanced understanding: rain is necessary, but its benefits must be protected, and its risks responsibly managed.

Prayer and policy are not rivals. Faith should sharpen our sense of responsibility. We may pray for beneficial rain, but we must also build and maintain the systems that keep it beneficial.

Mosques and other religious institutions can help translate this message into action. Sermons can promote responsible waste disposal, tree planting, water conservation and compliance with safety warnings. Faith communities can support affected families and participate in neighbourhood environmental initiatives. Religious leaders can also demand accountability from those entrusted with public resources.

The sermon further taught that a believer should help those affected by disaster because believers are like parts of a building, each strengthening the other. This ethic should shape community solidarity and public policy. In economic terms, climate change creates negative externalities and imposes high social costs. Climate disasters affect poor and marginalised people most severely, even though they often contribute least to environmental degradation. Climate governance must therefore be inclusive and centred on protecting vulnerable citizens.

The accountability beyond the rain

Rain exposes more than blocked drains. It exposes the strength of our institutions, the quality of our urban planning and the seriousness of our commitment to human life.

When the same communities flood repeatedly, it suggests that lessons have not been fully translated into action. When forecasts do not produce early interventions, information has failed to become policy. When illegal developments remain until disaster strikes, it raises concerns about the consistency and effectiveness of regulatory enforcement.

The spiritual lesson of rain is ultimately one of accountability. As the sermon reminded us, the earth that comes alive after rainfall points to resurrection and the day when every person will be called to account for what he or she has done.

Public office is also a trust for which an account must be rendered. Officials entrusted with planning approvals, environmental protection, infrastructure and emergency management carry responsibilities that affect lives. Citizens, developers and businesses are equally accountable for how their actions affect the wider community.

Rain will continue to fall. Whether it reaches our farms as nourishment, our reservoirs as water security or our homes as a destructive flood will depend partly on the climate, but also significantly on the decisions we make.

If rain is a blessing, gratitude requires us to preserve its benefits. If it is a trial, wisdom demands preparedness. And if it offers a lesson, good governance demonstrates that we have learned it.

AbdulAzeez Aliyu Elayo is an economist, policy analyst and environmental sustainability advocate. He writes from Maccido Estate, Galadimawa, Abuja.

The views expressed in this article are personal and do not represent those of any institution with which the author is affiliated.

World.title: HURIWA kicks against proposed concession of King’s College
World.content:
By Chioma Obinna

The Human Rights Writers Association of Nigeria, HURIWA, has called on the Federal Government to suspend moves to concession the management of King’s College, Lagos, to the school’s Old Boys’ Association under a proposed Public-Private Partnership, PPP.

HURIWA also demanded the immediate publication of the legal and contractual framework backing the proposed arrangement, insisting that Nigerians should know who would control the school, for how long and under what legal authority.

The rights group, in a press statement by its National Coordinator, Comrade Emmanuel Nnadozie Onwubiko, said an alumni association could not automatically assume the role of proprietor or de facto manager of a federal school simply because it had contributed to the institution’s development.

The group said King’s College was a national institution within Nigeria’s public education system and should not be transferred or subjected to a management arrangement without strict adherence to due process, applicable laws and public accountability.

HURIWA’s position comes amid reported controversy over the proposed PPP arrangement involving the school and its Old Boys’ Association.

The association’s president, Kashim Ibrahim-Imam, has reportedly maintained that the arrangement does not amount to a sale or privatisation of the school.

But HURIWA said the description of the arrangement as a PPP did not, by itself, answer fundamental questions about the proposed management structure.

The group asked: “Who will control the school? For how long? Under what law? Who will determine policy? Who will control finances? Who will employ or transfer teachers? Who will determine fees? What happens to the school’s public assets? And what happens when the PPP expires?”

It said the questions must be answered publicly before any concession arrangement was allowed to proceed.

HURIWA urged the Federal Government, if it intended to proceed with the concession, to ensure that the process was transparent, competitive and compliant with applicable procurement and public-sector rules.

The organisation also rejected what it described as any attempt to give an individual alumni association preferential access to a national public institution without a transparent process.

According to HURIWA, financial contributions by old students towards the development of their alma mater should not automatically translate into ownership or management rights over a federal institution.

The group said such contributions could instead be structured through a properly governed development fund or endowment, with clear rules on how the money would be managed and deployed.

“Money donated to a public institution does not become a title deed to that institution,” HURIWA said.

The rights group also cautioned against using PPP arrangements as a means of transferring the Federal Government’s responsibility for public education to alumni organisations.

It urged the government to provide adequate funding, infrastructure and personnel for public schools while ensuring that any partnership with private organisations was structured around improving facilities and educational standards without compromising public ownership and accountability.

HURIWA also expressed concern over reports of tension between workers and the Old Boys’ Association concerning the future of King’s College.

The group said disagreements surrounding the management of a federal school should be resolved through dialogue and due process and not through intimidation or the deployment of security personnel to enforce a disputed arrangement.

It therefore called for an immediate dialogue involving workers, parents, students, the Old Boys’ Association, education authorities and other relevant stakeholders.

HURIWA further demanded that no irreversible decision concerning the ownership, control or management of the institution be taken until the legal and public-interest issues surrounding the proposed PPP had been addressed.

The group said: “King’s College is not an inheritance to be shared among former students. It is a national institution.

“It belongs within Nigeria’s public education system and must remain accessible, accountable and subject to lawful public oversight.”

HURIWA urged the Minister of Education to disclose the proposed concession agreement, approval documents, legal basis, duration, financial obligations, management structure and safeguards for students and workers.

It also called on the Federal Government to ensure that any future partnership aimed at rehabilitating King’s College was designed to improve the institution without compromising public ownership and accountability.

HURIWA said it would oppose any arrangement which, in its view, used the language of PPP to achieve what would effectively amount to transferring control of a national educational asset to a private association.

The group said: “King’s College is not for sale. King’s College is not an alumni estate. King’s College is a national institution, and its future must be determined openly, lawfully and in the public interest.”

World.title: U-20 Women’s World Cup: 2 Quarter-Final Fixtures Confirmed
World.content:
Two quarter-final fixtures have been confirmed at the 2026 FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup following the latest round of matches.

South Korea will face Italy in the first confirmed quarter-final on Saturday, September 19, while Brazil will take on Spain later the same day.

South Korea and Italy will meet at Arena Sosnowiec in Sosnowiec, with kick-off scheduled for 2pm WAT.

Brazil will then face Spain at the same venue at 5:30pm WAT.

The remaining two quarter-final ties will be decided after Thursday’s round-of-16 matches.

Nigeria booked their place in the last eight after thrashing England 3-0 at Bielsko-Biala Stadium.

Tosin Rafiu opened the scoring for the Falconets in the eighth minute before Seimeyeha Janet

Akekoromowei doubled Nigeria’s lead shortly after half-time.

Mary Mamudu added a third in the 73rd minute to seal Nigeria’s progression.

The Falconets will face the winner of the Poland vs Colombia round-of-16 clash in the quarter-finals on Sunday, September 20, at 2pm WAT at Stadion Miejski ŁKS Łódź.

Canada will also play in the quarter-finals after defeating France 3-1 on Thursday. They will face the winner of the DPR Korea vs Japan tie at 5:30pm WAT on September 20.

Confirmed quarter-final fixtures

Saturday, September 19

South Korea vs Italy — 2pm WAT, Arena Sosnowiec

Brazil vs Spain — 5:30pm WAT, Arena Sosnowiec

Sunday, September 20

Nigeria vs Poland/Colombia — 2pm WAT, Stadion Miejski ŁKS Łódź

Canada vs DPR Korea/Japan — 5:30pm WAT, Stadion Miejski ŁKS Łódź
