Mark Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg at 11.30 a.m. Strasbourg time, an hour his office had published the day before. A prime minister kept an appointment made before the threat arrived.

Donald Trump had threatened tariffs a day earlier if he thought the arrangement “at all a hostile act”, and had signed a procurement memorandum on Canadian goods. Two governments spent the day describing each other to third parties.

Read across the Prime Minister of Canada’s own speech text and media advisory, two White House fact sheets, and the Federal Reserve’s projections and press-conference transcript. Then United States Treasury and Department of Labor releases, Bank of Canada rates, Elections Alberta, and our Washington, Ottawa and Strasbourg reading.

Ottawa Answers From Another Continent

Ursula von der Leyen had told the same chamber on 16 September that Canada should become “the first associate member of the European Union”. She said the two “share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world”.

Carney told the chamber that Canada welcomes the ambition Ursula von der Leyen set out on 16 September, in his office’s published text. Euronews reported him saying the same day that the terminology is Europe’s to choose.

That text says Canada and Europe are “not fair-weather allies” and do not pursue zero-sum deals. He said he is not proposing a third bloc “in order to become a great-power rival – only with better manners”.

The same text sets out critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, artificial intelligence and computing, energy security, space and payments as the fields for cooperation. He offered liquefied natural gas and hydrogen “at large scale” to European buyers.

It says Canada has deposits of “over 34 critical minerals” and is among the top producers of the ten most essential ones. A resource list is the part of an alliance that can be counted.

Afterwards he said Canada is “not in a position, nor seeking, to become a full member of the European Union”, United Press International reported on 17 September. Euronews quoted him saying that what matters is the substance.

Asked about Trump’s criticism, he said Canadians are united that “nobody is going to tell us what language we speak”, the Associated Press reported. The same report quotes him saying: “No one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally.”

Euronews reported on 17 September that Article 217 of the European Union’s treaties is the route officials name for association agreements. Ireland’s foreign minister Helen McEntee said she welcomed the announcement “to explore associate membership for Canada”.

France’s foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the status “will need to be debated, examined in detail and analysed” before France takes a position. Euronews reported that Spain backed the offer on the same day.

Backing the offer and backing its legal form are two different questions. No member state had published a position on the legal form, so far as this desk could establish by midday on 17 September.

A European Commission spokesman answered Washington that the partnership is “not against anyone else, but for our common strength”, Euronews reported. Roberta Metsola announced on 14 September that the Parliament will open an office in Ottawa, the Canadian Press reported.

Washington Shuts A Door It Owns

Trump signed a presidential memorandum on 16 September 2026 titled “Restoring Reciprocity in Government Procurement”. The White House fact sheet of the same date sets out what it directs.

It directs the Office of Management and Budget and the United States Trade Representative to remove “Canadian-origin items” from the federal civil procurement system. The fact sheet the desk read carries no deadline for that work.

The phrase it uses is the federal civil procurement system, which on its face does not reach defence or state contracts. It names no other part of federal buying.

That fact sheet says Canadian companies hold preferential access to over 280 billion United States dollars of the American government procurement system. Trump’s own post put the annual figure at more than 50 billion dollars, BNN Bloomberg reported on 16 September.

The two numbers are not the same measure, because one describes access and the other describes yearly awards. Neither document the desk read shows how either was calculated.

Gabriel Brunet, a spokesman for Dominic LeBlanc, said Canada would “review these measures” in the interest of Canadian businesses and workers. The Canadian Press carried that response on 16 September.

Mélanie Joly said Canada is “still engaging with U.S. counterparts” but that “we need to stand on our two feet”. BNN Bloomberg carried those words on the same day.

The two governments were still talking as the measures landed, on Joly’s own account. A door shut in procurement is not a table cleared.

The White House fact sheet of 8 September bans certain Canadian alcoholic beverages and dairy products from the American market on 29 September 2026. It rests the measures on Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930.

That same fact sheet took rock salt and cement off the tariff list on 15 September, and added all-terrain vehicles and further dairy products. A list that moves both ways is still being argued over.

That fact sheet says the tariffs apply “regardless of whether a good originates under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement”, and puts Canadian retaliation at about US$20 billion of American exports. The Council of the European Union lists an EU-Canada summit for 29 and 30 October 2026, and its listing names no venue.

The United States Census Bureau put American purchases of Canadian goods at US$233.7 billion in the first seven months of 2026. The two measures name alcoholic beverages, dairy products and federal civil purchasing.

Spirits Canada said on 9 September that about half of Canadian spirits production depends on American demand. It puts the sector’s employment at nearly 48,800 full-time equivalent jobs across Canada.

Spirits Canada’s president, Cal Bricker, said in July that tariffs “impact farmers, manufacturers, hospitality businesses, retailers, governments and ultimately consumers in both countries”. A measure arrives as a number and lands on a payroll.

The memorandum and the ban fall within a fortnight of each other, and both come before that summit. A government that shuts one market is arguing for another.

The Market Answers The Committee

The United States Treasury’s daily reading put the two-year government borrowing rate at 4.74 per cent on 16 September, from 4.67 per cent the day before. The ten-year rate moved from 5.00 to 5.01 per cent over the same two days.

The thirty-year rate fell from 5.36 to 5.35 per cent on that reading. Short money answered the committee and long money did not.

Lenders for two years now ask for more, and lenders for thirty years ask for slightly less. The desk reads that as a market pricing the committee’s resolve rather than its failure.

The Associated Press put the Standard and Poor’s 500 index at 7,551.81 at the close on 16 September, down 0.4 per cent. The Dow Jones industrial average closed at 51,461.90 and the Nasdaq composite at 25,978.42.

The Dow fell 631.21 points, or 1.2 per cent, on those same Associated Press figures. The industrial index took the decision harder than the technology index did.

The Bank of Canada’s daily rate put the Canadian dollar at 1.3947 per United States dollar on 16 September, from 1.3917 on 15 September. A currency reads a rate gap before a parliament does.

The committee’s statement went out at 2 p.m. New York time on 16 September, and Trump posted on Truth Social at 4.38 p.m. New York time. Two hours and thirty-eight minutes separated the decision from the demand.

He wrote that American rates should be “1%, or less”, and Axios reported that he did not insult the chairman he appointed. The post ends in capitals: “LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!”

Kush Desai, a White House spokesman, called the decision “rather unfortunate” on Fox News on 16 September. He said it was not “backed by a particularly compelling economic case”.

He added that higher rates would “stop any significant progress” the country has made under the President. A government that cannot set a rate can still grade it.

The Chairman Says Less, On Purpose

The Federal Reserve published the preliminary transcript of Chairman Kevin Warsh’s press conference of 16 September 2026. The version the desk read carries his opening statement and no questions.

It ends on his own line, “And with that, I’ll take a few of your questions”. A chairman who dislikes central-bank talk has cut his own.

That statement has him saying that the plain fact is that inflation is “too high and has been for too long”. It carries his line that the committee’s unanimous vote “shows our resolve to achieve price stability on a timelier basis”.

American Banker’s live coverage quotes him calling data-point dependence “a dangerous preoccupation” and saying that trends matter. He is arguing for fewer words rather than different ones.

The Summary of Economic Projections of 16 September puts the median federal funds rate at 4.1 per cent for the end of 2026. Its full range of participants runs from 3.9 to 4.4 per cent.

The midpoint of the range set that day is 3.875 per cent, which rounds to the bottom of that projection range. No participant projects a lower rate by the end of this year.

The central tendency, which drops the three highest and three lowest projections, runs from 4.1 to 4.4 per cent for 2026. American Banker reported that sixteen of eighteen participants expect at least one further rise this year.

The table records eighteen participants, and says one of them did not submit projections for 2028 and 2029. The document names no participant anywhere.

The United States Department of Labor reported on 17 September that initial claims for unemployment benefit fell to 196,000 in the week to 12 September. The release puts the previous week’s level at an unrevised 206,000.

The four-week moving average stood at 203,250, and insured unemployment fell to 1,730,000 in the week to 5 September. The first labour reading after the decision argued for the decision.

The Pipeline Turns Before The Pump

Brent crude for November settled at US$105.83 a barrel on 16 September, down 2.7 per cent from US$108.75 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate for October settled at US$102.43, down 3.2 per cent from US$105.83 a barrel.

Those are settlement figures on Bloomberg’s wire, published by Rigzone on 16 September. The desk carries settlements because an intraday quotation changes while a page stands still.

A nozzle in a car’s filler at a filling station. The American Automobile Association put the national diesel average at US$6.3103 a gallon for 16 September 2026, against US$3.7008 a year earlier. Photo: Rama, CC BY-SA 2.0 fr

Saudi Arabia is seeking to return about half the capacity of its damaged East-West pipeline within days, and full operations in six weeks. A person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg so on 17 September.

Reuters reported on 17 September that Saudi Arabia is offering Asian refiners more crude through ship-to-ship transfers off Oman’s Sohar port. It cited people familiar with the matter, and said the repair timetable remained unclear.

United States Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the line would restart soon, CNBC reported on 15 September. Crude answered the sentence before the pipeline did.

The American Automobile Association put the national diesel average at US$6.3103 a gallon for 16 September, against US$5.9424 a week earlier. Its page still carried that date when the desk read it on 17 September.

Regular petrol stood at US$4.3672 a gallon against US$3.1862 a year earlier, on the same association figures. A barrel falls in an afternoon and a pump falls over a month.

Two Senators Name A Country

Senators Tim Kaine and Adam Schiff filed a war powers resolution on 16 September 2026 to bar hostilities in or against Oman. Kaine’s own release of that date carries the text.

The resolution says Congress “has not declared war upon the Sultanate of Oman”, Stars and Stripes reported on 16 September. Kaine’s release quotes him saying the President has ordered strikes “in more countries around the world than any President in recent history”.

Schiff said in the same release that Congress “has not authorized any of these commitments of our armed forces”. Two senators have put a name to the next war before it starts.

The Senate’s published schedule for Thursday 17 September lists votes on a college sports bill and on a district judgeship, and no war powers vote. The chamber was due to convene at 10 a.m. Washington time.

The House of Representatives passed a different war powers resolution on Tuesday 15 September by 220 votes to 204. The clerk records roll call 307 on H.Con.Res. 93, which directs the removal of American forces from hostilities with Iran.

A concurrent resolution never reaches the President’s desk, which is why it cannot be vetoed and cannot bind. Congress is building a record rather than a limit.

Alberta Prices Its Own Exit

Alberta’s government released a report on 16 September costing separation at C$50 billion to C$170 billion, about US$36 billion to US$122 billion. The province’s own release puts that range over the first five years after separation.

The University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy wrote it for C$1.5 million, about US$1.1 million, of provincial money. It says a new state would need at least 70,000 civil servants.

The report models two paths and puts the effect on provincial output after twenty years between plus 3.4 and minus 16.2 per cent. Jason Nixon, the finance minister, said the government supports “a strong and sovereign Alberta within a united Canada”.

Elections Alberta puts ten questions to voters on 19 October, one asking whether the province should begin the legal process for a binding separation vote. A government that commissions the bill is not expecting to pay it.

Quebec votes on 5 October, and Éric Grenier’s tracker put the Parti Québécois near 29 per cent on 16 September. His model projected an average of 46 seats across ten thousand simulations, short of a majority.

Two provinces hold votes this autumn while Ottawa negotiates with two capitals abroad. A federation argues loudest about itself when it is busiest elsewhere.

What This Means From Latin America

Brazil’s Copom cut the Selic rate (Brazil’s benchmark interest rate) to 13.75 per cent on 16 September in a unanimous vote. The Federal Open Market Committee raised its own target range on the same afternoon.

The distance between those two decisions is the distance between an inflation that is falling and one that is not. Regional borrowers now pay more in dollars and less at home.

American diesel at US$6.3103 a gallon for 16 September is the freight cost that carries Brazilian soy and Chilean fruit north. Food prices in this region follow that number after a delay of weeks.

Canada spent Thursday accepting a European offer twelve days before American import bans on its alcohol and dairy begin. Several governments in this region have made the same calculation with less ceremony.

Mexico is the third party to the agreement whose origin rules that fact sheet of 8 September sets aside. A rule that does not shield Ottawa is worth reading in Mexico City.

Carney landing back in Ottawa tonight — his office’s media advisory puts him leaving Strasbourg at 4.30 p.m. Strasbourg time and reaching the National Capital Region at 7 p.m. Ottawa time. What he says on landing is Canada’s first answer to the procurement memorandum.

What has Washington done to Canadian trade this week, and when does it bite?

Two things, on two dates. Donald Trump signed a presidential memorandum on 16 September 2026 titled “Restoring Reciprocity in Government Procurement”. The White House fact sheet of that date directs the Office of Management and Budget and the United States Trade Representative to act on it. They work with the Federal Acquisition Regulatory Council to remove “Canadian-origin items” from the federal civil procurement system. The fact sheet the desk read carries no deadline. How did markets and politicians answer the Federal Reserve’s rise?

Short borrowing costs rose and long ones did not. The United States Treasury’s daily reading put the two-year government borrowing rate at 4.74 per cent on 16 September, from 4.67 per cent the day before. The ten-year rate moved from 5.00 to 5.01 per cent, and the thirty-year rate fell from 5.36 to 5.35 per cent. What would Alberta’s referendum on 19 October actually decide?

Whether to start a process, not whether to leave. Elections Alberta puts ten questions to voters on 19 October 2026. One asks whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada. The alternative is that the provincial government begin the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution for a binding referendum on separation. A vote for that second option would open the process rather than end it. Key Facts — What the Federal Reserve did on Wednesday. It raised its target range by a quarter point to between 3.75 per cent and 4.00 per cent on 16 September. That was the first increase since 2023, the vote was twelve to nothing, and officials signalled one more rise this year. — What the Bank of Japan decides on Friday. Its board began a two-day meeting in Tokyo on Thursday and publishes the outcome on 18 September. The rate has been around 1.0 per cent since 16 June. — What Seoul and the energy agency launched today. It covers shared monitoring, early warning and coordinated stockpiling. — Why the Strait of Hormuz decides Asia’s fuel bill. A National Barometer Survey of 1,002 adults, released on 10 September, found 45 per cent against sending military assets and 36 per cent for. — What Japan paid for its imports in August. Imports rose 28.0 per cent on a year earlier, to 11,153.9 billion yen or about US$71 billion. The value of crude oil imports rose 58.7 per cent, on figures Japan’s Ministry of Finance published on 16 September. — Where the Korean won and the Kospi finished. The Kospi closed at 6,715.41 on Thursday, 2.56 points below Wednesday’s 6,717.97. The won closed at 1,382.2 per dollar, 13.6 won weaker, on the Korea Times of 17 September. — What oil did after the Saudi pipeline news. Brent’s previous close was US$105.83 a barrel, and the desk read US$102.01 during Thursday’s session, which is a reading rather than a settlement. A state dinner is set for that evening, and its account says the Chinese business delegation is still unsettled.

The full Asia Intelligence Dossier — the editor’s leader, the deep dive, the country health check and the people who matter — is updated daily by the Rio Times Intelligence Desk. Open the dossier · Read it on the web

Asia spent Thursday between two prices it does not set. Washington made money dearer overnight, and the strait most of the region’s fuel comes through is still shut.

The Federal Reserve raised its target range to between 3.75 per cent and 4.00 per cent on 16 September. The Bank of Japan publishes its own decision on Friday, and Seoul answered the week by signing an energy pact rather than sailing a fleet.

Read in English and Korean this morning, with material from other capitals taken in English editions or agency translation. The desk also read its own Asia file of 16 September.

South Korea: An Agency Signed, A Navy Argued Over

President Lee Jae Myung met Fatih Birol, executive director of the International Energy Agency, at Cheong Wa Dae in Seoul on Thursday. About 70 per cent of Korea’s Middle East crude passes through the Strait of Hormuz, the Korea Herald reported the same day.

Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment and the agency signed the memorandum at the Four Seasons Hotel Seoul that day, under Minister Kim Sung-hwan. It is to monitor oil, gas and grid supply together, and to build shared early warning and stockpiling.

Lee said the Middle East crisis “appears to be posing a major obstacle” to Korea’s shift towards renewable power. Birol said the world is “entering the age of electricity”, and that “Korea is a very good example of that”.

Birol plans to propose at the climate conference in Turkey that electricity reach 35 per cent of energy use by 2035. That share is about 23 per cent now, the Korea Herald reported on 17 September.

The agency’s members released 400 million barrels from emergency reserves in March, the largest coordinated release in its history, and Korea joined it. Korea also reinstated fuel price caps dropped in the 1990s and limited public employees’ car use, the Associated Press reported in March.

Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said at Incheon International Airport on Thursday that “nothing has been decided yet” on a Hormuz deployment. He said Korea “will participate in international cooperation”, with priorities of “the safety of our people and freedom of navigation”.

Woo Won-shik of the Democratic Party of Korea told a foreign ministry question session that this is “rather a war the United States started”. Lee Ki-heon said the party is “absolutely opposed to taking direct part in a war”, the Seoul Economic Daily reported on 17 September.

The desk found no vote, resolution or party position on the record, only two lawmakers speaking at a question session. The presidential office had already taken the question off the National Security Council agenda, the Seoul Economic Daily reported.

Gallup Korea polled 1,000 people from 8 to 10 September and found 55 per cent against a deployment and 32 per cent for it. The Korea Herald carried that release on 11 September.

A National Barometer Survey of 1,002 adults, taken from 7 to 9 September, asked about sending a maritime patrol aircraft or a logistics support ship. It found 45 per cent against and 36 per cent for, and the Korea Herald carried it on 10 September.

Lee holds a news conference at Yeongbingwan at 10 a.m. Seoul time on Friday 18 September, his seventh, running about 90 minutes. The National Assembly confirmed Kim Sung-soo as a Supreme Court justice on Thursday by 227 votes to 28, with 13 abstentions.

Japan: The Eve Of A Decision

The Bank of Japan’s policy board began a two-day meeting in Tokyo on Thursday and publishes its decision on Friday 18 September. The statement is due around 11:30 a.m. Tokyo time and the governor speaks at 3:30 p.m. Tokyo time.

The bank set the uncollateralised overnight call rate at around 1.0 per cent on 16 June and held it there on 31 July. The vote in July was eight to one, with Takata Hajime proposing around 1.25 per cent.

The Bank of Japan’s head office in Nihonbashi, Tokyo. Its board began a two-day meeting on 17 September 2026 and publishes the decision on 18 September. The statement is due around 11:30 a.m. Tokyo time. The rate has been around 1.0 per cent since 16 June 2026. A Reuters poll of 68 economists taken from 1 to 8 September found 66 expecting around 1.25 per cent. That is a forecast, not a decision.

A Reuters poll of 68 economists taken from 1 to 8 September found 66 expecting a rise to around 1.25 per cent. That is a forecast by economists, and we do not yet know what the board will choose.

Japan’s Ministry of Finance reported on 16 September that August imports rose 28.0 per cent on a year earlier. That came to 11,153.9 billion yen, about US$71 billion, and the value of crude oil imports rose 58.7 per cent.

Exports rose 19.3 per cent to 10,048.4 billion yen, about US$64 billion, a twelfth consecutive month of growth. The trade deficit came to 1,105.6 billion yen, about US$7.1 billion, and was the fourth in a row.

The yen’s previous close was 156.26 per dollar, on Trading Economics data read on 17 September. Thursday’s quotations differed across outlets, so the desk carries only that close.

Japan’s Statistics Bureau publishes August consumer prices on 18 September, on its own release schedule. The July rate was 1.9 per cent, on Trading Economics data read on 17 September.

The Price Of Money: A Gap That Widened Overnight

The Federal Reserve raised its target range by a quarter point to between 3.75 per cent and 4.00 per cent on 16 September. It was the first increase since 2023, the vote was twelve to nothing, and officials signalled one more increase this year.

Chair Kevin Warsh told his news conference that day that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”. Officials’ own projections put the rate at 4.1 per cent by the end of 2026, against 3.8 per cent in June.

The Kospi closed at 6,715.41 on Thursday, 2.56 points below Wednesday’s 6,717.97, while the Kosdaq rose. Its range ran from 6,697.85 to 6,795.53 and Seoul largely shrugged the increase off, the Seoul Economic Daily reported.

Foreign investors sold a net 2.28 trillion won, about US$1.6 billion, in a seventh consecutive session of selling. The won closed at 1,382.2 per dollar, 13.6 won weaker, and past 1,380 for the first time in three weeks.

The Bank of Korea’s policy rate is 3.0 per cent after increases in July and August, a gap of up to one percentage point with the American rate. Kim Myung-sil of iM Securities said the August minutes show the bank weighing “the timing and the pace” of further rises.

Bank Indonesia decides on 23 September with its policy rate at 5.75 per cent, unchanged since 19 August. The rupiah’s previous close was 17,677.00 per dollar and the rupee’s was 96.13, on Trading Economics data read on 17 September.

India’s government has been giving households priority over businesses for cooking gas and absorbing most of the price rise. Shortages have forced some eateries to shorten hours or drop dishes, the Associated Press reported in March.

Asia’s central banks now follow a rate set in Washington, in a month when their fuel bill is set in the Gulf. A region that exported its way to surpluses is importing its monetary policy.

China: A Summit Being Assembled In Public

National Public Radio reported on 17 September that Xi Jinping’s state visit is seven days away, which puts it on 24 September. Its account says briefing materials and the Chinese business delegation are still unsettled.

Two American deadlines sit just behind the meeting. A moratorium on rare-earth export controls and a delay to semiconductor export controls both expire on 10 November.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in that report that rare earths “are not flowing as freely as they could”. A Chinese commitment to buy at least 200 more Boeing aircraft is held up by American reluctance to sell replacement spare parts.

At the foreign ministry’s briefing in Beijing on 16 September, spokesperson Guo Jiakun took questions on Japan, European cyber-security rules and Taiwan. The desk read that transcript in full and found no question on the Washington visit, which is an absence rather than a denial.

More than 80 per cent of the oil and gas that leaves the Strait of Hormuz is bound for Asia, the Associated Press reported. Beijing is preparing a summit about chips and rare earths while its oil comes past a war.

Thailand And The Philippines: A Telephone Call And A Subpoena

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said at the Interior Ministry at 10:30 a.m. Bangkok time on Thursday that he may speak to President Donald Trump soon about tariffs. He will discuss the detail with Commerce Minister Suphajee Suthumpun on 18 September, Khaosod English reported.

Thailand faces a 12.5 per cent American tariff under Section 301 of the United States Trade Act, tied to forced-labour import rules. Chotima Iemsawasdikul of the Department of Trade Negotiations said the 10 per cent gap with Malaysia and Indonesia would cost exporters, Thansettakij reported.

The National Bureau of Investigation has flagged 47 of 100 flood-control projects in the Davao City district of Representative Paolo Duterte. Its director Melvin Matibag said so on Thursday, of a programme worth 1.9 billion pesos, about US$30 million on the desk’s conversion.

Matibag said one project carried “one coordinate and five budgets, each with a different title”, and that about six had clear problems. The bureau plans to summon 51 people from three contractors, the public works department and the audit commission.

Rodrigo Duterte appeared in person at the International Criminal Court in The Hague on 16 September. It was his first physical appearance since his arrest in March 2025, on three counts of crimes against humanity covering 76 deaths.

Palace press officer Claire Castro said on Thursday that Duterte “seems to be in good condition” and appeared to accept that the trial would proceed. His own lawyers have argued that he is unfit to take part.

The Quiet Files: Jakarta, Kuala Lumpur And Singapore

President Prabowo Subianto replaced Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa with Suahasil Nazara on 14 September, his third finance minister in under two years. The Jakarta Post reported on Thursday that the state’s planned stake in the Jakarta-Bandung railway is unsettled again.

Worsening haze has delayed a Japanese firefighting mission to West Kalimantan, the same paper reported on Thursday. Indonesia’s fire season and its fuel bill are arriving in the same quarter.

DBS Bank, Bain and Company and Vriens and Partners published a forecast on 16 September for the six largest South-East Asian economies. They would grow 4.8 per cent a year to 2035, with Vietnam at 6.2 per cent and Thailand at 2.2 per cent.

Malaysia plans talks with Myanmar on returning Rohingya refugees, Asia News Network reported on Thursday. The desk could not find a date for those talks in that report.

Singapore’s forecast is 2.7 per cent a year, and its income per head is the highest in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Those two numbers together are the ordinary shape of a mature economy.

What This Means From Latin America

Asia’s fuel bill is now set by a strait on the other side of the world, and Latin American producers sell into the same market. Brent‘s previous close was US$105.83 a barrel, and that is the number regional producers budget against.

The Federal Reserve’s move to between 3.75 per cent and 4.00 per cent makes dollars dearer for everyone who borrows in them. Brazilian, Mexican and Colombian borrowers have met that arithmetic in every previous American tightening.

If the Bank of Japan raises its rate on Friday, as 66 of 68 economists in a Reuters poll expect, money borrowed cheaply in yen becomes costlier to hold. Unwinding those positions has moved the Brazilian real and the Mexican peso in past cycles.

Korea’s new programme is about monitoring and stockpiles as much as about climate, and electrification consumes copper and lithium. Chile, Peru and Brazil sell both, and a buyer who plans for shocks buys differently from one who reacts to them.

What We Are Watching

The Bank of Japan’s decision on Friday — Whether the board moves from around 1.0 per cent, set on 16 June, to around 1.25 per cent. A Reuters poll of 68 economists taken from 1 to 8 September found 66 expecting that rise.

— Whether the board moves from around 1.0 per cent, set on 16 June, to around 1.25 per cent. A Reuters poll of 68 economists taken from 1 to 8 September found 66 expecting that rise. President Lee’s news conference in Seoul — Ninety minutes at 10 a.m. Seoul time on Friday 18 September at Yeongbingwan, his seventh. Whether he answers on a Hormuz deployment is the question the day turns on.

— Ninety minutes at 10 a.m. Seoul time on Friday 18 September at Yeongbingwan, his seventh. Whether he answers on a Hormuz deployment is the question the day turns on. Japan’s consumer prices for August — Japan’s Statistics Bureau publishes them on 18 September, in the same hours as the rate decision. The July rate was 1.9 per cent.

— Japan’s Statistics Bureau publishes them on 18 September, in the same hours as the rate decision. The July rate was 1.9 per cent. Whether Korea sends ships to the Gulf — Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said on 17 September that nothing has been decided yet, before leaving for the United States. Two governing-party lawmakers said the same day that they are opposed, and the presidential office took the question off the National Security Council agenda.

— Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said on 17 September that nothing has been decided yet, before leaving for the United States. Two governing-party lawmakers said the same day that they are opposed, and the presidential office took the question off the National Security Council agenda. Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington — National Public Radio reported on 17 September that the visit is seven days away and the Chinese delegation is not yet fixed. The rare-earth and semiconductor deadlines of 10 November sit behind it.

— National Public Radio reported on 17 September that the visit is seven days away and the Chinese delegation is not yet fixed. The rare-earth and semiconductor deadlines of 10 November sit behind it. Bank Indonesia’s decision on 23 September — Whether a policy rate of 5.75 per cent holds after an American increase. The rupiah’s previous close was 17,677.00 per dollar, and this is the new finance minister’s first test from outside the cabinet.

— Whether a policy rate of 5.75 per cent holds after an American increase. The rupiah’s previous close was 17,677.00 per dollar, and this is the new finance minister’s first test from outside the cabinet. The Saudi East-West pipeline’s return — Saudi Arabia could restore about half the damaged capacity within days and the rest within six weeks, Bloomberg reported on 16 September. The desk read Brent at US$102.01 during Thursday’s session, against a previous close of US$105.83.

The Bigger Picture Asia built its prosperity on cheap freight and cheap money, and both were rented rather than owned. Thursday was the day the rent came due in two currencies at once. The region has been here before, in 1973 and again in 1979, when an oil shock and dearer dollars arrived together. What followed each time was a decade of building stockpiles, pipelines and terminals. That is the cycle Korea’s new programme belongs to, and its own timetable reaches only to 2028. Institutions built during a squeeze usually outlast the squeeze that built them. None of this is a reason for a reader to move money this week. It is a reason to expect the next quarter’s figures to look different from the last one’s.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Federal Reserve decide, and why does Asia care?

The Federal Reserve raised its target range by a quarter point on 16 September 2026, to between 3.75 per cent and 4.00 per cent. It was the first increase since 2023 and the vote was twelve to nothing. Chair Kevin Warsh told his news conference that day that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”. Officials’ own projections now put the rate at 4.1 per cent by the end of 2026, against 3.8 per cent in June. Asia cares because much of the region’s trade finance is priced in dollars, and because a wider gap between American and local rates pulls money out of local markets. Foreign investors sold a net 2.28 trillion won of Korean shares on 17 September, about US$1.6 billion. That was a seventh consecutive session of selling, and the won closed 13.6 won weaker at 1,382.2 per dollar.

Why is the Strait of Hormuz an Asian problem?

Because most of what passes through it is going to Asia. The Associated Press reported in the Korea Herald on 29 March 2026 that more than 80 per cent of the oil and liquefied natural gas transiting the strait is bound for Asia. The Korea JoongAng Daily put that share at roughly 90 per cent on a different basis, and we carry the lower figure. The Korea Herald reported on 17 September 2026 that about 70 per cent of Korea’s Middle East crude comes through the same water. Japan’s August import bill shows the effect. Its Ministry of Finance reported on 16 September that imports rose 28.0 per cent on a year earlier, to 11,153.9 billion yen or about US$71 billion. The value of crude oil imports rose 58.7 per cent, and the trade deficit came to 1,105.6 billion yen, about US$7.1 billion.

What is the new Korean energy programme, and what does it do?

Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment and the International Energy Agency launched it in Seoul on 17 September 2026. It is called the Resilient and Integrated Strategy for Energy Security in Asia. It provides for joint monitoring of oil, liquefied natural gas and clean-energy supply chains, together with power-grid reliability. It also provides for shared early warning and coordinated stockpiling, for electrification plans in smaller economies, and for a standing policy forum. Its own timetable finishes the cooperative structure in 2027 and the crisis protocols in 2028, with building work after that. It moves no oil this week, and it is a monitoring compact rather than a supply guarantee. President Lee Jae Myung and the agency’s executive director Fatih Birol discussed it at Cheong Wa Dae the same day.

What does any of this change for someone living in Latin America?

Three things, in plain terms. First, dollar borrowing became dearer on 16 September, and Brazilian, Mexican and Colombian borrowers have met that arithmetic in every previous American tightening. Second, a Reuters poll of 68 economists taken from 1 to 8 September found 66 of them expecting the Bank of Japan to raise its rate to around 1.25 per cent on 18 September. If it does, money borrowed cheaply in yen and held elsewhere costs more to hold. Unwinding those positions has moved the Brazilian real and the Mexican peso in past cycles. Third, Asia’s answer to its energy squeeze is electrification, stockpiles and grids, which consume the copper and lithium that Chile, Peru and Brazil sell. None of these is a reason to act today, and all three are reasons to read the next quarter closely.

Sources: The Korea Herald, Korea JoongAng Daily, Seoul Economic Daily, The Korea Times and SBS News. Also National Public Radio, Nation Thailand carrying Thansettakij, Khaosod English and Thailand Business News. And Philippine Daily Inquirer, Philippine Star, Daily Tribune, The Jakarta Post and Asia News Network carrying The Straits Times. Also Al Jazeera, FXStreet carrying the Reuters poll, Trading Economics and investingLive. Those outlets carried reports from Reuters, Bloomberg, Kyodo News and the Associated Press. Primary documents: the Federal Open Market Committee statement of 16 September 2026. Also the Bank of Japan’s statement on monetary policy of 31 July 2026 and its published 2026 meeting schedule. Also the International Energy Agency’s collective action decision of March 2026 to release 400 million barrels, as carried by the Korea Herald. Also Japan’s Ministry of Finance trade statistics for August 2026 and Japan’s Statistics Bureau release schedule. And the Chinese foreign ministry’s regular press conference transcript of 16 September 2026, read in full. Reporting from 11 to 17 September 2026. Currency conversions are desk calculations against rates read on 17 September 2026 and are approximate.

Africa Intelligence Brief — Thursday, September 17, 2026

A health worker in protective equipment giving an Ebola vaccination in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The World Health Organization counted 6,757 confirmed cases and 3,267 deaths in the country to 7 September. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control counted 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 deaths to 13 September, with 5,659 of them in Ituri. Photo: MONUSCO Photos, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Africa Intelligence Dossier — Thursday, 17 September 2026 · Web edition Take it with you. The full dossier is published on the web. Read the web dossier → · The dossier archive →

Key Facts — How many people the Congolese epidemic has killed. The World Health Organization counted 6,757 confirmed cases and 3,267 deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo to 7 September. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control counted 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 deaths to 13 September. — What the two delegations in Geneva were meeting about. The seventh Joint Security Coordination Mechanism ran in Geneva from 16 to 17 September. It monitors the Washington Accords of 4 December 2025 between the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda. — How many women have been found dead in Ekurhuleni. Police found a ninth body at Dawn Park on the morning of Thursday, 17 September. Independent Online counted nine women in nine weeks in and around the East Rand. — How many people died at the Sudanese mine. The Kordofan Observatory counted at least 70 dead on 16 September. A Rapid Support Forces source, speaking anonymously to Agence France-Presse, gave at least 82 killed and 50 wounded. — What the American central bank decided on Wednesday. The Federal Open Market Committee raised its target range a quarter point, to between 3.75 and 4 per cent, on 16 September. The vote was twelve to nothing, and it was the first rise since July 2023. — What a barrel of Brent crude settled at. Brent crude for November settled at US$105.83 a barrel on Wednesday, 16 September, US$2.92 below Tuesday. The session ranged from US$104.00 to US$105.83. — When Morocco votes and how many voters are registered. Morocco’s thirteen-day campaign closes at midnight on 22 September and the country votes on 23 September. The register holds 15,801,162 voters for 395 seats.

The full Africa Intelligence Dossier — the editor’s leader, the deep dive, the country health check and the people who matter — is updated daily by the Rio Times Intelligence Desk. Open the dossier · The dossier archive

The Democratic Republic of the Congo is running three emergencies through one government. Geneva holds the war talks, Ituri holds the epidemic, and Kinshasa holds the argument about the constitution.

Elsewhere the day was about counts and prices. Sudan cannot agree how many of its miners died, and Washington has raised the cost of borrowing in dollars.

Read in English, French, Arabic, Portuguese and Swahili, across the continent’s largest outlets and our own Africa desk. Every figure below carries the source that published it and the date.

DR Congo: A War In Geneva, An Epidemic In Ituri

The seventh meeting of the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism opened in Geneva on Wednesday, 16 September, and closed on 17 September. Delegations from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda attended, with the United States, Qatar, Togo and the African Union Commission.

The mechanism monitors the Washington Accords, signed on 4 December 2025, which reaffirmed a peace agreement of 27 June 2025. Kinshasa undertook to neutralise the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda, a Rwandan Hutu armed group in eastern Congo.

Olivier Nduhungirehe, Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, said on 15 September that Kigali would continue to defend itself. He said the Congolese government still arms that group, and that Rwanda has lifted some of its own measures.

Patrick Muyaya, the Congolese Minister of Information and government spokesperson, said Kinshasa is meeting its commitments and accused Rwanda of expansionist ambitions. Al Jazeera carried his account on 16 September, with President Paul Kagame calling the arrangement on that armed group insufficient.

Al Jazeera reported on 15 September that neither central security commitment has been declared complete, and that fighting continues in North and South Kivu. Whether Geneva issued a joint statement, as the sixth meeting did in August, was not known when this edition closed.

Those same eastern provinces carry an epidemic. The World Health Organization counted 6,757 confirmed cases and 3,267 deaths in the country to 7 September, publishing on 10 September.

The organisation gave a case fatality ratio of 48.3 per cent for the country, the share of confirmed patients who died. Its wider count, which adds 20 cases in Uganda and one in France, was 6,778 cases and 3,269 deaths.

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control counted 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 deaths to 13 September. Ituri holds 5,659 of those cases and North Kivu 1,281, on the European centre’s figures.

The two counts are the same national reporting series read six days apart. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus of the World Health Organization gave higher figures again on 16 September, of more than 7,200 cases.

He put the deaths at more than 3,500 across seven provinces. He spoke at an online news conference and led with progress, saying the organisation is starting to see encouraging signs.

Transmission is going down in the most affected parts of Ituri, and South Kivu has reported no new cases since May. He said more than 1,700 people have recovered and that vaccine trials should begin in the coming weeks.

He said the area is so vast that it is hard to speak of a single epidemic. Weekly cases in North Kivu have doubled over two weeks, from 100 to more than 200.

He then said: “But make no mistake. The epidemic continues to grow, and continues to kill.”

He said the epidemic has been contained mostly in north-eastern Congo after four months, apart from a small Ugandan outbreak that was stopped quickly. The European centre said that outbreak was declared over on 25 August, after a 42-day countdown.

The European centre also counted 1,726 recoveries and 905 people in hospital isolation, with 78.6 per cent of contacts under follow-up. Meg Doherty, who directs science and research at the organisation, said it has vaccinated more than 3,000 health and front-line workers.

They were given Merck’s Ervebo, which is licensed against Zaire ebolavirus. Its effect on the Bundibugyo strain driving this outbreak is not known.

Julien Harneis, the United Nations Special Ebola Coordinator, called it a deadly and massive epidemic, with progress in some areas and growth in others. TimesLIVE carried his remarks on 16 September, with those of Olivier le Polain of the World Health Organization.

Le Polain said it is too early to say a peak has passed, and that full control would take many months. Jean-Jacques Muyembe, who directs the National Institute for Biomedical Research, said the indicators in Ituri are turning green.

Kinshasa also policed its own streets this week. Al Jazeera reported that police fired tear gas as hundreds protested in the capital on Tuesday, 15 September, against proposed constitutional changes.

The same report gave at least ten arrests, with demonstrations also in Lubumbashi and Uvira. Critics say the changes could allow President Félix Tshisekedi to seek a third term, which the two-term limit now bars.

The marches were a nationwide day of action called by the C64 coalition, forged by opposition parties to defeat that attempt. Parliament made a change possible in June by allowing constitutional amendment through a referendum, and the Catholic Church has condemned the proposal.

Mohamed Eyenga of the Envol party, a senior figure in C64, said many activists were arbitrarily arrested. General Blaise Kilimbalimba, the provincial police commander, said peaceful demonstrators had not been arrested.

Tshisekedi announced a national dialogue three weeks before the marches, bringing in opposition parties, civil society groups and religious leaders. That dialogue excludes M23 and other armed groups, and Kinshasa is running a separate dialogue with the political alliance behind M23.

One government is negotiating, counting and policing at the same time. Three files, three cities, and only one of them has a closing date.

South Africa: A Year Of Police Evidence, And A Ninth Body

The Madlanga Commission marked one year of hearings on Thursday, 17 September. Independent Online counted 110 witnesses across 174 hearing days, and 1,894 calls to the commission’s hotline.

A South African Police Service patrol van. The Madlanga Commission of Inquiry marked one year of hearings on Thursday, 17 September. It examines criminality, political interference and corruption in South Africa’s criminal justice system, and has heard 110 witnesses over 174 hearing days.

The commission also holds 750 bundles of documentary evidence, on the same count. It examines criminality, political interference and corruption in the criminal justice system, and reports to President Cyril Ramaphosa.

Jeremy Michael, the commission’s spokesperson, said the one-year mark is significant because real consequences have followed while the inquiry is still under way. The South African Government News Agency carried his remarks on 17 September.

The commission exists because Lieutenant General Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi, the KwaZulu-Natal police commissioner, made allegations at a media briefing on 6 July 2025. Ramaphosa announced the inquiry that month.

On 15 September the National Prosecuting Authority withdrew four charges under the Public Finance Management Act against General Fannie Masemola, the suspended national police commissioner. Andy Mothibi, the National Director of Public Prosecutions, ordered the withdrawal.

The Daily Maverick reported on 15 September that the police health-services tender was budgeted at 360 million rand, with 228 million rand awarded. That is about US$22 million and US$13.9 million at 16.37 rand to the dollar, the close Trading Economics reported for 16 September.

The prosecuting authority said it was satisfied there were no reasonable prospects of a successful prosecution. It also withdrew charges against Lieutenant General Dumisani Khumalo and six crime intelligence officials.

Lesiba Thobakgale of the South African Police Union told Independent Online on 17 September that the prosecutions were meant to demean and damage the leadership. Ian Cameron, who chairs the parliamentary police committee, warned against calling every failed prosecution a weaponised one.

Police found a ninth woman’s body at Dawn Park in Ekurhuleni on the morning of Thursday, 17 September. Major General Fred Kekana, the acting Gauteng provincial commissioner, said the remains had been dumped there.

Independent Online reported the same day that nine women have been found dead in and around the East Rand over nine weeks. Three have been publicly named: Itumeleng Kekana, Elizabeth Moselakgomo and Dineo Evelyn Motapane.

Zizipho Ntoyanto, a resident, told Independent Online that people are scared and living in fear, and asked for soldiers. Lieutenant General Tebello Mosikili, the deputy national commissioner, said investigators are very much able and capable.

The South African Human Rights Commission put the number of women killed between April and June 2026 at 569, with 1,052 survivors of attempted murder. It said South Africa is not a safe place for women, in figures Independent Online carried on 17 September.

The commission has joined the Commission for Gender Equality and the CRL Rights Commission in a national inquiry into gender-based violence and femicide. The CRL body covers cultural, religious and linguistic communities, and the inquiry runs from 28 September to 2 October.

It will examine how cases are reported and investigated, what support victims receive, and how the justice system handles cases before trial. The commission also said 8,814 rape cases were reported in the first quarter of the year.

Police said one suspect has been arrested and a second identified, without clarifying which of the nine cases either is linked to. They have formed a multidisciplinary team to investigate the deaths and to establish whether the cases are connected.

The rewards on offer reached a combined 900,000 rand, about US$55,000 at the same rate. The Democratic Alliance’s Ekurhuleni mayoral candidate, Khathutshelo Rasilingwane, offered 500,000 rand for information leading to a successful prosecution, and the police 400,000 rand.

Pixie du Toit, a criminologist and criminal profiler, said the killings fit the pattern of a serial killer. She said the guidelines require three murders “within a very short period in the same area”, and much the same method.

Crezane Bosch, the Democratic Alliance’s spokesperson on community safety, said serious and violent crimes remain a concern at several Gauteng police stations. She said that is so despite declines in major crime categories across the province.

Janey du Plessis, a Kempton Park resident, said the deaths had changed how people go about their days. She said it is so close to home that she walks to her local shop with her daughter, and that “everyone is vigilant”.

The Presidency said on 16 September that Ramaphosa had been advised by his medical team to rest, after returning from the BRICS summit in India. He has asked ministers to represent him at scheduled public engagements.

A year of testimony has produced 110 witnesses and a withdrawn indictment against the man who ran the police. The state is learning what it is faster than it can act on it.

Sudan: Three Counts Of The Same Dead At Al-Zara

An unregulated gold working at al-Zara, near al-Nuhud in West Kordofan, gave way on Tuesday. The Kordofan Observatory reported it on Wednesday, 16 September, and counted at least 70 dead.

A source in the Rapid Support Forces, which controls the area, told Agence France-Presse that at least 82 people were killed and 50 wounded. The source requested anonymity, and both Al Jazeera and France 24 carried that agency copy.

Al-Amin Suliman, a miner, said 60 bodies had been recovered by Wednesday morning and that people were still stuck inside. The Sudan Doctors Network said search efforts were continuing and that the casualty figure could rise.

Khair al-Sayyed Jabara, a survivor, told Agence France-Presse that he and fellow miners dug through the night with their own tools. He said heavy equipment was needed, and that they did not know how many more were still inside.

The Kordofan Observatory said no specialised rescue teams had joined the effort, and that residents with rudimentary tools were struggling in loose, sandy soil. The Rapid Support Forces have controlled West Kordofan since April 2023, and smuggled gold is a key source of revenue.

The Sudan Doctors Network said the site was missing basic safeguards and condemned the negligence it said put miners at serious risk. It said mining under that control makes mining a direct threat to civilians.

A war economy runs on gold, and this gold is dug by hand. The one figure nobody has settled is how many men were under it.

Nigeria: A Refinery Sells Shares Into A Dearer Dollar

Dangote Petroleum Refinery opened a public share offer on the Nigerian Exchange on Monday, 14 September. Vanguard put the offer at 2.15 trillion naira, about US$1.6 billion if fully subscribed, at 525 naira a share.

That gloss uses 1,329.86 naira to the dollar, the official rate Naija News reported from the Central Bank of Nigeria for Wednesday, 16 September. Forbes Africa reported on 9 September that the offer closes on 13 October, with a listing planned for November.

The refinery runs at 700,000 barrels a day, with an expansion to 1.4 million planned by 2028. Aliko Dangote called it an offer “for the people”, meant to widen ownership among Nigerians and other eligible investors.

The Federal Open Market Committee raised its target range by a quarter point, to between 3.75 and 4 per cent, on Wednesday, 16 September. The vote was twelve to nothing, and it was the first increase since July 2023.

The committee said inflation remains elevated and that the action supports a timelier return to its 2 per cent goal. Kevin Warsh has chaired the Federal Reserve since 22 May 2026.

Nairametrics reported on 17 September that Nigeria’s own rate decision falls on 21 and 22 September. The Central Bank of Nigeria retained its policy rate at 26.5 per cent at its meeting of 21 July.

Muda Yusuf of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise told Nairametrics that portfolio money may move towards the United States. He also said Nigeria’s high domestic yields could limit that movement.

Brent crude for November settled at US$105.83 a barrel on Wednesday, 16 September, US$2.92 below Tuesday’s US$108.75. The session ranged from US$104.00 to US$105.83, on the settlement data DTN Progressive Farmer published.

Bloomberg reported on 16 September, citing an unnamed person, that Saudi Arabia is working to restore half the pipeline’s capacity within days. It put the East–West line at seven million barrels a day, against four to five million in Al Jazeera on 12 September.

Nigeria’s 2026 budget assumes US$64.85 a barrel, on the figure allAfrica reported on 9 September. A barrel above one hundred dollars is revenue for Abuja and a bill for Nairobi.

The African Peer Review Mechanism opens the Africa Credit Rating Agency in Port Louis, Mauritius, on 7 October. Nairametrics reported on 2 September that it is to rate sovereign and corporate debt in local currency.

The African Union says skewed risk perception has made African states pay an unfair premium on global capital. A new rating agency and a higher American rate reach the same borrower from opposite directions.

Morocco: Thirteen Days Of Campaign Before The Vote On 23 September

Morocco’s official campaign opened at midnight on 10 September and closes at midnight on 22 September. Morocco World News reported that twenty-seven parties are contesting 395 seats in the House of Representatives.

The same report put the register at 15,801,162 voters, 54 per cent male and 55 per cent urban. Al Jazeera reported on 17 September that 4 per cent are aged 18 to 24, and 29 per cent are 60 or over.

Al Jazeera gave youth unemployment at 37.3 per cent and overall unemployment at 13 per cent for 2025. It gave real growth of 4.9 per cent in 2025 and a projection of 4.4 per cent for 2026, without naming the forecaster.

The governing coalition is the National Rally of Independents, the Authenticity and Modernity Party and Istiqlal. They took 102, 87 and 81 seats in 2021, when the Justice and Development Party fell from 125 seats to 13.

Parties are campaigning on employment, purchasing power and public services, on Al Jazeera’s account of 17 September. The register’s over-sixties outnumber its under-twenty-fives seven to one.

Guinea And Equatorial Guinea: A Channel Banned And Two Applications Blocked

Guinea’s Haute Autorité de la Communication, the state broadcasting regulator, banned France 24 from Guinean territory with immediate effect on Thursday, 17 September. It withdrew at the same time the accreditations of all the channel’s correspondents, special envoys and collaborators in Guinea.

The regulator cited what it called the channel management’s manifest, deliberate and characterised refusal to apply the formal notice it issued on 16 September. Guinéematin named its president as Boubacar Yacine Diallo, and the Guinean reports the desk read did not print the disputed word.

That notice had objected to a description of President Mamadi Doumbouya in a news broadcast the day before. Doumbouya took the oath as Guinea’s civilian president on 18 January 2026, after an election in December 2025.

The regulator also withdrew the accreditation of Jeune Afrique’s permanent correspondent in Guinea, Mamadou Diawo Barry, in a communiqué of 16 September. It accused him of grave violations of the ethical obligations that govern journalism on national territory.

In Equatorial Guinea, Facebook and TikTok have been unreachable for more than two weeks, and internet speeds have been restricted since 2 September. Agence France-Presse reported on 16 September that the blocks followed a video accusing Vice-President Teodoro Nguema Obiang of corruption.

The woman who posted the video was arrested, and the agency said the information ministry did not answer its questions. WhatsApp and Instagram remain reachable with limits, and a virtual private network still gets past the blocks.

Two governments spent the week narrowing what may be said about them. A ban and a blocked application are the same instrument at different ranges.

What This Means From Latin America

The Federal Open Market Committee’s quarter-point rise reaches Bogotá and Lagos through the same channel. A dearer dollar raises the cost of servicing dollar debt for commodity exporters on both sides of the Atlantic.

Brent at US$105.83 is revenue for Brazilian and Colombian producers and a fuel bill for Kenya and Morocco. Nigeria’s 2026 budget assumes US$64.85, so the same barrel reads as surplus in Abuja and as subsidy arithmetic in Nairobi.

The Africa Credit Rating Agency opens in Port Louis on 7 October to contest the ratings that price African debt. Latin American issuers are rated by the same three houses.

What We Are Watching

Whether Geneva publishes a joint statement — the seventh Joint Security Coordination Mechanism closed on 17 September, and the sixth meeting issued a joint statement in August.

— the seventh Joint Security Coordination Mechanism closed on 17 September, and the sixth meeting issued a joint statement in August. Whether North Kivu’s weekly case count turns — weekly cases there doubled from 100 to more than 200 in two weeks, while Ituri’s transmission is going down, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.

— weekly cases there doubled from 100 to more than 200 in two weeks, while Ituri’s transmission is going down, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said. Whether police connect the nine Ekurhuleni deaths — one suspect has been arrested and a second identified. A multidisciplinary team is examining whether the cases are connected, and the rewards on offer total 900,000 rand.

— one suspect has been arrested and a second identified. A multidisciplinary team is examining whether the cases are connected, and the rewards on offer total 900,000 rand. How many bodies Sudan finally counts at al-Zara — three published counts run from 60 bodies recovered to at least 82 killed, and the Sudan Doctors Network said search efforts were continuing.

— three published counts run from 60 bodies recovered to at least 82 killed, and the Sudan Doctors Network said search efforts were continuing. What the Nigerian rate committee does on 21 and 22 September — the policy rate has stood at 26.5 per cent since 21 July, and Washington has since raised its own.

— the policy rate has stood at 26.5 per cent since 21 July, and Washington has since raised its own. Whether Morocco’s young voters turn out on 23 September — 4 per cent of the register is aged 18 to 24, against 29 per cent aged 60 or over, Al Jazeera reported.

— 4 per cent of the register is aged 18 to 24, against 29 per cent aged 60 or over, Al Jazeera reported. When the Africa Credit Rating Agency opens in Port Louis — the launch is set for 7 October, and it is to rate sovereign and corporate debt in local currency.

The Bigger Picture Three of the day’s African files were about counting rather than deciding. Congo counted its dead, Sudan published three counts that disagree, and Morocco counted the people entitled to vote. The Congolese state is being asked to do three difficult things at once with one set of officials. Geneva wants a security commitment, Ituri wants epidemiologists, and Kinshasa wants police on its own streets. What the desk could not establish is named where it belongs. Geneva’s outcome was unpublished at press time, and no Guinean report the desk read printed the word France 24 used. For a reader with money or family in these places, the practical movements were a rate, a barrel and a share offer. All three changed the price of borrowing in a week when the cost of governing rose in three places.

Frequently Asked Questions

How bad is the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo?

The World Health Organization counted 6,757 confirmed cases and 3,267 deaths in the country to 7 September, a case fatality ratio of 48.3 per cent. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control counted 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 deaths to 13 September, the same series six days later.

What are the delegations in Geneva meeting about?

The seventh Joint Security Coordination Mechanism ran in Geneva from 16 to 17 September, with the two governments and four outside parties. It monitors the Washington Accords of 4 December 2025, under which Kinshasa neutralises one armed group and Kigali disengages its forces.

How many people died at the Sudanese mine?

The Kordofan Observatory counted at least 70 dead, and an anonymous Rapid Support Forces source gave Agence France-Presse at least 82 killed and 50 wounded. A miner said 60 bodies had been recovered by Wednesday morning, and the Sudan Doctors Network said search efforts were continuing.

What does the American rate rise mean for African borrowers?

The Federal Open Market Committee raised its target range to between 3.75 and 4 per cent on 16 September, its first rise since July 2023. Muda Yusuf of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise told Nairametrics that portfolio money may move towards the United States.

Sources: World Health Organization, European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, Federal Reserve Board, Central Bank of Nigeria, South African Government News Agency, United States Department of State. Also Al Jazeera, TimesLIVE, Independent Online, Daily Maverick, News24, Courthouse News Service, France 24. And allAfrica, Nairametrics, Vanguard, Forbes Africa, Naija News, DTN Progressive Farmer, Trading Economics, Morocco World News, Guinéematin, Guinee360, Africanews, Security Council Report · 10-17 September 2026.

World.title: Europe Intelligence Brief — Thursday, September 17, 2026
World.content:
Europe Intelligence Brief — Thursday, September 17, 2026

A child at a tablet computer. Ursula von der Leyen and Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen presented the EU KIDS Act on 17 September 2026. The proposal would bar social media platforms from reaching children under 13 and set 15 as the age for an account held without a guardian.

Europe Intelligence Dossier — Thursday, 17 September 2026 · Web edition Take it with you. The full dossier is published on the web. Read the web dossier → · All Europe dossiers →

Key Facts — What Brussels proposed for children online. The European Commission tabled the EU KIDS Act in Strasbourg on 17 September 2026. Its own notice says the text bars social media platforms from reaching children under 13, and sets 15 as the age for an independent account. — Who now has to prove a service is safe. Ursula von der Leyen said the proposal reverses the burden of proof, so that platforms must show they are safe by design. The Commission’s title for it reads EU Keeping Internet Digital Spaces Accountable and Trustworthy. — How Sweden’s election finally ended. The Election Authority’s updated preliminary result gave the four opposition parties 176 of the 349 Riksdag seats against 173 for the governing bloc. Ulf Kristersson asked the speaker to relieve him of his duties as prime minister on 17 September 2026. — What Canada was offered in the European Parliament. Mark Carney told the chamber at 11.30 a.m. Strasbourg time on 17 September 2026 that Canada welcomes the Union’s ambition of associate membership. Donald Trump had called the proposal laughable the day before and threatened tariffs on Europe. — Why the Dutch prime minister is still short of votes. Rob Jetten answered the second day of the general political debate in The Hague on 17 September 2026 without choosing between left and right. His minority cabinet needs ten more votes in the lower house and sixteen in the senate, DutchNews.nl reported on 14 September 2026. — What drivers are paying at European fuel pumps. Diesel in Germany reached 2.404 euros a litre (about US$2.77) at the start of the week, the motoring association ADAC said. Two days later the same association put petrol and diesel together at 2.45 euros a litre (about US$2.83), Euronews reported. — Where interest rates now stand on both sides of the Atlantic. The European Central Bank raised its deposit rate a quarter point to 2.50 per cent with effect from 16 September 2026. The Federal Reserve raised its target range to between 3.75 and 4.00 per cent the same day, by a vote of twelve to nothing.

The full Europe Intelligence Dossier is updated daily by the Rio Times Intelligence Desk. It carries the editor’s leader, the deep dive on the day Europe put an age on the internet, the country health check and the people who matter. Open the dossier · All Europe dossiers

Europe spent Thursday turning Wednesday’s speeches into paper. A law about children was tabled in Strasbourg, a Swedish count produced a resignation letter, and a Canadian prime minister came to explain his invitation.

Three of the four files this desk was watching closed during the day. The fourth, a Dutch budget without a majority, spent another day being argued.

Read across the European Commission’s own publications, the Federal Reserve’s own statement and the Canadian prime minister’s own text of his speech. Read also across Dutch, Swedish, Canadian and Brazilian outlets, with the Dutch budget debate followed in Dutch, and our own Europe desk.

Brussels Puts An Age On The Internet

The European Commission tabled the EU KIDS Act in Strasbourg on 17 September 2026, together with a communication on online child safety. The acronym stands for EU Keeping Internet Digital Spaces Accountable and Trustworthy.

The Commission’s own notice says the proposal prohibits social media platforms from accessing children under the age of 13. It also sets 15 as the Union-wide age at which a minor may open an account without a guardian.

Ursula von der Leyen said the act reverses the burden of proof, so that it is for platforms to show they are safe by design. She said Europe’s children are using technology “that was never created with their wellbeing in mind”.

The Commission’s overview page puts the case for the law in hours. Adolescents aged 13 to 18 average 4.5 hours a day on screens on school days and 6.1 at weekends.

Only half of children aged 9 to 16 across Europe say they feel safe online, that page reports. Cyberbullying is consistently the main reason for contacting the Safer Internet Centres, and 38 per cent report difficulty falling asleep because of social media.

The same page says the act will apply to social media, video-sharing platforms, online games, AI chatbots or companions, app stores and operating systems. Some services are proposed to be exempt, among them encyclopaedias, educational platforms and digital news.

The narrower list is the reach of the age rules alone. The Commission’s questions and answers say those apply to social networking and video-sharing services with proven risky features.

The overview page publishes the age rules as a staircase, under the heading Age access phases. From 3 to under 13 there are no accounts, and from 15 to under 18 a minor may open one without prior parental consent.

A guardian may still permit a child under 13 limited access to child-friendly video services through the guardian’s own account. The Commission says under-13s are not cut off from the online world, but will have no social media accounts.

Between 13 and 15 a minor may have what the overview calls mini social media and video-sharing accounts, set up and supervised by a guardian. The questions and answers add parental tools always on, a daily limit of at most one hour, and parental approval of contacts.

The Commission’s pages make a minor’s content visible only to accepted contacts and bar livestreaming by default. Geolocation switched off is United Press International’s and The Next Web’s detail, which this desk did not find on the Commission’s pages.

The questions and answers say fines can reach six per cent of total worldwide annual turnover. An expedited procedure applies for services the Commission supervises, with preliminary findings within 30 days and a final decision targeted within 90.

Daniel Friedlaender, who heads the Computer and Communications Industry Association in Europe, answered the proposal on 17 September 2026. He said “Children deserve a safe internet, but promises of privacy and security are not enough”, and asked what data an age check would collect.

The European Parliament and all twenty-seven governments must agree a text before any of this binds a platform. France’s Conseil constitutionnel struck down a national ban on accounts below fifteen on 14 August 2026, and the question has now moved to Brussels.

Stockholm Counts The Last Ballots And Loses A Government

Sweden’s Election Authority finished counting late and overseas ballots on 17 September 2026, four days after the vote. The Associated Press and Sweden Herald reported the result as 176 of the 349 Riksdag seats for the four opposition parties against 173.

Ulf Kristersson asked to be relieved of his duties as prime minister, in a letter to the speaker posted on X. Sweden Herald published it at 13.47 Central European Summer Time on 17 September 2026.

The count moved while it ran. ABC News in Australia reported early on 17 September 2026 that the blocs stood at 175 seats to 174, with 26,169 votes between them.

The Associated Press reported that the Social Democrats hold 99 seats and that the Sweden Democrats lost eleven to finish on 62. Speaker Andreas Norlén now conducts the talks on forming a government.

Kristersson and his ministers remain in office as a transitional government until a new one takes office, Sweden Herald reported. Norlén begins individual talks with representatives of the parliamentary parties on Friday.

Ebba Busch of the Christian Democrats wrote that “Currently, there is no one who can gather a majority in the Riksdag”. The Liberal leader Simona Mohamsson wrote that it was “up to Magdalena Andersson to show whether she can put together some basis for government”.

Kristersson wrote that the speaker “will lead the next steps towards forming a new government”, and Magdalena Andersson is expected to be asked first. The Associated Press reported that the Centre Party opposes governing alongside the Sweden Democrats or the Left Party.

Sweden took 131 days to elect a prime minister after the election of 9 September 2018, when Stefan Löfven was chosen on 18 January 2019. A country that counts slowly also forms governments slowly.

The newly elected Riksdag meets for the first time on 28 September 2026, holds a roll-call and elects a speaker. A majority of three holds only while nobody is away.

Strasbourg Hears A Guest, And Washington Answers

Mark Carney addressed the European Parliament at 11.30 a.m. Strasbourg time on 17 September 2026, a day after being offered the Union’s first associate membership. He told the chamber: “Canada welcomes this ambition.”

The European Parliament’s buildings in Brussels. Mark Carney addressed the Parliament in Strasbourg at 11.30 a.m. Strasbourg time on 17 September 2026. He told the chamber that Canada welcomes the ambition of a closer alliance, and that he was not proposing a third bloc.

He said he was “not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival”. At a news conference afterwards he said an enhanced partnership would go to a debate and a final vote in Parliament, BNN Bloomberg reported.

Canada’s own published text of the speech offers Europe deposits of more than 34 critical minerals and liquefied natural gas at large scale. It also proposes Canadian membership of the Erasmus+ and Horizon research programmes and closer integration of financial services.

Donald Trump called the proposal laughable on 16 September 2026 and said that if the intention were bad, “we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe”. BNN Bloomberg carried that wording in its live coverage of the day.

A Commission spokesperson answered that the partnership “is not against anyone else, but for our common strength”, Euronews reported. An alliance announced on Wednesday had acquired a tariff threat by Thursday morning.

Pierre Poilievre, who leads Canada’s Conservatives, said his party wanted “no EU taxes, no EU laws, and no EU open-border rules on immigration in Canada”. What associate membership would contain remains open, and this desk found no published definition in Brussels or in Ottawa.

Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador-designate to the Union, told reporters that the name would come later. He said the two sides had to reach “the point where we know what we’re describing”, in BNN Bloomberg’s record.

The Hague Spends A Second Day Counting To Ten

Rob Jetten answered the second day of the general political debate in the Dutch lower house on 17 September 2026. His minority cabinet needs ten more votes in that chamber and sixteen in the senate, DutchNews.nl reported on 14 September 2026.

He declined to choose between the left and the right, and Hart van Nederland’s live record timed the words at 10.47 a.m. Amsterdam time. He told the chamber, in Dutch, that making that choice today would shortchange the country.

In the same 10.47 entry NOS recorded him saying the cabinet would send invitations that evening to seven opposition parties. It listed them as Pro, 50Plus, Volt, ChristenUnie, SGP, JA21 and BBB.

Mirjam Bikker, who leads the ChristenUnie, told the house at 11.01 a.m. Amsterdam time that the cabinet must first agree with itself. “If the cabinet carries on like this, we will all end up in the mud,” she said, in Hart van Nederland’s record.

At 1.07 p.m. Amsterdam time he committed an extra 10 billion euros (about US$11.5 billion) to infrastructure, NOS reported. Money is the answer a minority cabinet can give without choosing a side.

Geert Wilders of the Party for Freedom announced the motion of no confidence on 16 September 2026, NOS reported. Its entries at 15.43 and 18.05 Amsterdam time that day both record him saying he would table it.

Jesse Klaver of Pro criticised the invitation and asked the prime minister to pick a direction, saying it was there to hold the coalition together. He did not refuse it, and NOS recorded him saying the route to an overall package was still open for him.

Underneath the debate, the police and the domestic intelligence service are still working on the sabotage that stopped Dutch trains on 15 September 2026. Sources told NOS they had seen farmer groups discussing fixing metal pipes to train lines on Prinsjesdag, DutchNews.nl reported on 16 September 2026.

Officials confirmed to NOS that farmer protest groups were one scenario under consideration, and farming organisations condemned the actions and denied involvement. The justice minister, David van Weel, pledged to catch the culprits.

Sanne Buisman, an associate professor of criminal law in Amsterdam, told de Volkskrant the likely charge is endangering rail traffic, NL Times reported. Article 164 of the Dutch criminal code carries fifteen years, rising to thirty years or life where a terrorist intent is uncovered.

The Pump Is The Argument Underneath All Of It

Diesel in Germany reached 2.404 euros a litre (about US$2.77) at the start of the week, the motoring association ADAC said. Petrol reached a record 2.286 euros a litre (about US$2.64) on the same reading, which The Local carried on 15 September 2026.

The same association put petrol and diesel at 2.45 euros a litre (about US$2.83) on 17 September 2026, Euronews reported. Euronews also reported that Saudi Arabia had closed its 1,200-kilometre East-West oil pipeline after attacks.
