An analyst quoted in that report put between 3.5 and 4 million barrels a day of exports at risk. Emmanuel Macron announced what he called a mobilisation on fuel prices.

Giorgia Meloni abolished stamp duty on small and medium-powered cars, calling the measure structural and permanent. Spain doubled its diesel tax cut to twenty cents a litre from 1 September 2026, in the same Euronews account.

Friedrich Merz said Germany must act and that a proposal would come very soon, in the account The Local carried on 15 September 2026. He said that “For many people who need their car every day, the limit has been reached.”

German gas stores stood at 53 per cent full on 1 September 2026, their lowest September level in fifteen years. A year earlier they stood at about 71 per cent, on figures from Initiative Energien Speichern and the Federal Network Agency.

The same association puts 77 per cent by 1 November as the minimum fill level for a normal winter. The gap between the reading and the target is the winter’s whole argument.

The Federal Reserve raised its target range for the federal funds rate to between 3.75 and 4.00 per cent on 16 September 2026. The vote was twelve to nothing, and its own statement said inflation remains elevated.

The European Central Bank raised its deposit rate, its overnight rate for banks, to 2.50 per cent with effect from 16 September 2026. Its own table shows 2.25 per cent in force from 17 June 2026, a quarter point lower.

The bank’s own reference rate was US$1.1537 to the euro on 16 September 2026, published at around 4 p.m. Frankfurt time. A litre of diesel is priced in that euro before it is priced in anything else.

Brent crude settled at US$105.83 a barrel on 16 September 2026, against US$108.75 the day before, on Investing.com’s futures series. This desk could not establish Thursday’s intraday direction, and Euronews reported Brent above US$113 a barrel on supply risk.

European share indices opened higher on 17 September 2026 and the dollar reached a seven-week high, Euronews reported that morning. A pump price is the part of a rate decision that a household can read without help.

What This Means From Latin America

Brazil signed its own children’s internet law exactly one year before Brussels tabled one. The Brazilian statute is Law 15,211 of 17 September 2025, and the EU KIDS Act was tabled on 17 September 2026.

The Brazilian law ties the account of any user aged sixteen or under to a legal guardian. It also forbids age checks resting on self-declaration alone.

Brussels proposes a guardian up to fifteen and no social media account below thirteen. The two rulebooks disagree about the age and agree about the gatekeeper.

Brazil’s data protection authority supervises the law, and administrative sanctions are due to begin in November 2026. That timetable is the law firm Mayer Brown’s reading, published in April 2026, and fines run to ten per cent of a group’s Brazilian revenue.

Platforms that rebuilt their sign-up screens for São Paulo have already paid part of the European bill. The work done for one regulator is rarely wasted on the next.

The European Parliament referred the Union’s agreements with Mercosur to the Court of Justice on 21 January 2026. Its consent to the wider partnership is still pending, so a Strasbourg debate about association is also a South American question.

Brent settling at US$105.83 a barrel is an income question for Brazil, Colombia and Guyana and a cost question for Chile and Peru. The same barrel is read as good news in one capital and bad news in the next.

What We Are Watching

Whether the Kids Act keeps its two ages — the European Parliament has previously called for sixteen, and Estonia opposes age-based bans, The Next Web reported. Twenty-seven governments must still agree the text.

— the European Parliament has previously called for sixteen, and Estonia opposes age-based bans, The Next Web reported. Twenty-seven governments must still agree the text. How age checks are actually to be done — whether the Commission answers the industry association on what data a check collects, and when the verification tool ships.

— whether the Commission answers the industry association on what data a check collects, and when the verification tool ships. How Sweden forms its next government — whether Speaker Andreas Norlén asks Magdalena Andersson first, and whether the Centre Party’s refusal to sit with the Left Party holds.

— whether Speaker Andreas Norlén asks Magdalena Andersson first, and whether the Centre Party’s refusal to sit with the Left Party holds. What associate membership actually contains — whether Brussels or Ottawa publishes a definition, a scope or a timetable for the status Mark Carney was offered on 16 September 2026.

— whether Brussels or Ottawa publishes a definition, a scope or a timetable for the status Mark Carney was offered on 16 September 2026. Whether the Dutch budget finds ten votes — whether the seven invited opposition parties come to the table, and what happens to the motion of no confidence Geert Wilders has announced.

— whether the seven invited opposition parties come to the table, and what happens to the motion of no confidence Geert Wilders has announced. Who placed the pipes on the Dutch track — whether the police or the prosecution service confirm the line of inquiry into farmer protest groups that sources described to NOS.

— whether the police or the prosecution service confirm the line of inquiry into farmer protest groups that sources described to NOS. Union sanctions on Russia on 22 September 2026 — whether France and Slovakia still withhold agreement on listings covering nearly 3,000 people and entities, over the delisting of Alisher Usmanov.

— whether France and Slovakia still withhold agreement on listings covering nearly 3,000 people and entities, over the delisting of Alisher Usmanov. What Europe does about fuel prices — whether Friedrich Merz’s promised relief arrives, and whether the closure of the Saudi East-West pipeline lasts long enough to reach the pump.

The Bigger Picture Europe has spent two years answering platforms with enforcement and is now answering them with an age. Enforcement asks a company to behave, while an age asks it to check a document. This desk cannot yet tell you what an age check will collect or cost, because the verification tool is still being built. Nor could it establish who placed the pipes on Dutch track, where farmer protest groups are one scenario under consideration. Sweden took four days to turn a Sunday vote into a resignation letter, and a cabinet takes longer than a count. Slow counts are what a country does instead of arguing about the result afterwards. Canada was offered a seat on Wednesday and a tariff threat followed the same day, which is the price of accepting an invitation in public. The offer still has no text, and a status without a text is an intention with a nice name. Underneath all of it, a German driver paid about two and a half euros for a litre of diesel. Europe asks households to carry an energy bill and a policy rate together.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the European Commission propose on 17 September 2026?

It tabled the EU KIDS Act, which its own notice says would prohibit social media platforms from accessing children under the age of 13. The same text sets 15 as the Union-wide age at which a minor may hold an account without a guardian.

When would the new rules on children’s accounts actually apply?

Not yet: the European Parliament and all twenty-seven governments must agree a final text before it binds any platform. The Commission’s questions and answers set the first deadline against that date, giving platforms six months to check existing account holders.

Who will govern Sweden after the election of 13 September 2026?

That is not yet settled: the Election Authority’s updated preliminary result gave the opposition 176 seats to 173. Ulf Kristersson asked to be relieved of office, and Speaker Andreas Norlén now runs the talks on forming a government.

What did Mark Carney say in Strasbourg about associate membership?

He told the chamber “Canada welcomes this ambition”, and said he was not proposing a third bloc to become a great-power rival. At a news conference he said an enhanced partnership would go to a debate and a final vote in Parliament, BNN Bloomberg reported.

Sources in English: the European Commission on the EU KIDS Act, with its own proposal page, its policy overview and its questions and answers. Also the Federal Reserve statement of 16 September 2026, the Swedish parliament and the Prime Minister of Canada. The Swedish Election Authority’s results page carries no seat numbers, and the 176 to 173 is the Associated Press’s and Sweden Herald’s reporting of it. Kids Act reporting from United Press International, Bytes Europe, IO+, The Next Web and Health Policy Watch. The industry response is from the Computer and Communications Industry Association, and the French decision is Conseil constitutionnel decision 2026-911 DC, read in French. Sweden via Sweden Herald, the Associated Press and ABC News in Australia. Canada and the tariff threat via BNN Bloomberg and Euronews. Dutch reporting from NOS and Hart van Nederland, read in Dutch. Also NL Times, reporting de Volkskrant, and DutchNews.nl on the rail sabotage and the budget arithmetic. Fuel prices from The Local and Euronews, with German gas storage from Tech Times. Market figures from Investing.com, with the European Central Bank’s official interest rates and its euro reference rates. Brazil via Law 15,211 of 17 September 2025 and Mayer Brown. Mercosur via White & Case · 14–17 September 2026.

World.title: Central America Drought Kills Cattle and Threatens Food Supply
World.content:
Animals are dropping dead amid the worst drought in living memory for many Central Americans, who are dealing with the unforgiving effects of the powerful El Nino weather pattern. “Sometimes I break down in tears. Sometimes you eat, sometimes you don’t,” said Lidia Ochoa in San Lorenzo, southern Honduras.

The same scene is playing out across the Central American Dry Corridor, which includes parts of Honduras, Guatemala, El Salvador, Nicaragua and Costa Rica. More than 10 million people live here, and 80 percent of small-scale producers in the corridor are poor, United Nations figures show.

Extreme weather events are common in this part of the world, but this year’s El Nino — expected to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago — has bewildered locals. “We had never seen anything like this,” said 76-year-old Ochoa. At this time of year, corn should be growing abundantly on the plot belonging to fellow resident Francisco Molina. But the field lies barren, surrounded by livestock carcasses decaying under the boiling heat. The same disaster is unfolding in El Salvador.



Maria de la Paz Portillo manages an increasingly thirsty water tank that supplies the northeastern El Matazano community, where temperatures have reached a record-breaking 42C. “This is the first year that we’ve seen this shortage and this need for water,” the 31-year-old said.

Harvests lost

El Nino raises surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean and causes global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions. Farmers, no longer able to depend on excess crops to feed themselves, are cutting down on how much they eat.

Governments have declared national emergencies but are facing accusations of neglecting affected communities, with many depending on NGOs for help. “All the corn harvests are going to be lost,” said Indigenous leader Elvira Pasa from a remote village in the municipality of Cunen, northern Guatemala.

Pasa’s country suffers serious child malnutrition problems that are being exacerbated by the drought.

Outrageously expensive

He says some villagers are already buying corn at prices 50 percent higher than normal. Back in Honduras, the same predicament troubles Ochoa. “We eat with just one tortilla and then we don’t eat again because everything is outrageously expensive,” she said.

El Matazano’s tank used to supply around 50 families and fill a pond where locals raised tilapia, a freshwater fish, to sell and to eat. But the latter project has been abandoned and the water is being saved for other, more pressing needs. “It’s affecting us because… we’re not eating tilapia, and also financially because it was a source of livelihood,” said 32-year-old resident Maria del Carmen Portillo.

Sixteen million people across Latin America could face food shortages due to El Nino, said Lena Savelli, regional director of the UN World Food Programme. The climate phenomenon is predicted to peak at the end of the year, but experts say the consequences will stretch far into 2027.

Skin and bone

The drought is also killing off malnourished livestock, and some San Lorenzo farmers are rushing to sell their cattle before they perish. The Honduran village has seen around 100 cows die in recent months, their skeletons littering the parched fields as farmers milk the scrawny creatures that remain.

Since conditions intensified in June, Darwin Cruz has had to sell two of his dairy cows, while another one died. The three cows left produce just a quarter of their usual output. That marks a heavy blow to a small producer like him, with his wife and two daughters dependent on his dwindling income.

Cruz doesn’t know what to do if the rain doesn’t come. The less-than-ideal solution, he says, is to “sell my little cows.” El Matanzo resident Vilma Ortiz is trying to adapt by producing crops that require less water. The 53-year-old is growing chili peppers, which she believes are “braver” than her usual choice of tomato plants in the face of drought.

Indigenous leader Pasa meanwhile cannot escape the anxiety seeping from the cracked ground in Guatemala. “The truth is, I’m starting to get scared because we don’t know what we’re going to live on,” he said.

World.title: Costa Rica Businesses Warn Strong Colón Is Threatening Jobs
World.content:
Costa Rica’s unemployment rate remains low by recent standards, but a closer look at the labor market shows fewer people participating in the workforce and fewer people employed than before the pandemic. At the same time, manufacturers say the strong colón is making it harder to protect jobs and justify new investment.

The latest figures from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC), covering May through July 2026, put national unemployment at 6.7%. Labor force participation, however, stood at just 54.3%, meaning slightly more than half of Costa Ricans age 15 and older were either working or actively looking for work. INEC said the main labor indicators did not show statistically significant changes compared with the same period a year earlier.

That relatively low unemployment rate masks a longer-term problem. Costa Rica had 2,227,240 employed people in February 2020, shortly before the COVID-19 pandemic. By the quarter ending in June 2026, the figure stood at 2,182,916, according to the International Center for Economic Policy for Sustainable Development (CINPE) at the National University (UNA). That means the country had about 44,000 fewer employed people despite growth in the working-age population.

CINPE researchers point to the falling labor force participation rate as a major reason unemployment can decline without a comparable increase in employment. Participation has fallen from around 60% in 2022 to roughly 54% in 2026. The center warned that the decline in unemployment should be “interpreted with caution” because it has happened alongside a shrinking share of the population participating in the labor market.

A separate report published in June by UNA’s Economic and Social Observatory, or OES, reached a similar conclusion. Based on first-quarter comparisons, the study found that Costa Rica’s labor force had shrunk by 70,615 people from a year earlier and by 203,047 compared with the first quarter of 2020.

Women have been particularly affected as the number of women in the labor force fell by 141,534 between 2020 and 2026, compared with a decline of 61,513 men. The OES report also found that the number of employed people fell by 56,376 during the year ending in the first quarter of 2026, including 45,229 women and 11,147 men.

The latest INEC data do not show that the labor market is currently deteriorating sharply from one year to the next. They do, however, confirm that participation remains well below earlier levels, leaving Costa Rica with an unusually small labor force relative to its working-age population. Against that backdrop, businesses are increasingly raising another concern: the strength of the Costa Rican colón.

The colón has appreciated substantially against the U.S. dollar since 2022. OES calculated that the average monthly exchange rate fell by about 34% between June 2022 and May 2026, reaching roughly ₡454.4 per dollar. By mid-September, the reference rate remained near ₡450 to the dollar.

That creates particular problems for companies that earn revenue in dollars while paying wages, utilities and other expenses in colones. Each dollar of revenue converts into fewer colones, squeezing margins unless companies can raise prices, reduce costs or increase productivity.

The Costa Rican Chamber of Industries (CICR) found that 70.2% of companies surveyed this year considered the exchange rate a negative factor affecting competitiveness, making it the industry’s most frequently cited concern. The survey covered 115 formal industrial companies between April 9 and July 15.For some businesses, the pressure has already reached employment.

About 13.3% of the companies surveyed said they had reduced their workforce because of exchange-rate conditions. Among companies operating under Costa Rica’s Free Trade Zone Regime, the figure reached 23.1%. More companies said cuts could come if the exchange-rate situation continues. About 25.6% of respondents expected they would need to reduce staff in the short term, rising to 38.6% among free-trade zone companies.

Investment is also being affected as roughly 31% of manufacturers reported suspending expansion plans or new investments, while nearly half of the free-trade zone companies surveyed had put investments on hold. Six in 10 companies reported receiving fewer colones when converting dollar revenue, and 55% said their profitability had fallen.

World.title: What the Red Sea Oil Halt Could Mean for Costa Rica
World.content:
Saudi Arabia has not exported crude oil through its Red Sea ports since Saturday, after drone attacks damaged its East-West pipeline, according to maritime intelligence data. The disruption adds new uncertainty for Costa Rica, which imports all of the fuel it consumes. The halt follows months of restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Chevron chief executive Mike Wirth warned that the global mechanisms used to ease the fuel crisis have been exhausted.

International oil prices rose yesterday amid the attacks on Saudi infrastructure and continuing uncertainty over Hormuz. For Costa Rica, the connection to world markets is direct. The Regulatory Authority for Public Services (Aresep) sets fuel prices each month based on import costs reported by the state refiner Recope.

Aresep has said that factors outside Costa Rica, including armed conflicts and weather, affect the international price of oil. Those factors in turn affect the price of gasoline, diesel and cooking gas in Costa Rica. September’s adjustment already pushed some prices higher. Aresep approved an increase of ₡82 per liter for diesel, raising it from ₡606 to ₡688, about $1.53 per liter ($5.79 per gallon).

Super gasoline rose ₡22 to ₡726, about $1.62 per liter ($6.11 per gallon). Regular gasoline was the exception, falling ₡51 to ₡707, about $1.57 per liter ($5.95 per gallon). The price of an 11.3-kilogram (25-pound) cooking gas cylinder rose ₡82 to ₡7,071, about $15.73.

That adjustment was calculated from shipments made between Aug. 17 and Sept. 10, before the latest disruption to Saudi exports. Recope had previously pointed to tensions in the Middle East, higher seasonal demand and lower inventories of refined products as drivers of its costs.

Higher energy costs come as the government faces a constrained fiscal outlook. In its Medium-Term Fiscal Framework 2026–2031, updated Sept. 1, the Finance Ministry projected under its base scenario that tax revenue will grow more slowly than the economy. It also projected that public debt will remain above 60% of gross domestic product.

The ministry is now headed by former president Rodrigo Chaves, who also serves as Minister of the Presidency. It projects that the tax burden will fall from 12.8% of GDP in 2025 to 12.6% this year and keep declining to 11.7% by 2031.

The government also faces heavy debt payments over the coming decade. Finance Ministry data as of May show that 72% of the ₡32.4 trillion the ministry has borrowed, about ₡23.4 trillion or $52.1 billion, comes due between 2027 and 2036. The same data show that 34% of the ministry’s financing depends on movements in the exchange rate.

That exposure links the fuel market to the colón. In April, former Central Bank president Rodrigo Cubero said rising oil prices could act as an external force capable of breaking the dollar’s downward trend and pushing the colón toward depreciation. The Central Bank’s reference exchange rate stood at ₡444.46 to buy and ₡449.49 to sell on Wednesday.

Aresep’s next monthly adjustment will be based on the import costs Recope reports for its upcoming shipments.

World.title: International News: New data reveals where 4.5 million migrants went after crossing U.S.-Mexico border
World.content:
International News: New data reveals where 4.5 million migrants went after crossing U.S.-Mexico border

By Zoila Palma: An unprecedented surge in migration along the U.S.-Mexico border has reshaped communities across the United States, with new data obtained by The Associated Press providing a detailed look at the backgrounds and destinations of 4.5 million migrants released into the country between October 2018 and July 2025.

The migrants came from more than 150 countries, contributing to significant changes in the demographic makeup of cities and communities across the country.

The AP obtained the federal records through a Freedom of Information Act request. The data includes migrants’ self-reported destination ZIP codes, citizenship, age, gender, dates of encounters with authorities and the border regions where they were processed.

While some migrants may not have gone to the addresses they provided, many remained in their initial destinations, while others later moved to different parts of the country or left the United States.

The records show a major shift in the origins of migrants arriving at the southern border. Border Patrol encountered people from 174 countries in a single year, compared with earlier periods when migration was dominated by people from Mexico and Central America.

Cities such as New York and Philadelphia received migrants from numerous countries, while smaller communities including Elkhart, Indiana; Knoxville, Tennessee; and Dodge City, Kansas, also experienced significant changes.

Florida remained the most popular state among the migrants in the data, but many moved to other parts of the country.

Cuban migrants, for example, were concentrated in Florida but also went to communities including Louisville, Kentucky, Grand Island, Nebraska, and Odessa, Texas. Colombian migrants went to Aurora, Colorado, while Peruvians were drawn to Paterson, New Jersey.

The data also shows that women and children accounted for nearly six in every 10 migrants released at the border, representing a shift from earlier years when arrivals were predominantly men.

The data also highlights the diverse migration patterns of specific nationalities.

Chinese migrants largely settled in New York City, particularly Queens and Brooklyn, and in communities around Los Angeles.

Meanwhile, immigration enforcement has varied among destinations that experienced large migrant arrivals, with cities including Miami and New York seeing arrests, while other migrant destinations such as Silicon Valley, Madison, Wisconsin, and Stamford, Connecticut, have received comparatively less enforcement attention.

World.title: Caribbean Sugar Refinery says first Belize sugar production on track for 2026
World.content:
Caribbean Sugar Refinery says first Belize sugar production on track for 2026

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Caribbean Sugar Refinery says its new sugar refinery in Belize remains on schedule, with production of its first refined sugar targeted for the third quarter of 2026.

The company says full commissioning of the facility is anticipated during the fourth quarter of the year.

As the refinery moves toward full operations, waivers allowing refined white sugar imports will remain in effect until April 1, 2027.

According to Caribbean Sugar Refinery, the transition period was developed in collaboration with future buyers and the CARICOM Private Sector Organization. It is intended to give commercial customers time to adjust their procurement arrangements while the company completes commissioning, product quality certifications and regional distribution channels.

During the transition, the refinery will process raw sugar feedstock while expanding its distribution network across the Caribbean.

A new sugarcane crop cycle expected to begin by March 1, 2027, is also anticipated to strengthen regional sugar supplies.

Caribbean Sugar Refinery says the Belize facility is intended to do more than provide another source of refined white sugar. The company believes regional production can strengthen trade among CARICOM countries, improve supply stability for manufacturers and reduce dependence on suppliers from outside the region.

The company also expects the investment to contribute to employment, investment and more resilient regional supply chains.

World.title: Belize Immigration officers complete MIDAS training to strengthen border management
World.content:
Belize Immigration officers complete MIDAS training to strengthen border management

By Zoila Palma: About 125 immigration officers from across Belize have completed specialized training on the Migration Information and Data Analysis System (MIDAS), as the Department of Border Management and Immigration Services (DBMIS) moves to strengthen border management operations and standardize procedures at the country’s ports of entry.

The training followed a technical mission organized by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), led by MIDAS Headquarters Representative Boran Simsek and Regional Expert Antonio Meono, with IOM Program Officer Idelki Familia Jimenez participating alongside DBMIS personnel.

The mission combined a performance assessment of MIDAS with practical training on the system and the Standard Operating Procedures governing its use.

The initiative was carried out under the project “Border Management: Effective and Sustainable Management of Belize’s Southern and Western Borders,” implemented by IOM in partnership with the Government of Belize with financial support from the European Union under the Belize-European Union Multi-Annual Indicative Program.

Technical assessments were conducted at DBMIS headquarters in Belmopan, the Western Border and Philip Goldson International Airport, including reviews of MIDAS workstations and servers, document processing, secondary inspections, data exchange and Advance Passenger Information integration.

Lawrence Thompson, Director of Border Management and Immigration Services, said the training will help ensure officers apply consistent procedures across Belize’s ports of entry. “Our officers work at the frontline of Belize’s border management system every day, and their ability to use MIDAS effectively is critical to how we process travellers, manage information and maintain the integrity of our ports of entry,” Thompson said. “This training gives officers from across our border stations and the international airport a common set of procedures that they can apply in their daily work.”

MIDAS is used by DBMIS to register, process and manage traveller movements at the Northern, Western and Southern Borders, Philip Goldson International Airport, Big Creek Port and San Pedro seaport. Officers received training in traveller registration, arrival and departure processing, entry and exit requirements, data protection, information management, secondary inspections and exceptional cases. The sessions included live demonstrations, practical exercises and discussions using a dedicated training database.

The mission follows recent hardware upgrades to Belize’s MIDAS infrastructure and the integration of Advance Passenger Information data exchange, with IOM expected to document the findings, corrective actions, training outcomes and recommendations in a mission report.

World.title: San Ignacio and Santa Elena Basketball Association to tip off 21st annual tournament
World.content:
San Ignacio and Santa Elena Basketball Association to tip off 21st annual tournament

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Basketball action is returning to San Ignacio as the San Ignacio and Santa Elena Basketball Association prepares to tip off its 21st annual basketball tournament at the Victor Galvez Stadium.

The tournament will feature 42 teams competing across 15 divisions, bringing together young players, female teams, senior athletes and workplace teams. Games will be played on Thursday, Friday and Saturday nights, with some games also scheduled for Sunday afternoons.

Opening weekend action gets underway on Friday, September 25, with five games on the schedule.

The Under 8 division will start the action at 6:30 p.m. with Tolacca/Yute Expeditions taking on Elite. At 7:00 p.m., Elite will face Oye FM/Universal Hardware/Hodes in the Junior Females division.

The Under 11 matchup will see Belize Eco Cultural Tours/ICB facing Elite, followed by KG Equine Supplies/SMCU/Habet Service Station against Elite in the Under 13 division. Police and Sacred Heart College will close Friday night in the Inter Office division.

Another five games are scheduled for Saturday, with competition in the Under 15, Over 45, Under 17 and Under 21 divisions.

All opening weekend games will be played at the Victor Galvez Field in San Ignacio Town.

World.title: Red, white and blue take over as schools prepare for National Children’s Rally
World.content:
Red, white and blue take over as schools prepare for National Children’s Rally

By Zoila Palma: Patriotism is in full effect across primary schools countrywide as students, teachers, parents and young entrepreneurs put the finishing touches on their preparations for tomorrow’s National Children’s Rally and Uniform Parade, as Belize celebrates 45 years of independence under the theme, “Look at Me, I Am Belize at 45.”

In communities across the country, the colors of the Belizean flag are taking center stage, with children proudly preparing red, white and blue hats, decorating bicycles and creating colorful accessories for the celebrations.

Young entrepreneurs are also getting into the Independence spirit, selling T-shirts, earrings, horns and other patriotic items as Belizeans get ready to showcase their civic pride.

The National Children’s Rally and Uniform Parade provides an opportunity for Belize’s youngest citizens to participate in the country’s Independence celebrations while expressing their creativity and love for Belize.

From handmade decorations to patriotic clothing and accessories, the preparations highlight the enthusiasm of children and communities as they mark the nation’s 45th year as an independent country.

The celebrations will continue on September 19 with National Service Day, held in honor of George Cadle Price, the Father of the Nation.

National Service Day encourages Belizeans to give back to their communities and uphold the values of unity, service and love for country that characterized Price’s life and leadership.

On September 21, 1981, the Union Jack was lowered and the Belizean flag was raised for the first time, marking Belize’s achievement of independence.

The historic moment represented the realization of Price’s vision for a free and sovereign Belize and followed years of struggle for the rights of Belizeans to vote, self-govern and build a nation of their own.

Throughout his life, Price received numerous national and international recognitions, including the Order of National Hero, Belize’s highest honor.

His legacy continues to be reflected in the values of service and national unity, while National Service Day serves as a reminder that building Belize is a responsibility shared by every citizen.

As Belize prepares to mark 45 years of Independence, the energy of its children offers a colorful reminder that the future of the nation is already taking shape—one flag, one bicycle, one T-shirt and one expression of civic pride at a time.

World.title: Twelve students receive refrigeration and air conditioning scholarships
World.content:
Twelve students receive refrigeration and air conditioning scholarships

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Twelve students have been awarded scholarships under the Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Scholarship Programme administered by the Department of the Environment through its National Ozone Unit.

The recipients were formally recognized during an award ceremony held on September 16.

The scholarships support students enrolled in refrigeration and air conditioning programmes at ITVET centres in Belize City, Orange Walk and Stann Creek.

Each scholarship covers one academic year, from 2026 to 2027, and includes tuition as well as a toolbox with servicing tools and personal protective equipment.

Three of the 12 recipients are female trainees, which the Department of the Environment says is an important step in a field where women remain underrepresented.

The award ceremony was held on World Ozone Day, which marks the signing of the Montreal Protocol and highlights efforts to reduce substances that damage the ozone layer.

This year’s theme, “Global Action for a Cooler Planet,” also marks 10 years of sustainable cooling under the Kigali Amendment.

Chief Environmental Officer Anthony Mai said the students represent an investment in the future of Belize’s cooling sector.

He said the training and tools will help build a profession that protects both people and the environment.

The scholarships are funded under the HCFC Phase-out Management Plan, Phase II, with support from the Multilateral Fund for the Implementation of the Montreal Protocol.

World.title: Belize stays hot as unstable conditions bring some rain
World.content:
Belize stays hot as unstable conditions bring some rain

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize can expect sunny skies mixed with cloudy spells today as slightly moist and somewhat unstable conditions affect the country.

The National Meteorological Service says a few showers and isolated thunderstorms are possible mainly along some coastal areas this morning.

By this afternoon, the activity is expected to shift mostly inland.

Temperatures will remain warm, with inland areas reaching a high of around 95 degrees Fahrenheit. Coastal temperatures will peak near 89 degrees, while the hills will reach around 84 degrees.

Tonight will be partly cloudy, with generally isolated showers or thunderstorms. A few more could develop over southern Belize and some coastal areas late tonight.

Similar conditions are expected on Friday, although skies will become cloudy at times. Showers and thunderstorms should remain generally isolated, with slightly more activity possible over the south.

Forecasters say tropical cyclone formation is not expected over the region during the next 48 hours.

World.title: Young Anthony William Perry shot and killed on Wednesday night in Belize City
World.content:
Young Anthony William Perry shot and killed on Wednesday night in Belize City

By Jose Luis Cruz: 20-year-old Anthony William Perry is the old capital’s latest murder victim.

Perry was shot earlier on Wednesday night on Louise Bevans Street in Belize City.

He was rushed to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital (KHMH) but died as a result of the gunshot injuries received.

Perry joins a growing list of young Belizean men who have been robbed of their future due to gun violence.

World.title: Bouncing back fast
World.content:
WILLIAMS...I see quarters that are becoming less negative and that is a good sign.

CITING data that shows Jamaica 18 months ahead of schedule in recovering from the destruction Hurricane Melissa unleashed on several parishes last year, Finance Minister Fayval Williams on Wednesday painted a rosy picture of the country’s economy. She acknowledged, however, that “not everybody is feeling it just yet”, a nod to critics who have argued that the pace of the recovery and rebuilding is much too slow.

During her upbeat PowerPoint presentation at Wednesday’s post-Cabinet news briefing the minister reeled off data to support her claims.

“When I look at this chart, I see quarters that are becoming less negative and that is a good sign,” Williams stated.

“And, no, this is not a picture of a recession. The Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ) already debunked that notion,” she added.

Williams highlighted that in the quarter following the hurricane, the economy contracted 7.1 per cent, then 4.1 per cent in the next quarter and just 2.9 per cent in the quarter, after that. She said the 2.9 per cent projection should be finalised by the Statistical Institute of Jamaica (Statin) by the end of September.

The finance minister argued that the shrinking year-on-year numbers are themselves proof that the economy is recovering. She argued further that “an economy in decline produces deepening figures, not improving ones”.

Williams urged Jamaicans to remember that immediately after the hurricane, PIOJ projected that the country would not get back to its pre-Melissa level of output until the last quarter of 2028. She noted that the PIOJ now expects that the economy will begin to see growth by the second quarter of 2027 — “six quarters earlier, a year-and-a-half earlier”. According to her, the PIOJ “has been able to revise their forecast because the out-turn keeps getting better”.

The finance minister highlighted that where it was projected that the fiscal deficit would have been 3.8 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) immediately after the hurricane, it instead came in at 2.5 per cent. At the same time the primary surplus was projected to be 1.3 per cent but came in at 2.3 per cent, while public debt-to-GDP was projected to rise to 68.9 per cent but came in at 65.6 per cent.

Regarding the public debt-to-GDP number, Williams said, “That number matters, it is not a one-off, it’s because we had stronger nominal GDP, the economy itself is bigger than we assumed, and that is the kind of improvement that will persist.”

She also pointed to the positions taken by the big three international ratings agencies with Moody’s upgrading its assessment of Jamaica just seven weeks after the hurricane, which it described as a “temporary setback”. Standard & Poor’s held its rating for Jamaica in December 2025 and moved the outlook to stable, while Fitch affirmed its BB-rating for Jamaica in February 2026 with a stable outlook.

Williams also pointed out that while unemployment rose from 3.3 per cent to 3.7 per cent following the hurricane, it remained at record lows. She acknowledged that unemployment in the hardest-hit parishes was higher.

“I want to assure them that the Government continues to work night and day to restore the west — to restore roads, water, housing, all the services, employment, schools and so on,” she said.

Williams also noted that the response from the Diaspora helped to stabilise the economy, as is evidenced in the record level of remittances that were sent to Jamaica in the aftermath of the hurricane. A breakdown of the numbers shows that, in November, the Diaspora sent remittances totalling US$273 million, up 16 per cent. December saw a record US$296 million being sent. The figure was up 16.3 per cent for the month. Of note is that all of the hardest-hit parishes received more in remittances than before the hurricane.

In the first three months after the storm, Jamaicans abroad sent home US$93 million more than they sent in the same three months a year earlier.

On the matter of inflation, the finance minister insisted that, while it was expected that food prices “would run away” following the devastating hurricane, they did not. She pointed out that inflation moved to 2.9 per cent in October 2025, 4.4 per cent in November 2025, and 4.5 per cent in December 2025 — all within the target range for the Bank of Jamaica. This, she said, was because agricultural production recovered faster than expected.

“Because of that, the price shock was contained,” the minister remarked.

However, Williams acknowledged that by July 2026 the picture had changed completely, with headline inflation surging to 7.5 per cent — the driver being the transportation division, which was up 13.6 per cent. She said based on figures released by Statin on Tuesday, whereas transportation had pushed up inflation in July, it was higher food prices, as a result of the ongoing drought, which drove inflation in August.

While transportation is still a factor, the finance minister said the August inflation number is directly attributable to the upheaval in international markets, driven by the United States war on Iran which has pushed up oil prices since February.

World.title: Blessing in disguise
World.content:
Sharon Logan, director of sales and marketing at Half Moon Resort, speaks during a JAPEX partner media update on Tuesday. (Photo: Aceion Cunningham)

WHEN Hurricane Melissa swept through Jamaica last October it left tourism businesses counting losses and racing to recover. But nearly a year later, Half Moon resort and Chukka Jamaica are looking beyond the devastation, using the disruption to refresh their properties, redesign experiences, and rethink their operations.

For Half Moon, the forced recovery has gone beyond repairing hurricane damage. The Montego Bay resort has used the interruption to undertake a broad refresh of its property, while Chukka Jamaica says the experience forced it to examine its processes and find ways to operate more efficiently.

Speaking during a Jamaica Product Exchange (JAPEX) 2026 Partner Media Update on Tuesday, director of sales and marketing for the Half Moon resort Sharon Logan said the hurricane created an opportunity for the resort to undertake work that would otherwise have been difficult to complete while guests were on property.

“One of the things that I look on is the silver lining behind the cloud, which is that we got the opportunity to do a complete refresh and regrowth of the property since the reopening,” said Logan.

She explained that while some projects, including renovation work on some of the resort’s villas, had already been under way before the hurricane, other major improvements came directly out of the damage caused by the storm.

“The villas were already a project that we were working on. But the other parts of the property, like the original part of the hotel, that has a complete refresh and that is all as a result of the hurricane,” added Logan.

The result, she said, has included improvements across much of the 400-acre property, including its rooms, meeting spaces, lobby, roadways, and pool areas.

One of the more unusual benefits, she identified, came from the movement of sand during the hurricane.

“There are so many open spaces. All the plants have been sprung up fresh and nice…We even got new beaches because we got sand that washed up. That would have cost the hotel millions of dollars to purchase. We got 30 truckloads of sand, free, so we have expanded beaches, so we’re excited about that,” explained Logan.

The resort, which reopened on April 2, is continuing a phased reopening of its facilities. Logan said half of the original Founders’ Cove section is already open, with the remaining section scheduled to open on October 1.

The hurricane also gave the resort an opportunity to tackle work that had previously required interruptions to operations. Logan pointed specifically to the pool at the Eclipse section, which had experienced problems with its tiles.

But while Half Moon’s gains have been visible in its physical transformation, Chukka Jamaica’s experience has produced a different kind of reset.

The attraction operator, which describes itself as a nature adventure company, was particularly exposed to the effects of the hurricane because its business depends heavily on the natural environment.

Group Digital Platform Manager Ilia Tomlinson said the recovery was especially difficult at Chukka’s river locations. At Good Hope in Trelawny, for example, the site was inundated and its river operations were disrupted.

Chukka began reopening locations in November, according to Tomlinson, with its final reopening taking place in June. She said the river-based operations were among the hardest to restore because of the overflow of the waterways.

But the disruption also prompted the company to scrutinise how it worked, with greater productivity emerging as one of the main lessons from the recovery.

“I would say the silver lining is…we operated a little bit more efficiently. We have had to. Nobody wants to cut back, it’s hard decisions to make, but cutting back and being efficient almost go hand in hand where there’s a middle spot where it’s productivity,” said Tomlinson.

“We have had to look at things we have never thought we have had to look at, and in a way we’re thankful for that. You know, it really has had us reflecting on our own processes and procedures and being more efficient in how we deliver our experiences,” added Tomlinson.

That reassessment has taken place alongside changes to Chukka’s tourism products.

In Ocho Rios, the company has redesigned parts of its offering following the hurricane and has expanded its portfolio through its acquisition of the Green Grotto Caves, which it took over just two days before Melissa struck Jamaica on October 28.

The caves, located near Discovery Bay in St Ann, are being incorporated into Chukka’s wider network of experiences in the resort area, adding a stronger history and culture component to its nature and adventure products.

Meanwhile, at Good Hope, the company has rebranded the attraction as a river outpost reflecting its location and the experiences offered there, including river tubing, bamboo rafting, ziplining, and dune buggies.

Tomlinson said the storm also reinforced the importance of preparation, particularly for a company whose operations are so closely tied to Jamaica’s landscape.

“We didn’t know we were so good at preparing. That was the lesson learned on the value of our standards of procedures and policies that we put into place that we probably otherwise take for granted,” she added.

World.title: J-House Vol 1 puts Jamaica on a new global dance floor
World.content:
Freddy Browne

There are collaborations, there are compilations — and then there are projects whose star-studded line-ups pack such a heavy punch that they position themselves for global attention long before anyone hears a single track.

Keen on taking Jamaican voices into the billion-dollar world of electronic music, Freddy Browne’s ambitious J-House Volume 1 is poised to do just that.

With Patra, Beenie Man, Tessanne Chin, Busy Signal, T.O.K, Agent Sasco, and more in the mix, the project, set for release on September 18, aims to take unmistakably Jamaican voices and personalities into the international house music arena.

Rather than simply placing Jamaican artistes over electronic beats and calling it fusion, Browne has been building J-House as its own musical proposition.

According to the American producer, DJ, and JHouse Entertainment CEO, the project stretches across generations of Jamaican music while refusing to stay comfortably inside any one of them.

Each artiste represents a different era in Jamaica’s rich musical history. Patra carries the weight of an artiste who helped push dancehall into mainstream international spaces during the 1990s. Beenie Man has spent decades as one of the genre’s most recognisable figures, while Busy Signal has built a catalogue around his ability to move between hard-core dancehall and broader musical territory. Ding Dong, meanwhile, brings an energy rooted heavily in dance and movement.

Then there is Tessanne Chin, whose victory on The Voice introduced her powerhouse vocals to millions internationally. T.O.K, whose harmonies became integral to dancehall’s crossover era; Richie Stephens, bringing decades of reggae experience; and Agent Sasco, one of the genre’s most respected lyricists.

Newer voices J’Calm and AcYn ensure the project is not only honouring Jamaica’s musical legacy, but also looking towards its future.

Browne, who has previously spoken about imagining artistes such as Ding Dong performing before audiences at major electronic music festivals, described J-House as an opportunity to carry Jamaican talent into spaces it may not traditionally occupy.

“This is crazy,” he said. “We’re creating a blueprint for other producers and record companies. The goal is to open doors for artistes, producers, and the industry as a whole.”

That ambition extends beyond the music itself. House music connects artistes to a vast international network of DJs, clubs, festivals, streaming platforms, radio, play lists, licensing opportunities, and electronic music audiences. J-House is designed to place Jamaican talent directly within that ecosystem, making the project as much about market expansion as it is about musical experimentation.

With J-House Volume 1 distributed through The Orchard/Sony Music the project also has access to an established international distribution network. And Volume 1 is not being treated as the endgame.

Browne shared that Jamaica represents the first instalment of a wider international concept. The United Kingdom is planned as the focus of the second volume, Japan the third, with Africa completing the four-part series. If the vision unfolds as planned, Jamaica will not simply be participating in another global musical movement. It will be the starting point.

World.title: Jamaica, US finalise operating procedures related to TCNs
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith confirmed that the United States and Jamaica have finalised operating procedures related to the memorandum of understanding for TCNs that was signed earlier this year..

JAMAICA could soon receive its first batch of third-country nationals (TCNs) from the United States (US) as Foreign Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith confirmed that both governments have finalised operating procedures related to the memorandum of understanding (MOU) that was signed earlier this year.

Jamaica now joins 30 countries, including several members of the Caribbean Community (Caricom), which have similar arrangements with the US Government amid its ongoing crackdown on illegal immigration.

“After internal consultations and thoughtful negotiations, both governments have now finalised operating procedures related to the MOU in order to settle the guard rails and parameters underpinning the agreement. The arrangements were also finalised, taking into account Jamaica’s capacity constraints and our belief in the principles of safe, orderly, and lawful migration,” said Johnson Smith, speaking at a post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House on Wednesday.

The agreement, Johnson Smith clarified, will see 25 TCNs entering the country biweekly. While here, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) will provide basic services, like health care and counselling, to help with their transition.

The minister reiterated that under no circumstance will more than 25 TCNs be present in the island.

“We have also not agreed to receive 10,000 individuals. We have negotiated guard rails to address capacity constraints, and have, therefore, agreed to a maximum of 25 individuals per two-week period, which the IOM will, of course, be on a continuous basis making arrangements for their return.

“Furthermore, this arrangement will be suspended if 10 TCNs apply to remain in Jamaica through asylum procedures or other humanitarian applications. This, again, is specifically negotiated by Jamaica,” said Johnson Smith.

She further explained that TCNs were not deportees but the nationals of other countries who entered the US unlawfully and are being returned to their home countries through the IOM’s Assisted Voluntary Return Programme.

Johnson Smith added that while she is aware that some countries have opted to accept TCNs with criminal records, Jamaica will only facilitate those with no previous convictions.

“The Government reiterates its commitment to working with the IOM and the Government of the United States of America to ensure that all arrangements for the next stage of TCN implementation are appropriately governed and implemented in accordance with both our domestic laws and international law,” she said.

Additionally, while acknowledging Minister of National Security Dr Horace Chang’s previous commitment to release the agreement, Johnson Smith explained that the MOU’s bilateral status prevents it from being made public.

“As indicated, this is not a unilateral arrangement; it is a bilateral arrangement, and one in which they [the United States] have not generally released their agreements, and they have not agreed to release this one,” she said.

“I give you every assurance as well that we have all shared all the relevant and material matters, provisions, in relation to the matter. So there’s nothing being hidden per se, but as you would note, even under the ATI [Access to Information Act], bilateral agreements, security agreements, arrangements that are sensitive to relations between countries and otherwise are treated differently from other agreements,” explained Johnson Smith.

Despite not being able to give an official start date for when the first TCNs are expected to arrive, Johnson Smith affirmed that Jamaicans will be regularly updated as conversations advance.

World.title: NEXT LEVEL
World.content:
Jamaica 100m sprinter Jonielle Smith competes in the women’s 4x100m relay heats during the World Athletics Championships in Tokyo, Japan, on September 20, 2025. (Photo: AFP)

After breaking into the ranks of Jamaica’s fastest women ever, national 100m sprinter Jonielle Smith says she’s looking to carry her strong form into next season with the World Athletics Championships looming.

Smith ended her impressive 2026 season over the weekend at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, finishing fourth in the women’s 100m final and helping Jamaica land silver in the 4×100 metres mixed relay.

The 2025 North American, Central American and Caribbean (NACAC) 100m champion moved to 14th all time in Jamaica’s all-time list when she clocked a personal best 10.89 seconds at the Eugene Diamond League in July.

Prior to this year, Smith had never gone under 11 seconds in the event. However, she managed to dip under the mark six times, including at the Ultimate Championship where she registered 10.94 seconds both in the semi-final and final.

Smith, a finalist at this summer’s Commonwealth Games in Scotland and March’s World Indoor Championships in Poland, believes improving her confidence level was key in her success this year.

“I’m proud of myself [for] having confidence in myself,” she told the Inside Lane UK. “As good as last year was, it took me a while to start to trust my body and I feel like from day one this year in the background, I told myself that I was a champion and I was going to get what I wanted done and I think that’s what I’m most proud of, just being confident.”

The 30-year-old, who won 4x100m silver at last year’s Tokyo World Championships, says writing out her goals has helped change her perspective, which was on display at the recent Ultimate Championship.

“I journalled every day before practice and I had to do that [for the 100m final] also,” she said. “After the 4x100m, I felt bad because I really wanted us to win and I wasn’t able to pass [USA’s] Kayla [White]. She’s a phenomenal athlete, but I wanted us to win [0:44] to be honest, so I genuinely felt bad. My people were like ‘you split nine [seconds], that was so good’. But regardless, it was just like we didn’t win.

“So I went back to what I was used to and I journalled, I told myself that I’m a champion and I reminded myself what we were doing, trying to have fun and stuff like that. And I felt like that made me come out a whole lot more confident since the last month and the results showed.”

Describing 2026 as “phenomenal”, Smith says she’s excited for what’s to come in 2027.

“I got my 10.8, I got top three at the national trials and Ultimate finalist,” she said. “I just didn’t get [a] Commonwealth [medal] but that was out of my control, so I got to give myself some grace for that. But I feel like I finished off extremely well and I started even better indoors, so it’s a great thing to build off going into next season.”

Smith will likely be eyeing an individual spot at the 2027 World Championships in Beijing, having last done so in 2019 in Doha.

World.title: Shan’s Garlic, Thyme & Scotch Bonnet Butter Ribeye
World.content:
Shanice Gore completes the spread, serving up the garlic, thyme, and Scotch bonnet butter ribeye. (Photo: Alan Smith)

Get ready for a flavour-packed feast Mia Hair Artistry principal Shanice Gore shares her Garlic, Thyme & Scotch Bonnet Butter Ribeye recipe with Thursday Food.

“Ribeye is one of my favourite cuts of steak because of its beautiful marbling and rich flavour. In my home, we love our steak cooked medium rare, so I focus on getting a good, flavourful sear on the outside while keeping the centre juicy and tender. My garlic, thyme and Scotch bonnet compound butter is the finishing touch — it melts beautifully over the hot steak and adds a delicious Jamaican kick,” says Gore.

Ingredients

•1 ribeye steak, approximately 1–1½ inches thick

• Salt, to taste

• Freshly cracked black pepper, to taste

• 1 tablespoon olive oil

For the Compound Butter:

• ½ cup unsalted butter, softened

• 2 cloves garlic, finely minced

• 1 tablespoon fresh thyme leaves

• ½–1 Scotch bonnet pepper, finely minced, depending on desired heat

Method

1. Begin by preparing the compound butter. Combine the softened butter with the garlic, thyme and finely minced Scotch bonnet pepper. Mix well until everything is evenly incorporated. Place the butter onto parchment paper, shape into a log, roll tightly and refrigerate until firm.

2. Remove the ribeye from the refrigerator about 30 minutes before cooking and pat dry with paper towels. Season both sides generously with salt and freshly cracked black pepper.

3. Heat a heavy skillet or cast-iron pan over high heat until very hot. Add the olive oil and carefully place the steak into the pan. Sear undisturbed until a deep golden-brown crust forms, then flip and sear the other side.

4. For a ribeye approximately 1–1½ inches thick, cook for approximately three to four minutes per side for medium rare, four to five minutes per side for medium, or six to seven minutes per side for well done. Cooking times will vary depending on the thickness of the steak, so a meat thermometer can be used for accuracy.

5. Once the steak has been seared on both sides, reduce the heat or remove the pan from the heat and place a generous spoonful of the garlic, thyme and Scotch bonnet compound butter directly on top of the steak. Allow butter to melt over the hot meat, spooning the melted butter over the steak.

6. Remove the ribeye from the pan and leave it to rest for five to 10 minutes before slicing. Slice against the grain and serve with the melted compound butter spooned over the top.

Shan’s Tip: For the juiciest ribeye, don’t skip the resting time. And in my home, medium rare is the preferred doneness — the combination of the tender, juicy steak and the spicy, garlicky compound butter is hard to beat.

World.title: Family services shake-up
World.content:
The Ministry of Education has severed ties with the heads of two of its primary family services agencies — the Child Protection and Family Services Agency (CPFSA) and the National Parenting Support Commission (NPSC) — reportedly to undertake a major shift in their operations, the Jamaica Observer has learnt.

As part of that shake-up, chief executive officer of the CPFSA Laurette Adams-Thomas, who took the helm of the agency in October 2023, will demit office next month.

In a brief response to the Observer, Adams-Thomas said her contract expires on October 1, 2026 and she was “officially notified on July 23, 2026” that it would “not be renewed”.

The CPFSA is an executive agency which was formed from the merger of the Child Development Agency (CDA) and the Office of Children’s Registry (OCR). Adams-Thomas, an educator and social worker, took over its leadership following an eight-year stint as general manager of the largest infirmary in the Caribbean — Jamaica’s Golden Age Home — where she had oversight responsibly for protection and welfare services for more than 450 indigent people from the parishes of Kingston and St Andrew. Prior to assuming that position, she was interim executive director/registrar at the OCR, where her focus was centred on ensuring that an effective system was maintained to facilitate the confidential receipt, assessment, and referral of reports of known or suspected cases of child abuse.

She holds a master’s degree in business administration, bachelor of science in human resource management, and a number of certifications in leadership, corporate governance and strategic planning.

In the meantime, the Observer was reliably informed on Monday that NPSC CEO Kaysia Kerr “is no longer with” the entity. Efforts to get an official response from Kerr were unsuccessful. A pre-recorded message on her personal mobile phone directed all callers with queries related to the commission to contact the education ministry or the commission itself.

A source with knowledge of the development said the ministry had decided to disengage with Kerr due to a breakdown in relations.

She took the helm of the commission in 2017, succeeding Dr Patrece Charles. In an interview with the

Observer at the time, Kerr said she hoped to craft and design programmes for parents and children of all 13 categories of disabilities, move the organisation out of eastern Jamaica to serve other parishes, take some of the programmes internationally, and get the unit to a stage where it generates income.

The former NPSC head has a solid background in education and has completed studies in business and professional management at Nova Southeastern University, along with a first degree in special education and a master’s in administration and supervision from Western Carolina University.

The commission coordinates a wide range of services for parents and also delivers programmes that build parenting skills and promote parental involvement in education.

The Government of Jamaica mandated the establishment of the NPSC in response to the 2004 task force report on the status of education in Jamaica.

The NPSC began operating in January 2013.

World.title: Global aviation squeeze
World.content:
Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) Deputy Director of Tourism for the Americas Philip Rose says Jamaica needs more airline seats to meet strong demand as carriers face aircraft shortages and higher fuel costs amid the impact of the war in the Middle East.

Addressing the media during the Jamaica Product Exchange (JAPEX) forum in Ocho Rios on Tuesday, Rose said Jamaica’s immediate challenge is not a lack of demand, but having enough airline seats to bring visitors to the island.

“The immediate thing that we do need is more seats into the destination. The good news is, and I really want this to land, the good news is the airlines know this. The airlines are preparing because they don’t want to leave business on the table. The airlines know that the demand is there. The airlines are preparing to put in additional flights,” he said.

His comments come as Jamaica’s tourism industry continues its recovery following last year’s Hurricane Melissa, with hotel capacity gradually returning and airlines looking to adjust their schedules accordingly.

Rose said the global aviation industry is itself under pressure, making it difficult for airlines to simply add capacity whenever demand rises. He pointed to higher fuel costs linked to developments in the Middle East, as well as problems affecting aircraft engines, servicing and maintenance.

“As you all know, there are global pressures now on the aviation space. What’s happening out there in the Middle East has really impacted oil prices, which impacts fuel prices. In the best of days, the margins are exceedingly thin for airlines. You’re going to add this increase in jet fuel, it puts additional pressure on the industry,” he explained.

“Along with that, there is a shortage of aircraft because of issues to do with the engines, which I won’t really bore you all with. There are some service and maintenance things that are going on, which means a lot of aircraft have been pulled out of service,” he added.

The result, he said, is that Jamaica cannot depend on unlimited airline capacity, even as demand remains strong

“Airlines across the world don’t have infinite aircraft. That means that seats are not infinite. When the seats are full, the seats are full. Because of the demand that we have been generating for Jamaica, the vast majority of the flights into Jamaica are full,” he added.

Still, Rose said the outlook for airlift is positive, with airlines preparing to increase service as more hotel rooms become available.

He said airlines are also preparing to return to the flight schedules that existed before Hurricane Melissa, although they first have to resolve their own aircraft availability issues and factor in Jamaica’s accommodation capacity.

World.title: Security for Ireland’s easy-access politicians dealt a blow
World.content:
Healy-Rae had his window rolled down and was talking on the phone to his son Jackie, a Kerry councilman, as a man walked into the road and started punching the politician in the face. While the attacker fled on foot, police helped Healy-Rae reach a nearby hospital to have his facial wounds stitched up.

Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the attack on Healy-Rae — who had been a junior minister in his coalition government before his surprise resignation in April — could mark a watershed in how Irish politicians operate in public.

“We’ve never had this before in our society,” said Martin, who has represented the southwest city of Cork in parliament since 1989.

Reflecting the relative informality and openness of Irish political life, the prime minister spent part of this own week pressing the flesh with thousands of farmers at the National Ploughing Championships, one of the country’s perennial events featuring face-to-face contact with politicians from all parties. But there, too, Martin, faced an attempted assault and a suddenly beefed-up security detail.

“Our democracy is relatively unusual in the sense that our members of parliament, and indeed ministers and myself, can walk through our streets unhindered,” said Martin, who called the attack on Healy-Rae “a significant moment that we have to take very seriously.”

Healy-Rae, who was recovering Thursday at his Kerry home, issued a statement vowing he would “not be deterred” from politics.

World.title: European Investment Bank chief heads to Ottawa amid warming EU-Canada ties
World.content:
Coming after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed admitting Canada as an associate member of the EU, Calviño’s trip is significant given that the EIB typically only operates in developing countries or members of the European Union or European Economic Area.

Ahead of this year’s G7 summit, Canada extended a behind-the-scenes offer to alliance members for “priority access” to its critical minerals stockpile, according to a letter seen by POLITICO from Hodgson.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney named boosting critical raw materials as one of the areas in which he wants to boost collaboration between Ottawa and Brussels in a speech to the European Parliament on Thursday.

“Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defense industrial capacity, AI and computers, energy security, space and payments,” he said.

Carney told an investment summit in Toronto on Tuesday that EU and Canadian leaders would get down to serious business at an end-October summit that he will host in Montreal.

“The real deepening and discussions will be launched with our summit,” Carney said in Toronto. “And then go for it from there.”

Mike Blanchfield contributed reporting from Ottawa.

World.title: Immunity of Greek ex-commissioner lifted amid Qatargate probe
World.content:
Greek parliament then voted unanimously to lift his parliamentary immunity, and, in response to questions from POLITICO, Avramopoulos said he would appear before the Belgian authorities once a date has been set.

He added that he regrets not appearing when he was first summoned around a year ago, stating that had he testified then, there would be no arrest warrant today.

The Belgian arrest warrant for Avramopoulos, dated June 21 and seen by POLITICO, accuses him of membership in a criminal organization, bribery of an official, and money laundering. It also alleges a financial benefit totaling approximately €73,000.

Allegations center on Avramopoulos’ cooperation with Fight Impunity, a non-governmental organization and which the arrest warrant links to the ongoing Qatargate investigation. Avramopoulos was an honorary board member of the NGO and resigned as soon as the scandal broke.

The Qatargate scandal broke out in December 2022 — after Avramopoulos had left the Commission — when Belgian police launched a series of raids on properties and offices in Brussels, arrested key suspects, and seized bags of cash in one of the biggest corruption investigations to hit the EU. The core allegations are that suspects linked to the European Parliament accepted money or gifts in exchange for doing Qatar’s bidding.

Pier Antonio Panzeri, a former MEP from Italy who founded Fight Impunity, Greek former MEP Eva Kaili, and her husband, Francesco Giorgi, were arrested in Belgium in 2022. They are facing charges of corruption, money laundering, and participation in a criminal organization as part of the Qatargate investigation.

They have been released from jail pending trial, but there has been little progress in the case over the last couple of years. Panzeri admitted guilt and has struck a plea deal with the Belgian prosecutor to exchange information for a reduced sentence. Kaili has repeatedly maintained her innocence.

World.title: New taxes crucial to preserve EU budget, says Irish PM
World.content:
But the Taoiseach added that an agreement on new levies, also referred to as own resources, would be “very complicated,” highlighting tensions in the negotiations.

The European Commission put forward five new taxes in 2025, expected to raise €60 billion per year. But the proposal was met with resistance by national governments, reluctant to back new levies that would overwhelmingly affect their domestic industries.

Ireland, which holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU and is steering the budget talks, will announce a new negotiating document, or negobox, with revised figures in the coming weeks.

"When we meet all the various Member States, they have ambitions, they have asks, they have requests, and ... we cannot satisfy those requests if there's not a sufficiency of new own resources," Martin added, setting the tone for the next European leaders’ meeting on Oct. 15, where Costa aims to nail down several own resources that have strong backing among EU countries.

World.title: Carneys Vorstellungen über Handel in einer assoziierten Partnerschaft
World.content:
„Wir begrüßen dieses Ziel“, sagte er mit Blick auf von der Leyens Vorschlag. „Umfragen zeigen, dass eine überwältigende Mehrheit der Kanadier deutlich engere Beziehungen befürwortet.“

Carneys Liste potenzieller Bündnisse war ein früher Versuch, einem bislang noch weitgehend undefinierten politischen Vorhaben konkrete Inhalte zu verleihen.

Die Idee eines „assoziierten Mitglieds“ hatte am Mittwoch für Verwirrung gesorgt, da die Kommission dies zuvor nicht mit den europäischen Hauptstädten abgestimmt hatte und ein solcher Status derzeit nicht existiert. Später am Mittwoch erklärte US-Präsident Donald Trump, er könnte mit „erheblichen Zöllen“ reagieren, sollte Kanada eine engere Anbindung an die EU anstreben.

„Ein Bündnis für die Zukunft ist ein einzigartiger, positiver Ansatz, den wir gemeinsam definieren werden, indem wir auf unseren gemeinsamen Stärken aufbauen und uns auf gemeinsame Werte stützen“, sagte Carney.

Ministerin Joly will Zölle vermeiden

Kanadas Wirtschaftsministerin Mélanie Joly deutete am Mittwoch gegenüber Reportern in Toronto an, dass Ottawa zusätzliche Garantien im Handelsbereich anstrebt – was möglicherweise neue Gesetze erfordern könnte.

Auf die Frage nach der Möglichkeit einer „assoziierten“ EU-Mitgliedschaft merkte Joly an, dass Länder mit Freihandelsabkommen dazu neigen, sich stärker abzuschotten, um ihre eigenen Industrien zu schützen, wenn sie mit Zöllen belegt werden. Sie hob insbesondere die EU hervor.

World.title: Jensen Huang: Don’t regulate AI like social media
World.content:
“Unlike social media, which is a product, AI is a technology that's behind all of these other tech, all of these products — and so, regulate the products,” Huang said.

He said authorities should monitor for when an AI deployment “goes wrong” and “whenever new laws are necessary, add to the existing laws,” but pointed out that there are existing regulations in sectors where AI is deployed such healthcare, transportation, and entertainment.

Rigorous testing systems are needed, he said, in contained testing labs. “That's engineering, good old-fashioned engineering. It's not more than that. It's not less than that,” he said, adding the sector has to ensure that there is the “rigor of testing these products properly before we release it to the public.”

“This is no different than, you know, an omelet's not ready to be released, or a car is not ready to be released, an airplane engine's not ready to be released,” Huang said. “You should properly test it.”

Huang reiterated his point about holding back models until they're safe to release in his formal address to the event, in front of King Charles and representatives from OpenAI and Anthropic.

“When a product is not safe enough, we should hold it back and keep engineering. We've always done that, and we should continue to do that,” he said.

World.title: Carney to Trump: No one tells Canadians what to do
World.content:
“Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language to speak,” Carney continued, nodding to reports that the White House had sought to interfere with the French language spoken in Quebec. “No one is going to dictate our culture, or with whom we can strike agreements.”

Von der Leyen’s proposal to make Canada the EU’s first “associate member” left capitals scrambling and seemed to take even Ottawa by surprise.

Carney name-checked the term in his speech on Thursday, praising von der Leyen for “opening the door to Canada becoming the EU’s first associate member,” and adding that he welcomes the ambition.

Pressed by reporters on whether he preferred calling the new EU-Canada relationship an “Alliance for the Future” or “associate membership,” he shrugged off the distinction.

“President von der Leyen used both terms, alliance for the future and associate membership. The nomenclature is a question for Europe; what terms they use,” he said. “What matters is the substance. What are we actually building together.”

World.title: Left alliance wins Swedish election as PM Kristersson quits
World.content:
That may not be easy as two of these potential allies are at odds: The Left Party has named its price as having ministers in the government — and that’s something the liberal Center Party says it cannot accept.

Andersson said “a new era of cooperation between the political parties” would be needed.

In his resignation letter to the speaker of parliament, Kristersson, the conservative center-right leader, appealed for talks between “all parties” because pre-existing red lines would make finding a coalition hard. Although he didn’t name Andersson or the dispute between the Green and Left parties, it’s likely that he had these issues in mind.

“A constructive openness will now be needed from the parties in the Riksdag for a prime minister to be tolerated — and for a new government to gain support for its state budget,” Kristersson wrote. “Talks will need to be held with all parties to find ways around these deadlocks and create the conditions for a stable and effective government.”

One option sometimes discussed by commentators in Sweden is for the main center left and center right parties — Andersson’s Social Democrats and Kristersson’s Moderates — to come together to form a grand coalition, removing the need for support from either end of the political spectrum.

But even if they did agree to work together, these two parties would still need backing from a third to get a majority, and collaboration between the two rival camps is seen as highly unlikely by political insiders.

Negotiations could last weeks. The earliest a new prime minister can be sworn in is Sept. 29. Barring an unlikely unravelling of those negotiations, the result heralds the end of conservative Kristersson’s hopes of holding onto his job. He is expected to take a caretaker role until a new government is formed.

This article was updated.

World.title: UAE presidential adviser Gargash says trust with Iran will take years to rebuild
World.content:
Trust between the United Arab Emirates and Iran will take years to rebuild, UAE president's diplomatic adviser Dr Anwar Gargash said on Thursday.

 

Speaking at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai, he said relations with Tehran had to continue because the two countries were neighbours, but that confidence was a separate question after the attacks on the Gulf states.

Gargash said the UAE was managing the crisis while also assessing the future of the relationship.

“At the end of the day, we are neighbours, geographically neighbours. We have very complex relations with Iran, and certainly there is a collapse in the security regiment in the region. Thus, we have to find some new channels of understanding,” he said.
