He set out the UAE approach in three parts. “Our role, or rather our approach, is based on three elements. First, to defend our sovereignty, and then to be flexible,” he said. The third was continuity of economic development through the crisis, he said, citing the president's visit to Germany.

“We have to try. To maintain our development, our economic uproar, and the visit of our president to Germany was successful because we don't want to stop our economy in the midst of this crisis,” he said.

Asked about his 7 September statement that UAE confidence in Iran was broken, Gargash said he had drawn a deliberate distinction.

“Actually, I differentiated between the relations and the trust, and I said that the relations are a must and we should have communication and relations with Iran based on open dialogue and a dialogue that would overcome the daily matters,” he said.

“Confidence building, I believe, will take us a long time. We need years to rebuild this trust.”

“The Iranian president said that the aggression from Iran on the GCC countries was a big mistake,” he said.

“I think it is a geostrategic mistake that created a more complex situation for Iran that would affect its future.”

'UAE is a nice country but not an easy target'

He said Iran's use of proxy militias kept it close to the aggression, and that the Gulf states would be the parties to broker Tehran's return to its international place, trade and commerce, once the attacks stopped.

“They can't negotiate a new future while they are still threatening and being aggressive against the neighbourhood,” he said.

Asked whether the UAE had taken any measures of its own against Iran, financial or political, he said it had not.

“No, we have only defended ourselves, and we continue to defend ourselves, and we still extend our hands for friendly relations”, he said.

Gargash said Iran was made of different circles and that decision-making there was no longer held in one place, as it had been under the previous Ayatollah Ali Khamenei since 1989, and that the voices arguing against confrontation with the Gulf needed to be louder.

On the meeting between Sheikh Khalid bin Mohamed and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian at BRICS, Gargash said the two sides had agreed on the direction if not on everything.

“There was not a complete agreement between them. But there was an agreement on the fact that we should start a new page and look to the future,” he said.

“The future should never be like what we have now. It is not in the interest of Iran nor the GCC countries.”

He said President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed had set the balance between flexibility and strength from the beginning of the war.

“The UAE is a nice country, but we are not an easy target,” Gargash said. “He was so clear in saying that Iran is going to be away from stability for decades to come.”

Houthi control of Bab el-Mandeb 'concern for everyone'

Asked about the drone and rocket fire that triggered alerts in Saudi Arabia's city of Jeddah and Islam's holiest site of Mecca, Gargash said that "targeting Mecca is completely denounced and rejected.”

“The security and the sovereignty of Saudi Arabia is part of our security, and the stability of the GCC countries is interconnected,” he said.

The region had suffered from militias, Gargash said, naming Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen, and that “any arms outside the state are harmful for the countries and the region”.

“Yes, the channels are open. And as you are aware, and strategically speaking, the safety, security, and prosperity of Saudi Arabia is in our interest,” he said, asked whether relations with Riyadh remained open.

On the Houthis' offensive to take control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, Gargash said that "the Houthis' control over the strait is a concern for everyone," and not just a regional issue.

"This is not related to the region, but rather to the international economy," he said. “We go back to the basic principle that these straits are international. This is the international definition."

Gargash set out no timetable for further contacts with Tehran, saying the UAE did not choose the war but defended itself when it started, and that “this is a beginning for a political dialogue that should be started”.

World.title: Brussels seeks 'credible' outcome in EU-China talks after key negotiators’ call
World.content:
The European Commission stepped up pressure on China on Thursday, calling for tangible results with Beijing following a one-hour video call between Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao.

 

The EU executive hopes to secure commitments from Beijing to rebalance the trade relationship, as the bloc's trade deficit with China has been widening by €1 billion a day.

However, Beijing wants to secure access to the EU’s market of 450 million consumers, resisting calls from the Europeans to reduce its exports.

“While genuine engagement remains a priority, it is equally important that first concrete outcomes are delivered at the second session of the Trade and Investment Council in Beijing in October, which the Commissioner will co-chair – a signal that we are moving from rhetoric to results,” the Commission said in a statement after the call.

“That outcome needs to be credible,” the statement added.

The EU-China Trade and Investment Council was launched in June as a dialogue between the two sides, with the Commission setting October as a deadline to reach tangible results.

During the call on Thursday, Šefčovič and Wentao discussed market access on both sides and Chinese export controls on rare earths.

China has a near-monopoly over the production and processing of these strategic materials, which are essential to the EU’s green technology, defence and automotive industries, giving Beijing significant leverage in the negotiations.

The EU is seeking assurances that China will not halt its exports of rare earths again, a year after blocking them amid a trade war with the US. Securing the necessary export licences is essential for EU businesses.

EU leaders expect results

The coming weeks will be crucial for the negotiations, with EU officials expected to make another trip to China for technical discussions before Šefčovič himself travels to Beijing on 8–9 October.

In her State of the Union address to MEPs on Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also pushed for concrete results in the EU-China talks.

“Words are good. But deeds are better,” she said, making clear that the EU was ready to use all its trade defence instruments to rebalance the trade relationship.

China is also expected to feature prominently on the agenda when EU leaders meet in October. They have tasked the Commission with securing tangible results from its dialogue with Beijing.

In an interview with Euronews, Šefčovič also made clear that, without a “deliverable” to present to EU leaders,“the political interest would be to look for the solution through other instruments.”

The EU has several trade defence instruments such as anti-dumping duties or tariffs against unfair subsidies.

A diversification tool is also in the pipeline, aimed at reducing EU firms’ reliance on Chinese critical minerals for strategic technologies by helping them diversify their sources of supply.

Such a move would come as relations between Beijing and Brussels remain strained, following the Commission’s introduction of several legislative proposals aimed at protecting the EU market. One of them would introduce a European preference for products made in Europe, prompting China to threaten retaliatory measures.

Last summer, China also urged its companies to stop cooperating with the Commission in antitrust investigations, after the EU executive opened a probe in May into e-commerce giant JD.com over concerns about subsidies.

World.title: Air raid siren sounded for residents of eastern Poland
World.content:
Residents in parts of the Lublin and Podkarpackie provinces received a Government Security Centre alert at midday on Thursday warning of a possible air attack.

 

Earlier, the Operational Command of the Armed Forces reported that Polish military aviation had been activated in response to Russian strikes on Ukrainian territory.

Alert for residents

Residents of parts of Lublin and Podkarpackie provinces were sent an SMS reading: "ATTENTION! ATTENTION! ATTENTION! Threat of an air attack. Find a safe place. Follow the instructions of the emergency services. Await further announcements."

Alarm sirens were also activated in Lublin and Rzeszów.

The alert was lifted at around 12:50 local time. "There is no threat on Polish territory," officials declared.

According to the Operational Command of the Armed Forces, the deployment of Polish air power was a reaction to Russian strikes on western Ukraine. The statement noted that, in connection with the use of jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles against western Ukrainian territory, military aircraft began operating in Polish airspace.

The Command stressed that the measures taken were preventive. Their aim is to safeguard Polish airspace, with particular emphasis on areas close to regions under threat.

The Operational Command also underlined that it is continuously monitoring the situation and that its forces and assets "remain ready for an immediate response".

Tusk on Russian attack close to the Polish border

Prime Minister Donald Tusk also addressed the situation at a press conference following his meeting with Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker. He referred to the recent Russian attack on western Ukraine as "massive, extremely brutal".

Tusk said the strike took place in an area very close to the Polish border. "Near Yahodyn, which is by Dorohusk, a petrol station was apparently hit again, there was a very powerful explosion, and our aircraft were also scrambled," the prime minister said.

He added that a similar Russian air raid had taken place two days earlier, as well as during the night from Wednesday to Thursday. In his view, this means that 17 September, which marks the anniversary of the Soviet Union's aggression against Poland, is "unfortunately an exceptional day also in terms of today's security situation".

Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote on X: "Russia is not letting up in its aggressive actions. Today it carried out an attack just a few kilometres from the Polish border. There was no violation of our airspace. That is why in recent weeks I decided to strengthen the protection of Polish skies – we have increased the activity of F-16s and helicopters and are reinforcing air-defence and rapid-reaction systems."

Airports in Lublin and Rzeszów temporarily halt operations

Both airports in Lublin and Rzeszów were also temporarily restricted. The Polish Air Navigation Services Agency (PANSA) explained that this was necessary to ensure freedom of action for military aircraft.

"Due to the need to ensure the freedom of action of military aviation, airports in Lublin and Rzeszów temporarily suspended flight operations," PANSA said in a statement published on X.

World.title: Watch: Carney backs closer EU ties, draws applause at European Parliament
World.content:
Addressing the European Parliament in Strasbourg on 17 September, Carney backed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal to explore making Canada the EU’s first associate member, describing it as part of a broader effort to strengthen their sovereignty and resilience.

 

He called for deeper cooperation on critical minerals, defence, artificial intelligence, energy, space and financial systems, while proposing closer digital trade and stronger links between universities and young people.

Carney also made clear that the partnership was not intended to create a new geopolitical bloc.

“I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival – only with better manners,” he said, drawing applause. “We do not seek power to dominate others.”

The speech came just hours after Trump threatened “very serious tariffs” against the EU if Brussels pursued the proposed relationship with Canada.

Carney nevertheless presented the initiative as a long-term project that could extend beyond trade and defence. He said a Canada-EU alliance could become a “beacon” for other democracies, built around “freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability” and a shared commitment to international law.

World.title: Scotland halts new hyperscale AI data centre approvals amid environmental concerns
World.content:
No new hyperscale artificial intelligence (AI) data centres are expected to be approved in Scotland for up to a year, after lawmakers backed a pause on planning decisions while new national rules are developed.

 

Hyperscale data centres are among the largest facilities of their kind, designed to provide vast amounts of computing power and typically requiring tens of megawatts of electricity or more.

The Scottish Parliament on Wednesday said no planning or consenting decisions on hyperscale data centre applications should be made until the government publishes national guidance, which is due within 12 months, according to the motion passed by lawmakers.

The move comes as Scotland sees a surge in proposed data centres linked to the global AI boom. More than 20 large facilities have been proposed, including one project in Fife, in eastern Scotland, that has been described as potentially the second largest in the world.

Data centres provide the computing power needed to train and run AI systems, but they can also consume huge amounts of electricity and water.

That has prompted growing concern over whether Scotland’s energy grid can cope with rapidly rising demand, as well as over the impact of new projects on carbon emissions and nearby communities.

The Scottish government has separately introduced mandatory environmental impact assessments for all new data centres with a power capacity above 50 MW.

Scotland responds to AI infrastructure boom

The decision follows growing pressure from campaigners and local communities calling for clearer rules around the development of large AI data centres.

Hundreds of people protested outside the Scottish Parliament earlier this month, calling for a pause on new projects until the government sets out national planning standards and defines what should count as a “green” data centre.

The vote was a “landmark day” for communities concerned about projects being proposed in their areas, Kat Jones, director of the environmental group Action to Protect Rural Scotland, told the Guardian.

“There’s much still to be done, but this is a huge step forward,” she added.

The pause is not a permanent ban on new data centres. The Scottish government has been asked to report on the development of national planning guidance by the end of 2026 and publish the full guidance within 12 months.

According to the Guardian, Daniel Johnson, economy spokesperson for the Scottish Labour Party, said that the economic potential of the AI boom needed to be considered alongside its impact on the environment, communities and energy demand.

The debate reflects a wider challenge facing governments as technology companies invest heavily in the physical infrastructure needed for AI.

Countries are trying to attract new data centres and AI investment while also managing concerns over electricity demand, water consumption and climate targets.

World.title: How a Saudi pipeline attack is putting Europe’s oil security to the test
World.content:
Europe is bracing for a potential oil supply shock after Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline, also known as Petroline, following drone attacks earlier this month from Iran-backed allied Houthis and Iraq.

 

The Saudi energy ministry announced a precautionary shutdown on 10 September after drone attacks on the pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions the previous day.

The siege knocked out one of the kingdom’s most important alternatives to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz – the transit ruote for 20% of the world's oil and gas supplies – since the US and Israel launched military attacks on Iran on 28 February.

The pipeline has recently been carrying around 4–5 million barrels per day, roughly 4–5% of global oil supply, and the disruption to it is exposing once again that the EU's energy diversification strategy provides only one layer of security.

What happened to Saudi Arabia's oil pipeline?

While diplomatic talks to end the war in Iran keep stalling, Tehran and its regional proxies are executing a coordinated strategy targeting Saudi energy infrastructure in an attempt to completely block Saudi's oil exports through its eastern flank via the Red Sea.

The attack that shut the 1,200-kilometre East-West pipeline has disrupted the route carrying crude from the kingdom’s eastern fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, effectively bypassing Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline was built in 1981, after the Iranian Revolution, to provide an alternative route for crude exports that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz.

Running from the kingdom’s oil-producing east to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, it allows Saudi oil to reach global markets without passing through the Hormuz chokepoint.

East-West crude oil pipeline from Abqaiq to Yanbu. International Energy Agency

What are the implications for Europe?

European refineries have been forced to rethink their crude supply since Saudi Arabia began cancelling some oil cargoes from Yanbu, following the outage of the kingdom’s East-West oil pipeline.

Energy pricing agency Argus reported on 15 September that at least three European refiners had cargoes scheduled for late September cancelled or postponed, in some cases until November, citing unnamed market sources.

Poland's Orlen, one of the biggest buyers, has bought 16 additional cargoes from Norway, Britain, Algeria, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and the Americas to keep its refineries operating through October.

"We inform you that oil deliveries to Poland and the remaining refineries of the Orlen Group are being carried out on an ongoing basis and fully cover their demand," read a statement from the Polish energy refiner on X on 16 September.

Refineries are the facilities that turn crude oil into diesel, petrol, jet fuel and other products used across the economy. And they are not interchangeable machines: different refineries are configured to process different types of crude.

Why does Europe need Saudi oil?

Europe relies on Saudi crude partly because some Saudi grades have qualities that fit the configuration of European refineries, particularly their ability to process medium and heavier, relatively sour crude.

Replacing those barrels is possible, but finding equivalent grades in sufficient volumes can be costly and may require refiners to adjust their operations – a complex endeavour while the continent is already enduring high energy prices.

Without Saudi oil, Europe's refiners may have to blend several different crude grades to recreate the characteristics of the Saudi barrels they have lost.

"European refineries that have been reliant on Arab crude via the Red Sea have to find alternatives. But not all crudes are made equal," said June Goh, senior oil market analyst for the market intelligence Sparta Commodities.

Why are prices about to surge again?

Oil prices are set in global markets, so disruptions to supply can feed through to prices far beyond the country where they occur.

When traders and investors anticipate a tighter market – particularly if spare capacity or inventories are limited – prices can rise even before any physical shortage materialises.

Before the damage to the Saudi pipeline, it could move several million barrels a day – approximately 5.5 million – and has become particularly important with the Strait of Hormuz effectively blocked.

Now, with energy analysts estimating that about 3.5 to 4 million barrels per day are at risk, the gap has led to a surge in prices, with Brent crude oil recently trading above $113 a barrel due to mounting supply risks.

Several European countries are trying to cushion the impact of rising diesel prices, which are being felt at the gas pump as a direct consequence of the shutdown of Saudi Arabia's pipeline.

How serious could this crisis get?

That depends on whether energy infrastructure becomes a new target of military attacks and how quickly the Saudis can restore the pipeline to function at its normal capacity.

While minor damage to the pipeline has reportedly been repaired, restoring the damaged pumping stations and full pipeline operations could take up to six weeks, according to market intelligence firm Kpler's head of oil analyst Homayoun Falakshahi.

In the meantime, as Kpler noted on 14 September, a bypass pipeline around the damaged pumping station is serving as a temporary ﬁx in the short term.

"(Saudi) West Coast reﬁneries reduce throughput and increasingly rely on inventories, while Yanbu exports are partially disrupted, including northward ﬂows," Kpler stated.

Kepler said it had assessed Yanbu's oil terminal inventories at 9 thousand barrels of crude oil and other West Coast refinery inventories at 16.5 thousand barrels of crude oil.

"Assuming no additional piped throughput, these would be enough to sustain the current pace of loadings and runs for three and nine days, respectively," according to Kpler.

Related European leaders rush to counter looming diesel price surge as Saudi pipeline attacked

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia said on 16 September it expects to fix half of the pipeline's capacity in the coming days, leading analysts to a more positive outlook. However, its infrastructure could still face additional attacks.

If the damage to the pipeline is not repaired soon, Europe could face higher crude and refined-fuel prices and renewed inflationary pressure.

Until the pipeline resumes normal flows, what might normally be a regional logistics problem could become a potential squeeze for European refiners – and another test of how much room governments have to shield consumers and industry.

World.title: Sweden's centre-left win election as right wing bloc suffers narrow defeat
World.content:
Sweden's bloc of centre-left parties has won a parliamentary majority in the tightly contested general election.

 

The alliance is led by Magdalena Andersson and her party, the Social Democrats. It also includes the Left Party, Greens and the Centre Party. They now hold a three-seat majority in the 349-seat Riksdag (Sweden's parliament) over outgoing prime minister Ulf Kristersson's right-wing alliance.

After the final count, the result was very close with only around 50,000 votes separating the two opposing blocs nationwide.

For Andersson, the hard work starts now. She must form a government with the other parties in her alliance, which is likely to involve some very difficult negotiations because of because of major ideological differences within the bloc. The Centre Party says it will not support a government that gives cabinet posts to the Left, while the Left Party wants ministerial representation.

Social Democrats party leader Magdalena Andersson speaks during the Social Democrats' election night watch party. 13 September 2026 Jonas Ekströmer/TT News Agency via AP

She said voters had chosen “a new direction” for Sweden.

The outgoing prime minister Kristersson has now resigned, but if Andersson fails to form a workable cabinet, Kristersson could still attempt to form an alternative.

Kristersson said he would respect Andersson's attempts to form a government, wishing her luck given the divisions among her alliance.

As if often the case with coalition governments in Sweden, forming a government could take weeks. In 2022, it took more than five weeks. After 2018's election, it took almost 20 weeks.

An election worker counts early votes and overseas votes in Stockholm City Hall, in Stockholm. 16 September 2026 Christine Olsson/TT News Agency via AP

Waning support for parties on both sides

Despite winning as part of the centre-left bloc, for Andersson's Social Democrats party, it was their worst result in more than a century losing eight seats and with just 28% of the overall vote. The Social Democrats ruled the country for most of the 20th century and remain Sweden's largest party.

The far-right Sweden Democrats also lost support, for the first time since entering parliament in 2010, with their share of the vote falling to 17.5% and losing 11 seats in parliament.

International reaction

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez welcomed the result, presenting it as a victory for social democracy and the welfare state.

World.title: Moldova, Greece and Ireland: Where tourist arrivals are on the rise in Europe this year
World.content:
International tourism grew just 0.4% in the first half of 2026, with Europe seeing a 3% uptick in arrivals, according to the latest World Tourism Barometer from UN Tourism.

 

The continent was among the strongest performers, with only Africa seeing a larger growth of 4%.

Some 350 million international tourists visited Europe between January and June this year – but that growth wasn’t uniform.

Both Southern Mediterranean Europe and Central Eastern Europe saw a 4% growth, with Northern Europe up 3%.

On the flip side, arrivals in Western Europe declined 1%, with UN Tourism noting this was “partly due to heatwaves in June and weaker long-haul demand in some destinations during Q2 2026”.

The Middle East saw a 22% drop in arrivals, with South Asia down 5% and South East Asia down 1%.

“The Middle East situation has touched destinations far beyond the region itself and serves as a clear reminder that, in such a connected world, resilience needs to be built everywhere and not just when a crisis begins,” UN Tourism Secretary-General Shaikha Al Nuwais said.

The report notes that in Europe and Asia Pacific, the conflict has “partly shifted tourism demand toward nearby and more accessible destinations”.

Which destinations saw the biggest growth?

In Europe, Moldova had the biggest uptick in tourist arrivals, with a 25% rise in the first half of the year. Greece and Ireland both saw a 15% increase.

Globally, the destinations seeing the biggest rises include El Salvador (+37%), Paraguay (+34%), Bhutan (+31%), Vanuatu (+30%), Palau (+29%), Mongolia (+27%), Uzbekistan (+25%) and South Korea (+21%).

International arrivals are predicted to grow between 1% and 2% for 2026 – down from a forecast of 3% to 4% reported in January.

World.title: Germany's judges seek to prevent AfD justice abuse
World.content:
German judges and prosecutors have warned that the government needs to reform the laws around how state prosecutors to prevent extremist parties like the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) abusing them.

The official association of German judges, the Deutscher Richterbund (DRB) , has called on the federal government to tighten up the law to stop state governments from abusing prosecution powers to potentially influence criminal cases.

The prospect of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) taking over the government in Saxony-Anhalt, which appears highly likely after the party's resounding election win in early September, has raised fears that "extremists in government" could steer "criminal investigations in one direction or another through directives," according to the DRB.

The AfD, sections of which are considered a threat to the German constitutional democratic order by domestic intelligence agencies, is set to take control of a government for the first time ever in Saxony-Anhalt. This has sparked concern in the judicial system that the party could, for instance, push prosecutors away from pursuing cases against right-wing extremists.

"The top priority now is to prevent the misuse of public prosecutors' offices in Germany for partisan political purposes," DRB executive director Sven Rebehn said in a statement emailed to DW. "Currently, the law allows state justice ministries to interfere even in individual criminal proceedings. While there is a political tradition of self-restraint when issuing directives to prosecutors, this tradition can be abandoned at any time and offers no effective protection."

New report backs ban of German far-right party To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

State prosecutors — not independent

In Germany, unlike in many other countries, state prosecutors, along with the police, are part of the executive branch of government. This puts them under the authority of the state or federal Interior Ministries, and subject to parliamentary oversight. This dependence is seen by many constitutional lawyers as a democratic principle, as it means that prosecutors' actions can be checked by a democratically elected body. But others see it as a problem, as it opens the possibility of political influence.

German Interior Ministries, both at the federal level and in the 16 states, have the power to issue directives to prosecutors in individual cases. For instance, if some evidence has been supplied by an intelligence agency, the Interior Ministry can issue a directive to the prosecutor to keep that fact out of a court case, as disclosing it could compromise the work of the agency.

The German domestic intelligence agency, the Verfassungsschutz, which reports to the Interior Ministry, has long been a focus of the AfD's ire, as they consider it politicized. The agency is charged with keeping tabs on extremist tendencies in the country. By the same token, German Justice Ministries can make a ruling over how prosecutors interpret a certain law, or how investigations are to be pursued.

One such controversial directive was made in 2015, when the then federal Justice Minister Heiko Maas told the federal prosecutor to withdraw a report that found that state secrets had been compromised in a particular case. Maas denied that this had been the directive, and federal prosecutor Harald Range was dismissed in the ensuing power struggle.

As things stand, there is still no way to check the ministry's directives, which some see as a problem. Berlin's state prosecutor, Margarete Koppers, also has strong opinions on this point, and sees the danger as acute: "The rule of law is at risk when its rules are politically abused," a spokesperson for Koppers told DW by email. "A look at European countries that have, at various times, been under authoritarian-populist leadership — and where the structures of the rule of law were subsequently eroded — shows that this is not an unrealistic scenario." When the far-right Law and Justice (PiS) party took over in Poland, it triggered a constitutional crisis by trying to appoint judges to the constitutional court. The government of Viktor Orban in Hungary also tried to intervene in the judicial system.

EU, Poland row over judicial committee To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Another option: Make directives transparent

Both the DRB and Koppers believe removing the ministries' right to take directives is long overdue, but others in the judicial community are not so sure.

"I can understand the fear that a sword like this in the hands of the wrong people makes the executive branch a danger," said Gül Pinar, a criminal lawyer based in Hamburg who in 2020 offered expert testimony in the Bundestag on the issue.

But Pinar agrees that reform is necessary, but mainly because ministries' directives are not documented. "The people who are affected by the criminal procedures don't know that certain actions taken by the prosecutors stem from a directive, from the government, or the federal prosecutors, or the Interior Ministry," she told DW.

But if the directives were documented, Pinar argued, it would be possible for lawyers to examine whether they were legally sound, or whether they overstepped their authority. "We have to insert new mechanisms to check what is happening," she said.

"But the solution is not to make the state prosecutors independent," she underlined. Hardly anyone in the judiciary, Pinar said, doubts that the right to issue instructions stems from the principle of democracy. But she added that there were many voices, particularly amongst judges and public prosecutors, who advocate for an independent public prosecution service.

For its part, the current federal government has not shown any inclination to change the law. In a statement to the Legal Tribune Online, the Federal Justice Ministry said that the current laws provided plenty of safeguards: Ministries are prohibited from issuing "unlawful" directives, and prosecutors from following them.

In fact, the ministry said, keeping prosecutors as part of the executive branch was important, because it meant that they were more accountable and subject to parliamentary oversight.

Inside the AfD To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The European arrest warrant problem

The relatively unique position of Germany's state prosecutors has come up at the European level before: In 2019, the European Court of Justice warned that European arrest warrants could be compromised by political influence because German state prosecutors were not independent enough — while European arrest warrants are supposed to be issued by state prosecutors, in Germany, only judges are allowed issue them.

According to Pinar, allowing state prosecutors to issue arrest warrants is "not compatible with our legal system." In fact, she thinks the German system safeguards more civil freedoms: "In Germany, withdrawing someone's freedom is always under the authority of the judge," she said. "I think it would better if other countries adapted their systems to ours, so that the executive branch can decide on the freedom, but was under a judge's authority."

Edited by Rina Goldenberg

World.title: Germany cuts development aid despite growing crises
World.content:
The budget of Germany's Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) is set to shrink for the fifth consecutive year. Aid organizations warn that the cuts could have dramatic consequences for millions

Germany's Development Minister, Reem Alabali Radovan, opened her latest speech in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, with a litany of catastrophes and suffering: floods in Nepal, heat waves, forests engulfed in flames, rivers running dry, and crop failures caused by drought and lack of rainfall.

"Millions of people are facing hunger," said the minister from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD). "And one thing is clear: the climate crisis is threatening the entire world. No country can tackle it alone."

Radovan opened the debate on the federal government's proposed 2027 budget for her ministry with a stark assessment. The budget is set to shrink for the fifth consecutive year, falling from just over €10 billion to just under €9.5 billion. In 2022, it still stood at nearly €14 billion. Since then, the ministry's budget has been reduced by roughly one third.

Fighting to end suffering in Africa's conflict zones To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How does this sharp decline square with the dramatic picture painted by Germany's development minister herself? She points to the new strategy she unveiled in January, when she declared: "Development policy will become an even more important pillar of German security, alongside diplomacy and defense."

Funding for humanitarian aid stagnates

Aid organizations reacted skeptically to this policy shift when it was first announced, and their concerns have deepened in light of the latest funding cuts. "The renewed reductions in funding for international cooperation are further exacerbating an already critical situation," said Michael Herbst of VENRO , the umbrella organization representing around 150 development and humanitarian NGOs.

Herbst also criticizes the stagnant budget for humanitarian aid administered by the German Foreign Office. While it exceeded €3 billion in 2022, it has remained at just €1 billion since 2025. In light of worsening global crises, VENRO is calling for a change of course. "Next year, we will need to invest more in combating hunger because the conflict involving Iran and the dry summer are expected to trigger a sharp decline in agricultural yields," Herbst said, explaining the organization's demand for substantially higher funding.

Ten million people left without assistance

The impact of the cuts is already clearly visible, the umbrella organization stresses, citing a survey of its member organizations. The number of funded projects is declining significantly. "Our sample of 34 organizations shows that, among these organizations alone, more than ten million fewer people are being reached with assistance."

"And many local partner organizations, which are indispensable to effective development cooperation and humanitarian assistance, are no longer able to operate," Herbst added. He also stressed that the full impact of these far-reaching cuts is unlikely to become apparent for another three to four years.

Should the development budget be exempt from Germany's 'debt brake'?

The federal government's belt-tightening across virtually all ministries is a consequence of the Zeitenwende announced by then-Chancellor Olaf Scholz(SPD) in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Since then, Germany has embarked on a major military buildup, increasing its defense budget year after year, while nearly all other ministries have had to make do with significantly less funding.

Herbst, a member of VENRO's executive board, is calling on the German Bundestag to exempt both development cooperation and humanitarian assistance from the country's so-called 'debt brake'. "After all, exceptions have already been made for the modernization of the Bundeswehr and for military aid to Ukraine," he points out. Herbst hopes that such a move would enable Germany to once again assume greater responsibility on the international stage.

Germany's Radovan warns SDGs unlikely to be met by 2030 To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Less money, less impact?

Jamila Schäfer, a member of parliament from the opposition Green Party, made a similar argument during the Bundestag debate on the development ministry's budget. Climate action and development cooperation, she argued, are not acts of charity but are firmly in Germany's own interest.

"Germany must invest in its defense capabilities, but security is not created through investments in the defense budget alone," Schäfer argued. "Those who strengthen military security while cutting support for international stability have a blind spot in their security policy."

Nicolas Zippelius, a lawmaker from the governing centre-right conservative alliance, the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), sees the ongoing cuts to development spending differently. In his view, every ministry must contribute to consolidating the federal budget. "Less money does not necessarily mean a smaller impact. Instead, it should encourage us to focus more clearly on priorities and critically review existing structures."

Zippelius dismisses demands to exempt the development ministry from Germany's 'debt brake'. "The key question is whether every euro spent is directed to where it can make the greatest difference." The Christian Democrat argues that success in development cooperation, as in other areas of policy, should be judged not by the size of the budget but by the impact it achieves.

German Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan in Kenya To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The case for more prevention

Jan Sebastian Friedrich-Rust, who heads the humanitarian and development aid organizationAction Against Hunger , has a very different view. "The cuts planned for the 2027 budget are short-sighted and dangerous. As a result, up to 22.6 million people worldwide could die by 2030," he said in a written statement to DW.

Cuts to development cooperation and humanitarian aid are also fiscally short-sighted, Friedrich-Rust argues. "Hunger, crises and instability generate long-term costs that far exceed the cost of prevention. Those who cut spending today are merely postponing the bill and ultimately making it much more expensive," he warned.

To underscore its concerns, the alliance Action Against Hunger delivered a petition to the leaders of the governing coalition of SPD and CDU/CSU parliamentary groups on the eve of the Bundestag's budget debate. The appeal, titled "Don't Balance the Budget at the Expense of Solidarity: Strengthen International Aid!", garnered around 100,000 signatures.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Exotic animal smuggling baffles activists in India
World.content:
Orangutans, rare reptiles and other exotic animals are popping up in India, suggesting the country is becoming a major destination for trafficked wildlife.

Five infant orangutans, a species found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra and on Borneo, were found in a forest by rangers patrolling in the Balasore district of India's eastern Odisha state last week.

Indonesia's Forestry Ministry has asked India to establish the origin of the abandoned orangutans, known for their shaggy red fur, and return them if they are found to have come from their usual habitat abroad.

The rescue of the rare apes has raised fresh questions about how exotic animals enter India and how the country is used in the illegal wildlife trade.

How did five baby orangutans end up in India?

"The discovery on the eastern coast of India is a bit mind-boggling. It's like that time a few years ago when live kangaroos were found wandering along the highways of West Bengal," Kanitha Krishnasamy, Southeast Asia director at wildlife trade monitoring network TRAFFIC, told DW.

"What are orangutans doing in India? Were they smuggled from their native Malaysia or Indonesia or did they come from a facility?" she asked.

The youngsters appeared to be healthy and were being cared for at a zoo after their rescue Image: ANI/IMAGO

The Odisha government has asked the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate how the critically endangered animals reached the state.

"These animals are not found in India and are mostly seen in the rainforests of Malaysia, Indonesia, Borneo and Sumatra in Southeast Asia," said Odisha's Forest and Environment Minister Ganesh Ram Singh Khuntia.

"We suspect that they might have been released in the Balasore district forest… by an international wildlife smuggling racket."

Indian officials seize pythons, parrots, giant tortoises

The orangutans are the latest in a series of exotic wildlife being seized in India.

In November 2024, authorities in the Indian city of Bengaluru seized 40 rare animals arriving from the Malaysian capital, Kuala Lumpur, including Aldabra giant tortoises, gibbons, American alligators and iguanas.

In June 2025, Mumbai Customs seized 284 exotic animals arriving in four consignments from the Thai capital, Bangkok, including snakes and tortoises.

In July 2025, customs officials in the Indian city of Pune intercepted 20 exotic animals from passengers arriving from Bangkok. They included 14 green tree pythons, four double-eyed fig parrots and two Sumatran striped rabbits.

'Shocking' volume of trafficked wildlife found in India

According to figures from TRAFFIC, 7,272 individual animals, alive and dead, were seized from passenger baggage in smuggling attempts between Thailand and India between January 2022 and May 2025, with more than 80% of interceptions taking place in India.

The animals included reptiles, birds and mammals — many apparently destined for the exotic pet trade.

"We have found hundreds of species and thousands of individuals being trafficked into India through air and land routes. This changed drastically from around 2020," conservation researcher and practitioner Uttara Mendiratta told DW.

"Both the volume of this trafficking, and the number of species involved, many of which are endangered, have been shocking."

Law enforcement lagging behind smugglers

TRAFFIC says India and Malaysia were the countries most implicated in an illegal gibbon trade chain identified in 2025, with gibbons being moved from Malaysia to India.

Trishala Ashok, a conservation filmmaker and science communicator, says the scale of the trade remains difficult to establish.

"Our enforcement systems haven't evolved at the same speed as the trade," Ashok told DW. "We are still reacting to individual seizures rather than mapping the networks, financiers, suppliers and buyers behind them."

Tito Joseph of the Wildlife Protection Society of India says the situation is escalating.

"Smuggling of exotic species was always there in India," Joseph told DW.

At the same time, he noted that it has increased significantly since 2018.

He identifies routes running from Myanmar through northeast India into other parts of the country, as well as movement from Bangladesh into India. By air, Thailand and Malaysia are important sources of trafficked wildlife.

The routes into India also extend beyond airports. Exotic animals are also reaching India through its northeastern land borders.

"What is new is the large volume of incoming live wildlife. There are indications that some of the traders who were involved in smuggling live animals like star tortoises out are now also involved in sourcing [other] exotic wildlife," said Mendiratta, the conservation researcher.

Social media fans illegal animal trade

Demand is being fueled by growing ownership of exotic pets and unregulated digital marketplaces, according to a June 2026 analysis of India's exotic pet trade by Humane World for Animals India, an NGO that works to tackle the root causes of animal cruelty.

"Internationally, social media platforms have aided and abetted the growth of illegal trade in wild animals by providing a platform for people to display and boast about the animals they collect," wildlife biologist and conservation scientist Ravi Chellam told DW. "These platforms are also serving as an online marketplace for the illegal trade to flourish."

"The problem is exacerbated by the senseless and obscenely huge personal collections of animals from around the world by the rich and the famous," Chellam noted.

Establishing where an animal came from can become particularly difficult once it has crossed several borders.

"A seizure cannot be the end of the investigation. It should be the beginning," said Ashok, the conservation filmmaker.

"Who supplied the animals? Who arranged the movement? Who paid? Who was waiting for them?" she asks. "Until we start following those links, we will keep catching consignments without dismantling the networks behind them."

World.title: Fact check: How disinformation fuels Houthi-Saudi conflict
World.content:
As fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia escalates, old and repurposed videos have flooded social media, with many presented as fresh footage from the front lines.

The conflict between Yemen's Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia has sharply escalated in recent days, with Houthi forces making rapid gains along the Red Sea coast and taking control of key areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Saudi Arabia has responded with airstrikes. Houthi forces have launched drones and missiles towards Saudi territory. The renewed fighting has also raised concerns about global trade via the Red Sea.

The conflict has also spread online, where significant disinformation has circulated.

DW's fact-checking team examined what is circulating and why a conflict that is so hard to observe independently leaves so much room for this kind of disinformation.

Nine-second viral clip

One nine-second clip has gone viral. It shows a huge explosion between buildings, with fireballs and screaming in the background.

Claim: A user posted the video on X with the Arabic caption "Yemeni forces are carrying out the strongest strikes in various areas in Saudi Arabia, including Abha." The video has more than 340,000 views.

It was also posted in other languages , falsely claiming that it showed real footage from the current fighting.



Toward the end of the clip, a lamppost emerges out of nowhere, a clear sign that the video was AI-generated Image: X

DW Fact check: Fake and AI-generated

The video is not only old, but also artificially generated. There are several visual clues in the clip such as the pattern of the explosions and the uniform way the smoke spreads.

A large-scale explosion of this kind would also have generated a very bright flash, and nearby buildings would likely have collapsed or at least had their windows shattered. Neither appears to have happened.

One can also see, in the final seconds of the video, how a lamppost appears out of nowhere in the middle of the frame.

The audio is mostly unintelligible, but the speaker's tone does not appear to change after the huge explosion. Such a large explosion would normally be expected to trigger some audible reaction in the speaker's voice.

On the technical side, Hive Moderation's AI detection analysis also confirmed that the video was artificially generated.

According to AI detection platform Hive Moderation, there are clear indications that the video was generated using artificial intelligence Image: Hive Moderation

The very same video was shared this June , then claiming to show explosions in Iran, as we found with a reverse image search.

Not enough verified information from Yemen

The recycling of old or unrelated footage is not new to the Yemen conflict.

Hannah Porter has spent years researching fake news and disinformation in Yemen and the country's wider information environment. She says this has been happening for years.

"There is less international attention in Yemen than there might be in other conflicts around the world. And, because there is not sufficient attention paid to Yemen, I think that allows more space for disinformation to spread not only within Yemen and in the region, but globally about Yemen," Porter told DW.

The Houthis seized Yemin's capital, Sanaa, and expanded their control in 2014. Saudi Arabia intervened militarily in 2015 in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.

A UN-brokered truce in 2022 sharply reduced fighting, but it did not resolve the conflict. Fighting has since intensified again.

The Houthis now control large parts of northern and western Yemen. Saudi Arabia supports forces opposing them, while Iran has provided the Houthis with military support.

Experts and media watchdogs such as Reporters Without Borders have repeatedly pointed out that reporting from parts of Yemen remains extremely difficult. Journalists face threats, and independent media outlets are under intense pressure. This contributes to the spread of disinformation.

It is "very difficult to get reliable information, especially now and especially in the north [of Yemen]," Porter said.

She said researchers and the international community were struggling to establish what is happening in northern Yemen.

Military exercise becomes ambush

The second video that DW Fact check examined shows how genuine footage can become a source of disinformation.

Claim: A 30-second clip posted on X shows a convoy of military vehicles passing through a desert. Moments later, large explosions erupt and several vehicles are engulfed in smoke and flames. The caption reads: "The most beautiful thing I've seen: Houthis ambush against the Saudi-Backed Mercenaries' convoy in Yemeni."

This video does not show an ambush by the Yemeni rebel Houthis Image: X

DW Fact check: False

The video is old and unrelated to the ongoing conflict.

A timestamp visible in the video points to March 10, 2024. A reverse image search led DW to an older video published on YouTube in April 2024.

That video claims to show a Houthi military exercise. Its caption, written in Arabic, describes a simulated ambush on Israeli positions and attacks on US and British forces. Israeli and American flags can be seen in the footage.

DW also traced the sequence to a 42-minute video published by Yemeni War Media, an outlet affiliated with the Houthi movement.

Interestingly, the audio of that clip was changed. The version that is now circulating contains dramatic commentary, which is actually sports commentary from a football match played in 2018, as clips from that match show.

As is often the case, the clip with the convoy has also been used previously in different contexts .

Houthi gains in Yemen threaten key Red Sea shipping route To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With much of Yemen's media landscape weakened by the conflict, reliable information about events can be difficult to obtain.

That makes it harder for people to independently assess footage circulating online, Porter said. She added that unverified and misattributed videos can significantly shape perceptions of how battles are unfolding elsewhere.

"Any image or video that you see that is purported to be of a specific battle in Yemen, you have to be really skeptical," Porter said. "And you have to find a way to fact check it."

Emad Hassan contributed to this article

Edited by Uta Steinwehr and Thomas Sparrow

World.title: South Africa: Police find 9th body of woman amid spree fears
World.content:
Police in South Africa have discovered the bodies of nine women east of Johannesburg in two months, stoking fears of a serial killer or group of killers.

Police in South Africa on Thursday found the body of another woman near the airport east of Johannesburg.

The woman's body was found stabbed, beaten and partially naked.

The body is the ninth that has been discovered in the area in the last two months, raising fears that the killings could be connected and that a serial killer — or group of killers — might be active.

What do we know about the latest discovery of a woman's body near Johannesburg?

The bobies were all discovered in Ekurhuleni, a municipality immediately east of Johannesburg, the country's largest city.

Both Ekurhuleni and Johannesburg lie in Gauteng province.

Fred Kekana, the provincial police commissioner, said the woman's body was found near a construction site by a passerby, who alerted police.

The victim, who has not been identified, appeared to be around 30 years old and had a stab wound to her side. Her throat also appeared to have been cut, Kekana said, although the cause of death has not yet been officially determined.

Previously, investigators had said similarities in the killings of the first eight victims were "sufficiently concerning for the police to issue a public warning."

Police said the latest find early Thursday would be "added to the investigations into the deaths of women in Ekurhuleni."

A lockdown has been put in place in Kempton Park in Ekurhuleni and police have set up roadblocks, after three of the bodies were discovered in recent days.

"We cannot continue picking up bodies," deputy police chief Tebello Mosikili told journalists at the scene on Thursday.

Residents of the area have been left shaken by the killings Image: Emmanuel Croset/AFP

Killings send shockwaves through South Africa

Mosikili said investigators look at whether the latest find is linked to the earlier murders or if a so-called copycat killer is also active.

Police have offered a reward of 400,000 rand (about $25,000 or €21,400) for information leading to an arrest.

The premier of Gauteng province, Panyaza Lesufi, said Thursday that "someone has declared war against us, and we will push back, we are not going to surrender."

President Cyril Ramaphosa said Tuesday that "no stone will be left unturned" to solve the crimes.

"These incidents are causing fear and uncertainty in our communities, and especially among women," Ramaphosa said.

South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world, and gender-based violence is also endemic. The country has declared a national emergency to tackle the issue.

The UN estimates that one in three women experiences physical or sexual violence during her lifetime.

World.title: Europe seeks stricter age limits for TikTok, Instagram and Facebook
World.content:
The European Commission wants to bar children under 13 from social media platforms and curb addictive features such as infinite scrolling. Companies that fail to comply could face hefty fines.

Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, unveiled a plan aimed at keeping children away from the risks associated with some social media platforms.

The initiative seeks to prevent children younger than 13 from accessing platforms such as Facebook, TikTok and Instagram.

"What we already have is a consensus that there needs to be a start date for the age children can join social media," von der Leyen said, calling for "age-appropriate restrictions."

The measure follows similar proposals introduced in Australia, the United Kingdom, China, India, Turkey, and several European countries, and responds to growing concerns about the impact social media can have on children's mental health.

"Today, our children are interacting with some of the most sophisticated technologies ever created, and they were not designed with their well-being and development in mind," von der Leyen said at a press conference.

The proposed reform to the EU Kids Act "will establish clear boundaries in the digital world, just as we do every day in the real world," she added.

Do European laws contradict each other?

The non-profit organization CCIA Europe, which represents major technology companies in Europe, including Google and Meta, warned about potential privacy risks stemming from the proposal and pointed to "conflicting requirements" under other European Union laws.

"Collecting age information, identity credentials, and data linking children to their parents or guardians on this scale would undoubtedly create an attractive target for cybercriminals," said CCIA Europe Director Daniel Friedlaender.

"The Kids Act creates legal overlap and regulatory duplication that ultimately weakens protections for children and consumers," he added.

Can AI tell if you're 18+ just from your hand movements? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

More parental control and stricter regulations

Von der Leyen's proposal would give parents greater control over the accounts of young people aged 13 to 15.

The initiative will be debated among EU member states and the European Parliament in the coming months before it can become law.

Social media accounts, video streaming services, online video games, and chatbots aimed at users under 18 would be subject to a set of stricter regulations.

These include banning features considered addictive, such as infinite scrolling and autoplay content. The proposal would also restrict algorithm-driven recommendations, personalized profiling, reward-based engagement mechanisms, and unsolicited contact from strangers.

Another demand from the European Parliament is that platforms be required to implement child-safe designs and algorithms, while also providing easy-to-use parental controls.

In addition, major technology companies would have to strengthen their age-verification systems for anyone seeking to open an account.

Companies that fail to comply could face fines of up to 6% of their global annual revenue.

They would also be required to dedicate greater resources to content supervision and moderation.
