World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019029/Token of Trust: Beijing Links AI Usage to Company Loans
World.title: Token of Trust: Beijing Links AI Usage to Company Loans
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019029/Token of Trust: Beijing Links AI Usage to Company Loans
World.content:
A zone in Beijing has launched a program asking several banks to extend billions of yuan in credit to multiple companies across the AI industry chain, partly based on their token usage.

Termed “token loans,” the financing scheme was recently implemented by the Beijing Economic and Technological Development Zone, also known as Beijing E-Town, in the city’s southeast, and involves extending nearly 2 billion yuan ($300 million) in credit to several AI companies, domestic media reported Monday.

A token is the smallest unit of data an AI large language model can process. In March, the National Data Administration officially adopted “ciyuan” — combining “word” and “currency” — as the Chinese term for “token.” The move was largely seen as putting an economic spin on AI-led computing power.

In June of this year, China’s daily token consumption already exceeded 500 trillion, according to data from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. A Saturday report by the China Telecom Research Institute estimates that that number could rise to 100 quadrillion, or 200 times that figure by year-end.

Six domestic banks, including the Agricultural Bank of China, China CITIC Bank, Industrial Bank, Bank of Beijing, China Minsheng Bank, and Huaxia Bank, provided the loans. The credit is intended for AI companies with “high research investment and high technological barriers,” as well as growing computing needs, but without the physical assets or profits typically required to obtain bank financing.

In addition to token consumption, the banks also awarded the loans based on technological barriers, team strength, and companies’ business development prospects.

Guoqi Zhikong, a developer of automobile-focused connected cloud platforms and autonomous driving vehicles, received a 30-million-yuan credit line from China CITIC Bank. Meanwhile, Shenzhou Guangda, which provides computing infrastructure and enterprise-level AI agent solutions, received the same credit amount from Industrial Bank.

The rapid growth of the AI industry has created a dilemma for tech startups, which often struggle to obtain traditional loans, an anonymous staff member from Beijing E-Town’s business and finance bureau told domestic media. Conventional lending models rely heavily on collateral and corporate profit statements, so even companies with strong technological capabilities often lack physical assets to pledge. In contrast, their opportunities for technological development and business expansion are constrained by profits that have yet to fully materialize.

In August, Bank of China’s branch in the southern city of Guangzhou launched the country’s first token loan scheme. Aimed at small- and medium-sized computing companies, it covers token supply, applications, and related services, with successful applicants eligible for up to 30 million yuan in credit.

Looking ahead, Lou Feipeng, a researcher at the Postal Savings Bank of China, said that before such loans can be adopted more broadly, the country must address several major issues, including exaggerated token-use data, inaccurate assessments of computing power consumption, and overestimation of borrowers’ repayment ability.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018999/From Monkey Kings to Little Demons: China’s New Age of the Supporting Character
World.title: From Monkey Kings to Little Demons: China’s New Age of the Supporting Character
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018999/From Monkey Kings to Little Demons: China’s New Age of the Supporting Character
World.content:
In the classic Chinese novel “Journey to the West,” little demons are nobodies. They serve powerful demon kings, perform menial tasks, and are easily dispatched by heroes like Sun Wukong, better known as the Monkey King. Most do not even have names.

But increasingly, these once-forgotten characters are moving to the center of the story. Across Chinese films, TV shows, games, and books, little demons are being transformed from anonymous supporting characters into protagonists in their own right.

Take Black Myth: Wukong, the Chinese AAA video game that became a global hit. The game features a compendium of 203 supernatural creatures, including 90 classified as “little demons,” each with its own biographical profile. It is almost like an archive assembled from the gaps in “Journey to the West,” a who’s who of forgotten characters.

Another example is 2024’s “The Great Nobody,” a Chinese comedy series spinoff that grew out of the variety show “Amazing Night.” In it, a group of little demons living on the fictional Flower Neck Mountain waits in vain for the monk Tang Sanzang and his disciples to arrive on their pilgrimage to retrieve Buddhist scriptures. The reworking of the classic tale becomes a commentary on supporting comedians struggling to make their mark in the entertainment industry.

But perhaps the most striking example is “Nobody,” a Chinese animated film that grossed 1.7 billion yuan ($240 million) at the box office last summer. Expanded from the first episode of “Yao-Chinese Folktales,” an animated anthology series released on the video platform Bilibili in 2023, the film follows a “knock-off” pilgrimage team of demons comprising a pig, a toad, a weasel, and a gorilla.

Seen in the broader history of “Journey to the West” adaptations, this renewed interest in little demons represents the third major approach to interpreting the classic since the turn of the millennium.

The first was what might be called “post-revolutionary interpretations.” Emerging in the late 1990s, this approach is represented by Stephen Chow’s “A Chinese Odyssey” (1995) and the online novel “The Legend of Wukong,” which began serialization in 2000. These works focused on Sun Wukong’s struggle for individual autonomy, symbolized by his decision over whether to don the golden headband, a device used by Tang Sanzang to rein in his mischievous nature. At their core was the tragic rebellion of the neoliberal individual against the grand narrative of the pilgrimage, as well as a playful deconstruction of earlier “revolutionary” interpretations of “Journey to the West.”

The second consisted of “gothic interpretations,” represented by films including “Journey to the West: Conquering the Demons” (2013), “The Monkey King 2” (2016), and “Journey to the West: The Demons Strike Back” (2017). Through digital spectacle, these films created fantastical worlds and recast the classic as a monster movie. Their dark, horror-filled atmosphere can be seen as a cultural expression of the crisis of neoliberalism.

The third approach is what I call “system-based interpretations.” These works portray the Heavenly Palace and Vulture Peak, the respective seats of the Taoist and Buddhist hierarchies, as parts of a vast network of relationships. Tang Sanzang and his disciples’ pilgrimage to obtain the scriptures becomes a meticulously planned project, while the 81 trials they encounter along the way are recast as conspiracies orchestrated by the powers that be.

Ma Boyong’s bestselling novel “The Annoyance of the Gods” (2023), for example, portrays Taibai Jinxing, a deity associated with the planet Venus, as a project manager exhausted by office politics. In doing so, the novel reframes the pilgrimage as an internal struggle within a sprawling bureaucracy characterized by maneuvering, competition, and checks and balances.

The focus on little demons emerged from this same “system-based” approach. Rather than subverting the logic of the original text, these works stand in the shadows of its grand narrative and construct detailed accounts of the lives of those who remain nameless.

This interpretation is closely connected to the current social mood. Since 2020, growing uncertainty has weakened faith in nixi, or the idea that ordinary people can beat the odds and dramatically improve their fortunes. As economic growth has slowed, such aspirations have increasingly given way to greater empathy for ordinary workers simply trying to get by.

If the era in which little demons were ignored corresponded to a period of economic expansion, when workers believed they too could “retrieve the scriptures and achieve Buddhahood,” then the era of empathizing with them belongs to the period after that peak. Ordinary people stuck on the periphery of systems recognize themselves in these little demons: operating at the margins, with limited control over events, and little guarantee that their efforts will be rewarded.

Take “Nobody,” for example. Close-ups of the little demons’ vacant eyes and sluggish expressions reflect the mental state of some workers today. Their circumstances , to a certain extent, closely mirror contemporary workplaces: routine and often modest tasks, represented by scrubbing pots and making arrows; shifting expectations and promises that do not always materialize; and the risk of being treated primarily as a functional part of a larger operation.

Identification with these little demons reflects a changing sense of where ordinary workers locate themselves within larger systems. Rather than always imagining themselves as protagonists destined to rise above their circumstances, they may find greater resonance in supporting characters who navigate constraints, make compromises, and carve out limited forms of agency within the roles available to them.

This sense of being a supporting character also underlies the popular idea that “the world is just a ragtag troupe.” Some individuals may struggle to fully identify with the current situation while also finding it difficult to imagine viable alternatives. For those who remain within these structures, a common response is to learn how the rules operate and navigate the available room within them in order to maintain a workable position.

This shift toward accepting a supporting role has already manifested in forms of spectatorship common online. “Roasting” other people’s stories allows individuals to mock them from a safe distance while releasing some of the psychological pressure they themselves face.

Posting “bullet comments” that scroll across videos in real time creates a more distanced form of viewing while giving spectators a sense of collective belonging. “Eating melon,” a Chinese internet expression for following gossip and online drama as a bystander, similarly turns public events into spectator entertainment. Rather than emphasizing individual agency, these forms of spectatorship encourage people to watch from the sidelines.

This consciousness has also spread into contemporary cultural production, with little demons being just one example. In the 2024 web novel “The Diary of a Female Zombie’s Hiking Adventure,” the protagonist has no desire to become involved in other people’s storylines and instead chooses simply to observe. Meanwhile, in the animated film “Chang An” (2023), the figure who guides the audience through the splendor of the Tang dynasty (618–907) is the diligent and orderly poet Gao Shi rather than Li Bai, the personality who most fully embodies the era’s poetic spirit. Through Gao Shi’s eyes, Li Bai’s wildness and romanticism are viewed with a sense of incomprehension and detachment.

The audiences for these works are people navigating rapid social change, uncertainty, and shifting forms of connection. They are not merely digital natives, but individuals searching for a sense of place and meaning in this “era of supporting characters.”

Translator: David Ball.

(Header image: Visuals from Douban and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019024/After Beijing Bowel Accident, Hyrox Changes Its Rules
World.title: After Beijing Bowel Accident, Hyrox Changes Its Rules
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019024/After Beijing Bowel Accident, Hyrox Changes Its Rules
World.content:
Hyrox has amended its official rulebooks after the winner of a recent Beijing event experienced bowel incontinence mid-race yet continued competing. The incident sparked widespread debate in China over sportsmanship and the organizer’s handling of potential hygiene risks.

On Monday, Hyrox updated its online rulebook to state that a race director may withdraw an athlete if their “blood, vomit, urine, or faeces pose a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers.”

The change comes in the wake of controversy surrounding the women’s solo elite race on Saturday, in which Australian athlete and Hyrox world record holder Joanna Wietrzyk finished first with a time of 1:01:23. Footage circulating online showed fecal matter staining Wietrzyk’s clothing and legs as she performed various exercises.

Hyrox has recently surged in popularity across China. Founded in Germany, the sport features eight 1-kilometer runs, each followed by strength training stations including sled pulls, rowing, and burpees. China’s first official race was held in Beijing in 2024 and drew 1,700 entries. Participants at this weekend’s Beijing event exceeded 11,000, with standard individual registration costing roughly 800 yuan ($125).

Competitors and social media users questioned organizers’ decision to let Wietrzyk continue racing. The Women’s Pro division won by Wietrzyk began at 2:40 p.m. Saturday, with other heats scheduled until 8:40 p.m. and another full day of competition Sunday.

“As someone who works in the public health sector, my biggest concern is that if she had a bacterial or viral infection, contamination like this could spread pathogens very quickly,” a Beijing-based athlete in her 20s, surnamed Wang, whose race began about an hour after Wietrzyk, told Sixth Tone.

Toilets were available at the venue, she noted, but using the bathroom counts toward an athlete’s total race time.

In a post made via its official account on microblogging platform Weibo Saturday night, Hyrox’s China division said organizers had “immediately” closed and disinfected affected areas and removed contaminated equipment. Wang said she had seen nothing “noticeably unusual” on the course.

Wietrzyk later posted an Instagram Story of herself receiving an intravenous infusion from what appeared to be a hospital. An accompanying caption read: “a win is a win.”

This drew further criticism from some Chinese social media users, who saw the remark as dismissive of concerns over other competitors’ health and safety.

Italian Hyrox pro-athlete Sara Gandola, who competed in the same race, told Sixth Tone that Wietrzyk should not be blamed for the incident.

Gandola said the responsibility of athletes is to perform at their highest level within the rules, while “it is the sport’s responsibility to set those rules and define what is acceptable.”

“If you disagree with the rules, debate the rules,” she said. “But attacking an athlete for doing exactly what elite athletes are supposed to do is completely backward.”

On Monday, Hyrox’s global headquarters issued a statement on Instagram, describing the incident as an “unforeseen situation” and adding that those who threatened its athletes would be permanently banned from future events.

However, Chinese social media users criticized their stance for not directly acknowledging failures in how it handled the incident at the time.

Later that day, Hyrox China admitted on Weibo that the incident exposed “shortcomings” in its competition rules and said it had proposed revisions to its global headquarters. The previous Hyrox rulebook imposes a two-minute penalty for littering, spitting, or blowing one’s nose onto the floor, but does not address fecal incontinence.

Hyrox China added that the venue’s carpets had been replaced and that the entire venue had been deep-cleaned overnight, pledging to disinfect both venues before future events and any shared equipment.

Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste also issued an apology via Instagram on Monday, admitting that “Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race.”

In a Sunday commentary, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV said the incident highlighted a growing tension between the “rapid expansion” of commercial sporting events and “gaps in competition rules.”

Additional reporting: Xie Anran; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019025/The Chinese Dating App Promising Marriage — or Your Money Back
World.title: The Chinese Dating App Promising Marriage — or Your Money Back
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019025/The Chinese Dating App Promising Marriage — or Your Money Back
World.content:
A new Chinese dating app is betting that AI can do more than keep users chatting — it wagers it can see them married in three years or less.

If it fails, the team behind Liangpei — roughly “good match” in Chinese — promises to refund the user’s one-time fee of 2,000 yuan ($275). The guarantee comes as marriage rates fall in China, with only 6.76 million couples tying the knot in 2025, about half the number a decade earlier.

Launched this past July, Liangpei begins with a roughly 20-minute voice conversation with an AI matchmaker. Users answer 25 questions about their relationship history, marriage plans, and even whether they intend to buy property. The system then uses their answers to build a detailed profile, calculate compatibility scores, and recommend potential partners.

Once two people match, they can talk only until one decides to move on, a restriction the app’s developers say is intended to keep them focused on one relationship rather than constantly searching for alternatives.

“We want to get the users off the platform as soon as possible,” founder Zeng Xinxun told Sixth Tone.

Before launching Liangpei, the 32-year-old worked on AI search technology at Kimi, one of China’s best-known generative AI platforms. His 18-person team now uses similar technology to draw out information that basic dating-app tags such as age, occupation, and location cannot capture.

Approximately 91% of users who start Liangpei’s interview finish it, Zeng said, going on to create profiles averaging 516 Chinese characters, about four times as long as those on several major Chinese dating apps.

About one in 10 users has reached an exclusive one-on-one match, according to Zeng. Those conversations last more than 10 days on average and run to more than 200 messages.

“One-on-one allows both parties to invest more focus and effort into building a relationship,” Zeng said. “Even if it doesn’t work out, it’s a conclusion reached after genuine communication.”

So far, he said, Liangpei has more than 9,300 active users across 300 cities. Men account for 57% of users, and women 43%. The two largest age groups are 26 to 28 and 29 to 31.

China’s established dating and social platforms operate at a much larger scale. Tantan, one of the country’s oldest dating apps, had 10.7 million monthly active users in March 2025, while Soul draws large audiences with broader offerings that combine dating, social discovery, entertainment, and shared interests.

Liangpei also requires real-name registration, a marital status check, and live photo verification. The company has blocked 487 people found to be married, Zeng said. It also uses AI to watch for signs of fraud once conversations begin.

Wang, a Shanghai-based user who asked to be identified only by her surname for privacy reasons, has tried more than 10 dating apps. Liangpei was the first on which she was willing to answer so many questions.

“It has helped me understand myself better and clarified exactly what I’m looking for,” she said.

Within a week, Wang entered an exclusive one-on-one match. She said the format made online dating less exhausting and allowed her to focus on getting to know her counterpart. But with no other matches to turn to, the arrangement depended on that person keeping the conversation alive.

“Once matched, your slot is locked,” Wang said. “If the other person isn’t proactive, you’re left waiting with nowhere for the conversation to go.”

On Xiaohongshu, the lifestyle app also known as RedNote, Liangpei has drawn sharply mixed reactions. Some users described it as a welcome option for people anxious about finding a spouse, while others questioned whether treating marriage as a fixed target made dating too rigid.

Free users can send only one “like” a day, according to posts reviewed by Sixth Tone. The app also prominently displays compatibility scores, which some users said made them more reluctant to start conversations.

Despite the compatibility score, several users admitted they still ended up judging potential partners by appearance.

Three-year itch

Six years ago, Zeng said he became frustrated trying to meet someone online — a period that lasted a year. He wrote a lengthy profile, but few people seemed to read it, and even fewer replied.

“Profiles were too bare to spark interest,” he said. Zeng eventually expanded his own to around 2,000 Chinese characters, then came across a woman whose profile was just as detailed.

“We quickly went from strangers to a close connection,” Zeng said. By the time they met in person, he thought the relationship might go somewhere.

They are now married. And Liangpei uses that same outcome as its measure of success.

His team had considered a first date or the start of a relationship instead. Marriage, Zeng said, was different: “It’s legally verifiable and undisputed.”

The three-year cutoff came after his team interviewed 150 couples obtaining marriage licenses at a civil affairs bureau in the southern city of Shenzhen. More than 70% said they had married within three years of meeting, Zeng said.

Liangpei has been operating for only a few months, so none of its users have yet to reach that deadline. For now, the company is reviewing the data it does have, including whether higher compatibility scores are associated with more likes, replies, and longer conversations.

“For example, among 1,500 users in Shenzhen, the AI can directly rank the top 10 people most likely to succeed with you,” Zeng said. “You don’t have to browse everyone — just start with the highest scores.”

To address relationship anxiety, Liangpei offers an “icebreaker” feature that suggests questions when a conversation stalls. An “AI wingman” can also analyze an exchange and offer advice.

But the “AI wingman” will not compose replies. Zeng said someone who struggles with online banter might still make a good partner in person, but AI should only carry early exchanges far enough for both people to find out.

Du Shichao, an assistant professor of sociology at Shanghai’s Fudan University, said Liangpei’s focus on marriage could appeal to people who already know what they are looking for. He also saw value in matching people using more than surface-level information.

“It may not address everyone’s pain points, but it can at least solve problems for some people and offer them more choice,” Du said.

But he was more cautious about AI taking on a larger role in relationships.

“This ‘enhancement’ can easily slide into ‘replacement,’” Du said. “When this kind of use is taken to an extreme, people need to be wary of ceding their capacity for emotional connection to technology.”

Whatever help an AI assistant can provide online, he said, people still have to learn about each other in person. “Ultimately, people must rediscover each other and themselves through real-world interaction.”

Du said technology may help with some of the difficulties individuals face in meeting and communicating with partners, but it cannot address the forces shaping marriage more broadly, including demographics, economic pressure, and family expectations.

“It may benefit some, but won’t significantly change China’s marriage patterns,” he said.

Zeng is making a more modest claim. “We don’t need to serve everyone,” he said. “We can’t help those with particularly poor prospects, or those with unrealistic expectations. If the people in between can find success in Liangpei, that’s good enough.”

Whether they do will become clear in 2029, when Liangpei’s first users reach the end of its three-year guarantee.

Additional reporting: Xu Ruishuo; editor: Apurva.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019020/China Approves Obesity Drug for Severe Fatty Liver Disease
World.title: China Approves Obesity Drug for Severe Fatty Liver Disease
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019020/China Approves Obesity Drug for Severe Fatty Liver Disease
World.content:
China has approved the weight-loss drug Wegovy, a brand name for the medication semaglutide, to treat a severe form of fatty liver disease, making it the country’s first and only glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) drug approved for the condition.

The drug, approved Sept. 10 by the National Medical Products Administration, covers adults with moderate to advanced liver damage from metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) — the result of inflammation caused by excess fat — but no cirrhosis, or permanent scarring.

The move comes as obesity drugs become more widely available internationally and growing competition pushes drugmakers to differentiate products to treat a broader spectrum of diseases.

China has one of the world’s largest burdens of fatty liver disease, affecting about one in three adults and over 80% of people with obesity. An estimated 6.7% of Chinese adults have MASH, the disease’s more severe form, and may not qualify for GLP-1 drugs under previous weight-management indications.

The share of global liver cancer cases caused by MASH is forecast to rise from 8% to 11% by 2050, according to a report by the Lancet Commission on liver cancer published last year.

Effective drug options for fatty liver disease have long been limited, with treatment until now largely dependent on patients making lifestyle changes, Jia Jidong, director of the Liver Research Center at Beijing Friendship Hospital, told domestic media. He added that approval of the drug could help to raise public awareness of fatty liver disease, as the illness can be “silent and asymptomatic” in its earlier stages.

Semaglutide was originally developed to treat diabetes but has become widely used for weight management in recent years. It does so by mimicking the hormone GLP-1, released in response to eating, binding to the hormone’s receptors and suppressing appetite.

The medication is sold by Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk as Ozempic for diabetes and at a higher dose as Wegovy primarily for weight management. Wegovy was approved in China for weight management in June 2024.

The latest approval was based on a trial involving 1,197 MASH patients with moderate-to-advanced liver scarring. About two-thirds of patients who took semaglutide saw their MASH resolve, while slightly more than a third experienced reductions in liver scarring.

Other drugmakers are also exploring GLP-1 medications as potential treatments for fatty liver disease, with Chinese regulators fast-tracking approval for U.S. pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide in January.

Chinese biotech firm Innovent Biologics has also reported fatty liver reduction with its drug mazdutide, which was approved in the country for weight management last year.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019019/A Crab Farmer and His Uninvited Guests
World.title: A Crab Farmer and His Uninvited Guests
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019019/A Crab Farmer and His Uninvited Guests
World.content:
Thanks to years of ecological restoration, endangered Oriental storks have been expanding their range around Gaoyou Lake in the eastern Jiangsu province. In recent months, dozens have descended on crab farmer Hu Dingsong’s ponds, bringing him online fame — and huge economic losses.

Hu first spotted two or three storks in April. After learning they were a nationally first-class protected species, he was delighted. “I even joked online that my pond had crabs to spare,” he said.

But the numbers quickly grew: over 20 by mid-May, to more than 40 by early June, to their present numbers of around 80. Hu estimates that the birds collectively eat roughly 2,400 crabs a day, costing him 30,000 to 40,000 yuan ($4,200-$5,600) daily. His agricultural insurance does not cover wildlife damage.

Forestry officials have also banned Hu from using firecrackers to drive the birds away, as they are a protected species. Netting such large ponds is also impractical, and offering the birds other food sources — such as fish — introduces disease risks, leaving him with little recourse.

Lu Changhu, a wildlife ecology professor at Nanjing Forestry University, said storks staying in the province during summer is not new. Once mainly winter visitors, more have begun staying around Gaoyou Lake and nearby wetlands as their population has grown. Some may skip migration when food is plentiful, he said.

Local officials have provided Hu with a drone to monitor the flock and are helping address his losses, but farmers currently lack official channels to pursue compensation for wildlife damage.

Hu is now urging authorities to work with farmers on solutions that protect both the birds and their livelihoods.

World.title: PH still deadliest country in Asia for environmental defenders for 13th straight year
World.content:
PROTEST. Community and church partners of EcoWaste Coalition reenact the Way of the Cross along the streets of Tondo, Manila, on March 31, 2026, to call for just and lasting solutions to the nation’s worsening waste, climate, energy, and corruption issues.

The latest report from watchdog group Global Witness says violence against defenders in the Philippines in 2025 was linked to the government's counterinsurgency programs and extractive projects

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines recorded 12 killings of land and environmental defenders in 2025, the highest in Asia, according to a report by watchdog group Global Witness released on Wednesday, September 16.

This is the 13th consecutive time the Philippines ranked as the deadliest country for environmental defenders in Asia.

These are the environmental defenders identified by Global Witness in its 2025 report:

Ali Jejhon Macalintal

Davie Ugking

Fernando Promboy

Hulyo Agtay

Joan Escuadro

Juan Sumilhig

Nickasio Tayas Mindo

Ramon Lupos

Rico Malubay

Rudolph Dela Cruz Espe

Veronico Anterio

Warlita Jimenez

Global Witness said violence against defenders in the Philippines was linked to the government’s counterinsurgency programs and extractive projects. Five of the killings involved the suspected participation of members of the Philippine military, according to the report.

Kalikasan People’s Network for the Environment, in a statement on Thursday, September 17, condemened the attacks against environmental defenders.

“The right to defend the land is the right to defend life. The right to protest is a fundamental right, never a crime,” the group said.

Kalikasan also accused state institutions, including security and legal agencies, of being used to target communities through what it described as fabricated charges, terrorist accusations, and intimidation.

Last September 10, five paralegals were arrested, while dozens were hurt in a protest against Pax Silica. The protest was held outside an event where President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. was meeting investors for the Luzon development project.

Environmental groups have raised concerns over the environmental impacts of Pax Silica in the country.

The Global Witness report said at least 124 land and environmental defenders were killed globally in 2025, with Colombia remaining the deadliest country with 39 cases, followed by Brazil with 26 cases. The Philippines tied with Honduras at third with 12 cases. – Rappler.com

World.title: Team Japan forced to look at alternate accommodation options at home Asian Games
World.content:
ATHLETES' UNITS. A person walks near wooden container units built to house athletes, including those for Japanese and Filipino athletes, ahead of the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan.

Abandoning plans to set up an Athletes' Village, 2026 Asian Games host Nagoya sets up alternative accommodation options, including a chartered cruise ship and shipping-container style huts

NAGOYA, Japan – Accommodation issues continued to plague the lead-up to the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Thursday, September 17, with even the host Japan team looking at alternative arrangements after cases in which male and female athletes were allocated shared rooms.

Local organizers, having decided not to build a dedicated Athletes’ Village, looked to creative accommodation options to house the 17,000 competitors and officials arriving for the Games, which officially open on Saturday, September 19 .

The Italian cruise ship Costa Serena, which will host 4,000 participants, arrived on Tuesday, September 15, and 2,000 other athletes and officials will be accommodated in shipping-container style huts in the dock area of Japan’s biggest port.

“Since the cruise ship village opened yesterday, athletes have been arriving and going through the entry procedures,” Japan’s deputy chef de mission Hisashi Mizutori told a news conference on Thursday.

“However, the process took a significant amount of time, and due to issues with activation of their credentials, we have received reports that some athletes were left waiting for several hours.

“There have been cases where coaches, team officials, and athletes have been assigned to the same room. There are also situations where room assignments were made purely based on the numbers, such as assigning five twin rooms for a group of five men and five women.

“While the numbers match on paper, practically it creates challenging situations such as men and women being assigned together, coaches being assigned with athletes, or trainers who need to accommodate a lot of medical equipment being assigned together.”

The local organizing committee maintains that the accommodation issue arose because they were expecting 15,000 athletes and officials for the Games, only for numbers to increase as new sports were added.

In a joint statement with the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) last week, the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games Organizing Committee said numbers would be capped at 17,000 with all of those guaranteed a place to stay.

Mizutori said the Japanese Olympic Committee (JOC) had anticipated accommodation “challenges” and had secured hotel rooms in the city as a backup.

“We heard that the accommodation allocations are extremely tight,” said the former Olympic champion gymnast, who also sits on the JOC executive board.

“We are currently working to coordinate and negotiate adjustments wherever possible. For cases where that proves too difficult, we are considering using the backup accommodations that Team Japan prepared in advance as alternatives.”

Organizers pledge to address complaints

Last Tuesday, Asian Games organizers said they were committed to addressing complaints from athletes and officials about accommodation.

There have been media reports of complaints from South Korean basketball players about the size of the beds in the shipping container-style huts on land that will be home to some 2,000 of the visitors.

“We are fully aware of the dissatisfaction and concerns voiced by the athlete delegations,” accommodation manager Yuta Matsuo told Reuters.

“However, we are not merely acknowledging these issues, we are already taking concrete steps to improve the environment for the athletes, including their living conditions during their stay.”

Matsuo said the core concept of the accommodation program had been sustainability and that while everything had been approved by the Japanese Olympic Committee, he understood that other delegations would have specific needs.

A resident center operating 24 hours a day would be available to address any complaints or problems from athletes or officials, Matsuo said.

“In this way, we are making every effort to ensure that athletes do not have to remain anxious or worried for prolonged periods of time,” he said.

Matsuo suggested that some of the cabins on the Costa Serena might be quite small but urged athletes to make the most of the extensive shared space on the ship.

“We hope the delegation will consider the ship’s facilities and relaxation options — taking a comprehensive view rather than focusing solely on cabin size,” he said.

The local organizing committee maintains that the accommodation issue arose because they were expecting only 15,000 athletes and officials for the Games, only for numbers to increase as new sports were added.

In a joint statement with the Olympic Council of Asia last week, the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games Organizing Committee said numbers would be capped at 17,000 with all of those guaranteed a place to stay.

The weather has not helped with several hundred athletes and officials briefly evacuated from their accommodation after torrential rain battered Nagoya last week.

The Games, the third edition to be held in Japan, will run from Saturday until October 4. – Rappler.com

World.title: [READOUT] Where businesses can plug into the Luzon Corridor
World.content:
Of the initiative’s roughly $20 billion worth of disclosed opportunities, 99% are in transport, logistics, and energy projects, underscoring how much of the corridor’s high-tech potential still depends on getting the basics right first

The government’s much-touted Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) comes with an eye-catching number: about $20 billion (more than P1 trillion) worth of disclosed opportunities stretching across Subic, Clark, Metro Manila, and Batangas, if its investment dealbook is to be believed.

But for business leaders, that headline number may not be the most useful metric since the opportunities are scattered across different stages of development.

Rappler’s analysis, conducted alongside independent research analyst and strategic advisor Cesar Tolentino, found that less than $5.1 billion (P320.4 billion) of roughly $21.4 billion (P1.34 trillion) in identifiable project values could already be classified as pledged, being spent, implemented, or completed.

Much of the rest is still looking for investors, undergoing studies, or awaiting procurement. So rather than treating the corridor as $20 billion of investment that is definitely coming, it may be more useful to ask where your business can already plug in.

First, LEC is looking for much more than investors.

Rappler’s review of the 31 detailed opportunities shows that many projects are simultaneously seeking different kinds of private sector participation.

27 identify opportunities for investors

24 are looking for suppliers

18 are seeking locators

A smaller number are explicitly looking for customers, offtakers, or other partners

That opens the corridor to companies beyond those interested in bankrolling an airport or railway. For instance, equipment providers could supply projects. Manufacturers and logistics firms could locate around new infrastructure. Operators could compete for long-term concessions. Energy users could become customers or offtakers.

READ: Billions on paper: How much of Luzon Corridor’s $20-B pipeline will become real?

Second, forget the government’s high-tech rhetoric for now. The near-term LEC opportunity is mostly about the basic infrastructure businesses need to operate.

Of the 31 projects, 17 are in transport and logistics and seven are in energy. There are only four digital connectivity projects and two classified under advanced manufacturing. In dollar terms, transport, logistics, and energy make up almost 99% of the pipeline with disclosed values.

That means the projects worth watching are mostly railways, ports, airports, power infrastructure, fuel pipelines, warehouses, and industrial facilities.

They may be less exciting than artificial intelligence or semiconductor design, but they are the investments that could eventually make Subic, New Clark City, and the country’s industrial parks more attractive to locators.

Third, pay attention to project stage, not just opportunity value.

Four huge opportunities account for around four-fifths of the dealbook’s disclosed value:

$4.1 billion (P257.6 billion) Sangley Point International Airport

$4 billion (P251.3 billion) North-South Commuter Railway operations and maintenance opportunity

$3 billion (P188.5 billion) Metro Manila Subway O&M concession

$3 billion to $6 billion (P188.5 billion to P377.0 billion) Subic-Clark natural gas ecosystem

But most other large projects remain years away. Studies for the proposed Subic-Clark-Manila-Batangas freight railway are expected to run until 2029, while Metro Manila Subway Phase 2 is also still undergoing feasibility work.

For businesses looking for nearer-term opportunities, the smaller projects may thus be more relevant. The Clark National Food Hub has already secured an initial $65 million (P4.08 billion). Civil works are complete for a $20-million to $25-million (P1.26-billion to P1.57-billion) insulated panel factory expansion in Pampanga, with equipment already in transit. Development of a $30-million (P1.88-billion) Subic fuel depot began in May.

The Philippines and United States also signed a separate $60-million (P3.77-billion) grant for energy sector reforms during the LEC forum. It may be nowhere near the size of the headline infrastructure pipeline, but crucially, it’s actual committed funding aimed at fixing one of the biggest constraints businesses face: high electricity costs.

READ: High-tech dreams, low-tech reality of the Luzon Economic Corridor

Finally, treat the corridor’s high-tech ambitions as upside rather than the present reality.

The government wants New Clark City to eventually attract AI, semiconductor, and advanced manufacturing investments. But those industries barely appear in the pipeline today. Pax Silica itself is not among the dealbook’s detailed projects.

For now, LEC is overwhelmingly an infrastructure story. But rail, ports, power, logistics, and connectivity are exactly the foundations the Philippines needs before higher-value industries will commit capital.

No less than Finance Secretary Frederick Go told Rappler that advanced manufacturing, electronics, and AI-related tech “won’t be handed to us on a silver platter. We have to work hard to deserve it and become a global player in these industries.”

We hope this readout helps inform your next strategy or boardroom decision. And as always, feel free to tell us what to tackle next, dear business leader. – Rappler.com

Readout is a new content series from data consultancy The Nerve, bringing you insights that bridge the gap between quick news headlines and dense technical reports. Readout tracks and explains business shifts in different Philippine industries. World.title: EU Commission proposes under-13s social media ban
World.content:
URSULA VON DER LEYEN. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen attends a press conference with Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for Technological Sovereignty, Security, and Democracy Henna Virkkunen (not pictured) to present the EU Kids Act, in Strasbourg, France September 17, 2026.

Under the proposal, which will need to be negotiated with EU countries and the European Parliament in the coming months before it can become law, accounts for children between 13 and 15 will be under parental control

STRASBOURG, France – European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Thursday, September 17, set out a sweeping plan to keep children safe from online dangers, proposing to ban under-13s from social media and require online services to design safe children’s accounts.

The move follows similar initiatives in Australia, Britain, China, India, Turkey and several EU countries underscoring rising concerns about the impact Meta’s Facebook and Instagram, TikTok, Google’s YouTube, and ChatGPT have on children’s mental health and safety.

Australia’s challenges in enforcing its world-first social media ban for children under 16 however could see Europe facing an uphill battle as well.

“Today, our children are engaging with some of the most sophisticated technology ever created, and it was not created with children’s well-being and development in mind,” von der Leyen told a press conference.

She said the proposed EU Kids Act “will set clear boundaries in the digital world just as we do it on a daily basis in the real world”.

Under the proposal, which will need to be negotiated with EU countries and the European Parliament in the coming months before it can become law, accounts for children between 13 and 15 will be under parental control.

Social media and video-sharing services, online video games, AI companions, and chatbots for children below 18 will be subject to a list of dos and don’ts.

These include a ban on addictive features, profiling-based recommender feeds, infinite scroll, reward tricks and unsolicited contact from strangers. AI companions and chatbots must be turned off by default.

Online platforms must design algorithms safe for children and provide easy-to-use parental controls and tools to block and mute users. – Rappler.com

World.title: NEA seeks extra P7 billion to eliminate non-technical system losses
World.content:
Electric company contractors install wires for newly installed electric meters on a utility pole along Jose Abad Santos Avenue in Manila on September 3, 2026.

NEA says eliminating non-technical system losses will require a phased transition, with cooperatives needing billions in loans for metering and other upgrades before they can absorb the costs

MANILA, Philippines – The National Electrification Administration (NEA) is asking Congress for an additional P7 billion to help electric cooperatives eliminate non-technical system losses, an amount larger than the agency’s entire P6.49-billion proposed budget for 2027.

The P7 billion is not included in the National Expenditure Program (NEP) submitted by the executive branch to Congress. Under the proposed 2027 budget, NEA only has P850 million in national-government equity earmarked as loans to electric cooperatives, alongside P5.64 billion in subsidies and other funding under its National Rural Electrification Program.

NEA Administrator Antonio Mariano Almeda told senators during deliberations on the Department of Energy’s proposed 2027 budget that the agency is now seeking the P7 billion in addition to its existing loan equity fund to cushion electric cooperatives from the financial impact of removing non-technical system losses from consumers’ electricity bills.

Play Video

“The P7 billion is a fund in addition to the loan equity fund of the National Electrification Administration to loan to the electric cooperatives,” Almeda said on Thursday, September 17.

Under NEA’s proposed 2027 budget, the P850-million equity infusion is already intended to finance loans to electric cooperatives. The agency targets facilitating P850 million worth of loans to 18 cooperatives next year, up from P810 million targeted in 2026.

There is no separate allocation in the NEP for system loss reduction.

Non-technical system losses refer to electricity that goes unaccounted for because of factors such as pilferage, illegal connections, and inaccurate or missing meters. They differ from technical losses, which naturally occur as electricity travels through distribution lines and cannot be completely eliminated.

System loss has become a hot policy issue after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. used his July State of the Nation Address to call for an immediate amendment of the Electric Power Industry Reform Act in order to prohibit utilities from passing system loss charges, including the corresponding VAT, on to consumers.

The directive has put pressure on energy agencies and regulators to work out how those charges can be reduced or removed without undermining the finances and operations of electric cooperatives and other distribution utilities.

Why electric co-ops need these loans

Almeda said electric cooperatives would have to spend heavily on metering as the government moves to stop passing non-technical losses on to consumers, including installing meters for currently unmetered connections and replacing meters as authorities crack down on electricity theft.

NEA estimates its four-stage program would require around P7.5 billion in capital expenditures. Almeda said the first phase, which would reduce non-technical system losses to 25%, would require around P4 billion. Another P1 billion would be needed for each of the next two stages, followed by P1.5 billion for complete elimination.

The proposed assistance would not be a subsidy. Instead, NEA would lend the money to electric cooperatives for investments needed to reduce their losses.

At an earlier DOE press conference, Almeda said NEA estimated that 62 of the country’s 121 electric cooperatives could suffer financial losses if 25% of non-technical system losses could no longer be recovered from consumers.

Almeda has pointed to the Zamboanga City Electric Cooperative as an example of what the program could achieve. He said its system loss rate fell from around 20% in January 2026 to roughly 13% by July following interventions that included additional metering, capital infusion, and management measures. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: No lockdown in Malacañang after court ordered VP Sara’s arrest
World.content:
No credible reports confirm that barricades and barbed wire were installed around Malacañang due to the issuance of Duterte's arrest warrant, contrary to the claim

Claim: Malacañang was placed under lockdown following the issuance of an arrest warrant against Vice President Sara Duterte.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The video bearing the claim has already received 648,000 views, 26,000 reacts, 2,600 shares, and 1,400 comments as of writing. It was posted on September 6, days after a Quezon City trial court issued an arrest warrant against the Vice President.

The video shows a photo of Duterte on her arrival at the Quezon City court to post bail. Images of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., his mother Imelda Marcos, and Ilocos Norte 1st District Representative Sandro Marcos can also be seen in the video’s graphics.

The narrator of the Facebook reel says, “Sa kabila po ng pag-aresto kay VP Sara, nag-lockdown ang Malacañang. Opo, nagkaroon na naman po ng barikada, ng mga barbed wire ang Malacañang, mga kababayan, kasunod ng pag-aresto kay VP Sara, kasunod ng paglabas ng warrant of arrest kay VP Sara.”

(Following the arrest of VP Sara, Malacañang went into lockdown. Yes, barricades and barbed wires have once again been set up at Malacañang following the arrest of VP Sara, following the issuance of the arrest warrant against her.)

Some Facebook users believed the claim. One comment reads, “Lumalabas na sila takot. For the first time, siya lang nag lockdown na Presidente.”

(It turns out they are afraid. For the first time, he was the only president to impose a lockdown).

The facts: Malacañang has not imposed a lockdown following the issuance of Duterte’s arrest warrant on September 4 and her posting of bail on September 5. No credible reports confirm that barricades and barbed wire have been installed around the area.

The Palace has previously implemented heightened security measures due to rallies such as the September 2025 and November 2025 anti-corruption rallies as well as the July 2026 protest by the United People’s Initiative.

More recently, police conducted a simulation exercise and installed metal barricades and razor wire on roads leading to the Malacañang Complex as preparation for National Heroes Day activities on August 31.

Following the issuance of Duterte’s arrest warrant, several supporters gathered at the Quezon City court on September 5 and on September 11 for her arraignment, which was later deferred.

Grave threats case: The warrant of arrest against Duterte was issued after the Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98 found probable cause to hold the Vice President for trial on three counts of grave threats.

The case stemmed from Duterte’s November 2024 warning that she allegedly hired an assassin to kill President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House speaker Martin Romualdez.

The Vice President posted bail of P360,000 — P120,000 for each count.

On the same day she posted bail, Duterte said that she does not feel safe, citing previous alleged security threats. “I do not feel safe. I do not feel safe anywhere. Pumunta lang ako [rito] kasi sabi ninyo pupunta ako sa court (I only went here because you told me I needed to appear in court),” she said.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla told the media that they accorded Duterte the respect “that her position deserves.” He added, “We have all the body cam footages of her warrants being served. We have all the body cam footages of her arrival to post bail.”

Previous fact checks: Rappler has previously fact-checked similar false claims about the Vice President:

– Angelee Kaye Abelinde/Rappler.com

Angelee Kaye Abelinde is a student journalist based in Naga City, and an alumna of Rappler’s Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expands International Air Connectivity With New Routes to Türkiye and UAE
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is set to expand international air connectivity with new and resumed passenger and cargo services linking the country with Türkiye and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), as airlines increase capacity on key routes.

Turkish airline SunExpress plans to launch regular flights between Astana and Izmir with flights scheduled twice a week on Wednesdays and Saturdays using Boeing 737 aircraft, while increasing the frequency of its existing Almaty–Izmir service.

The plans were discussed during a Sept. 15 meeting between the Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Civil Aviation Committee and representatives of SunExpress, according to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport.

Meanwhile, Air Astana plans to resume regular flights between Kazakhstan and Dubai in October. The Almaty–Dubai service is scheduled to restart on Oct. 1, followed by the Astana–Dubai route on Oct. 2. The airline plans to gradually increase frequencies during the month, with Almaty–Dubai flights rising from four to 12 per week and Astana–Dubai flights from three to 10 per week by the end of October. The airline said the schedule could be adjusted depending on developments in the Middle East.

The expansion also includes air cargo connectivity between Kazakhstan and the UAE. FlyDubai plans to launch weekly cargo flights on the Almaty–Dubai route from Oct. 2 using Boeing 737 aircraft. The service will transport both import and export cargo between the two countries, according to Kazakhstan’s Civil Aviation Committee.

The new cargo route is expected to provide additional logistics options for Kazakh businesses and support trade and economic ties between Kazakhstan and the UAE. Kazakhstan’s Transport Ministry has identified the development of air cargo transportation as a priority for strengthening the country’s transport and logistics potential, increasing its transit attractiveness and supporting the development of aviation hubs.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Face Thailand in Davis Cup Tie With First World Group Place at Stake
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s tennis team will face Thailand in a Davis Cup World Group 2 tie in Astana on Sept. 18–19, with the winner advancing to the World Group 1 playoffs. The official draw has determined the order of the singles and doubles matches at the National Tennis Center’s Arena.

The official draw for the tie was held in Astana on Sept. 17, determining the order of the five matches. The tie consists of four singles matches and one doubles match, reported the Kazakhstan’s Tennis Federation.

The first day on Sept. 18 will feature two singles matches, beginning at 1 p.m. Astana time. Kazakhstan’s Alexander Shevchenko will face Thailand’s Maximus Parapol Jones in the opening match. He will be followed by Timofey Skatov, who will play Kasidit Samrej.

The second day will begin with the doubles match. Kazakhstan will be represented by Denis Yevseyev and Beibit Zhukayev, who will face Thanapet Chanta and Pruchya Isaro.

The final two singles matches are scheduled to follow, with Shevchenko facing Samrej and Skatov taking on Jones. The tie will conclude on Sept. 19, with play starting at noon.

The winner of the Kazakhstan–Thailand tie will advance to the World Group 1 playoffs for the 2027 Davis Cup season. Kazakhstan currently occupies 42nd place in the Davis Cup rankings, while Thailand is ranked 60th. The two teams are meeting in the Davis Cup for the first time since 2009.

Ahead of the tie, Zhukayev said he had spent about three weeks preparing for the competition and was looking forward to partnering with Yevseyev in the doubles match.

“I prepared for this Davis Cup for about three weeks. I am looking forward to our match with Denis against Thailand. We had good training sessions, played practice sets and worked on different exercises. Overall, I feel good on court and hope we can produce a quality performance,” Zhukayev said.

Yevseyev highlighted the pair’s familiarity with each other as one of their strengths.

“This year has been difficult for us. We lost in February, and now it is important to draw the right conclusions and show what we are capable of. Beibit and I have known each other for a long time and have played together many times in both singles and doubles. We understand each other on court, and I consider that an advantage. We will try to make the most of our opportunities and give everything for the victory,” he said.

The matches will be played on hard courts at the National Tennis Center in Astana.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s National Fund Sees Investment Income Nearly Catch up With Oil Taxes, Expert Says
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s National Fund is increasingly generating income not only from the country’s oil sector but also from the capital accumulated over years of resource revenues, with investment returns in the first half of 2026 coming close to the amount raised through oil-sector taxes, Kazakh economist Ruslan Sultanov writes in his Telegram channel, analyzing Kazakhstan’s national statistics.

The National Fund received 3.21 trillion tenge (US$7.1 billion) in the first six months of 2026. Oil-sector taxes accounted for 55.6% of total inflows, while investment income reached 43.7%.

The figures point to an important shift in the role of the fund: as its accumulated assets grow, returns generated by investing those assets can become a source of income comparable in scale to current revenues from the oil sector.

Capital itself is becoming a source of income

The 1.4 trillion tenge (US$3.13 billion) investment return exceeded the revenue generated by any individual oil-sector tax during the period.

The largest individual oil-related contribution was corporate income tax from the oil sector, which amounted to 798.9 billion tenge (US$1.78 billion). The mineral extraction tax generated 267.2 billion tenge (US$596.6 million), while the rent tax on exports brought in 172.5 billion tenge (US$385.1 million).

Against these figures, the investment return of 1.4 trillion tenge (US$3.13 billion) represents a separate and increasingly significant source of resources for the National Fund, according to Sultanov. The scale of the underlying capital is central to this development. The fund’s assets stood at 37.34 trillion tenge (US$83.9 billion) at the beginning of 2026.

The investment income generated during the first six months was equivalent to approximately 3.8% of that starting capital. This means that even a relatively modest percentage return on a very large asset base can translate into hundreds of billions or trillions of tenge.

The fund financed the budget while its capital grew

The National Fund simultaneously continued to perform its traditional fiscal role during the first half of the year. A total of 1.87 trillion tenge (US$4.05 billion) was used from the fund, of which 1.86 trillion tenge (US$4.03 billion) went to the national budget as a guaranteed transfer.

At the same time, the fund’s capital, Sultanov writes, increased from 37.34 trillion (US$80.88 billion) to 38.68 trillion tenge (US$83.80 billion). The combination is significant: despite the transfer to the budget, the fund’s capital increased during the period. Investment income played an important role in that outcome.

From oil revenues to an asset-based model

The National Fund was created to accumulate part of Kazakhstan’s natural-resource revenues and provide a financial buffer for the economy. Its traditional role has therefore been closely associated with oil: when hydrocarbon revenues rise, the fund receives more money; when the economy requires support, part of those savings can be transferred to the budget.

The latest figures illustrate another dimension of that model. Once the fund reaches a sufficiently large asset base, the accumulated capital itself begins to generate significant income. The source of that income is therefore no longer directly tied to the production or taxation of another barrel of oil.

That distinction matters for the long-term role of sovereign savings. Oil revenues are linked to production volumes, commodity prices, export conditions and the fiscal regime. Investment income, meanwhile, depends on the size and composition of the portfolio, asset performance and the quality of asset management. As the capital base expands, the second factor becomes increasingly important.

World.title: Kazakhstan Wants More Oil Refining: Its Next Challenge Is Securing Feedstock
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan plans to more than double its annual oil refining capacity to 39 million tons by 2040, seeking to move the energy sector toward deeper processing and higher-value products. But the scale of the planned expansion also raises a fundamental question: how will the country secure sufficient economically viable crude supplies for its future refineries while maintaining incentives to invest in exploration and production?

The issue was highlighted at the 13th annual Central Asia and Caspian Oil and Gas Petrochemistry and Refining Summit 2026, where the Ministry of Energy presented the main provisions of Kazakhstan’s Concept for the Development of the Oil Refining Industry for 2025–2040.

The concept envisages increasing annual crude processing from 18 million to 39 million tons and raising the ratio of oil production to refining from 5:1 to 2.5:1.

Refining expansion depends on a growing resource base

The strategy is intended to modernize and expand refining capacity, increase the depth of crude processing, improve fuel quality and develop petrochemical production. By 2040, the government targets an increase in refining depth from 89% to 94%, upgrades in motor fuel quality to the K5+ environmental class, and higher production of benzene and paraxylene.

The ambition is clear: Kazakhstan wants more of the value generated from its hydrocarbons to come from processing rather than the sale of crude alone. The economics of supplying those future facilities, however, may prove equally important.

Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy estimates the country’s geological oil reserves at 13.2 billion tons, of which nearly 4.4 billion tons are recoverable, reported the Kazinform news agency. These figures are subject to revision as geological exploration continues and reserve assessments are updated.

KazMunayGas has launched a large-scale exploration program for 2026–2030, including the drilling of 26 wells, as part of efforts to replenish the country’s resource base.

The question is not simply whether Kazakhstan has oil underground, but whether sufficient volumes can be developed and supplied to domestic refineries on economically sustainable terms. That issue becomes more important as the planned refining capacity approaches 39 million tons annually.

The economics of domestic crude supplies

Energy analyst Abzal Narymbetov argues that Kazakhstan’s current fuel-market reforms need to be considered alongside the government’s refining ambitions. In his analysis published on his Energy Analytics Telegram channel, Narymbetov points to the decision to move away from state regulation of fuel prices in February 2025. According to his account, the reform was intended in part to make supplying crude to domestic refineries economically attractive for producers, helping address chronic fuel shortages and create conditions for investment in refining.

“However, the subsequent introduction of an additional excise in December 2025, equivalent to 50% of the additional margin generated by resource holders, and discussion of raising the share to 95%, have raised concerns among oil producers,” he wrote.

Narymbetov says such a policy could reduce the economic benefit producers receive from supplying crude to the domestic market.

Investment incentives become part of the refining equation

The broader issue, according to Narymbetov, is how the fiscal treatment of domestic crude supplies could affect investment decisions in oil production and exploration. He argues that if producers are required to direct a large share of their output to domestic refineries while the state subsequently captures most of the additional margin generated by higher fuel prices, companies may face weaker incentives to invest in exploration and production.

This could become significant for Kazakhstan’s future refining plans because new processing capacity requires a reliable long-term supply of crude.

“If the state administratively obliges oil producers to supply crude to refineries while simultaneously reducing the economic return from those supplies, it effectively increases investment risks in the very industry that must provide crude for future refining,” Narymbetov wrote.

From raw materials to higher-value products

The government’s refining strategy itself reflects an effort to address a longstanding structural feature of Kazakhstan’s energy economy: the large gap between crude production and domestic processing. Under the new concept, six priorities have been identified. They include ensuring the domestic economy is supplied with petroleum products, increasing petrochemical output, developing applied research, strengthening human capital, adapting the sector to technological trends and expanding export opportunities.

The planned increase in refining depth from 89% to 94% is intended to improve the efficiency of crude processing, while higher production of petrochemical feedstocks such as benzene and paraxylene could support the development of downstream industries.

The government expects the program to create jobs, strengthen the sector’s scientific and technological base and establish conditions for increasing exports of refined and petrochemical products.

World.title: From Craft to Industry: Kazakhstan Looks to Unlock its Jewelry Potential
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is moving to bring a larger share of its jewelry industry into the formal economy by tightening controls over precious-metal turnover and improving access to legally sourced gold for jewelers, as the domestic jewelry market reached nearly $168 million in 2025.

The rise of the production was discussed at a government meeting chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin on combating the shadow economy and illegal circulation of precious metals on Sept. 16.

According to the Ministry of Industry and Construction, Kazakhstan’s domestic jewelry market grew 3.4% in 2025, while jewelry production increased 31% to $7.2 million. Jewelry exports amounted to $65.4 million. At the same time, market participants estimate that a significant share of jewelry turnover remains in the shadow economy.

Government targets transparency in jewelry trade

The authorities are considering measures to increase transparency across the jewelry supply chain, including the handling of precious-metal scrap and waste. In 2025, pawnshops transferred nearly 3.2 tons of precious-metal scrap and waste to Tau-Ken Altyn for processing, down from 3.8 tons in 2024.

Against this backdrop, participants proposed working with the Agency for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market on mandatory transfer of precious-metal scrap and waste to refining entities, as well as improving the rules governing their acceptance and sale. The proposals are intended to strengthen oversight of the movement of precious metals and reduce opportunities for their circulation outside the formal economy.

Jewelers seek access to legal gold

Zhumangarin stressed that efforts to formalize the industry should also ensure that jewelers have practical conditions to operate legally.

“Jewelers are true artisans whose profession is passed down from generation to generation. We have major jewelry centers, and it is important to preserve this heritage and bring the industry into the formal sector as much as possible,” Zhumangarin said.

He emphasized the need to provide jewelers with access to a legal and affordable source of gold.

“Creating transparent conditions for their work will be one of the key steps toward formalizing the industry,” he said.

The comments reflect the authorities’ focus not only on enforcement but also on ensuring that businesses can obtain raw materials through legal channels.

Hallmarking remains limited

Mandatory hallmarking was another focus of the meeting. The number of businesses submitting jewelry for hallmarking increased sharply from 45 in 2024 to 959 in 2025. However, the number remains relatively small compared with the total number of taxpayers engaged in the jewelry trade.

There are currently 3,520 taxpayers operating in the jewelry sector, meaning that approximately 27% underwent mandatory hallmarking in 2025. The authorities proposed working with the Committee for Technical Regulation and Metrology to identify high-risk businesses and conduct relevant inspections.

Particular attention will be given to the possible reintroduction of processed jewelry into circulation, an area identified as requiring additional control.

Broader measures target shadow economy

The jewelry sector is part of a wider government effort to reduce the shadow economy through digitalization and closer integration of state information systems. According to the State Revenue Committee, 24 regulatory legal acts have been adopted and 20 information systems modernized over the past five years as part of efforts to combat the shadow economy.

The share of the shadow economy in GDP declined from 17.58% in 2023 to 15.69% in 2025. The government is also introducing digital tracking mechanisms in agriculture, oil and gas, energy, trade and construction to improve transparency and traceability.

Following the meeting, Zhumangarin instructed government agencies to ensure implementation of the Comprehensive Plan on Combating the Shadow Economy for 2026–2028 and strengthen interagency cooperation. He also ordered further work on proposals to improve regulation of precious-metal circulation and the jewelry market.

World.title: Experts Explore Health, Energy Security Challenges of Kazakhstan’s Coal Dependence
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s continued reliance on coal is creating challenges that extend beyond decarbonization, affecting the flexibility of the power system, public health and the way households consume energy, experts said at a panel session titled The Role of Coal in Kazakhstan’s Decarbonization during the third Regional Central Asian and European Decarbonization Forum on Sept. 16.

Coal and the renewable-energy challenge

Tatiana Lanshina, project lead in Agora Energiewende’s Power System Transformation team, said Kazakhstan’s growing renewable-energy capacity could play a greater role in the electricity mix, but warned that a system dominated by inflexible baseload generation could constrain the integration of wind and solar power.

“The more coal-fired power plants and also nuclear power plants that operate in baseload mode, the less room there will be for large-scale deployment of solar and wind energy,” Lanshina said.

Kazakhstan is simultaneously moving ahead with new and modernized coal generation. The national project on coal-fired generation envisages around 7.8 gigawatts (GW) of new and modernized capacity, while renewable generation continues to expand. In 2025, renewable facilities generated 8.6 billion kilowatt-hours, accounting for 7% of total electricity generation, according to the Ministry of Energy.

Lanshina said the transition is particularly complicated in the heating sector, where replacing coal-fired combined heat and power plants requires finding alternative sources for both electricity and heat.

“If we want to replace an old coal-fired power plant with something else, we need to solve not one problem, but two problems. We also need to find a source of heat,” she said.

She pointed to heat pumps, geothermal energy, solar thermal technologies, biogas and electrified heating as potential alternatives.

Coal’s cost for air quality

Zhuldyz Saulebekova, Almaty Air Initiative CEO, brought the discussion to the immediate health consequences of coal combustion, arguing that climate policy and air-quality policy should not be treated as separate agendas.

“Very often, when I attend different conferences, especially climate conferences, I hear a lot about efforts to address climate change and decarbonization. But very rarely do I hear about air pollution,” Saulebekova said.

She highlighted Almaty’s CHP-2 and CHP-3 plants, which together burn more than 3.5 million tons of coal annually. The coal comes from Ekibastuz and, according to figures she presented, has an ash content of around 42%.

Saulebekova said converting CHP-2 from coal to gas could reduce relevant air pollution by around 12 times.

She also presented figures from Climate TRACE showing the scale of particulate emissions from several major sources. According to the figures in her presentation, Almaty CHP-2 emits nearly 94 tonnes of PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) annually, compared with 633 tons from Ekibastuz GRES-2 and around 3,700 tons from Qarmet in Temirtau. She said Qarmet’s emissions were higher than those of 99.8% of point sources tracked by Climate TRACE, with approximately nine days of Qarmet emissions equivalent to one year of emissions from Almaty CHP-2.

Saulebekova also stressed the human-rights dimension of air pollution.

“The right to clean air is a guaranteed right in many countries around the world, including Kazakhstan. It is protected not only by our Constitution, but also by the Aarhus Convention, which Kazakhstan ratified more than 20 years ago,” she said.

She cited estimates that around 14,000 premature deaths annually in Kazakhstan are associated with air pollution, including approximately 2,000 in Almaty.

Changing the energy mindset

Mongolian Parliament member Tsenguun Saruulsaikhan highlighted another dimension of the transition: changing how people think about energy consumption.

“It is not just only changing coal that is the main goal. We also have to change the people’s mindset that energy, however, from any source it comes from, we need to save it, we need to make it efficient,” she said.

She argued that artificially low heating costs can discourage households from conserving energy, making energy efficiency and insulation an important part of the transition.

“We shouldn’t be focusing on the fuels, on how to heat it. We have to actually focus on insulation, so that we do not need so much energy consumption,” Saruulsaikhan said.

Her comments point to a broader challenge shared by Kazakhstan and Mongolia: the energy transition is not simply about replacing coal with another fuel. It also requires modernizing grids and heating systems, improving efficiency, attracting investment and addressing the health and social costs of the existing energy system.

For Kazakhstan, the challenge is to reconcile growing electricity demand and energy security with a gradual reduction in coal dependence-while ensuring that the transition also delivers cleaner air and more efficient energy use.

World.title: Knowledge Partnership Korea and Central Asia Must Build Before Astana 2028
World.content:
The first Korea-Central Asia summit gave the relationship a permanent structure and tied Central Asian minerals to Korean technology. Kazakhstan will host the next summit in 2028, and the years in between will show whether the partnership builds industrial capability in the region.

The presidents of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan met South Korean President Lee Jae Myung in Seoul on Sept. 16 for the first Korea-Central Asia summit held at head-of-state level. The six leaders adopted the Seoul Declaration, which sets a 30-year cooperation agenda and commits them to summits every two years. Kazakhstan offered to host the second summit in Astana in 2028, and the other participants agreed. The declaration also creates a C5+1 Industrial Ministers’ Consultative Mechanism, with ministerial meetings between summits tasked with reviewing implementation.

The format took nearly two decades to reach this level. Seoul launched the Korea-Central Asia Cooperation Forum in 2007 at the vice-ministerial level and gave it a permanent secretariat in 2017. The summit is the outcome of that gradual institution-building.

The declaration covers supply chains, energy, trade, emerging technologies and security. Its most consequential economic passage concerns critical minerals. The leaders expressed interest in combining Central Asia’s mineral resources with Korea’s advanced technologies and in facilitating exchanges of skilled personnel. That pairing of resources with people points to where Korea can matter most for Central Asia. Korean capital remains modest next to Chinese lending or the portfolios of the multilateral development banks. Korean experience in turning skills into industrial capability is harder for the region to find elsewhere.

Bilateral packages that match each country’s resources

The bilateral meetings held around the summit produced distinct results for each country. Kazakhstan brought the largest commercial package. During President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s state visit on Sept. 15, the two countries signed commercial agreements worth $19 billion and upgraded relations to a future-oriented comprehensive strategic partnership.

The headline figure combines signed agreements with announced projects at different stages of development. QazaqGaz and Hyundai Engineering agreed to build a gas processing plant at Karachaganak with capacity of five billion cubic meters a year, and KazMunayGas and Samsung E&A signed on expanding the Pavlodar refinery to nine million tons a year. On minerals, Tau-Ken Samruk and the Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources agreed on joint drilling at the Bakennoye lithium deposit, while POSCO Holdings signed a memorandum on rare-earth processing and refining.
