World.title: Smart glasses ban looms as Labor sets out new AI rules
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A ban on smart glasses capable of covertly recording people is being considered for Commonwealth buildings amid concerns about the technology's privacy and security risks.

Restricting the use of wearable devices is among a wide range of technology issues on the federal government's agenda, with ministers progressing plans for Australia's uptake of artificial intelligence and related workplace protections, data centres, investment and online safety.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will travel to the US on Friday for high-level talks with tech executives and world leaders while major employers gather in Canberra for a roundtable and separate consultation begins on national AI standards for data centres and frontier model training.

AI will also feature in the upcoming 2026 Intergenerational Report due to be released next week, with Treasurer Jim Chalmers revealing he met with an Anthropic official to discuss the technology's economic opportunities and potential risks.

Mr Albanese said AI and online safety would be a major theme of his visit to Apple's headquarters in California and attendance at the United Nations General Assembly in New York next week.

"We want Australia to be a country that helps shape the AI age rather than simply responding to it," he said.

Labor mulls smart glasses ban

With growing community backlash over the increased availability of more affordable smart glasses capable of secretly recording people, the government has made its first move to rein in the technology.

Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has asked the Australian Public Service Commission for advice on the use of smart glasses across Commonwealth workplaces, including whether the technology should be "prohibited" and what exemptions might be appropriate.

A ban on smart glasses in government buildings is being considered. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

Ms Gallagher said the Australian Public Service should always set the standard as a "model employer".

"Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information, and we need clear and consistent guidance for public servants," she said.

The government has already asked the nation's Privacy Commissioner to give the use of smart glasses "priority consideration" amid widespread community concerns about their potential impact.

National standards for data centres and training frontier AI

The government has also opened consultation on national AI standards covering large data centres and the training of frontier AI models in Australia.

The proposed rules would set mandatory requirements for data centres covering power supply, energy costs, water use, location, community engagement and skills.

They would also impose safety, security, transparency and local investment conditions on frontier AI training.

Consultation will remain open until October 9 with the government planning to legislate the standards early in the new year.

Anthropic to use Queensland data centre A $32 billion data centre proposed for a site west of Brisbane will be used by AI giant Anthropic.

Industry Minister Tim Ayres said the standards were about ensuring Australia captured the technology's "enormous opportunities" while maintaining the trust and confidence of the community.

"By setting high standards now, Australia can shape the future of this technology rather than simply adopting standards made overseas," he said.

Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton said the government had been "clear" about welcoming AI investment, provided it was on "Australia's terms".

AI will be 'defining influence' on Australia's economy

AI will also feature prominently in next week's 2026 Intergenerational Report, which will examine what the technological shift could mean for productivity, jobs and investment in decades to come.

An excerpt of the report described AI as a "defining influence" on the economy over the next 40 years.

Mr Chalmers said Australia had a "big opportunity" to lift productivity, investment and living standards, but must not be "complacent" about potential downsides.

"The global AI boom is worth hundreds of billions of dollars and we are positioning Australia to capture more of that supply chain," he said.

This week Mr Chalmers met with Anthropic special envoy Jeff Bleich, which the treasurer said was a "really valuable opportunity" to discuss both the economic opportunities of AI and importance of safeguards.

Mr Bleich said Anthropic was committed to realising the "enormous potential" of AI in a "safe, responsible way".

"Working with like-minded countries such as Australia is an important part of that," he said.

Mr Bleich said Australia brought a skilled workforce, strong institutions and a "clear-eyed approach" to new technology.

"We want to invest in those strengths and to keep working with the government so that Australians share in the gains from AI," he said.

Major employers gather to talk AI

Meanwhile, Microsoft, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and the Commonwealth Bank of Australia are among the major employers will be attending an AI roundtable hosted by Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth on Friday.

The meeting is one of five consultations being held this month with unions, employers, small business and academics to help develop Australia's first best practice guidance for AI in the workplace.

Discussions will focus on the lessons from businesses already adopting AI, how to build trust and confidence in the technology and ensuring any benefits reach workers as well as employers.

Ms Rishworth said the consultations would ensure the guide reflected the "realities of modern workplaces".

"Labor believes workers should have confidence that the adoption of AI will improve the way we work, not simply train their replacement," she said.

World.title: UN-backed experts find US strike on Minab school amounts to war crime
World.content:
Human rights experts commissioned by the United Nations say they have found "reasonable grounds" to believe the United States committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including on a school in the southern city of Minab.

The human rights experts also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.

Amnesty demands Iran strikes probe Amnesty International is demanding formal investigations into three American and Israeli attacks on densely packed suburbs of Tehran, which killed at least 41 civilians.

The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined the US's conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government's response to nationwide unrest that started in late December.

It said Iranian civilians were caught between "gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government and the nation's deadly conflict with the United States and Israel".

The Iranian and US permanent missions in Geneva did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

US officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.

Loading...

Strike on Minab school 'reckless'

The UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe US forces were responsible for an attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the city of Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including about 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials.

The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.

Iranian authorities say about 120 children were killed by a US strike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School. (AP: Abbas Zakeri/Mehr News Agency)

According to the report, the US relied on intelligence suggesting a senior Iranian military commander was present at the site but failed to adequately verify the information before launching the strike.

Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence and confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.

" Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen. "

In June, US President Donald Trump said that "nobody" purposefully attacked a girls' school in ​Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident.

US media ‌reported that an initial internal US military investigation showed US forces were likely responsible for the fatal strike in Minab in southern Iran.

The Pentagon has ​since elevated the probe but it has not published any ​preliminary findings.

What is known Iranian girls' school air strike Iran says the death toll from an attack on a girls' school it claims was launched by the US and Israel has surpassed 165.

UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.

The experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd.

The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians.

It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.

US Central Command said in a statement in March that US forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on the day a sports centre was bombed. (US Air Force via Reuters)

US Central Command said in a statement in March that US forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.

Widespread abuses by Iranian authorities

The UN mission probe found that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.

Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shi'ite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution.

Deaths in Iran protests reach at least 5,000, Iranian official says The death toll includes about 500 security personnel and exceeds that of any other round of protest or unrest in Iran in decades.

Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes the US and Israel.

The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was likely far higher than official figures, which say 3,038 people were killed and 25,000 people injured.

The Iranian government's response to the protests, including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty, marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

The team also said that killings by state security forces occurred on a "staggering scale" in Iran, and alleged crimes against humanity committed by the Iranian government.

The fact-finding mission on Iran, chaired by jurist Sara Hossain of Bangladesh, is made up of independent experts and was created in 2022 by the Human Rights Council, the UN's top human rights body.

Reuters/AP

World.title: Woman charged after baby found dead in Sydney bin
World.content:
A woman believed to be the mother of a baby found in a Sydney bin last month has been charged.

Emergency services were called to Harrow Road, Auburn, at 11:20am on August 31 after reports a baby's body was discovered in a garbage bin of a unit block.

In a statement on Thursday, NSW Police said a 24-year-old woman "believed to be the mother of the infant" was located and taken to hospital for assessment.

"Upon release from hospital, the woman was arrested and taken to Auburn Police Station," it read.

She was charged with mother alone conceal birth by disposing body.

She has been granted conditional bail to appear before Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday October 27, 2026.

Acting Superintendent of the Auburn Police Area Command Darren Sly told reporters at the time the unclothed baby boy's body was found in a plastic bag.

He said the body may have been there for up to 36 hours and it was not known whether the infant had been born alive.

"It's very traumatic for that particular lady who found that baby," Acting Superintendent Sly said.

"It's a newborn baby who now has passed away and of course it's sad and a horrific set of circumstances."

World.title: Man charged with murder after alleged assault in Tasmania's north
World.content:
A 42-year-old man has been charged with murder after allegedly assaulting a man at a house in Tasmania's north.

Tasmania Police said shortly after 8.30am on Wednesday, emergency services attended a private residence following reports that a man had been assaulted at Railton, south of Devonport.

The alleged offender had left the scene and was arrested at a nearby location a short time later, police said in a statement.

Police said the victim and offender were known to each other, and there was no ongoing threat to the wider community.

On Thursday night, police said the Tarleton man had been charged with murder after the 48-year-old victim, a man from Railton, died at the Royal Hobart Hospital.

The man was set to appear in the Devonport Magistrates Court on Thursday night.

World.title: Backpacker cuts slammed as 'low blow' for farming and tourism
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Federal limits to backpacker numbers have sparked fears in regions reliant on holidaying workers for farming and tourism.

On Thursday Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke outlined an overhaul of the working holiday-maker visa system, introducing a ballot for backpackers seeking to extend their stay and reducing overall numbers.

A cap of 45,000 will be applied to those looking to stay a second year, down from the 57,000 who qualified this year.

Tony Burke announced the changes in an address to the National Press Club on Thursday. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Those seeking a third year will be capped at 5,000, down from 31,000 this year.

Mr Burke said the government would prioritise migrants that have skills Australia needs in areas such as construction and agriculture.

Backpackers provide a significant source of workers in regional communities across Australia. (Pixabay)

People who successfully secure an extension in the ballot will be required to undertake regional work.

Mr Burke said backpackers could not be exempt if the country was serious about lowering net overseas migration.

"Drastic cuts, wherever you make them, hurt the economy in every part, in every area," he said.

" Anyone who wants to pretend there's only an economic cost in the regions does not understand the Australian economy. "

But the National Farmers’ Federation (NFF) has warned the government is putting Australia’s food security, regional economies and farm safety at risk if it pushes ahead with its plan without "urgent" consultation.

Hamish McIntyre called the decision a "low blow" for farmers. (Supplied: National Farmers Federation)

The lobby group's president, Hamish McIntyre, said farmers were furious that the time-frame for processing visas would now take up to three months, as opposed to days.

“This is a low blow for farmers and the businesses that produce Australia’s food and fibre,” he said in a statement.

"A three-month processing target leaves farmers completely stranded, with harvest already underway in parts of Queensland and the main season only weeks away."

Federation chief executive Mike Guerin also warned of rising food prices if the industry struggled to find workers for harvesting.

"We will see a lift in the price of food. We will see emptier supermarkets," he said.

Slowdown leaving farms without workers

Esperance farmer Mic Fels said the slowdown of backpacker visa applications, which began last month, meant some farmers were going without the seasonal workforce needed to bring crops in.

“I think 'reform' is probably a generous word. I think 'deform' is perhaps a better one," he said.

" It's been quite catastrophic — and I'm not using hyperbole here — for the broadacre sector across Australia, especially Western Australia, where farms tend to be of larger scale. "

Mic Fels says the loss of workers across the agricultural sector will be disastrous. (ABC News: Emma Field)

Mr Fels, who contested the WA seat of Swan at last year's federal election, said assurance the government would prioritise applications for skilled agricultural workers was welcomed.

But he said the situation was time-sensitive.

“If we saw hundreds of applicants coming through over the next week, I think that would give everybody some breathing space,” he said.

Mr Fels said there were concerns across the sector that a lack of workers could lead to dangerous practices that the industry had attempted to stamp out.

“After COVID, when we just had all these inexperienced workers on farms and the death rates on farms doubled, and it's not hyperbole, this is what we're dealing with,” he said.

“These are massive machines with thousands of moving parts. You wouldn't put inexperienced operators on a dump truck on a mine site and say, 'Go for your life', and that's what they're effectively saying."

Securing workers is critical ahead of the harvest, Mic Fels says. (Supplied: Ash Bowman)

Tourism lobby warns of 'severe' impact

WA's tourism lobby said the state stood to lose 4,500 backpackers working in peak seasons, costing at least $62 million in tourism spend and 425 local tourism jobs.

“The cuts will be most severe for Exmouth, Broome, Kununurra and northern WA, which currently attract backpackers to work in tourism to earn a third visa," Tourism Council WA chief executive Evan Hall said.

Tourism Council WA says towns such as Broome will be particularly hard hit. (ABC Kimberley: Andy Seabourne)

Queensland's Tourism Council said the government had effectively dismantled the system sending thousands of young travellers to regional Australia.

"Why would a young traveller leave the city and complete three months of regional work when there is no longer certainty of receiving a second visa?" chief executive Natassia Wheeler said.

"The workforce impact will begin during their first year, long before the ballot is held.

"Working holiday-makers are also visitors. When we lose that workforce, we also lose the money they would have spent on accommodation, transport, hospitality, tours and experiences."

World.title: Disability advocate's tragic drowning spurs life-saving gesture
World.content:
A small but intimate ceremony was held at Ellery Creek Big Hole only five months after the death of disability advocate Ellen Fraser-Barbour, who tragically drowned while swimming in April this year.

Her mother, Susie Fraser, family and friends travelled to the site to unveil an automated external defibrillator (AED) and a plaque to honour the work and memory of Dr Fraser-Barbour.

Ms Fraser took the opportunity to thank the first responders and St John Ambulance service for providing the defibrillator.

"I'd like to thank you all for your initiative in doing this and for finding some way of making something positive come out of something which was so tragic," she said.

Susie Fraser and William Sears attended the ceremony at Ellery Creek Big Hole, 80 kilometres west of Alice Springs.

"I think your will and determination to do this is incredibly important to us and that something positive can come out of something so shocking."

Closure for family

William Sears, duty manager at Alice Springs Ambulance Station, was involved in Dr Fraser-Barbour's care.

"It was a tough day for ambulance because of the challenges involved in providing emergency healthcare in remote Central Australia," he said.

" There is no aeromedical response, so the next closest ambulance response is roughly an hour via road. "

Mr Sears said Dr Fraser-Barbour's family was supportive of the gesture to commemorate the work she had done in the disability sector.

"It's a good opportunity to not only provide some life-saving equipment in remote Central Australia, but to offer the family some closure and some help with their journey."

Jayde Stewart, Dave O'Toole, William Sears and Bessie Barrett were the first responders to help care for Dr Fraser-Barbour.

Abbey Studley, regional manager for St John Ambulance Northern Territory, said it was an honour to be included at the commemoration.

"It's not often, if not ever, that frontline workers get to speak with families after tragedies or even be a part of any commemoration services, and so it also forms part of our grieving process," she said.

"I think Dr Ellen Fraser Barber was a big believer in equal rights and something as simple as providing an AED in an area that doesn't normally have it, I think aligns really well with who she was."

An AED has been installed at Ellery Creek Big Hole to commemorate the disability advocate. (ABC Alice Springs Emma Haskin)

Deeply missed

At the time of her death, the 35-year-old was championed as a passionate disability advocate who loved travelling and hiking.

Dr Fraser-Barbour's sister Harriet shared the impact on her family and the community in a statement to the ABC.

"Ellen was a fierce and defiant force who made a lasting impact on all that she encountered," she said.

"We cannot describe the hole she will leave in our family, and she will be missed greatly by her community.

"She was an amazing friend to many and wise beyond her years with so much left to give.

"Ellen helped to shape so much of who I am today, and I will not be the same without her."

World.title: ‘I regret the decision’: Hyrox athlete apologises, forfeits event after soiling herself
World.content:
Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk has apologised for continuing to compete after soiling herself in the Hyrox indoor fitness race in Beijing, and has forfeited her points from the win.

Videos of the world record holder using communal equipment, including sandbags and kettlebells, while excrement was visible on her legs and arms, went viral after the event on September 12 and lead to Hyrox updating its rules to “prevent situations like this from happening again”.

Australian Joanna Wietrzyk took part in HYROX Beijing 2026 on September 12. Getty Images

Wietrzyk, in a now-deleted Instagram post, had initially written “a win is a win”. However, on Thursday night, she issued a lengthy apology to her fellow competitors, spectators and organisers “for what happened during the race”.

“I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness. Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognise that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused,” Wietrzyk said.

World.title: King warns AI leaders of ‘existential dangers’ if tech falls into wrong hands
World.content:
WorldEuropeAI King warns AI leaders of ‘existential dangers’ if tech falls into wrong hands Kate Holton and Paul Sandle September 18, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

King Charles has warned AI leaders of the “existential dangers” posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands, with potentially catastrophic consequences, saying safeguards were needed before it becomes “too late”. Charles was hosting the co-founders of Nvidia and Google DeepMind, along with leaders from OpenAI and Anthropic, in Scotland on Thursday as concern grows that AI safety efforts are lagging behind the development of increasingly powerful systems. King Charles III walks with Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang at the meeting in Scotland. Jonathan Brady/Pool PA via AP In recent weeks, the debate has centred on whether the industry can and should regulate itself, drawing interventions from global figures including Pope Leo XIV, Charles and US President Donald Trump. Charles said artificial intelligence had the potential to improve and save lives, particularly in life sciences and medicine.



Related Article AI ‘The world should trust us’: Silicon Valley billionaire’s plea as fight escalates But its creators were increasingly warning that it could develop darker capacities, “perhaps even to take life”, he said. “There seems urgency in adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways,” he told leaders gathered at his Dumfries House estate. “Surely, we need sufficient means of control before it is all too late?” Attendees included Nvidia founder and chief executive Jensen Huang, Google DeepMind founder and chairman Demis Hassabis, OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar and Britain’s Minister ​for Artificial Intelligence Kanishka Narayan.



Paolo Benanti, an adviser to the pope who has called for governments to slow AI development, was also expected to attend. The debate over AI has been thrust back ​into the spotlight after two Anthropic researchers warned that the rapidly advancing ⁠technology could lead to human extinction in the not-too-distant future. Related Article Analysis

AI ‘We must be stopped’: Why Australia needs to listen to the experts on AI Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has also called for companies to slow the pace of AI development. However, that has sparked an international debate over whether some executives have ulterior motives, such as setting rules that preserve the lead of particular companies, acting now to avoid a broader government backlash, or simply slowing spending in the race to develop AI.



While the meeting in Scotland is not expected to produce any binding agreements, and Charles is not known for his technological expertise, it highlights how he, first as Prince of Wales and now as King, has used his position to convene discussions on a range of global issues. In references to the risks around AI, Charles has also warned about the potential impact on the environment, reflecting his decades of campaigning on the natural world. Buckingham Palace said the discussions would consider whether a shared set of principles could guide the future application of AI, “not merely as a driver of capability and efficiency, but as a tool that upholds human dignity and contributes to the flourishing of both people and the planet”. World.title: Mother charged after newborn found dead in Sydney rubbish bin
World.content:
The mother of a newborn boy found dead in a rubbish bin outside a unit complex in Sydney’s western suburbs has been charged with concealing her son’s birth by disposing of his body, almost three weeks after giving birth.

The baby was found naked inside what resembled a bin bag outside the Auburn apartment complex on August 31. Detective acting Superintendent Darren Sly said at the time that the newborn may have been in the bin for up to 36 hours.

Police cordoned off Harrow Road, Auburn, following the grim discovery. Janie Barrett

The 24-year-old, found by police on Thursday after an exhaustive investigation, was taken to hospital before she was transported to Auburn police station. She was arrested about 6.30pm after answering questions from detectives, and charged later on Thursday night with “mother alone conceal birth by disposing body”.

The charge, which carries a maximum penalty of two years’ imprisonment, relates specifically to the disposal of a dead child’s body to conceal that a birth has taken place.

World.title: Albanese puts cyber safety at heart of bid for UN Security Council seat
World.content:
PoliticsFederalUnited Nations Albanese puts cyber safety at heart of bid for UN Security Council seat Rob Harris September 17, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia will put technology and online safety at the heart of its campaign for a seat on the United Nations Security Council as Anthony Albanese prepares to argue that cyberattacks, artificial intelligence and digital threats are becoming matters of international peace and security. The prime minister will travel to New York on Friday to launch the government’s formal campaign for a two-year term on the Security Council in 2029-30, with Australia seeking to turn its record on digital safety into a diplomatic selling point. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will meet Apple executive chairman Tim Cook on his US trip. Alex Ellinghausen Albanese will also visit Apple’s California headquarters at the weekend, when he meets board executive chairman Tim Cook to discuss new parental controls for children, partly inspired by Australia’s social media reforms. The government also confirmed he would meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at the UN, where the pair are expected to announce a bilateral security agreement.



The government will argue that rapidly evolving threats involving artificial intelligence, cyberspace and online safety will increasingly intersect with international peace and security by the time Australia takes its seat. Ahead of the 2028 vote, Albanese will co-lead high-level discussions on technology safety alongside international leaders at the UN General Assembly. He will promote Australia’s commitment to multilateralism and work with international partners on what the government describes as shared challenges, including building a safe digital future. Related Article Social media Apple credits Australia’s teen social media ban for its new controls The federal government is also preparing a sweeping new push to shape Australia’s response to artificial intelligence, with tougher rules for AI infrastructure and possible restrictions on recording smart glasses in Commonwealth workplaces. On Friday, it will open public consultation on the development of Australia’s AI standards, covering data centres, energy, water use, safety and transparency. Albanese will point to Australia’s previous term a temporary member of the Security Council, including its role during the international response to the MH17 disaster, as evidence of the influence middle powers can wield at the top diplomatic table.



Albanese emphasised the need to secure the economic and national security advantages of artificial intelligence while safeguarding Australia’s national interests. He added: “Now to do that, we have to be engaged with our friends in the United States, because the two big countries that are engaged, of course, are the United States and China in what is this extraordinary emerging technology that will change the way that society functions over our lifetime, but over the next decade.” Australia and Finland are so far uncontested for the two positions for the Western Europe and Others Group; however, the campaign will require a two-thirds majority of the UN General Assembly. Beyond technology, the government’s campaign will focus on middle-power diplomacy, climate action and support for Pacific neighbours, as well as stronger protections for international humanitarian personnel. Albanese will deliver Australia’s National Statement during the UN General Assembly High-Level Week, where he will also discuss fuel costs, climate change and conflict.



“Australia’s prosperity and security depend on a strong global system, where nations work

together, agreed rules are respected, and cooperation delivers shared benefits,” he said. “Australia is working to prevent online harm, particularly for our children, and I am proud that

Australia is setting the world standard for digital safety.” Albanese will also receive an Atlantic Council Global Citizen Award during the New York visit, alongside Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Formula One president and chief executive Stefano Domenicali and star of Wicked, Cynthia Erivo. Wicked star Cynthia Erivo will also receive a Global Citizen award. The awards will be presented at a dinner on September 23 during UN General Assembly week, with more than 700 senior government and business figures, military, media and civil society leaders expected to attend.



Atlantic Council president and chief executive Frederick Kempe said Albanese had embraced the challenges of the 21st century, describing him as pursuing a more resilient and forward-looking Australia while building strategic partnerships and reinforcing the country’s international engagement and role as a democratic voice in the Pacific. Foreign Minister Penny Wong will join Albanese in New York, promoting Australia’s work to build coalitions for the protection of aid workers and strengthen the international rules Canberra relies on for its security and prosperity. World.title: Real wild child in the ottoman aisle
World.content:
“Oh! The thrill of all these glimpses of the famous (C8),” enthuses Margaret Bellingham Holle of Woollahra. “As a teen I played hide-and-seek with Johnny O’Keefe among the furniture in his dad’s store in the city. Heady stuff! As an adult living with my family in the US Virgin Islands, I got to entertain John Wayne as a dinner guest. He was visiting his good friend Maureen O’Hara and her husband Charles Blair. Unfortunately, the menu was a little disastrous as it was only about two hours beforehand that Maureen informed me ‘The Duke doesn’t eat seafood’.”

Dominic Staun of Campbell (ACT) is well aware of the celebrity encounter of the negative kind: “I was in Malta in 1986 with premier Wran and another businessman, discussing an upcoming meeting with the government when Jill Hickson Wran walked into the room. We stood up and Neville said: ‘Darling, have you met these gentlemen?’ ‘No’ she replied, and walked past us. I refer to this as my brush-off with fame.”

In a case of “hold my Guinness”, Dermot Perry of Mount Keira supposes his having a meal with Liam Neeson in the dining room at Queen’s University, Belfast in the early seventies will not be taken seriously.

We’re hoping Stein Boddington of St Clair’s contribution to the street-side urination (C8) debate is an urban myth when he says, “My mother told me to avoid lumps in sugar, as they formed when dogs peed on the hessian bags of sugar stacked at the entrance to the grocer.”

“The list of the many cars abandoned at Sydney Airport, some from as far away as WA, includes Mercedes-Benz, Alfa Romeo, Lexus and Dodge,” notes Paul Duncan of Leura. “Seems that today it’s cheaper to abandon one’s car than to pay the parking fees.”

World.title: Four Melburnians linked to gun in mistaken-identity killing of Sydney student
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Four Melburnians linked to gun in mistaken-identity killing of Sydney student Lachlan Abbott September 17, 2026 — 8:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Four Melburnians have been linked to the gun used in a fatal shooting of an innocent university student in Sydney’s south-west as part of the city’s gangland war. Police alleged in Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Thursday that Vaifaalie Tuafuti, Omar Mohamed, Amenah Abusud and a child worked for the Alameddine crime family in a recent spate of violence against the so-called Coconut Cartel. Marco Tapia was shot dead while in bed at his family’s Glen Alpine home in Sydney on September 1. A police summary read out in Abusud’s extradition hearing revealed investigators have linked the four to a gun found at the family home in the suburb of Glen Alpine where Marco Tapia, 23, was shot dead in his bed early on September 1. NSW Police have said the wrong address was targeted in what is believed to have been a botched organised crime killing. Two teenagers were charged with murder early on Thursday over the incident.



The four Victorians mentioned in court have not been charged over Tapia’s death but are accused of a home invasion in the Sydney suburb of Hurstville and shooting cars in Turrella the night before. Related Article Updated

Crime ‘Trail of evidence’: Teens charged over mistaken identity murder of innocent student Ballistic analysis found discharged cartridge cases at the two scenes matched and were then “positively mapped” to the Glen Alpine homicide scene, where a firearm was found, a NSW Police investigator testified on Thursday. “Subsequent ballistic examination confirmed that the firearm was used to discharge rounds recovered from all three crime scenes,” he said. “Investigations relating to the homicide at Mount Sugarloaf Drive, Glen Alpine, remain ongoing.”



Police say Tuafuti, Mohamed, Abusud and a child left Donnybrook in Melbourne’s north late on August 29 and drove to Campbelltown in Sydney’s south-west, arriving at an Airbnb property about 5am on August 30. A senior constable from NSW Police’s anti-gang Raptor squad said the group were “contracted by a faction of the Alameddine organised crime network … for the purposes of committing extremely violent crimes targeting several Sydney-based close associates of the Coconut Cartel”. Court documents reveal Mohamed, Tuafuti, the child, aged 16, and an unknown fourth person are accused of breaking into a home in Hurstville about 2am on August 31. No one was home. “Offenders utilised a sledgehammer to gain entry to the premises and discharged a round of ammunition into a wall inside,” a statement of alleged facts says.



The court heard the break-in was filmed, and the occupant later received a WhatsApp message that said: “We were in your house to kill you if you were there, but God gave you life today. I promise you, we are going to make sure your kids grow up with no father.” Related Article Sydney's ganglands ‘It’s the Wild West’: How a shaken Sydney is grappling with the gang war The four allegedly then drove to a home in Turrella that police said was “well-known to law enforcement” for links with the Coconut Cartel. Police allege four shots were fired into parked vehicles outside the house before the quartet drove back to Campbelltown. The officer from the Raptor squad said the four Victorians later left their Airbnb about 1.50am on September 1 and returned about 4am, “where they appear to be in a rush to collect their belongings before all leaving”.



Tuafuti, Mohamed and Abusud were remanded in custody after NSW Police expressed fears they could flee the country if granted bail. Victorian police will drive them to Albury on Friday, where their charges will be formally filed with a NSW court. World.title: King warns AI leaders of ‘existential dangers’ if tech falls into wrong hands
World.content:
WorldEuropeAI King warns AI leaders of ‘existential dangers’ if tech falls into wrong hands Kate Holton and Paul Sandle September 18, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

King Charles has warned AI leaders of the “existential dangers” posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands, with potentially catastrophic consequences, saying safeguards were needed before it becomes “too late”. Charles was hosting the co-founders of Nvidia and Google DeepMind, along with leaders from OpenAI and Anthropic, in Scotland on Thursday as concern grows that AI safety efforts are lagging behind the development of increasingly powerful systems. King Charles III walks with Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang at the meeting in Scotland. Jonathan Brady/Pool PA via AP In recent weeks, the debate has centred on whether the industry can and should regulate itself, drawing interventions from global figures including Pope Leo XIV, Charles and US President Donald Trump. Charles said artificial intelligence had the potential to improve and save lives, particularly in life sciences and medicine.



Related Article AI ‘The world should trust us’: Silicon Valley billionaire’s plea as fight escalates But its creators were increasingly warning that it could develop darker capacities, “perhaps even to take life”, he said. “There seems urgency in adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways,” he told leaders gathered at his Dumfries House estate. “Surely, we need sufficient means of control before it is all too late?” Attendees included Nvidia founder and chief executive Jensen Huang, Google DeepMind founder and chairman Demis Hassabis, OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar and Britain’s Minister ​for Artificial Intelligence Kanishka Narayan.



Paolo Benanti, an adviser to the pope who has called for governments to slow AI development, was also expected to attend. The debate over AI has been thrust back ​into the spotlight after two Anthropic researchers warned that the rapidly advancing ⁠technology could lead to human extinction in the not-too-distant future. Related Article Analysis

AI ‘We must be stopped’: Why Australia needs to listen to the experts on AI Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has also called for companies to slow the pace of AI development. However, that has sparked an international debate over whether some executives have ulterior motives, such as setting rules that preserve the lead of particular companies, acting now to avoid a broader government backlash, or simply slowing spending in the race to develop AI.



While the meeting in Scotland is not expected to produce any binding agreements, and Charles is not known for his technological expertise, it highlights how he, first as Prince of Wales and now as King, has used his position to convene discussions on a range of global issues. In references to the risks around AI, Charles has also warned about the potential impact on the environment, reflecting his decades of campaigning on the natural world. Buckingham Palace said the discussions would consider whether a shared set of principles could guide the future application of AI, “not merely as a driver of capability and efficiency, but as a tool that upholds human dignity and contributes to the flourishing of both people and the planet”. World.title: Mother charged after newborn found dead in Sydney rubbish bin
World.content:
The mother of a newborn boy found dead in a rubbish bin outside a unit complex in Sydney’s western suburbs has been charged with concealing her son’s birth by disposing of his body, almost three weeks after giving birth.

The baby was found naked inside what resembled a bin bag outside the Auburn apartment complex on August 31. Detective acting Superintendent Darren Sly said at the time that the newborn may have been in the bin for up to 36 hours.

Police cordoned off Harrow Road, Auburn, following the grim discovery. Janie Barrett

The 24-year-old, found by police on Thursday after an exhaustive investigation, was taken to hospital before she was transported to Auburn police station. She was arrested about 6.30pm after answering questions from detectives, and charged later on Thursday night with “mother alone conceal birth by disposing body”.

The charge, which carries a maximum penalty of two years’ imprisonment, relates specifically to the disposal of a dead child’s body to conceal that a birth has taken place.

World.title: Albanese puts cyber safety at heart of bid for UN Security Council seat
World.content:
PoliticsFederalUnited Nations Albanese puts cyber safety at heart of bid for UN Security Council seat Rob Harris September 17, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia will put technology and online safety at the heart of its campaign for a seat on the United Nations Security Council as Anthony Albanese prepares to argue that cyberattacks, artificial intelligence and digital threats are becoming matters of international peace and security. The prime minister will travel to New York on Friday to launch the government’s formal campaign for a two-year term on the Security Council in 2029-30, with Australia seeking to turn its record on digital safety into a diplomatic selling point. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will meet Apple executive chairman Tim Cook on his US trip. Alex Ellinghausen Albanese will also visit Apple’s California headquarters at the weekend, when he meets board executive chairman Tim Cook to discuss new parental controls for children, partly inspired by Australia’s social media reforms. The government also confirmed he would meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at the UN, where the pair are expected to announce a bilateral security agreement.



The government will argue that rapidly evolving threats involving artificial intelligence, cyberspace and online safety will increasingly intersect with international peace and security by the time Australia takes its seat. Ahead of the 2028 vote, Albanese will co-lead high-level discussions on technology safety alongside international leaders at the UN General Assembly. He will promote Australia’s commitment to multilateralism and work with international partners on what the government describes as shared challenges, including building a safe digital future. Related Article Social media Apple credits Australia’s teen social media ban for its new controls The federal government is also preparing a sweeping new push to shape Australia’s response to artificial intelligence, with tougher rules for AI infrastructure and possible restrictions on recording smart glasses in Commonwealth workplaces. On Friday, it will open public consultation on the development of Australia’s AI standards, covering data centres, energy, water use, safety and transparency. Albanese will point to Australia’s previous term a temporary member of the Security Council, including its role during the international response to the MH17 disaster, as evidence of the influence middle powers can wield at the top diplomatic table.



Albanese emphasised the need to secure the economic and national security advantages of artificial intelligence while safeguarding Australia’s national interests. He added: “Now to do that, we have to be engaged with our friends in the United States, because the two big countries that are engaged, of course, are the United States and China in what is this extraordinary emerging technology that will change the way that society functions over our lifetime, but over the next decade.” Australia and Finland are so far uncontested for the two positions for the Western Europe and Others Group; however, the campaign will require a two-thirds majority of the UN General Assembly. Beyond technology, the government’s campaign will focus on middle-power diplomacy, climate action and support for Pacific neighbours, as well as stronger protections for international humanitarian personnel. Albanese will deliver Australia’s National Statement during the UN General Assembly High-Level Week, where he will also discuss fuel costs, climate change and conflict.



“Australia’s prosperity and security depend on a strong global system, where nations work

together, agreed rules are respected, and cooperation delivers shared benefits,” he said. “Australia is working to prevent online harm, particularly for our children, and I am proud that

Australia is setting the world standard for digital safety.” Albanese will also receive an Atlantic Council Global Citizen Award during the New York visit, alongside Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Formula One president and chief executive Stefano Domenicali and star of Wicked, Cynthia Erivo. Wicked star Cynthia Erivo will also receive a Global Citizen award. The awards will be presented at a dinner on September 23 during UN General Assembly week, with more than 700 senior government and business figures, military, media and civil society leaders expected to attend.



Atlantic Council president and chief executive Frederick Kempe said Albanese had embraced the challenges of the 21st century, describing him as pursuing a more resilient and forward-looking Australia while building strategic partnerships and reinforcing the country’s international engagement and role as a democratic voice in the Pacific. Foreign Minister Penny Wong will join Albanese in New York, promoting Australia’s work to build coalitions for the protection of aid workers and strengthen the international rules Canberra relies on for its security and prosperity. World.title: Real wild child in the ottoman aisle
World.content:
“Oh! The thrill of all these glimpses of the famous (C8),” enthuses Margaret Bellingham Holle of Woollahra. “As a teen I played hide-and-seek with Johnny O’Keefe among the furniture in his dad’s store in the city. Heady stuff! As an adult living with my family in the US Virgin Islands, I got to entertain John Wayne as a dinner guest. He was visiting his good friend Maureen O’Hara and her husband Charles Blair. Unfortunately, the menu was a little disastrous as it was only about two hours beforehand that Maureen informed me ‘The Duke doesn’t eat seafood’.”

Dominic Staun of Campbell (ACT) is well aware of the celebrity encounter of the negative kind: “I was in Malta in 1986 with premier Wran and another businessman, discussing an upcoming meeting with the government when Jill Hickson Wran walked into the room. We stood up and Neville said: ‘Darling, have you met these gentlemen?’ ‘No’ she replied, and walked past us. I refer to this as my brush-off with fame.”

In a case of “hold my Guinness”, Dermot Perry of Mount Keira supposes his having a meal with Liam Neeson in the dining room at Queen’s University, Belfast in the early seventies will not be taken seriously.

We’re hoping Stein Boddington of St Clair’s contribution to the street-side urination (C8) debate is an urban myth when he says, “My mother told me to avoid lumps in sugar, as they formed when dogs peed on the hessian bags of sugar stacked at the entrance to the grocer.”

“The list of the many cars abandoned at Sydney Airport, some from as far away as WA, includes Mercedes-Benz, Alfa Romeo, Lexus and Dodge,” notes Paul Duncan of Leura. “Seems that today it’s cheaper to abandon one’s car than to pay the parking fees.”

World.title: Four Melburnians linked to gun in mistaken-identity killing of Sydney student
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Four Melburnians linked to gun in mistaken-identity killing of Sydney student Lachlan Abbott September 17, 2026 — 8:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Four Melburnians have been linked to the gun used in a fatal shooting of an innocent university student in Sydney’s south-west as part of the city’s gangland war. Police alleged in Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Thursday that Vaifaalie Tuafuti, Omar Mohamed, Amenah Abusud and a child worked for the Alameddine crime family in a recent spate of violence against the so-called Coconut Cartel. Marco Tapia was shot dead while in bed at his family’s Glen Alpine home in Sydney on September 1. A police summary read out in Abusud’s extradition hearing revealed investigators have linked the four to a gun found at the family home in the suburb of Glen Alpine where Marco Tapia, 23, was shot dead in his bed early on September 1. NSW Police have said the wrong address was targeted in what is believed to have been a botched organised crime killing. Two teenagers were charged with murder early on Thursday over the incident.



The four Victorians mentioned in court have not been charged over Tapia’s death but are accused of a home invasion in the Sydney suburb of Hurstville and shooting cars in Turrella the night before. Related Article Updated

Crime ‘Trail of evidence’: Teens charged over mistaken identity murder of innocent student Ballistic analysis found discharged cartridge cases at the two scenes matched and were then “positively mapped” to the Glen Alpine homicide scene, where a firearm was found, a NSW Police investigator testified on Thursday. “Subsequent ballistic examination confirmed that the firearm was used to discharge rounds recovered from all three crime scenes,” he said. “Investigations relating to the homicide at Mount Sugarloaf Drive, Glen Alpine, remain ongoing.”



Police say Tuafuti, Mohamed, Abusud and a child left Donnybrook in Melbourne’s north late on August 29 and drove to Campbelltown in Sydney’s south-west, arriving at an Airbnb property about 5am on August 30. A senior constable from NSW Police’s anti-gang Raptor squad said the group were “contracted by a faction of the Alameddine organised crime network … for the purposes of committing extremely violent crimes targeting several Sydney-based close associates of the Coconut Cartel”. Court documents reveal Mohamed, Tuafuti, the child, aged 16, and an unknown fourth person are accused of breaking into a home in Hurstville about 2am on August 31. No one was home. “Offenders utilised a sledgehammer to gain entry to the premises and discharged a round of ammunition into a wall inside,” a statement of alleged facts says.



The court heard the break-in was filmed, and the occupant later received a WhatsApp message that said: “We were in your house to kill you if you were there, but God gave you life today. I promise you, we are going to make sure your kids grow up with no father.” Related Article Sydney's ganglands ‘It’s the Wild West’: How a shaken Sydney is grappling with the gang war The four allegedly then drove to a home in Turrella that police said was “well-known to law enforcement” for links with the Coconut Cartel. Police allege four shots were fired into parked vehicles outside the house before the quartet drove back to Campbelltown. The officer from the Raptor squad said the four Victorians later left their Airbnb about 1.50am on September 1 and returned about 4am, “where they appear to be in a rush to collect their belongings before all leaving”.



Tuafuti, Mohamed and Abusud were remanded in custody after NSW Police expressed fears they could flee the country if granted bail. Victorian police will drive them to Albury on Friday, where their charges will be formally filed with a NSW court. World.title: Gisborne District Council says government knows it's cash-strapped during storm recovery
World.content:
The Gisborne District Council says central government knows it's cash-strapped, as residents in the region struggle to recover from January's devastating floods, but East Coast MP Dana Kirkpatrick claims she hasn't received any request for help.

Council recovery manager Naomi Whitewood told RNZ Checkpoint it was actively having conversations with relevant agencies like the National Emergency Management Agency about the region's recovery.

Gisborne Council still tackling storm damage Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

"They are aware that we have been undertaking these assessments," she said. "They are aware that we need funding, and so they are also looking at opportunities or avenues to find additional funding that we do not have in our baselines."

The January storm caused widespread flooding and damage across the East Cape. According to research organisation Dragonfly, the sheer amount of rain that came down triggered more than 11,000 landslips in the area.

Seven months on, communities are still trying to clean up and fix the damage. In some settlements, like Te Araroa, residents also say they face new problems like ongoing flooding related to the storm.

East Coast MP Dana Kirkpatrick says she hasn't received any request for help from the council. Supplied

Whitewood said the council had undertaken "various assessments" of areas that had been affected, including Wairenga stream in Te Araroa, which filled with shingle from the January storm.

As a result, the water flowed freely across properties in the area. The problem worsened when it rained, with resident Lynda Akuhata-Brown telling Checkpoint her family's property had flooded five times since the January storm.

Whitewood said an assessment of the Wairenga stream was completed in July and would be released in the "next couple of weeks".

"We've been working through that report to ensure that all the facts, the recommendations and the information that's contained in that report are factual, they're technically correct, legally correct.

"We've only just recently been able to come to the point where that report is ready to be released, and that will be released to the affected whānau, the hapū and the communities."

Kirkpatrick has criticised the council's lack of communication with residents and her, as the local MP.

"It's now mid-September and we still don't have anything," she said. "I haven't seen any solution or any figure on what they need yet."

Whitewood said the council was following its own due process and keeping Kirkpatrick informed wasn't part of that.

"I would say that we haven't been pro-active in keeping her up to date, as we've worked through the various assessments and reviews," she said.

"There hasn't been the ability to share the information on an ongoing basis, because we've had to make sure that the right people are getting that information, before the rest of the public does.

World.title: Police officer facing charges over alleged $18 million fraud

An award-winning senior police officer is facing fraud charges over offending worth nearly $18 million.

Police said the man - who was suspended from duty in December 2025 - had been charged with 70 offences under the Crimes Act and Companies Act, which occurred over a 10- year period.

World.title: Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer ejected from Parliament for using c-word
World.content:
Te Pāti Māori's co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer has been ejected from Parliament after using the c-word.

Politicians have been debating the Move-On orders legislation under urgency.

Ngarewa-Packer admitted she used the word which had been used three times in Parliament and was asked to leave.

Labour's Willie Jackson also left the chamber after raising an objection then getting in a shouting match with other MPs, prompting Assistant Speaker Maureen Pugh to call for the Sergeant of Arms.

Te Pāti Māori's MP Oriini Kaipara had been making a speech and used the word "bullcrap", which prompted Pugh to remind her to "keep the language Parliamentary".

Green MP Julie Anne Genter then began her speech but NZ First's Casey Costello raised a point of order, saying Ngarewa-Packer had "used a word which I will not use that begins with C ... the fact that it has been used once in this house does not make it common use, I find it particularly offensive and disrespectful to you Madam Speaker."

She said "it was directed at you, Madam Speaker".

Ngarewa-Packer then raised her own point, saying "three times the word c--- has been used in this House, by the government ... so either that word is offensive or bullcrap is".

She was then asked to sit down and did so, saying, "Oh, hypocrites".

Pugh said: "And now I personally find that offensive and I'll ask the member to leave the chamber."

"Are you now going to challenge my ruling? I'm not going to entertain a conversation on this, the member will leave the Chamber," she said.

NZ First MP Casey Costello. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

Jackson then stood to say he did not wish to challenge the ruling, prompting Pugh to say, "That's good, it's a good time to sit down then", but he continued, saying the word had been used in front of the Parliament.

Pugh told him to "sit down, sit down now", but Jackson continued to argue the point, until Pugh ordered him to leave as well.

When he did not, and Jackson continued shouting across Parliament, Pugh calmly directed the Sergeant at Arms to "assist Mr Jackson".

She then sought clarification from Kaipara, who said she had not used the c-word, and Pugh apologised to her.

Ngarewa-Packer's original use of the word was not picked up by the microphones.

Speaking to reporters afterwards, she explained she had been objecting to Kaipara being "growled" for saying "bullcrap" and she had been complaining in an aside "oh crike's sake, they've used the word c--- in the House before".

"Casey then stood up and narked on me ... and told the speaker, who then stood up, and I think she thought - because Casey didn't name me - I think she thought Oriini said it."

She said she had not been using the word to refer to Pugh.

Jackson, speaking to reporters alongside Ngarewa-Packer, said Pugh had seemed to think she was.

"No, of course not. No," Ngarewa-Packer said. "I was talking to Oriini, and I said to Oriini ... 'whatever, they've used c--- in the House before and so ... if you want to look at the threshold, bullcrap's not up there."

Jackson said it was hypocrisy for Ngarewa-Packer to be ejected when ACT's Brooke van Velden had previously said the word and not been cautioned.

Ngarewa-Packer said she had used the word in Parliament twice before, "so today I think they're just extremely trigger happy".

Jackson said government MPs had been "screaming at me from the other side 'get out, get out'. Who do they think they are?"

He said he had "a lot of time" for Pugh but "then she was yelling at me to get out ... double standards, hypocrisy, the Speaker didn't want to hear that, I wanted to make it clear to her, then the National Party was saying 'you get out', and I said 'you get out, don't tell me to get out', then they said 'oh we'll call the Sergeant of Arms'.

World.title: Five Karangahape Road venues lose their liquor licences after police intervention
World.content:
Five venues on Auckland's Karangahape Road have lost their liquor licences, following objections from the police and an alcohol licensing inspector.

Mavana Group Limited (MGL) operates Family Bar, Family Down Under, G.A.Y. Club, Las Vegas Nightclub (Empire), and Phoenix Venue, all on Karangahape Road.

Family Bar is particularly iconic, having been a popular LGBTTQIA+ bar for more than 20 years.

After taking over the venues, MGL applied for temporary authorities to sell alcohol earlier this year, with permission granted on 7 May.

The company was warned at the time, however, that "no further compliance failures would be tolerated".

MGL, which has Dalavou Niuhulu as its director and Justine Niuhulu as its sole shareholder, had been seeking another grant of temporary authorities to sell alcohol. Opposition from the police and an alcohol licensing inspector resulted in a hearing in Auckland on 28 August, where a myriad of concerns were raised about multiple incidents at the venues.

The decision to reject the venues' liquor licences as a result of that hearing has just been released.

Police told the hearing that MGL had failed to address concerns raised by Auckland's District Licensing Committee. Police felt MGL "had not demonstrated the level of control, oversight and compliance expected of a licensee in one of Auckland's highest-risk alcohol environments".

While large portions of what police told the hearing have been redacted from the decision, as the statements relate to active investigations, a number of incidents have been disclosed since the venues were given temporary permission to sell alcohol in May.

Sergeant Simon Dillon said unlicensed security staff had been used by MGL, which "demonstrated inadequate employment vetting and failures in compliance".

There was also allegedly an assault on police during a compliance check at Black Velvet - another MGL-owned venue - on 7 June, where the patron admitted to consuming a full box of alcoholic drinks.

He also noted a driver with alleged excess blood alcohol that crashed into a parked car claimed to have had his last drink at Family Bar.

G.A.Y. Auckland has lost its licence. GOOGLE MAPS

Another "disorder job" occurred outside Family Bar on 4 July. The matter was now before the court.

Auckland Council senior alcohol licensing inspector Ashley Wilson addressed compliance monitoring at MGL's businesses.

He said while some issues may appear to be minor administrative breaches, he believed they showed defective systems, staff and training, and reflected negatively on MGL's attitude toward adhering to the rules.

Drunkenness at the venues witnessed by various agencies "showed MGL's unsuitability directly contributed to alcohol harm", he said.

Jon Wiles represented MGL at the hearing. He said police and licensing inspectors' submissions mostly related to isolated incidents, many of which did not involve MGL serving alcohol to those involved.

Many did not occur within the licensed premises either, he said.

Administrative issues identified the licensing inspector were minor, and had been fixed promptly, he said.

Allegations relating to intoxication were largely subjective, he said, and while the company acknowledged some incidents had occurred, MGL believed prompt and decisive corrective action had been taken, "including the replacement of the previous security provider with Sila and Sons Security Group".

Niuhulu, MGL's sole shareholder, said she had made a substantial personal and financial investment in Karangahape Road's hospitality sector, and had made a long-term commitment to the area.

She said she wanted to operate safe, professionally managed venues that contributed positively to the local community and hospitality environment.

The District Licensing Committee labelled what it had heard from police "alarming" and "disturbing".

"MGL was given an opportunity to show that it could deliver on its vision for the premises and the Karangahape community," the committee said.

"It has failed.

"We do not consider MGL is suitable to continue to hold the temporary authorities.

"The applications are declined."

World.title: Pahiatua Medical Centre staff threaten resignations unless under-resourcing addressed
World.content:
Staff at a Tararua district health centre say they will resign en masse, if its owners don't address problems arising from under-resourcing.

Pahiatua Medical Centre nurse practitioner Victoria Perry told RNZ Checkpoint failure to replace departing staff had put preventative screenings for bowel, breast and prostate cancer a year behind schedule, while regular patients were waiting three months for appointments.

The clinic's owner, Tararua Health Group, declined to comment.

Perry said the clinic's 16 staff were also demanding the Primary Health Organisation (PHO) - which contracts the clinic for its services - intervenes before the end of next week.

Staff at medical centre threatening to resign due to shortages Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

She said she feared people would die, if the clinic could not provide even its most basic of services and follow-up tests for its 5000 patients.

"By the time they do see someone in our practice, that problem may be overwhelming and be unfixable," Perry said.

"We're not responding to those sorts of things in close to safe timeframes. It makes us feel sick to the stomach that we can't practice like we've been trained to do and like we're ethically obliged to do."

She said an external workflow review proposed by the PHO amounted to further "bureaucratic delay", and would not address the management failures behind the clinic's understaffing and delays.

"At the moment, what we can't do is even immunise children or give the flu vaccines," Perry said. "We've got 1.6 nurses where we used to have five.

"Although the Minister of Health is saying, 'please go get your vaccines', we don't actually have capacity to administer them."

The clinic's staff wanted the PHO to expand its proposed review to include investigation of the clinic's management and guarantee a timely process - including direct and confidential consultations between the reviewers and frontline staff.

Perry said, if the PHO did not instigate the broader review, the entire frontline team would submit their resignations by 16 October.

"Please, please can you listen? Please can we have more clinicians?

"Please can we have more nurses? Please can we have more administrators to support us?

"It's not working. We're at the bottom here, crying out for help."

PHO chief executive Tony Wai said all parties, including Health New Zealand, were working together to understand the practice's challenges, and support staff and patients.

He said the organisation was looking at a range of options to help maintain services, including workforce support, local clinical cover, telehealth and locum support where appropriate.

It was also keeping in close contact with partners across the region and monitoring general practice capacity.

World.title: FENZ Minister Brooke van Velden questions CEO over withheld information
World.content:
FENZ Minister Brooke van Velden says she no longer has confidence in the organisation's chief executive, following a "serious breach" of the 'no-surprises' clause.

"It is of a nature that is so significant that I no longer have confidence in the chief executive of Fire and Emergency or have confidence that the information I'm receiving is correct," said van Velden.

She said chief executive Kerry Gregory withheld information from her for a "full year" on a matter of a "seriously significant incident". The matter had now been referred to the Serious Fraud Office.

Van Velden said information had also potentially been withheld from the board.

She couldn't provide detail on the issue, but said she became aware in the last fortnight that significant information had been withheld by the chief executive, "even after he received external advice telling him that he needed to let me know".

"I immediately contacted the board chair, as well as the chief executive, to let him know that I have no longer any confidence in the chief executive.

"Having information of a significant nature withheld from me is not something I would expect of a senior official within the public service."

She added it was a "serious breach of trust".

Van Velden asked the board to meet "immediately to maintain or restore my confidence". The board will meet in the next few days.

A scathing select committee report into FENZ recommended the government look at changing the organisation's board and whether it should be allowed to buy its own firetrucks.

Van Velden said the report was disappointing reading, but also noted some of the recommendations were "things that I can't actually do as a minister".

"I'm surprised that those recommendations are in there, because they're of such an operational matter that it would actually be a breach of the Crown Entities Act for me to be that involved."

Van Velden emphasised the breach of confidence was a separate issue to the report.

A FENZ spokesperson clarified to RNZ that the original incident, not Gregory, had been referred to the Serious Fraud Office.

"The matter referred to is historical, from prior to 2021, and relates to Fire and Emergency's administration of the levy scheme.

World.content:
A New Zealand national and a Samoan national have been charged by Samoa Police in relation to the alleged shooting murder of an Australian citizen and suspected gangleader in Vietnam in May.

In a joint statement, Samoa Police and the Australian Federal Police (AFP) said the two men, aged 31 and 33 years old, were charged with conspiracy to murder on 10 September. Under Samoa's Crimes Act, the offence carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment.

The two men appeared before a Samoan court on Wednesday and were granted conditional bail, the statement said.

Joseph Vaa, 27, admitted on Vietnamese television to gunning down suspected 'Coconut Cartel' ringleader Lorenzo Lemalu Tovia, outside a restaurant in Ho Chi Minh City on 21 May, while his associate, Steve Tofa, 23, then confessed to being his accomplice in the shooting.

"An investigation by international law enforcement authorities began following the death of an Australian citizen and serious injuries sustained by a second Australian citizen in a shooting in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, on 21 May, 2026," the joint police statement said.

"Vietnamese authorities arrested two Samoan nationals, aged 22 and 26, on 24 May, 2026, over their alleged roles in the shooting.

"On 27 May, 2026, Samoa Police first arrested and charged the 31-year-old in Samoa with misleading police and corruption offences as part of their investigation into the alleged murder. He was arrested while attempting to leave the country.

The statement said the AFP launched an investigation into the alleged murder to support international law enforcement authorities and identify any further individuals involved.

The AFP assisted the Samoa Police through the execution of a search warrant, financial inquiries, witness interviews and a forensic review of electronic material.

"These AFP activities, and further inquiries undertaken by Samoa Police, led to an additional charge of conspiracy to murder laid against the New Zealand man and 33-year-old Samoan national."

"Samoa Police will allege these men conspired with the Samoan men arrested in Vietnam to carry out the alleged murder in Vietnam," the joint statment said.

AFP acting commander Pacific Greg Davis said the charges reflected the strength of international law enforcement cooperation across the Pacific and broader region.

"Organised crime does not respect national boundaries, so law enforcement agencies must work together to combat them," he said.

"Criminal networks rely on international connections to facilitate serious offending, which is why regional partnerships are critical to disrupting and dismantling them.

World.title: Court battle looms for Socceroos star after drug test
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Cristian Volpato is set for a court battle with the Socceroos star's lawyer confirming he will challenge charges that he was driving with cocaine in his system.

The 22-year-old returned a positive roadside reading for cocaine after he was pulled over by police on Sydney's Anzac Bridge on July 24.

He had been driving at 109 kilometres per hour in a 60km/h zone.

He later underwent independent testing at a private clinic, where it was claimed he returned a negative reading.

However, Volpato was then sent for a secondary oral fluid test by police, which again confirmed a positive result for cocaine.

He copped a $722 fine as a result of the second positive test, but on Thursday his lawyer Paul McGirr confirmed to AAP that he had elected to take the matter to court.

Volpato has maintained his innocence, insisting he never knowingly ingested the substance.

He also undertook a test when he returned to Italy, which was negative, his club side Sassuolo said.

The Sydney-born player was a late inclusion for the Socceroos' World Cup campaign after switching his international allegiance from Italy to Australia on the eve of the tournament.

In a statement provided to AAP, a Football Australia spokesperson confirmed the organisation was aware of reports concerning Volpato and a "traffic matter currently subject to a police process".

"As the matter is ongoing, it would not be appropriate for Football Australia to comment further at this time," the spokesperson said.

Regardless, the positive reading on Volpato's secondary police test could have major ramifications for his availability heading into January's Asian Cup.

Sources have previously told AAP that Volpato could be hauled before FA's disciplinary and ethics committee, where the sport's governing body has the power to suspend him from national team action.

The 22-year-old is currently playing in Serie A with Sassuolo but is sidelined with a right leg injury sustained against Bologna this month.

AAP

World.title: 'Cinema' expected as rival wingers go to battle one last time
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Robert Toia will have a front-row seat to the last instalment of the battle between teammate Mark Nawaqanitawase and Ronaldo Mulitalo, and the Sydney Roosters centre is bracing himself for more box-office entertainment.

"Cinema, that's what I expect — [another chapter in] an ongoing battle and I think if we get the win that will top it off," Toia said.

Saturday's sudden-death semifinal could be Nawaqanitawase's last in the NRL, with the 26-year-old former Wallabies star switching back to the 15-man code with Japanese side Saitama Wild Knights.

Few could have imagined the impact Nawaqanitawase would have had in rugby league when he crossed codes after the Paris Olympics.

There have been highlights in just about every game — be it his grubber ahead and tip toe down the sideline against Canterbury last season that was named try of the year, or last weekend's tap-ahead intercept before climbing off the deck and racing away to score against Penrith.

"It's pretty hard to stay alert because you don't know what's going to happen," Toia said.

"I didn't expect him to do what he's been doing, I think he has shocked everyone."

Nawaqanitawase's long-running on-field feud with the sledge-happy Mulitalo — the pair of wingers openly admire each other off it — has made Roosters-Sharks games fixtures to savour.

"There's a bit of competitiveness there but I think that is what makes the game so great — it's the best of the best going at it with each other," said Roosters forward Siua Wong.

Toia's opposite number KL Iro said of Mulitalo: "He can get personal at times but after the game he always makes sure he clears it up straight away and shakes his hand.

"He loves getting in the mix, he's a huge competitor."

Nawaqanitawase has made the switch to rugby league look easy, having won caps for the Kangaroos, played State of Origin for NSW and scored 41 tries in 44 games for the Roosters.

The Roosters and Sharks battle on Saturday night from the Sydney Football Stadium.

AAP

World.title: Canberra is the greatest mystery of the NRLW finals
World.content:
Of all the teams in the fight for the NRLW premiership, Canberra shapes as the ultimate wildcard.

Ahead of the first finals series in club history, the Raiders are a difficult puzzle to solve; for themselves and opponents alike.

Darrin Borthwick's side enter the finals in fifth place with a 6-5 record that belies a strange tendency that developed over the season: more than any other team in the league, they play to their opponent's level.

Can anyone stop the Roosters in the NRLW? After completing the most dominant regular season in NRLW history, the big question around the Sydney Roosters is simple: can anyone hope to stop them?

The Raiders have a winning record against fellow top six teams, highlighted by a 28-4 win over third-placed Broncos, comfortably the Brisbane team's biggest ever NRLW loss.

They even put the gloves up against powerhouses Gold Coast and Sydney Roosters, losing to the two competition heavyweights by a combined 10 points, finishing close enough in both games that they would fancy their chances in a rematch.

But as easily as the Raiders can be inspired by the challenge of taking on the big dogs, they can be complacent when facing teams they should handle easily.

Canberra dropped games to stragglers Parramatta, North Queensland and Cronulla throughout the season, costing them a home final.
