I think things have moved a lot in the last six to 12 months. The more people use these models, the more the words that we’re all using to describe them actually might make more sense and feel more real. I guess most people on your podcast probably are using agents and real coding and stuff, but I do think more generally, the more people that get involved in using this stuff, the better.

[Laughs] There’s some big leap between free AI Overviews on Google Search and letting an agent go renegotiate your cable bill. Mustafa, you’re going to have to come back soon because I feel like all of this is changing really fast and this has been very, very useful. Thank you so much.

Pleasure, man. Great to see you. Super fun as ever.

Tech.title: AI is feared globally as the destroyer of jobs
Tech.content:
is a deputy editor and Verge co-founder with a passion for human-centric cities, e-bikes, and life as a digital nomad. He’s been a tech journalist for 20 years.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Pew Research has published a new global survey that sheds light on how people view AI, including its impact on jobs, life in general, and income inequality. The survey questioned 42,151 people across 37 countries from February 8th to May 13th — well ahead of recent apocalyptic warnings.

A majority sees AI as a threat to human employment. In 34 of the 37 countries surveyed, people are more likely to believe AI will lead to job losses over the next 20 years rather than create new ones. Worries run particularly high in wealthier countries like Australia (76 percent), South Korea (76 percent), and the US (71 percent). Not surprising, given Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s warning that AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs.

In general, respondents are more likely to say AI will increase the gap between rich and poor. People from wealthier countries that lean left on the political spectrum tend to believe this the most.

Age also tends to impact viewpoints. Older people are more likely to be more concerned about AI’s impact on daily life than younger people. Younger adults (ages 18–34) are most likely to have mixed feelings about AI and how it will shape the world they’ve inherited. They’re also growing increasingly anxious.

In countries like Sweden, Poland, Japan, Australia, Brazil, and the US, concern among younger demographics has risen sharply over the past year, making them more worried about AI-driven job loss and inequality as older generations in countries like the US and Sweden.

Nevertheless, public sentiment captured by the Pew survey is not wholly negative. Despite economic fears, a global median of 41 percent report feeling equally concerned and excited about AI’s growing presence in daily life, compared to 37 percent who are primarily concerned and just 13 percent who are primarily excited.

Tech.title: Lunacy Audio Nova is a place to build and sell your own AI-powered music plug-ins
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Lunacy, purveyor of fine VST plugins like Cube, a synth that you control by moving a ball around a 3D space, has just launched Nova, a platform where creators can build custom music tools using AI and sell them to others. At first, there will be a handful of instruments available, built either by Lunacy or a small selection of partner developers. But eventually, the company will launch Nova Builder, which will let anyone build their own plugins or remix existing ones.

There are 10 plugins available initially, covering everything from crunchy chiptunes, to warbly vintage synths, and evil ambient drones. None of them do anything particularly unique, but they all sound pretty solid. The lo-fi Drift Cassette synth and Silhouettes are my two favorites right off the bat. The former gets you nostalgic ‘80s tones, while the latter is all about sci-fi soundscapes. They all have pretty simple interfaces reminiscent of Native Instruments’ Play series, with bright colors and a handful of controls.

What makes Nova different is that plugins aren’t built using code in a text editor. Instead, they’re assembled using premade effects blocks and AI prompts. It’s not unlike Polyend’s Endless, except instead of vibe coding a guitar pedal, you’re creating music software anyone can use on their computer.

Nova instruments don’t require dedicated hardware. Heck, they don’t even require a digital audio workstation (DAW) and can run directly in a browser. That’s of limited use, though. So there’s also a Nova host plugin that runs in your DAW of choice. It lets you browse and load any Nova plugin from your library and swap between them quickly.

Lunacy envisions Nova as a tinkerers’ paradise. Cofounder and CEO Casey Kolb said in a press release that, “Say someone makes a step sequencer and shares it. You open it and wish you could add a custom shimmer reverb to the end of the signal chain. You can add that, then you can share your new version with a friend, and that friend expands it further. The tools are never fixed; they are always evolving.”

So far, though, the response from the music-making community to AI has been rather tepid. Tools like Endless have been met with, at best, cautious curiosity, and at worst, outright hostility. Lunacy is developing Nova out in the open, posting developer diaries and actively seeking customer input, in an attempt to avoid some of the same pitfalls and win over wary musicians.

Tech.title: Bose’s next open earbuds have more bass, more volume, and more battery life
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Bose announced a new version of its Ultra Open Earbuds that helped kick off the industry trend of clip-on wireless earbuds nearly two-and-a-half years ago. The new Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) feature a subtle redesign with improved performance in both sound quality and battery life. They’re also joined by a new cheaper alternative called the Bose Sport Open Earbuds designed to provide a more secure and stable fit during physical activities.

The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) will be available for preorder on September 19th for $299 with availability starting on October 1st. Color options include black, white smoke, cherry chocolate, olive green, and sky pink. Preorders and availability for the Bose Sport Open Earbuds are the same, but they’re $100 cheaper at $199. Colors include black, white smoke, and eucalyptus green.

The design of the Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) remains mostly the same aside from aesthetic improvements. Image: Bose

Like the original version, the new Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) feature a design that clips to your outer ear with a transducer that directs audio into your ear canal with “minimal sound leakage,” Bose claims. There’s still no ANC because these are designed to do the exact opposite and let you hear what’s going on around you while enjoying music or a podcast.

In addition to a refreshed design with a new beveled finish on each earbud’s metal cap, the 2nd Gen feature a new driver delivering higher volume with automatic adjustments and deeper bass. A new Cinema Mode simulates a “wider, more immersive soundstage” using Bose’s TrueSpatial technology while keeping dialogue clear and centered. Battery life with the buds alone has been boosted to up to nine hours (from seven hours) with an additional 19.5 hours of playback from the redesigned case that can now stand upright for use on a wireless charger.

An added bumpy texture on the Sport Open Earbuds’ customizable buttons makes them easier to locate by touch. Image: Bose

The Bose Sport Open Earbuds take a similar approach with a design that clips to your ear to project sounds inward, but they feature a thinner cuff with a “soft silicone matte finish” providing more grip to keep them in place. Bose says the Sport version will stay secure during head shakes, cartwheels, and running. They also feature automatic volume adjustments that adapt to ambient noise levels to ensure what you’re listening to isn’t drowned out, and the customizable shortcut button on the end of each battery barrel has an added texture, so they’re easier to find while working out. Battery life is rated at up to seven hours of playback plus an additional 22 hours with the wireless charging case.

Tech.title: Spotify’s Fresh Finds Forward gives artists free studio time and more
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Getting added to Spotify’s Fresh Finds playlists can be a huge break for artists trying to cut through the noise on streaming. Now Spotify is launching a program called Fresh Finds Forward, which aims to give artists the tools to capitalize on that exposure. Artists added to any Fresh Finds playlist after January 1st, 2026, can join the program and get 12 months of additional resources, the most extravagant of which is free studio time for US-based artists at Electric Lady Studios in NYC, The Lighthouse at Ocean Way Nashville, or Spotify Music Studios in LA.

Beyond that, artists will get early access to Spotify tools and features, priority access to tour and music video partnerships, as well as 12 months of Landr Studio Pro and Splice’s Creator Plan. Spotify is also offering artists six months of free therapy through BetterHelp, because we all know trying to make it as a musician is stressful and potentially soul-crushing, as scoring a Fresh Finds placement doesn’t guarantee there won’t be further rejections and failures.

Unlike with the so-called Discovery Mode, where artists were paid a “promotional royalty rate,” in exchange for higher algorithmic promotion, Spotify says the Fresh Finds Forward program doesn’t change royalty rates, and is provided completely free of charge to participating artists.

Tech.title: Grand Theft Auto VI’s soundtrack will feature 34 brand-new tracks
Tech.content:
is an entertainment editor covering streaming, virtual worlds, and every single Pokémon video game. Andrew joined The Verge in 2012, writing over 4,000 stories.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

GTA VI: all the news on Rockstar’s next entry in the Grand Theft Auto series

After teasing a music-related reveal a few days ago, Rockstar has officially announced the soundtrack for Grand Theft Auto VI. Called Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, the soundtrack will feature 34 songs, which Rockstar describes as “brand-new, original tracks.” Based on the first six singles, which are available today, it seems that the collection will span a pretty wide range of genres, with everyone from Keith Richards to Travis Scott contributing.

Here’s what’s been confirmed so far:

Yung Lean - “That’s It” (feat. Future & Metro Boomin)

Travis Scott - “RHYNO” (prod. by Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo)

CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, PinkPantheress, Fred again.. & Etienne de Crécy - “Sexy Magic”

Morgan Wallen - “Last Thing You Need”

Rauw Alejandro - “Macacoa 2000”

Keith Richards - “Bright Lights, Big City”

The soundtrack will be coming to all major streaming services, and Rockstar says that it’ll be available on both CD and vinyl. It’ll be launching on November 19th, the same day as the game.

Tech.title: I tried Tovala’s smart oven for two weeks — here’s whether it beats takeout
Tech.content:
I tried Tovala’s smart oven for two weeks to see if it could actually make dinner as easy as the company promises. It won’t replace the quality of a good home-cooked meal, and some dishes turned out better than others, but it’s hard to beat the convenience on days when you absolutely don’t want to cook.

This was exactly the challenge that Tovala co-founder and CEO David Rabie aimed to address.

“The idea originated from my own struggles in business school. I was often busy and sought a solution as convenient as takeout or frozen meals, yet still wanted the experience of a genuine home-cooked dish,” Rabie told TechCrunch via email.

“One afternoon, I was making a meal using several different appliances and realized that I was mostly just pressing buttons,” he said. “That’s what led to the idea for an end-to-end system: fresh, mostly prepped meals paired with a connected oven that could cook them automatically. The challenge became figuring out how to remove all that friction without sacrificing the experience of eating food that was actually cooked fresh at home.”

The idea is pretty simple: Tovala sends you meals with the ingredients already portioned out, and its smart oven handles the cooking.

Instead of chopping vegetables, measuring ingredients, figuring out cooking temperatures, and standing over a stove, you mostly just unwrap everything, follow simple instructions like adding packets of seasoning, put everything in the provided trays, scan a QR code using the companion app, and let the oven do the rest.

The countertop-sized oven follows the cooking instructions automatically, switching temperatures and cooking modes throughout the process. It can bake, broil, air fry, toast, and reheat. The regular oven costs $299, while the Smart Oven Pro costs $349 and adds a steam function.

Image Credits:Tovala

As for the meal-delivery side, there are more than 45 meals to choose from each week. For instance, steak and garlic mashed potatoes, salmon with vegetables, butternut squash soup, pasta dishes, and more.

There are also plenty of options when it comes to how much food you want delivered. Meal plans include 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, or 16 meals per week. You can skip deliveries, pause your plan, or cancel if you don’t need meals that week.

The meals aren’t exactly cheap, though. Single-serving meals start at $13.99, and two-serving meals start at around $8.99 per serving — $17.98 total — plus a $10.99 shipping fee. The company also recently launched family-sized meals, starting at $35.96. Unlike meal-delivery rivals like HelloFresh, Tovala is essentially betting that you’re willing to pay for the added convenience of having most of the cooking handled for you.

Taste and quality were the parts I was most skeptical about going in. I’m not a professional chef by any means, but I’ve recently gotten much more interested in cooking. Once you start learning how to properly sear meat, roast vegetables, and build flavor yourself, it’s hard not to be suspicious of a machine that promises to do all of that for you.

The biggest downside for me was the texture of the meats and how they cooked in the oven. I like a steak with a nice crust, so I finished mine in a steel pan for some extra browning. The steak was much better afterward, but that obviously defeats the point of a process that’s supposed to be mostly hands-off.

Not every dish had that problem, though. One of my favorites was the pineapple shrimp stir-fry. The rice was well cooked, and the sauce had plenty of flavor. It wasn’t necessarily something I’d rave about compared with a great restaurant meal, but it was easy, satisfying, and required very little effort.

Image Credits:Tovala

What I appreciated most, however, was the grocery-food feature that gives the oven some use beyond cooking Tovala-branded meals. The oven can recognize certain grocery-store products, so instead of guessing how long your frozen waffles need to toast, you can scan the barcode and let the oven automatically select the appropriate settings.

That’s what makes Tovala feel more like a genuinely smart oven, not just a machine built to cook its own meal kits. Even if you stop ordering Tovala meals, you can still use the oven with compatible grocery products.

Overall, if your alternative to cooking is ordering takeout because you’re too tired to cook, Tovala makes a pretty compelling case for itself.

Tovala is available on the company’s website and Amazon. It ships to most U.S. states, but it doesn’t currently ship to Alaska or Hawaii.

Tech.title: Huawei plans Q1 2027 launch of new AI chip as it takes on Nvidia
Tech.content:
Huawei is moving up the launch of its next-generation Ascend 960DT AI chip to the first quarter of 2027, as it races to challenge Nvidia, the company said on Thursday at its Huawei Connect conference.

The Chinese tech giant had previously planned to launch the chip in Q3 of 2027, a Huawei spokesperson told TechCrunch.

“The Ascend 960DT is expected to be ready in Q1 2027. Ascend 960 chips are launching ahead of schedule, doubling performance and advancing year by year,” the spokesperson said, adding that David Wang, Huawei’s rotating and acting chairman, announced the updated timeline at Huawei Connect on Thursday.

The announcement comes just a week before U.S. President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet on September 24 in Washington, DC.

Huawei is trying to turn hundreds of thousands, and eventually millions, of AI chips into one giant computer. The Chinese tech firm calls the approach its Peerium Computing Architecture. It relies on UnifiedBus, Huawei’s technology for linking processors with memory, storage, and networking hardware. Eric Xu, Huawei’s rotating chairman, said in the company’s statement that it is using its new Peerium Computing Architecture to build larger AI computing systems designed for both training and inference.

Huawei’s Atlas 950 SuperPoD and SuperCluster are the first systems based on the architecture. The company says an Atlas 950 SuperCluster can connect up to 256,000 accelerator cards.

The accelerated chip timeline comes with some questions about Huawei’s broader AI systems, however. China tech analyst Rui Ma said on X that Huawei had previously said its Atlas 960 SuperPoD would scale to 15,488 Ascend 960 chips, while this week’s announcement referred to a system with 4,096 chips. “The chip itself is coming WAY earlier, but the SuperPoD they announced is much smaller than what they originally laid out,” Ma wrote.

Huawei has continued to advance its chip ambitions despite U.S. restrictions on China’s access to advanced semiconductor technology. Ma said that those restrictions are unlikely to stop China from pursuing its own semiconductor technology.

“I think it’s futile to stop China’s development in semiconductors because the stakes for self-sufficiency are just too high at this point,” she wrote.

Trump has pushed back against calls from AI industry leaders to slow the development of the technology over safety concerns, arguing that the U.S. needs to maintain its lead over China. Meanwhile, Xu argued that China needs to accelerate AI development to catch up with the U.S., saying Chinese companies need to advance further before they can fully understand and address the risks posed by more powerful AI systems, according to Financial Times.

Tech.title: Rival AI agents, Instinct and Meta’s Muse, both add the ability to make calls
Tech.content:
Text-based AI assistants are a hot market, with Instinct, Wajo, Town, Ollie, and Meta’s Muse agent, which launched last week, vying for users’ attention and tasks. San Francisco-based Instinct is one of the most popular of the lot, attracting huge investor interest at what is reportedly a $10 billion valuation.

Instinct’s popularity may now grow even further, as it’s added a new calling feature that lets your agent place calls and act as a concierge. Meta’s Muse, another serious contender in this battle, has also done the same.

Instinct’s founder Noah Shinn announced on X that the buzzy startup’s new calling feature, Instinct Concierge, can do things like book restaurants that don’t take online reservations, get on your dentist’s cancellation list, or sort out problems with your cable bill. The feature is rolling out in early access to some users, with plans to expand to all users in time, he said.

Your Instinct can now handle phone calls.



Introducing Instinct Concierge – a white glove service meant to handle high-touch cases, such as making phone calls, high-end service booking, and more. You’ll be able to book the restaurant that doesn’t take online reservations, get on… pic.twitter.com/vGVnAJ1MF1 — Noah Shinn (@noahrshinn) September 16, 2026

Though Instinct is shipping fast, Meta’s Muse AI assistant is keeping up. It also just gained the ability to place calls to U.S. businesses. The tech giant said the feature will first roll out to users who ask Muse to make a call. (This essentially serves as a feature request mechanism, and Meta said that whenever Muse launches new features, they’ll be available first to people who ask Muse about them.)

These calling features arrive as a number of rivals had been touting their ability to make calls as an advantage over Instinct; but with Instinct’s Concierge feature rollout, they’re all now in parity with each other on this front.

we just expanded the @Muse beta for outbound calls to US businesses, prioritizing folks who'd asked their Muse to let us know they wanted it first :)



if you're in, give it a shot and tell us what you think. phone calling was one of our top requests and your feedback helped make… — Ryan Fox (@wailord) September 16, 2026

Last week, Instinct also rolled out email addresses to let Instinct handle account sign-up and management. The company additionally now allows its users’ assistants to contact other people’s assistants for managing certain tasks, by adding those users to a trusted network.

Both Instinct and Muse have seen great traction over the last few weeks. Instinct raised $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation last month, and it is reportedly in talks to raise $1 billion at a $10 billion valuation, with investors showing heavy interest in text-based assistants that can navigate different surfaces for users.

Analytics firm Sensor Tower noted that Muse outgrew the Meta AI app launch in the first few days. The app garnered over 730,000 downloads in the U.S., compared to the Meta AI app, which was downloaded 707,000 times post-launch in the first five days. The app even reached the No. 2 position in the top charts at one point.

Tech.title: Google, Nvidia, and Anthropic want Emerald AI to find space on the grid for more data centers
Tech.content:
Grid software unicorn Emerald AI has formed a coalition with Google and Nvidia that will use the startup’s technology to secure space on the grid for more data centers.

The AI Energy Management Alliance (AEMA) hopes to make demand response — a paradigm in which data centers temporarily reduce their electricity use — an integral part of data center development. Pausing noncritical tasks and shifting some compute loads, AEMA says, could allow an additional 100 gigawatts of data centers to connect to the grid.

The founding trio is joined by Anthropic, and a range of utilities including AES, Constellation, National Grid, and NRG Energy.

Demand response is an old concept that has been used by utilities for decades. It works because the grid is designed with peak loads in mind. For much of the year, demand is well below the maximum the grid can support.

Traditionally, demand response covered large electricity users like factories, which in times of high demand would agree to reduce their usage, typically by pausing production or switching to backup generators. In exchange, the utility would pay them for the service, often handsomely.

Today, data centers can also take advantage of those programs, usually by turning on backup generators.

Emerald AI has been proposing an alternative to dirty diesel generators. The company’s software coordinates requests from utilities with data centers, which can pause noncritical tasks or shift loads to other data centers where the grid has some headroom.

The startup isn’t the only one working on such technology. Google has been developing its own tools, and Enel X lets data centers tap their uninterruptible power supplies to round off peaks in power demand. Limiting max grid usage to 90% for a few hours at a time could let data centers free up 76 gigawatts of capacity, according to a study by Goldman Sachs published last year.

Emerald AI does have an advantage, though. Its software connects utilities directly to data centers, which should allow data centers to respond quickly to requests, much like batteries. The startup also recently raised $150 million in a Series A led by Energize Capital and DCVC, giving it the sort of funding needed to roll out the technology on a wider scale.

Given the peaky nature of AI compute loads, and data centers’ ability to quickly ramp up and down, the creation of something like AEMA is overdue. The coalition also promises to help tech companies and utilities find new sites for data centers, an effort that hasn’t been easy for either party.

Despite its promise, more sophisticated demand response won’t solve all of the grid’s problems today. Ayse Coskun, Emerald AI’s chief scientist, told TechCrunch that her company’s technology promises to blunt the industry’s need for new generating sources, but it won’t eliminate it entirely.

Tech.title: Lucid Motors has a potential robotaxi partner for Europe
Tech.content:
Lucid Motors has entered into a partnership with European mobility platform Bolt that could bring robotaxis made by the California company to the continent.

The two companies announced Thursday that Bolt “aims to deploy at least 25,000 fully autonomous vehicles” built on Lucid’s upcoming mid-size EV architecture, which is supposed to be smaller and cheaper than its current offerings.

The announcement follows a major restructuring at Lucid Motors under its new CEO, Silvio Napoli, who recently laid off nearly 20% of the company’s workforce and delayed the launch of the first vehicle to be built on the mid-size platform by almost a year to the second half of 2027.

Lucid Motors has yet to deploy a commercial robotaxi version of either of its two existing vehicles. The company has spent the last year working in partnership with Uber and autonomous vehicle firm Nuro to launch a robotaxi version of its Gravity SUV. That is supposed to happen by the end of 2026.

Napoli has said he believes the business of becoming a robotaxi provider would have margins that “vastly” exceed those of “the traditional retail model.”

Bolt intends to own and operate the fleet, according to a press release. The two companies “will work together from the product-development stage on an autonomous driving system (ADS)-ready vehicle platform,” it says.

The vehicles will use Nvidia’s autonomous vehicle compute and sensing architecture (called Hyperion), but the companies did not say which company (or companies) will provide the autonomous driving software. Lucid declined to offer any more information beyond what was in the press release.

No money has changed hands, and Bolt has not placed an order for the vehicles. There is also no public timeline for deployment — only that Bolt considers this a “major step toward” its “ambition of 100,000 autonomous vehicles on its platform by 2035.”

“Autonomous driving in Europe requires data, software, vehicles, and operations to work as one system built for European roads and regulation,” Markus Villig, founder and CEO of Bolt, said in a statement. “Lucid brings a world-class platform, and together, we will co-design the vehicle and software based on our data and more than a decade of operating experience across more than 850 cities. No one is better placed to operate autonomous mobility services efficiently at scale.”

Napoli, in a statement, said, “Bolt’s reach and operating expertise make it an ideal partner to scale autonomous mobility across Europe.”

.

Tech.title: How Bain Capital Ventures plans to deploy its fresh $1.6B fund
Tech.content:
Bain Capital Ventures (BCV), the venture division of private equity firm Bain Capital, has raised a new $1.6 billion fund, which is 14% larger than its previous $1.4 billion fund the firm announced three years ago.

Like many other venture investors, BCV says it will use the fresh funds to back startups primarily focused on AI. The firm believes artificial general intelligence (AGI), which it defines as agents performing many tasks as well as humans can, has already arrived, and the next wave of startups will not only harness its power, but also build the infrastructure needed to make it run efficiently.

Some of the main themes that will be the most relevant in what the firm calls “the post-AGI era” include infrastructure, healthcare, physical AI, and security, said partner Kevin Zhang.

He said BCV aims to fund compute infrastructure until intelligence becomes “too cheap to meter,” meaning that the cost of running AI drops to nearly zero. He pointed to one company in BCV’s portfolio that can help with this mission: data center developer Crusoe, which is reportedly valued at $30 billion and viewed as a near-term IPO candidate. BCV originally led Crusoe’s Series A in 2019, back when it focused on crypto mining.

The firm wants to focus on healthcare because it believes the sector may be vastly transformed by AI. Security, meanwhile, has recently become a matter of national debate after AI agents went rogue during training, and BCV believes there’s much potential to bet on in this space. Some of the firm’s significant investments in these sectors include Loyal, a longevity startup aimed at pets, and Dream, an AI-powered defender of national infrastructure.

BCV stands apart from other VC firms, according to Zhang, thanks to its affiliation with Bain Capital, which provides deep expertise and financial products across credit, real estate, insurance, and private equity. “BCV can support founders not just with equity capital, but with debt facilities, infrastructure partnerships, and real-economy relationships,” he said.

From the new fund, the firm’s 11th, BCV intends to invest in 30 to 40 companies, primarily at the seed through Series B stages. Unlike most VC firms where a single partner champions a deal, BCV’s partners often team up in pairs or trios to back a specific investment, Zhang said.

“We need to have enough mind space and time to really be thoughtful partners to every team we work with,” he said.

Tech.title: Apple Watch Series 12 Review: Finally, a Readiness Score (2026)
Tech.content:
Apple is also making the watch easier to navigate with one hand, adding a single-tap gesture to Apple’s existing double-tap and wrist-flick controls. Tap your index finger and thumb together to select widgets in Smart Stack; double-tap lets you scroll through them. A wrist flick can return you to the watch face, silence timers, or dismiss notifications. These gestures are particularly handy (ha) when you’re multitasking or if you want to use your watch discreetly.

Better at Reading You

The new S11 chip brings the standard round of faster CPU and GPU performance, along with a more efficient Neural Engine. S11 also powers a remodeled pedometer to improve step counts and distance measurements, particularly during indoor walks and runs. Compared to Series 11, I didn’t notice much difference in numbers. I do, though, appreciate the new Steps complication, which puts my real-time step count on the watch face, so I can check my progress without opening the Activity app.

Video: Boutayna Chokrane

The bigger hardware upgrade is Apple’s new Health Sensing System. The Series 12 has 32 electrodes for improved skin contact during ECG readings, compared with two on the Series 11. The photodiodes have been rearranged in a ring configuration for improved optical sensing, and larger green LEDs have been added for more accurate heart rate readings.

The result, and one of the watch’s biggest selling points, is that it takes more frequent readings. The Series 12 measures heart rate every five seconds, even while you’re moving, whereas the Series 11 takes readings every five minutes when you’re relatively stationary. The Series 12 can also measure heart rate variability (HRV) as often as every five minutes, compared with every two hours on the Series 11, and it measures two variants: recovery HRV and overall HRV. For health-conscious people, the higher sampling frequency gives you a more continuous picture of how your body responds to stressors throughout the day instead of a handful of isolated snapshots. You can see those readings in the Heart Rate app or through the new live heart rate complications.

Video: Boutayna Chokrane

Readiness has at last arrived for anyone who has been anticipating a unified recovery score from Apple. The new Readiness app pulls together activity, sleep, and other health data to estimate how prepared you are for the day ahead. It takes seven days of sleep data before the score becomes available, which is standard for wearables to determine a baseline.

I like having the score as a quick shorthand instead of attempting to contextualize the individual metrics myself, but I stay skeptical of any recovery score that simplifies complicated physiological states using a proprietary algorithm. That said, Readiness is useful as a prompt to pay attention to your body, and I’m glad Apple finally has one.

Apple is also planning a redesigned Health app later this year, including a new Longevity tab and metrics such as Health Age, which compares your health data with that of your demographic. I haven’t been able to test those features yet, but I have a feeling my Health Age will either be oddly gratifying or immediately anxiety-inducing.

A Little Too Attentive

Audio Intelligence may be Apple’s most controversial addition. The suite brings four audio-focused features, including accelerated Shazam and Sound Recognition, the latter of which has been available on the iPhone since 2020. The more intriguing additions are Siri Recap and Live Rewind, which push the Apple Watch into murky waters by using its microphone to capture and process audio. I haven’t been able to test either feature yet; both are slated to arrive later this year.

Siri Recap is Apple’s answer to the AI notetaking boom. When enabled, it can transcribe conversations and generate summaries using Apple Intelligence. I can see the appeal for meetings and classes. During a briefing, I saw Siri Recap turn a PTA meeting into a detailed set of notes and reminders that seemed genuinely useful.

Tech.title: What’s the Best iPhone to Buy or Avoid Right Now? (2026)
Tech.content:
What's New in iOS 27?

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

While last year's iOS 26 debuted the divisive Liquid Glass, iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 focus squarely on quality-of-life improvements, with a redesigned and much improved Siri AI assistant, easier Shortcuts, and lots of little tweaks to enhance speed and stability.

Siri AI doesn't just look different—now resembling a glass orb—it can also understand your personal context, pulling info from your messages, emails, or even photos, and helping you draft messages or find the right wine to pair with your dinner. Siri can also now pop up in the camera app to help you choose your next book or split a bill with friends.

Apple says iOS 27 is faster than ever, with app launches up to 30 percent faster, newly captured photos in your Photo Library loading up to 70 percent faster, and AirDrop transfers completing up to 80 percent faster. For more details, read our guide on the top features in iOS 27 and how to download it.

Charging Adapters for Your iPhone

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Apple hasn't offered a charging brick in the box since the iPhone 12, so if you don't have one, we've got you covered with a few recommendations. Most of these are 30-watt chargers that will fast-charge most iPhones. If you want the fastest speeds on the iPhone 18 models, you'll need a 40-watt charger, and we have some picks for you.

Anker 511 Nano 3 30-Watt Charger for $16: This is one of the tiniest chargers we've tested, and the prongs fold up for even more space savings. It comes in fun colors, and it's nice and cheap.

Counterpart The Charger for $44: Why carry a charger and cable separately when you can get both in one? Retractable chargers are popular, and I love this attractive model from Counterpart. You can get it in a few colors, and the USB-C cable extends up to 4 feet. The prongs fold so they won't scratch anything in your bag, and the 35-watt output is enough to fast-charge most iPhones and iPads. It'll recharge a MacBook, though a MacBook Pro requires a more powerful charger.

Apple 40W Dynamic Power Adapter Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Apple 40W Dynamic Power Adapter for $39: Apple's Dynamic Power Adapter will get you the fastest charging speeds possible on the iPhone 17 models. That's 50 percent in just 20 minutes, and I was able to replicate that in my tests. It's a smaller charger than prior models, and it's one of the few chargers with SPR AVS support (Standard Power Range Adjustable Voltage Supply). It's a mouthful, but essentially, it can boost power output up to 60 watts when needed. That means it's a more versatile charger that you can use for your MacBook Air and your iPhone.

The Right USB-C Cable

Photograph: Simon Hill Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Cable Matters USB-C to USB-C Thunderbolt 4 $30 Amazon

The problem with USB-C is that its capabilities are so vast, but not every USB-C cable supports every single function. You need to make sure the cable you buy supports video output, speedy data transfer, and fast charging if that's what you want. The cable Apple includes in the box can carry up to 60 watts of power, and that's pretty much it. You can use this cable to recharge a MacBook but maybe not a MacBook Pro under heavy load.

If you get a cable like this one from Cable Matters, you'll be covered for every scenario. It supports up to 100 watts of power so you can use it for all your gadgets, has DisplayPort to work with external monitors, and supports up to 40 gigabits per second of data transfer. It also comes in multiple lengths.

Read our Best USB-C Cables guide for more.

Get a MagSafe Portable Battery

The beauty of MagSafe is that you can pop a battery on the back of your iPhone, and you don't have to worry about any wires. This is our top recommendation, and it supports the Qi2 standard, so it will work with any device with Qi2. It has a 10,000-mAh capacity that is good to recharge an iPhone fully once and then some, and there's a built-in kickstand so you can continue watching your favorite show as it charges. Best of all is the built-in LED display, helpful for seeing how much juice the charger has left.

Read our Best MagSafe Power Banks guide for more recommendations.

Apple has a dedicated slim MagSafe Battery for the iPhone Air. It takes advantage of the Air's new design and fits perfectly on the back. (It will work with other iPhones, but you have to place the battery horizontally, making the whole thing awkward.) No, this $99 accessory isn't really worth it. You can find higher-capacity batteries for less money. In my tests, I was able to get 68 percent back on my iPhone Air before the 3,149-mAh MagSafe Battery died. However, it's still pretty dang slim, works reliably, and fits like a glove. Maybe catch it on sale.

Get a 3-in-1 Wireless Charger

If you have an iPhone, there's a chance you have another Apple gadget, like AirPods or an Apple Watch. If so, you really should get a 3-in-1 charger for your home. We have tons of options in our Best Apple 3-in-1 Chargers guide, but this Belkin MagSafe model is our favorite. It has an elegant design and charges the iPhone and Apple Watch at maximum speeds, and you can pop your earbuds on the base to top them up. It won't work with the iPhone 16e unless you get a MagSafe case, and even then, you won't be privy to the faster and more efficient charging speeds.

Carry a MagSafe Wallet

Photograph: Molly Higgins

Courtesy of Nomad Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Nomad Leather Mag Wallet $99 Nomad

Hate bringing a wallet with you everywhere? Stick it to the back of your iPhone! This Nomad leather wallet is classy and can hold about four cards. What makes it unique is that it features Apple's Find My, meaning you can track its location in the Find My app if you lose it. That does mean the wallet needs to recharge every once in a while, but you can conveniently recharge it with any MagSafe charger, no proprietary cable needed. (It should last around five months on a single charge.) Read our Best MagSafe Wallets guide for more options.

The MagSafe world is wonderful and weird. We have plenty more recommendations in our Best MagSafe Accessories guide, ranging from MagSafe camera cages and tripods to notepads you can magnetically stick to the back of your iPhone.

Avoid These iPhones AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The iPhone 14 and older iPhones are probably available somewhere, but you shouldn't take the bait. They don't have the processing power to keep up with the latest software, and even if they do, they will have a much shorter software shelf life or lack modern features like USB-C. The only older iPhones worth considering at the moment are the iPhone 15 or iPhone 16 series, even better if it's the Pro models, if you can find them at low prices. The iPhone 16e is also another option, though only if you can find it at a steep discount. The iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, and iPhone XR are cut off from receiving the iOS 27 update, so they're especially ones to avoid. Without software support, your device will slowly become less secure and could become a slow, buggy mess. The iPhone's Charging Port Is USB-C, Not Lightning AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The iPhone 15 range ditched the long-standing Lightning port for USB-C, and it's in every iPhone since. This is the same charging port on iPads, MacBooks, Android phones, Windows laptops, and many more personal tech gadgets. USB-C is often called the “universal port” because it can technically handle various responsibilities. For example, you can plug in external displays and extend the iPhone's screen or connect the same USB-C accessories you might be currently using on your laptop, like SD card readers. Sadly, it does mean your Lightning accessories won't work unless you get dongles. You can read more about what the port does here, but there are two important things to note: The iPhone 15, iPhone 15 Plus, iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16e, iPhone 17, iPhone 17e, and iPhone Air support the USB 2.0 standard just like the iPhones before, so you'll max out at 480 megabits per second of data transfer speeds. The iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo support the USB 3.0 standard and are capable of up to 10 gigabits per second of data transfer speeds. What’s the Deal With eSIMs? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron All iPhone 14 and newer devices completely ditch the physical SIM tray in the US, meaning you can no longer just pop your physical SIM inside to turn on cellular connectivity. Instead, you'll have to rely on an eSIM. You can read more about them here. This tech has been available in iPhones since the iPhone XS and XR, but now you have to use it. Apple has also started switching more global models to eSIM only, like the iPhone Air.) When you're setting up your new iPhone, you'll automatically be asked to transfer your number from your previous iPhone, and the whole process should take a few minutes without any hassle. (eSIMs are more secure than physical SIMs.) Once you transfer your number, your physical SIM card won't work anymore. There's a chance you may still run into some issues, especially if you're coming from an Android phone (or want to switch back to an Android phone). You'll have to check with your carrier to get your cellular connection working again. It shouldn't take long, but it's not as simple as popping in a physical card. How to Replace Your iPhone's Battery AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron If you don't want to spend the money to get a new iPhone, consider a fresh battery. If the biggest issues with your aging iPhone revolve around how long it lasts in a day, replacing the battery might make it feel brand-new. (Apple's iPhone 16, 16 Plus, and 16e have an easier-to-replace battery.) Replacements for older iPhones are $89, and $99 or $119 for newer models. If that doesn't do the trick, read our guide on ways to fix your iPhone's problems or our guide on selling your iPhone to get the most money for it. What Is the Action Button and Camera Control Button? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The Action Button debuted on the iPhone 15 Pro models, and it's now standard on every iPhone in the lineup. It sits above the volume rocker on the left edge of the phone. It effectively replaces the old Mute Switch, but think of it as just a configurable button. You can have it still control the mute function of the phone, or customize it (Settings > Action Button) to trigger the flashlight, a Voice Memo, or even launch an app or Shortcut. Camera Control is another newer addition that debuted on the iPhone 16 series. On the right edge of the phone below the power button, press it to launch the Camera app, and you can press it to capture a photo or start recording a video. A light tap and swipe can move through different camera lenses or modes, but I found this annoying. (You can configure it by heading to Settings > Camera > Camera Control.) Press and hold this button, and you'll trigger Apple's Visual Intelligence. It'll use the camera to identify subjects in front of you, very much like Google Lens, so you can ask questions via Google or ChatGPT about what you're looking at.
